---
name: muse-round
description: Run one round of the Muse agent on the MobileMoE-S kernels as a swarm. Explorers map the code and measurements into a shared analysis; then competing builders write and grade fused Metal kernels for the top inefficiencies. From round 2 on, the round starts from the previous rounds' results and must beat their best attempts. Both phases are tracked in shared documents.
---

# One round of the Muse agent: a swarm explores, then builds

*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Committed on main and tagged `muse-code-era` before the first Muse Code session; each later version is committed before the round that uses it. [Who made what](../../../PROVENANCE.md).*

**Skill version 10.** This file, the role cards and tracking.md are versioned together; [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) lists every version. Each round records the version it ran (see *Versions* in tracking.md).

You are the **lead** of a Muse Code session in your own worktree on the branch `muse-agent`. The first prompt names the Meta model you run as, the name your commit subjects start with, and the co-author line every commit ends with. `claude/muse-agent-brief.md` fixes the task, the slots, the tools and limits, the grader command and the pass criteria (G1, G2). Four ADRs change it in five ways:

1. **Harness** ([ADR 0006](../../../claude/adr/0006-muse-spark-in-muse-code.md)). You are a Muse Code session, not a Claude Code one. Muse Code adds no trailer, so you write the first prompt's co-author line on every commit yourself (see *Commits*).
2. **No attempt limit and no stop rule** (ADR 0006). The brief's *When a slot stops* no longer applies: you decide when a slot is done. Every graded attempt is committed, so the history shows every try.
3. **A swarm** ([ADR 0007](../../../claude/adr/0007-muse-spark-swarm.md)). Helpers explore and build; you coordinate and commit.
4. **Files** (ADR 0007, [ADR 0009](../../../claude/adr/0009-rounds-build-on-each-other.md)). Each round writes in its own **round folder**: round 1 at the top of `muse-spark/`, round N from 2 on in `muse-spark/round-<N>/`. It holds `exploration/` and `implementation/`, the round's shared documents, which replace `strategy.md`; `kernels/<slot-folder>/attempt-<M>/`; and `summary.md`. tracking.md writes it `<round>/`.
5. **Rounds build on each other** (ADR 0009). A finished round's files are frozen: read them and cite them, and the hooks refuse any change to them. From round 2 on, a slot may have a **baseline**: the best attempt so far that passes the current G2 and that Claude's G3 accepted: against the unchanged model and the compiled reference, faster in one phase, decode or prefill, and slower in neither ([ADR 0011](../../../claude/adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). A new attempt must beat it in the same grader run. A slot without one has a **starting point** instead: an earlier attempt to build from, which Claude's measurement names, with what kept it from being a baseline.

The rest of the brief stands. The goal: kernels that make whole requests faster. In the grader they pass G1 and G2 and have `beats_compiled` true, faster in one phase, decode or prefill, and slower in neither (ADR 0011), and where the slot has a baseline `beats_baseline` true too, because they remove a cause you can name. Then the **ready check**, the same G3 Claude runs after the round, run by you inside it, must pass them before they are `ready` ([ADR 0013](../../../claude/adr/0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)). A faster decode step bought with a slower prefill is no improvement, and a claim no one measured is no result. An attempt may hand the inputs outside a row range it names to the compiled reference: those above `max_rows`, such as prefill-sized ones, and from round 4 those below `min_rows`, such as the 1-row decode step (the brief's launch spec, [ADR 0015](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)). The Muse agent was Muse Spark in round 1, Muse Wonder in round 2 ([ADR 0008](../../../claude/adr/0008-muse-wonder.md)) and Muse Spark's contributor model in round 3 ([ADR 0012](../../../claude/adr/0012-muse-spark-contributor-unattended.md)), and is Muse Wonder again in round 4, the last round ([ADR 0014](../../../claude/adr/0014-muse-wonder-last-round.md)); the first prompt names the model you run as, and documents from earlier rounds say the model of their round. No one approves your tool calls during the round, so the rules here are yours to keep.

## The swarm

| Role | Name | Task | Card |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Lead** (you) | | Start the helpers, keep the two READMEs, settle clashes, commit | this file |
| **Explorer** | `explorer-<territory>` | Map one territory into entries, and find where it loses time | [explorer.md](explorer.md) |
| **Verifier** | `verifier` | Check every inefficiency against its sources | [verifier.md](verifier.md) |
| **Builder** | `builder-<n>-<letter>` | Write and grade one solution for one hypothesis: one attempt | [builder.md](builder.md) |
| **Boundary agent** | `boundary-<n>` | Write what a hypothesis's solution must keep identical, and check passing attempts against it | [boundary.md](boundary.md) |
| **Checker** | `checker-<n>`, `checker-final` | Check every speed claim against the file it cites: a hypothesis's before it closes, and the round's final claims | [checker.md](checker.md) |

You don't explore, build or grade yourself; the one GPU job you run is the ready check (step 4). Start each helper with a prompt of this shape:

> You are `<name>`, a `<role>` in round `<N>`'s swarm; this round writes in `<round folder>`. Read `.agents/skills/muse-round/<card>` and `.agents/skills/muse-round/tracking.md`, then: `<task>`.

[tracking.md](tracking.md) describes the shared documents (the two phase folders, their READMEs, entries and logs) and the rules every agent keeps. Read it before starting anyone. Up to 12 agents run at once, you included.

**A checkpoint** is what you do each time a helper returns, and whenever the log shows something to settle:
1. **Read the log.** Read the phase log since your last checkpoint.
2. **Settle clashes.** When two entries describe one cause, keep the fuller one and set the other's status to `superseded by <entry>`. When two helpers work on one item, redirect one of them (`subagent_send_message`). Log what you decided.
3. **Refresh the tracker.** Update the phase README's tracker table, and raise the version of each hypothesis entry that changed.
4. **Raise the version.** Raise the phase README to its next version, and add its line to `## Versions`, naming the entries that changed and their versions (see *Versions* in tracking.md).
5. **Commit** the phase folder, plus any attempt that came back, as that version (see *Commits*).

## The round

### 0. Find where you are

- Run `git log --oneline main -1`, then `git tag --list -n1 'muse-round-*'`, which lists the finished rounds. **This round** is one more than the highest; with none, it is round 1. Its folder is `muse-spark/round-<N>/` (round 1: `muse-spark/`).
- `git log --oneline --grep '^Muse ' muse-code-era..HEAD` lists the Muse agent's commits of every round.
- **From round 2 on,** read Claude's measurement of the previous round, `claude/findings/muse-round-<N-1>.md`. It has the G3 results and names each slot's baseline or starting point. If it is missing, stop and reply "Claude's measurement of round <N-1> is missing": this round builds on it.
- If this round's folder already exists, a session stopped partway: carry on from its READMEs' last versions.
- Read the brief.

**Done** when you can name the round number and its folder, and from round 2 on each slot's baseline or starting point and the latest G3 results.

### 1. The starting point (from round 2 on)

This is the round's plan, built on what the earlier rounds learned. Read:
- the previous rounds' final exploration and implementation READMEs and `summary.md`;
- the `notes.md` of each baseline or starting-point attempt;
- Claude's measurement.

Then write the opening of this round's `exploration/README.md` (set up as in step 2.1), a section **Starting point**:
- **Per slot:**
  - the baseline, or the starting point where there is none, and its piece timing;
  - its G3 effect, and how that compares with what was predicted, with the reason where Claude's measurement gives one;
  - what keeps a starting point from passing G2, and where the attempt still spends its time.
- **What is left:**
  - the confirmed inefficiencies not yet built or not fully removed, ranked by predicted saving against the baselines, or the reference where a slot has none;
  - the slots not yet tried, for example `routing+combine`;
  - the recommendations outside the slots.
- **Refuted claims,** which no one chases again.
- **Territories** this round opens (step 2.2), each with the line of this section that reopens it.

Commit it as exploration v1. **Done** when every slot has its baseline or starting point and every territory has its reason.

### 2. Exploration

1. **Set up the folder.** Write `<round>/exploration/README.md` with a heading, its version line (v1, with skill version 10), the tracker (one row per territory) and `## Versions`, and an empty `log.md`.
2. **Start the explorers and the verifier,** all at once.
   - **Round 1** starts with these territories:

     | Territory | Covers |
     |---|---|
     | `model` | `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py`: the decoder layer, `MoE.__call__` and everything around the slots |
     | `switch-layers` | `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/switch_layers.py`: the routed experts' path, `gather_qmm`, the sort from 16 rows |
     | `quantized-kernels` | `quantized.h` and `quantized_utils.h` in `.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/mlx/include/mlx/backend/metal/kernels/`: the `affine_gather_*` kernels behind `gather_qmm` |
     | `other-kernels` | the other Metal kernels in the same folder that the routing and combine slots launch: sort, softmax, reductions, elementwise, copies |
     | `vllm-metal` | `third_party/vllm-metal/vllm_metal/`: how the engine runs a decode step and a prefill chunk around the model |
     | `grader` | `bench/grader/`: the slot interface, what G1, G2 and the piece timing measure, and so the boundary every solution keeps |
     | `findings` | `claude/findings/` and `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/` |
     | `runs` | `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/`, `2026-10-29-baseline/` and `2026-10-30-micro/` |

   - **From round 2 on,** the starting point lists the territories:
     - `baseline-<slot>` for each slot: its baseline's kernels and `spec.json`, which are now the code in the slot, or its starting point's. Map them with the checklist, and find where they still lose time and, for a starting point, why it fails G2;
     - `g3`: Claude's measurement of the previous round, where the end-to-end change differs from the piece timing, and why;
     - of round 1's territories, only those the starting point reopens. An explorer starts from that territory's earlier entries and writes only what is new.
3. **Refocus as costs show up.** When an entry shows that one file holds most of a territory's cost, split it off as a territory of its own, with its own explorer. Merge or close a territory that turns out to hold nothing, and add one when an inefficiency points somewhere no one covers. Log each change and update the tracker.
4. **Checkpoint** each time a helper returns.

**Done** when every territory entry is `done`, the verifier has returned, and every inefficiency is `confirmed`, `refuted` or `superseded`.

### 3. The analysis

Write the final `<round>/exploration/README.md`. It is the round's report on the code, for this round's builders and for future improvements:

- **Tracker:** the final table.
- **Starting point** (from round 2 on), as written in step 1, with any correction exploration made.
- **Context:** the decode step and the prefill, the MoE block and its slots, and what the measurements say about where the time goes in each.
- **Territory map:** how the territories feed each other. For each territory: what it receives, what it passes on, and its measured cost.
- **Inefficiencies, ranked:**
  - the confirmed ones inside the slots, ranked by predicted saving as a share of the decode step, averaged over 1, 8 and 32 rows, or of the prefill chunk, averaged over 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows; from round 2 on, the saving is against the baseline where the slot has one;
  - each with what removing it does to the other phase, and whether a hand-off (`max_rows`) keeps that phase unchanged;
  - each with its cost, kind and entry;
  - Claude's findings marked as Claude's, earlier rounds' entries linked as theirs, and this round's own reading marked as yours.
- **Recommendations:** the confirmed inefficiencies outside the slots, with their evidence. They're for surucuonur's team.
- **Refuted claims,** in one line each, so no one chases them again.
- **Files read:** links to each territory entry's list.

Commit it. **Done** when every ranked item links a confirmed entry and every number in the README has its source.

### 4. Implementation

Take the ranked inefficiencies in order, at most two at a time, in different slots so their attempts never touch. Write `<round>/implementation/README.md` with a heading, its version line, the tracker and `## Versions`, and an empty `log.md`. For each hypothesis:

1. **Open the hypothesis.** Write `<round>/implementation/hyp-<n>-<slug>.md`, with status `boundary`, the inefficiency, the slot and, from round 2 on, the slot's baseline folder or `none`. Add its tracker row and log it.
2. **Draw its boundary.** Start `boundary-<n>` to write the boundary, and wait for it.
3. **Compete.**
   - Set the status to `building`.
   - Start 2 or 3 builders, `builder-<n>-a`, `-b` and `-c`. Give each a different direction drawn from the analysis: for example, fusing kernels, reading each weight byte once, or a different threadgroup shape. From round 2 on, a direction may start from the baseline's or starting point's kernels, or from scratch.
4. **Collect.** Each time a builder returns:
   - checkpoint, committing its attempt folder with the hypothesis entry, the README and the log;
   - if the attempt passed G2, start `boundary-<n>` to check it.
5. **Harden.**
   - Pick the best attempt: it passes G1, G2 and its boundary check, has `beats_compiled` true and, where the slot has a baseline, `beats_baseline`, and it is the fastest across the six sizes.
   - Set the status to `hardening`, and start a builder for that attempt's next single change.
   - Repeat while the attempt still has a cause you can name and remove.
   - **Change approach after three alike failures.** Keep the hypothesis entry's failure ledger at each collect: every graded attempt that lost, the size or phase it lost at, and its named cause. When three attempts have lost at the same phase for the same cause, the next one changes approach (another kernel structure, parallelisation or dataflow, not a tuning), and its `notes.md` says "approach change: from X to Y"; or you log why not. A cause renamed without a measurement that refutes the old one is the same cause.
6. **Close.**
   - **`candidate`:** the best attempt passes G1, G2 and its boundary check, has `beats_compiled` true and, where the slot has a baseline, `beats_baseline` true, and you can name no further change worth making. Write the **Decision**: the attempt, why it is best, and the change in whole requests you predict, labelled a prediction. Then start `checker-<n>` on the entry; the hypothesis is a candidate once its **Checks** section says `pass`.
   - **`dropped`:** say why. A slot whose hypotheses are all dropped keeps its baseline, or the reference where it has none.

Then open the next-ranked inefficiency.

**The ready check** ([ADR 0013](../../../claude/adr/0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)). Once no hypothesis is building or hardening and at least one is a `candidate`, run it yourself, over every candidate in one call:

```bash
.venv/bin/python bench/grader/check_ready.py <round>/checks/ready-<k> <slot>=<attempt folder> [<slot>=<attempt folder> ...]
```

It times the candidates in vLLM exactly as Claude's G3 will after the round, each alone and, with more than one, all together, then audits its own log and writes `ready-verdict.json`. It takes about 10 to 15 minutes per slot, more for an attempt with a slow prefill, and waits its turn for the GPU. Commit its folder at the next checkpoint.
- **Exit 0 or 1: a verdict, and it stands.** Cite the file.
  - **A set** ([ADR 0015](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)). With more than one candidate, when `muse-all` passes, all of them are `ready` together as a set, even where one fails alone. A set goes to G3 whole: all its attempts, or none.
  - **Alone.** Otherwise, a candidate whose `muse-<slot>` passes becomes `ready` on its own; one that fails goes back to `hardening` with the failure in its ledger, or to `dropped`. If some pass alone and `muse-all` fails, a second check may take only those.
  - An attempt that hands off 1 row (`min_rows`) runs MLX's own code for the whole 1-request workload, so it passes the ready check only in a set whose other kernels are faster with 1 request.
- **Exit 2: no verdict.** The run stopped or broke the protocol; run it again in a new folder.
- **At most two ready checks per round.**

**Done** when no confirmed inefficiency is left that you judge will pay, and every candidate has a ready-check verdict. Write why in the implementation README.

### 5. Finish

1. **The implementation README:** the final tracker, one paragraph per hypothesis, and a **Ready to test** section. It names the attempt per slot that goes to Claude's G3: a `ready` attempt, the baseline kept, or the reference, and says which `ready` attempts go together as a set. For the `ready` ones it shows the ready check's measured change in the four workloads (the decode step, the prompt time and the whole request, against the unchanged model and the compiled reference; for a set, its `muse-all`), citing `ready-verdict.json`, with your earlier prediction beside it, labelled PREDICTION, and the **Unverified** list. Nothing else in it is an end-to-end number.
2. **The exploration README:** add *What building taught*, the analysis corrected by what the attempts showed.
3. **`<round>/summary.md`:** a `## Round N` section with:
   - the model, the skill version this round ran, and the final versions of both READMEs;
   - the final attempt per slot;
   - the number of graded attempts per slot, this round and over all rounds;
   - the ready check's measured change, citing its file;
   - what you'd try next;
   - your recommendations outside the slots.
4. **Check, commit, reply.** Start `checker-final` on *Ready to test* and the summary, and fix what it finds until it signs `pass`. Then commit, and reply with this round's commits and the words "Round N finished".

## Your own rules

- **Writes:**
  - you write the two READMEs, the hypothesis entries' status blocks and decisions, and `summary.md`;
  - every helper writes only what its card names;
  - all of it stays in this round's folder.
- **Claude's G3 after the round is the authority;** your ready check is the same measurement, made earlier. vLLM runs only through the ready check.
- **The rules every agent keeps** are in tracking.md.

## Commits

You are the only agent that commits. Commit only on `muse-agent`.
- **What to add:** this round's phase folders that exist so far (only `exploration` until implementation starts) and the attempt folders that came back. An attempt another builder is still writing waits for its own commit. An entry that is mid-edit is committed as it stands, and finished in a later commit.
- **The message:**
  - every subject starts with the name the first prompt gives you, then a colon;
  - a checkpoint's subject is `<name>: <phase> v<N>: <what changed>`, the version it records;
  - every message ends with the first prompt's co-author line, exactly.

For example, in round 2 as Muse Wonder:

```bash
git add muse-spark/round-2/exploration muse-spark/round-2/implementation muse-spark/round-2/kernels/<slot-folder>/attempt-<M>
git commit -m "Muse Wonder: implementation v4: experts attempt 3 graded, beats baseline" \
  -m "Co-Authored-By: Muse Wonder (Meta Model API) <muse-wonder@meta-model-api.invalid>"
```

Use no other co-author. The hooks refuse a commit without a Muse agent's co-author, a commit outside `muse-spark/`, a change to a finished round's files, a new file outside this round's folder, and any merge. Push, merge, rebase, tags, git config and hook skipping stay with surucuonur.

104|8. **Verdict**, written by the verifier: each claim checked, and the result.
105|
106|### Hypothesis entry
107|
108|1. Status block. The lead owns it; the statuses are `boundary`, `building`, `hardening`, `candidate` (passes the grader's gates and its boundary check, signed by its checker), `ready` (a ready check passed it) and `dropped`.
109|2. **Inefficiency** it removes, the slot, and from round 2 on the slot's baseline folder, or `none` and its starting point.
110|3. **Boundary**, written by the boundary agent: what the solution must keep identical (see `boundary.md`).
111|4. **One section per builder:** its direction, its attempts (folder, predicted and measured µs per layer at the six sizes with each size's verdict, G1, G2, `beats_compiled`, and where the slot has a baseline its time and `beats_baseline`), and what each attempt taught.
112|5. **Boundary checks** of the attempts that passed G2.
113|6. **Decision:** the best attempt and why, with the change in whole requests it predicts, labelled a prediction; once a ready check has run, its `ready-verdict.json` and the measured change.
114|7. **Failure ledger,** kept by the lead: each graded attempt that lost, the size or phase it lost at, its named cause and its approach (`SKILL.md` step 4, *Harden*).
115|8. **Unverified:** what no one measured, the boundary's *can't see* list at least.
116|9. **Checks:** each checker's verdict, `pass` or its defects with file and line.
117|
118|## The checklist
119|
120|Fill it in for each piece of code you inspect, so that no piece is judged without its neighbours:
121|
122|- **Callers:** who calls it, and with what shapes at 1, 8 and 32 rows of a decode step and in a prefill.
123|- **Callees:** what it calls, down to the Metal kernel it launches.
124|- **Data:** each input and output with shape, dtype and layout. Where it is produced, and where it is consumed next.
125|- **Neighbours:** what runs just before and after it in the decode step, and what a replacement must keep identical.
126|- **Cost:** the kernels it launches, the bytes it reads and writes (weight bytes counted per read), and its measured time with the table the time comes from.
127|- **Invariants:** what correctness depends on: G2's bit-exact rule at every size, the tie rule for the 4th and 5th expert, the bfloat16 rounding points, and which MLX kernel the reference uses at each size.
128|
129|## The log
130|
131|Append one line per event with the shell, so lines from several agents never mix. In round 2:
132|
133|```bash
134|printf '%s | %s | %s\n' "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" "explorer-baseline-experts" "posted ineff-baseline-experts-2: each weight byte read 4 times at 32 rows" >> muse-spark/round-2/exploration/log.md
135|```
136|
137|Log when you start, claim something, post or confirm an entry, change direction (what from, what to, and which entry made you), grade an attempt (with its verdict), and finish.
138|
139|## Adapting to the others' work
140|
141|Before every new piece of work, and after every post:
142|1. Read the phase README's tracker and the newest 30 lines of the phase log (`tail -n 30`).
143|2. Then change direction when:
144|   - **someone else covers it:** another entry already covers the same code or cause, so append to that entry instead of starting a second one;
145|   - **its premise fell:** the claim your work rests on was refuted;
146|   - **something pays more:** an open item in your territory or task predicts a larger saving than what you're on, and nobody owns it.
147|3. When you change direction, log it with the reason, and write it in your own entry's status block.
148|
149|Two claims on the same item go to the lead, who settles them.
150|
151|## Rules for every agent
152|
153|- **Writes go only to this round's folder, in the files your role names.** Earlier rounds' folders, everything else in the worktree, and everything outside it are read-only.
154|- **Only the lead commits.** Helpers never run `git add` or `git commit`.
155|- **The grader and the ready check are the only GPU jobs.** Builders run the grader through the brief's command; the lead runs the ready check (`SKILL.md` step 4). Both wait their turn for the GPU. Start no other GPU work and load no model outside them: the machine has 16 GB and slows down sharply when memory runs short. A run of `time_candidates.py`, `breakdown.py` or any other timing script made directly is evidence of nothing.
156|- **Every number has a source,** and every speed number says its level and its kind:
157|  - **measured, piece:** the grader verdict that timed exactly that slot, `grade.json` in its attempt folder;
158|  - **measured, whole request:** the `ready-verdict.json` that timed exactly that slot or combination;
159|  - **prediction:** anything else. It counts only the candidate's own measured effect, shows its arithmetic, and stands beside the measured value once there is one.
160|
161|  A combination is measured as one, never added up from its slots. What no one measured goes under **Unverified**, never assumed free, neutral or zero. Other numbers cite a file and line, a table (path and row), or arithmetic shown in full.
162|- **Credentials stay unread:** `.env` files, `~/.config/muse/` and any key store.
163|- **The API-stage kernels** in the history before the tag `agent-era` are from an earlier, removed stage (PROVENANCE.md) and stay unread.

1|# Brief for the Muse Spark agent: write faster MobileMoE-S kernels, for decoding and prompt processing
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Committed and tagged `agent-era` before the Muse Spark session started. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|You are a Claude Code session powered by Meta's Muse Spark, working in your own git worktree on the branch `muse-agent`. This brief fixes your task, what you may change, where your work goes and how it is judged. It does not change during your session.
6|
7|## The task
8|
9|Meta's MobileMoE-S, int4, is served on an Apple M1 Pro (16-core GPU, 200 GB/s, 16 GB) by vLLM through vllm-metal, which runs the model with MLX. The findings below measure where each decode step's time goes. A step is about 870–1,090 small GPU kernels and is far from both the bandwidth and compute limits. The findings name the pieces that cost the most.
10|
11|A request goes through two phases: **prompt processing** (the prefill), which runs its whole prompt through the model, and **decoding**, one step per generated token. An improvement must hold in both: faster in one, and no slower in the other ([ADR 0011](adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). A kernel that speeds up the decode step but slows the prefill is not an improvement.
12|
13|1. **Choose.** Read the findings and choose one or two of the slots below to replace with your own fused Metal kernels. Write `muse-spark/strategy.md`: why, your design, and what each saves per step at 1 and 32 requests (your estimate). End it with the JSON block described under *Your files*. Commit it.
14|2. **Write and check.** For each chosen slot, write the kernels as files, run the grader on them, read its verdict, and improve. Up to **5 attempts per slot**; an attempt is a folder you graded and committed.
15|3. **Finish.** Write `muse-spark/summary.md`: your final attempt per slot and what you learned. Commit it.
16|
17|**Read these first** (all in your worktree):
18|- `claude/findings/bottleneck-explained.md` and `claude/findings/step-breakdown.md`: the measured findings;
19|- `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md` and `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md`: the raw tables;
20|- `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py` and `switch_layers.py`: the model code;
21|- MLX's custom-kernel documentation: `.venv/bin/python -c "import mlx.core as mx; help(mx.fast.metal_kernel)"`;
22|- `bench/grader/check_candidate.py` and `bench/grader/slots.py`: how you are graded.
23|
24|## The slots
25|
26|Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the call: 1 to 32 in a decode step, up to 2,048 in a prefill chunk. The grader flattens the inputs to the shapes below and restores the model's shapes afterwards. All arrays are row-contiguous.
27|
28|The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.
29|
30|### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights
31|
32|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
33||---|---|---|---|
34|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
35|| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
36|| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
37|| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
38|| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
39|
40|Reference:
41|
42|```python
43|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
44|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
45|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
46|weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
47|```
48|
49|The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.
50|
51|### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert
52|
53|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
54||---|---|---|---|
55|| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
56|| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
57|| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
58|| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
59|
60|Reference:
61|
62|```python
63|out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
64|```
65|
66|Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.
67|
68|### `routing+combine`
69|
70|Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.
71|
72|### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products
73|
74|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
75||---|---|---|---|
76|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
77|| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
78|| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
79|| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
80|| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
81|| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
82|| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |
83|
84|Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.
85|
86|Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:
87|
88|```python
89|y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
90|```
91|
92|As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.
93|
94|Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.
95|
96|## Tools and limits
97|
98|- **Only `mx.fast.metal_kernel`, MLX 0.32.4.** You write the Metal body; MLX generates the signature. Inputs arrive as `const device T* name` and outputs as `device T* name`. Shapes and strides come as `name_shape` and `name_strides` when the source uses them. The thread attributes are available, as in MLX's documentation: `thread_position_in_grid`, `threadgroup_position_in_grid`, `thread_position_in_threadgroup`, `threads_per_threadgroup`, `simdgroup_index_in_threadgroup`, `thread_index_in_simdgroup`, and so on.
99|- **The grader runs no Python of yours.** It reads your launch spec as data and compiles only your Metal.
100|- **Stay within the GPU's limits.** At most 1,024 threads per threadgroup and 32 KB of threadgroup memory. A grader run should take under 3 minutes, longer for an attempt much slower than the reference at the prefill sizes; stop one that runs past 15.
101|- **Hardware.** The Apple M1 Pro GPU (`applegpu_g13s`) has 16 cores and a SIMD width of 32. bfloat16 is available in Metal as `bfloat`.
102|
103|## Rules of this session
104|
105|These keep your work apart from everyone else's. Git hooks and an audit script enforce them, and a commit that breaks them is refused.
106|
107|- **Write only inside `muse-spark/`.** Never change `bench/`, `claude/`, `results/`, `tools/`, `third_party/`, or any other file. A copy of the grader you edit is never used.
108|- **Commit only on `muse-agent`,** with the co-author trailer your settings add: `Co-Authored-By: Muse Spark (Meta Model API) <muse-spark@meta-model-api.invalid>`. Start each subject with `Muse Spark:`. No other co-author.
109|- **Never push, merge, rebase, change git config, or skip hooks.**
110|- **Don't read `.env`** or any credentials file.
111|- One commit per attempt, after you've run the grader on it, so the history shows every attempt in order.
112|
113|## Your files
114|
115|```
116|muse-spark/
117|  strategy.md                                your choice and design, ending with the targets JSON
118|  kernels/<slot-folder>/attempt-<N>/
119|    block-0.metal, block-1.metal, ...        Metal kernel bodies (and headers), numbered from 0
120|    spec.json                                the launch spec
121|    notes.md                                 optional: what you tried and why
122|  summary.md                                 your final attempt per slot
123|```
124|
125|`<slot-folder>` is `routing`, `combine`, `routing-combine` or `experts`. Grade an attempt with:
126|
127|```bash
128|.venv/bin/python bench/grader/check_candidate.py muse-spark/kernels/<slot-folder>/attempt-<N> <slot>
129|```
130|
131|where `<slot>` is `routing`, `combine`, `routing+combine` or `experts`.
132|
133|**The targets JSON** at the end of `strategy.md`:
134|
135|```json
136|{
137|  "targets": [
138|    {"slot": "routing+combine", "why": "...", "expected_saving_ms": {"rows_1": 0.0, "rows_32": 0.0}, "design": "..."}
139|  ]
140|}
141|```
142|
143|List one or two targets, in the order you work on them.
144|
145|**The launch spec** (`spec.json`):
146|
147|```json
148|{
149|  "kernels": [
150|    {
151|      "name": "fused_routing",
152|      "source_block": 0,
153|      "header_block": null,
154|      "inputs": ["x", "w_router", "bias"],
155|      "outputs": [
156|        {"name": "inds", "shape": ["rows", 4], "dtype": "uint32"},
157|        {"name": "weights", "shape": ["rows", 4], "dtype": "float32"}
158|      ],
159|      "grid": ["rows*32", 1, 1],
160|      "threadgroup": [32, 1, 1],
161|      "template": {"T": "bfloat16"},
162|      "init_value": null,
163|      "atomic_outputs": false
164|    }
165|  ],
166|  "slot_outputs": {"inds": "inds", "weights": "weights"}
167|}
168|```
169|
170|- **`source_block` and `header_block`** are the numbers of your `block-N.metal` files.
171|- **Kernels run in list order.** A kernel's `inputs` may name slot inputs or outputs of earlier kernels.
172|- **`slot_outputs`** maps each output of the slot to the kernel output that provides it.
173|- **`max_rows`** (optional, an integer of at least 1): inputs with more rows than this skip your kernels and run the slot's reference under `mx.compile`. Use it to keep prefill-sized inputs on MLX's own code when your kernels are built for decode sizes; MLX switches its own experts kernel at 60 rows.
174|- **`min_rows`** (optional, from round 4; an integer of at least 1, at most `max_rows` when both are given): inputs with fewer rows than this run the compiled reference too, so your kernels run only from `min_rows` to `max_rows`. Use it when your kernels lose at the smallest decode sizes, such as 1 row ([ADR 0015](adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)). G3 times whole requests: with 1 request every decode step has 1 row, so an attempt that hands off 1 row runs MLX's own code for the whole 1-request workload, and can pass G3 only in a set whose other kernels are faster there.
175|- **A hand-off is checked like the rest:** bit-exact at every G2 size. The piece timing reports a size it hands off as `handed off` instead of timing it (*The piece timing*, below).
176|- **For `routing+combine`,** `spec.json` holds two specs, each in the format above for its own slot, `max_rows` and `min_rows` included: `{"routing": {"kernels": [...], "slot_outputs": {...}}, "combine": {"kernels": [...], "slot_outputs": {...}}}`. The original experts and shared expert run between the two parts. The grader tests each part on its own, and the combine part receives the reference routing weights.
177|- **Shape and grid entries** are integers, or products of integers and the names `rows`, `D`, `E`, `K` and `H`, such as `"rows*32"`. Nothing else is evaluated.
178|- **dtypes** are `float32`, `bfloat16`, `float16`, `uint32` or `int32`.
179|- **Template values** are one of those dtypes, an integer or a boolean.
180|- **`grid`** counts threads, not threadgroups, as in `mx.fast.metal_kernel`.
181|
182|## How each attempt is judged
183|
184|The pass criteria were fixed before the first round. From round 2, G2 is exact and also covers the prefill, and the piece timing chains the layers ([ADR 0010](adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md)); round 1 was judged by the earlier rules, in which G2 allowed small rounding differences and tested decode steps only. From round 3, the piece timing and G3 time both phases, decode and prefill ([ADR 0011](adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)); rounds 1 and 2 were timed on decode only.
185|
186|1. **G1, runs.** It compiles and runs on real inputs.
187|2. **G2, correct: identical to the reference, bit for bit.** The slot runs in every call of `MoE.__call__`, the prefill included, so it is tested on every layer's inputs at two kinds of size:
188|   - **a decode step:** inputs captured from all 20 layers during a real decode step, at 1, 8 and 32 rows;
189|   - **a prefill:** the first chunk of a prefill with 128-token prompts, recorded while the grader runs it, at 1, 8 and 32 requests: 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. From 60 rows on, MLX's own experts kernel changes (`gather_qmm_rhs` instead of `gather_qvm`), and so does its rounding.
190|
191|   At every size:
192|   - **`routing`:** each row's 4 experts and their 4 weights equal the reference's, in the same order, since combine sums the pairs in that order. That includes the reference's choice between tied 4th and 5th experts.
193|   - **`combine` and `experts`:** every element equals the reference's.
194|
195|   **Why exact:** the end-to-end check below asks for the same greedy tokens, and greedy decoding turns any difference into different tokens. In round 1, routing weights within 10⁻⁵ of the reference, relative, changed 7 to 9 of 32 sequences.
196|   - **Then, end to end:** the same greedy tokens as the original model over 24 generated tokens, at 1 and 32 requests, in both plain MLX and vLLM.
197|3. **G3, faster, in vLLM.** Each workload runs 5 times in shuffled order: 1, 8 and 32 requests with 128-token prompts, and 32 requests with 1,024-token prompts, 256 generated tokens each. Three times are measured per run:
198|   - the **decode step**, the median period between steady steps;
199|   - the **prompt time**, until every prompt was processed;
200|   - the **whole request**, from sending the requests to the last token.
201|
202|   Against both the original model and an `mx.compile` of the same reference code, the attempt passes when the decode step or the prompt time is faster in every workload, neither is slower in any, and no whole request is slower. Faster and slower mean that the ranges over the repeats don't overlap.
203|
204|   **From round 3, the same G3 runs inside the round too:** the lead's **ready check**, `bench/grader/check_ready.py`, with every candidate in one call. It also requires the same greedy tokens, and audits its own log. Only its passing verdict makes an attempt `ready`; Claude's G3 after the round decides. The skill says when the lead runs it ([ADR 0013](adr/0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)).
205|
206|   **From round 4, a set:** with more than one candidate, the ready check and G3 also time them all together (`muse-all`). When that passes, the candidates are ready together as a set, even where one fails alone, and G3 judges the set as one submission ([ADR 0015](adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)).
207|
208|**What the grader prints for an attempt** (JSON):
209|- `g1` false and the compiler's error message;
210|- or the correctness results per size: for routing, the rows that differ; for combine and experts, the elements that differ and the largest gap in units in the last place; with the first example;
211|- or, when the attempt is correct, `timing_us_per_layer` per size: its time per call next to the original's and the compiled reference's, its wins against the compiled reference and the verdict (`faster`, `same`, `slower`, or `handed off` for a size your spec hands to the compiled reference); then `phases_vs_compiled` and `beats_compiled`.
212|
213|**The piece timing** runs the slot at the six G2 sizes: the 20 layers' captured decode inputs at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and the 20 layers' first prefill chunk at 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. Each layer's call waits for the previous one's output, as in the model: one small kernel links them, the same for every function timed. Without that wait, the GPU overlaps the 20 calls and hides how long one takes; in round 1, an experts kernel 29% faster on overlapped calls was 66% slower on chained ones at 1 row.
214|- **Paired repeats.** Your attempt and the compiled reference run in alternating order, 30 times.
215|- **Per size:** your attempt is `faster` when it wins at least 22 of the 30 pairs, `slower` when it loses at least 22, and `same` otherwise. Medians alone would pass on noise: the same kernel timed twice differs by up to 5%.
216|- **Handed off** (from round 4): a size whose inputs your spec hands to the compiled reference (`max_rows`, `min_rows`) runs the bar's own code, so it is not timed against it. Its verdict is `handed off`, and your attempt's time there is the compiled reference's.
217|- **Per phase:** decode (1, 8, 32 rows) and prefill (127, 1,016, 2,048 rows) are each `faster` when every size it doesn't hand off is, and at least one isn't handed off; `slower` when any size is; `handed off` when all are; and `not slower` otherwise.
218|- **`beats_compiled`** is true when one phase is `faster` and neither is `slower`.
219|
220|It is a guide; the ready check in the round, and Claude's G3 after it, decide.
221|
222|**When a slot stops.** Work on a slot stops at the first attempt that passes G1 and G2 and has `beats_compiled` true, or after 5 attempts. Name your final attempt per slot in `muse-spark/summary.md`; it goes to the end-to-end and G3 checks, which surucuonur's team runs after merging your branch.

1|# Round 3 of the Muse agent, measured
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|In round 3 (2026-11-04, 17:35 to 19:00 UTC), the Muse agent ran skill version 8 ([ADR 0013](../adr/0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)). The model was Muse Spark's contributor model, `muse-spark-1.3-contributor`, at `max` effort, with tool approvals off ([ADR 0012](../adr/0012-muse-spark-contributor-unattended.md)). It started from [Claude's measurement of round 2](muse-round-2.md). There was no baseline in any slot, so the compiled reference was the bar everywhere. The round made 24 commits, the last `46679e7`, and graded 13 attempts: 5 for experts, 6 for routing and 2 for combine.
6|
7|For the first time, the swarm ran G3 itself before calling anything ready: the **ready check**, `bench/grader/check_ready.py` ([ADR 0013](../adr/0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)). Its two candidates each failed it alone, on overlapping ranges, and passed it together. The skill counted only candidates that pass alone, so the summary, [muse-spark/round-3/summary.md](../../muse-spark/round-3/summary.md), submits the reference in every slot. It reports the pair as measured but not submitted:
8|- **routing:** `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6`, round 2's attempt-4 kernels with `max_rows` 32;
9|- **combine:** `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/combine/attempt-2`, round 2's attempt-1 with its float contractions turned off.
10|
11|Claude measured the pair afterwards, alone and together, as G3 does.
12|
13|**Where everything is.**
14|- G3: [results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-3/](../../results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-3/), the verdict in `g3-vllm.json`.
15|- One request with long prompts: [results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-3-long/](../../results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-3-long/).
16|- The swarm's ready check: [muse-spark/round-3/checks/ready-1/](../../muse-spark/round-3/checks/ready-1/).
17|- The script: `bench/grader/time_candidates.py vllm <out> routing=… combine=…`, with `--settings 1x1024,1x7936 --max-model-len 8192` for the long prompts.
18|
19|**The machine.** The same M1 Pro, with Docker quit. 13.9 to 14.2 GB of 15.4 GB of swap were in use (`machine-*.txt`). vLLM ran with `VLLM_METAL_KV_COMMIT_PROBE=0`.
20|
21|## Summary
22|
23|- **Every kernel is bit-exact, and the tokens are unchanged.** Every variant, alone or together, gives the unchanged model's greedy tokens.
24|- **The pair is the best result of any round.** Against the unchanged model in vLLM, routing attempt-6 with combine attempt-2:
25|  - shortens the decode step by 16.5%, 5.4%, 2.8% and 1.6% with 1, 8 and 32 requests of 128 tokens and 32 of 1,024;
26|  - shortens whole requests by 14.1%, 5.6%, 2.1% and 2.4%;
27|  - processes prompts 1.6 to 3.1% faster, and is slower nowhere.
28|- **G3 still fails the pair, by one workload.** It passes against the unchanged model, but against the compiled reference (`compiled-all`) its decode step with 32 requests of 1,024 tokens is only 0.9% shorter, and the ranges of the 5 repeats overlap.
29|- **With one request and long prompts, the pair passes both bars.** With 1,024- and 7,936-token prompts its decode step is 14.8% and 11.3% shorter than the unchanged model's, and 8.1% and 6.3% shorter than the compiled reference's.
30|- **The ready check measured what G3 measures.** The swarm's decode changes match Claude's within 0.15 ms in every workload, and 2 of its 3 verdicts are the same. The third, the pair against `compiled-all`, passed in the swarm's run and failed in Claude's.
31|- **Experts never reached the ready check.** Its best attempt lost to the compiled reference only at 1 row (section 4).
32|
33|## 1. The ready check against Claude's G3
34|
35|Both runs time the same variants in the same four workloads, 5 shuffled repeats each. The decode-step change against the unchanged model, in ms, at 1×128 / 8×128 / 32×128 / 32×1024 (requests × prompt tokens; medians):
36|
37|| Variant | The swarm's ready check | Claude's G3 | Verdicts, swarm / Claude |
38||---|---|---|---|
39|| `muse-routing` | −0.38 / −0.31 / −0.59 / −0.48 | −0.41 / −0.31 / −0.61 / −0.62 | fail / fail |
40|| `muse-combine` | −0.53 / −0.59 / −0.44 / −0.26 | −0.56 / −0.51 / −0.45 / −0.48 | fail / fail |
41|| `muse-all`, both | −0.92 / −0.89 / −0.73 / −0.78 | −0.90 / −0.77 / −0.83 / −0.65 | pass / **fail** |
42|
43|**Why the verdicts differ.** Every failure in both runs is an overlap of ranges: no variant is slower than either bar anywhere.
44|- `muse-routing` fails against `compiled-routing` at 8×128 in both runs, and in Claude's also against the unchanged model at 32×1024.
45|- `muse-combine` fails in the swarm's run on one 1×128 repeat (5.892 ms, above the unchanged model's lowest, 5.430). In Claude's it fails against `compiled-combine` at 32×128 and 32×1024.
46|- `muse-all` against `compiled-all` at 32×1024: in Claude's run the 5 decode times are 38.59 to 39.08 ms and the compiled reference's 38.91 to 39.40, medians 0.9% apart. In the swarm's run the medians were 1.5% apart, and the ranges just missed each other.
47|
48|With gains of about 1%, 5 repeats decide by chance. Every median favours the kernels, but the rule asks for ranges that miss each other. That rule stays for round 4 ([ADR 0015](../adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md), *Considered options*).
49|
50|## 2. G3: whole requests and prompts
51|
52|Claude's G3, the change against the unchanged model (medians of 5 repeats; the unchanged step was 5.457, 14.337, 30.061 and 39.410 ms):
53|
54|| Workload | Variant | Decode step | Prompt time | Whole request |
55||---|---|---|---|---|
56|| 1×128 | routing | −7.5% | −2.7% | −6.9% |
57|| | combine | −10.2% | −1.0% | −7.7% |
58|| | both | **−16.5%** | −3.1% | **−14.1%** |
59|| | compiled reference, both slots | −8.5% | −4.1% | −8.0% |
60|| 8×128 | both | **−5.4%** | −1.6% | **−5.6%** |
61|| | compiled reference | −2.8% | +0.1% | −2.7% |
62|| 32×128 | both | **−2.8%** | −2.7% | **−2.1%** |
63|| | compiled reference | −0.9% | −1.4% | −0.8% |
64|| 32×1024 | both | **−1.6%** | −2.8% | **−2.4%** |
65|| | compiled reference | −0.7% | −0.3% | −0.6% |
66|
67|Bold: faster than the unchanged model beyond the spread of the repeats.
68|
69|- **The gain is about the same in milliseconds everywhere:** 0.65 to 0.9 ms per decode step. The share falls as more requests make each step longer.
70|- **Prompts gain a little, and lose nothing.** Routing hands every prompt-sized input to the compiled reference (`max_rows` 32), and combine attempt-2 is faster than the reference at every prefill size. Round 2's routing kernel made prompts 7 to 10% slower; this one doesn't.
71|- **Half the gain is compiling MLX's own code.** `mx.compile` of the two slots' reference code alone gains 8.5% at 1×128. The kernels add the other 8.8%.
72|
73|## 3. One request with long prompts
74|
75|G3's workloads stop at 1,024-token prompts with 32 requests. Claude also timed one request with 1,024- and 7,936-token prompts, the longest that fits the model's 8,192-token context with 256 generated tokens ([results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-3-long/](../../results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-3-long/)). `time_candidates.py` gained `--max-model-len` for this; G3's default is unchanged.
76|
77|| Prompt | Decode step | Prompt time | Whole request | Throughput |
78||---|---|---|---|---|
79|| 1,024 tokens | 5.7 → 4.9 ms, **−14.8%** | **−2.9%** | **−13.8%** | 152 → 176 tokens/s |
80|| 7,936 tokens | 8.2 → 7.3 ms, **−11.3%** | −2.1% | **−6.4%** | 56 → 60 tokens/s |
81|
82|Against the compiled reference, the decode step is 8.1% and 6.3% shorter. In these two workloads the pair passes G3's rule against both bars, and so does combine attempt-2 alone. The decode step saves about the same 0.85 to 0.93 ms however long the prompt is. A 7,936-token prompt takes about half the request, though, so the whole request gains less.
83|
84|## 4. Experts: lost at 1 row only
85|
86|hyp-2 graded 5 attempts and dropped the slot. The best, attempt-1, is round 2's fused kernel with `max_rows` 59. It is bit-exact, `same` as the compiled reference at every prefill size, and much faster at 8 and 32 rows, but slower at 1. Chained µs per layer, attempt against compiled reference:
87|
88|| Rows | 1 | 8 | 32 |
89||---|---|---|---|
90|| attempt-1 | 96.9 | 168.9 | 554.7 |
91|| compiled reference | 86.6 | 238.2 | 883.4 |
92|
93|`beats_compiled` needs one phase faster at every size, so the 1-row loss sank it. The round then tried to win at 1 row, in two ways:
94|- **a vectorised scalar path** (attempt-2) bought nothing;
95|- **an unfused path copying the reference's structure** (attempt-5) was twice as slow at 1 row.
96|
97|The round's lead concluded that "no third exists in the spec surface". The spec could not keep 1 row on MLX's own code while running the kernel at 8 and 32 rows; from round 4 it can (`min_rows`, ADR 0015). No experts attempt has been timed end to end since round 2's attempt-7, which shortened the decode step by 17.5% with 32 requests and processed prompts 6.6 to 14.5 times slower.
98|
99|## 5. How round 3 worked
100|
101|The new rules held:
102|- every end-to-end number in *Ready to test* comes from the ready check, and predictions are labelled;
103|- `checker-final` found 7 rounding slips in the last digit and had them fixed before the round ended;
104|- when the fused experts kernel kept losing at 1 row, attempt-5 changed approach to an unfused path, and its ledger line says so.
105|
106|What went wrong:
107|- **Builders were spent on directions exploration had already ruled out:** experts attempt-2 and routing attempt-3.
108|- **Extra kernel launches cost more than they saved.** Routing attempt-3's added copy launch, about 2 to 3 µs per layer, flipped its decode from `faster` to `same`. Experts attempt-5's five launches instead of two cost about 18 µs per layer, part of its 2× loss at 1 row (`hyp-2-experts-prefill.md`, `hyp-3-routing-prefill.md`).
109|- **The thread limit cost two attempts.** Metal's limit per pipeline depends on the kernel's registers, 640 and then 576 threads here, while the grader checks only for 1,024. Routing attempts 2 and 4 failed G1 on it.
110|- **The grader timed identical code against itself.** Above `max_rows` an attempt runs the compiled reference, and the grader still timed it against the compiled reference. That judged routing attempt-1 `slower` at 2,048 rows on 8 wins of 30, and cost a re-grade of a byte-identical copy (attempt-6). From round 4 such a size is `handed off` (ADR 0015).
111|- **The set had no rule.** The skill said submitting together needs `muse-all` to pass, but made only single candidates `ready`. The lead read it strictly and submitted nothing. From round 4 a passing `muse-all` makes its candidates `ready` as a set (ADR 0015).
112|- **Absolute grader times drift up to twice between runs** on this machine, so comparing attempts across runs misleads; the round learned to compare ratios against the compiled reference from the same run.
113|
114|## For round 4: baselines and starting points
115|
116|**The rule** is unchanged ([ADR 0011](../adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)): a slot's baseline is its best attempt so far that passes the current G2, has `beats_compiled` true in the grader, and passes G3. Round 4 adds sets and `min_rows` ([ADR 0015](../adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)).
117|
118|| Slot | Baseline | Starting point | Grader | G3 | Why it is no baseline |
119||---|---|---|---|---|---|
120|| `routing` | none | `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6` | `beats_compiled` true; decode 0.72 / 0.90 / 0.88 of the compiled reference at 1 / 8 / 32 rows, prefill `handed off` (Claude's re-grade with the round-4 grader, [results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/](../../results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/)) | fails alone: `same` as `compiled-routing` at 8×128 | G3 alone |
121|| `combine` | none | `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/combine/attempt-2` | `beats_compiled` true in both phases (round 3's grade) | fails alone: `same` as `compiled-combine` at 32×128 and 32×1024 | G3 alone |
122|| `experts` | none | `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1` | slower at 1 row, faster at 8 and 32, prefill `same` (section 4) | not timed | the 1-row loss |
123|
124|**The pair** routing attempt-6 with combine attempt-2 passes G3 against the unchanged model, and against the compiled reference everywhere but 32×1024, where it is 0.9% shorter with overlapping ranges (section 1). Under round 4's set rule it would be a `ready` set, but it is no baseline. Round 4's bar is the compiled reference in every slot.
125|
126|**What round 4 has to find out,** in Claude's reading of these results:
127|1. **experts with `min_rows`.** Whether attempt-1's 8- and 32-row speed carries into G3 once 1 row runs MLX's own code. With 1 request it then adds nothing, so it can pass G3 only in a set whose other kernels are faster with 1 request, such as the pair.
128|2. **All three slots at once.** In rounds 1 and 2, replacing all three slots lost about 2.8 ms with 8 requests, for an unknown reason ([round 2](muse-round-2.md), section 4). A set with experts meets that again.
129|3. **A margin at 32×1024.** The pair gains 0.25 to 0.3 ms over the compiled reference there, about 1%, which 5 repeats can't tell from noise. A set needs more than that with 32 long prompts.

# Muse Spark summary

## Round 3

- **Model:** Muse Spark (muse-spark-1.3-contributor). **Skill version:** 8. Final README versions: exploration v5, implementation v21.
- **Final attempts:** `experts` → the reference (hyp-2 dropped: `max_rows`-59 attempt-1 banks prefill `same` × 3 but misses 1-row decode, and the unfused 1-row fix came out 2× worse — the gap is structural); `routing` → the reference (hyp-3 dropped: `max_rows`-32 attempt-6 passes G1+G2+boundary with `beats_compiled` true, but the ready check fails it alone vs compiled-routing on the 8×128 range overlap); `combine` → the reference (hyp-1 dropped: pragma-devolatilized attempt-2 passes G1+G2+boundary with `beats_compiled` true, but the ready check fails it alone on a 1×128 outlier rep). No slot has a `ready` attempt and no slot has a baseline, so every slot keeps the reference.
- **Graded attempts per slot, this round and over all rounds:** experts 5 this round (1 G1 fail), 16 total; routing 6 (2 G1 fails), 12 total; combine 2, 6 total. Every graded attempt is committed in order (one grader run is one attempt).
- **Ready check's measured change** ([checks/ready-1/ready-verdict.json](checks/ready-1/ready-verdict.json), exit 1, verdict stands; 5 repeats, same tokens everywhere): `muse-routing` FAILS (vs base pass; vs compiled-routing fail) with decode medians −0.38/−0.31/−0.59/−0.48 ms vs base; `muse-combine` FAILS (vs base and vs compiled-combine fail) with decode medians −0.53/−0.59/−0.44/−0.26 ms vs base; no phase of either is `slower` anywhere — every failure is `not slower` on range overlap. `muse-all` (both together) PASSES vs base and vs compiled-all: decode −0.92/−0.89/−0.73/−0.78 ms, prompt −0.9/−6.2/−38.0/−174.0 ms, whole request −231/−227/−208/−390 ms vs base (decode `faster`, request `faster`, prompt `not slower`). Measured but not submitted: with no per-slot `ready`, per-slot submission is all-reference.
- **What I'd try next:** (1) the experts 1-row gap is THE blocker and needs a new idea — fused plateaued, unfused backfired, and the spec has no hand-off below a row count; (2) a joint `routing+combine` submission judged as one variant — `muse-all` passes G3's bar while neither passes alone; (3) the GEMM-sharing overhead hunt (barriers vs occupancy serialization, both slots' grouped paths are exact but 1.4–3.5× off); (4) accept that paired spread gates hand-off-identical code, and re-time would-be submissions in quieter runs before trusting a single overlap.
- **Recommendations outside the slots** (for surucuonur's team): attention K/V re-read per query head (up to ~2 ms at 32 rows); split-K partial traffic from 14 rows (≈2.4 ms upper bound at 32 rows, unmeasured); 60 q/k/v `[0]` gathers + copies (−0.21 ms measured at 8 rows, `squeeze(0)` fix); ~2 ms engine CPU per 1-row step (≈0.5 ms of Python fixes). Evidence in round 1's entries (see [muse-spark/exploration/README.md](../exploration/README.md) *Recommendations*). # Attempt 2 — builder-1-b, direction (b): FP-contract-off pragma barrier

First attempt in this direction (round 3, `hyp-1-combine-devolatilize`,
slot `combine`, baseline `none`). Builds on the starting point
`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/combine/attempt-1`, which passes G1+G2 and
`beats_compiled` but fails G3 (+1.051 ms/step in vLLM at 32 requests).

## What changed

Only the barrier mechanism. Grid (`rows*768`), threadgroup [256,1,1],
index/base lines, inputs/outputs and the final
`bfloat(acc) + shared[sbase]` line are verbatim from the starting
point. The seven `volatile float` locals (`p0..p3`, `s01`, `s012`,
`acc`) become seven plain `float` locals with the identical 7-op
sequence, and a new header block (`block-1.metal`, wired via
`"header_block": 1` — the only `spec.json` delta) disables FP
contraction for the kernel:

```metal
#pragma STDC FP_CONTRACT OFF
#pragma clang fp contract(off)
```

MLX emits `header` before the main function, so the pragmas precede the
kernel definition, which is where FP-option pragmas take effect. No
`volatile` anywhere in code, no `__attribute__((noinline))` helpers,
no extra functions, calls, or memory traffic of any kind.

Why this is contraction-proof: with contract(off) the backend may not
fuse any fmul+fadd into an fma — this is the compiler's own
contraction switch, so there is no transform left that can keep a
product unrounded into its consumer add. Each of the 7 statements is
then one rounded f32 op on register values: the same 7 materialisation
points, same fold order `((p0+p1)+p2)+p3`, same two bfloat16 roundings
as the starting point. Reassociation needs no pragma: it is off without
fast-math flags, and the grader sets none. The proof is G2 itself: any
surviving contraction shows the starting point's old signature (decode
0/2/2, prefill 6/50/130 differ).

## Inefficiency removed

`ineff-baseline-combine-1` (confirmed): the seven volatiles' 7 stores +
7 loads per output (56 B/thread of thread-private traffic, 43,008
B/row/layer) stall the decode step (+7.1/+25.4/+72.1 µs/layer vLLM)
and the 32×128 prompt (+1,501.7 ms twin). The pragmas keep every value
in registers — ~10 live floats, no spill pressure — so the barrier
costs zero bytes and zero instructions. Same fix covers both phases:
both run these identical lines.

## Prediction (µs per layer, chained paired basis)

Starting point (re-grade `grade-phases-combine-attempt-1.json`, via
`ineff-g3-1`): decode reference/candidate 52.8/45.7 @1, 71.2/47.9 @8,

62.8/226.5/273.0 vs compiled 66.1/271.6/520.4.

# From round 4, candidates that pass together are ready as a set, and an attempt may hand off small inputs too

*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../../PROVENANCE.md).*

**The change.** Round 3 showed three gaps in the rules ([Claude's measurement](../findings/muse-round-3.md)). On 2026-11-04 surucuonur chose to fix all three before round 4:

1. **Ready as a set.** Round 3's routing and combine candidates each failed the ready check alone, on overlapping ranges, while the two together (`muse-all`) passed it. The skill made a candidate `ready` only when it passed alone, so the round submitted nothing. From round 4, when `muse-all` passes the ready check, all its candidates are `ready` together as a **set**. A set goes to G3 whole, and G3 judges it as `muse-all`.
2. **Hand off below a row count too: `min_rows`.** `max_rows` already sends inputs with more rows to `mx.compile` of the slot's reference ([ADR 0011](0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). The new `min_rows` in an attempt's `spec.json` does the same for inputs with fewer rows, so the kernels run only from `min_rows` to `max_rows`. Round 3's experts attempt-1 lost to the compiled reference only at 1 row: 96.9 against 86.6 µs per layer, while it took 168.9 against 238.2 at 8 rows and 554.7 against 883.4 at 32. Its only way to pass was to win at the size it is worst at.
3. **A handed-off size isn't timed.** The grader timed each handed-off size, which runs the compiled reference, against the compiled reference: the same code twice. In round 3 that noise judged routing attempt-1 `slower` at 2,048 rows, on 8 wins of 30, and cost a re-grade of a byte-identical copy. Now such a size is reported `handed off`. A phase is `faster` when every size the kernels run at is faster, and it needs at least one; `beats_compiled` is still one phase `faster` and none `slower`. G2 still checks every size, bit for bit.

## How it works

- **`bench/grader/slots.py`:**
  - `build()` reads `min_rows` as it reads `max_rows`: an integer of at least 1, at most `max_rows` when both are given.
  - The function it returns has `hands_off(rows)`, which says whether inputs with that many rows run the compiled reference.
- **`bench/grader/check_candidate.py`:**
  - At each size, a function that hands the rows off is not timed. It takes the compiled reference's times, so for `routing+combine` the part that hands off adds the same time to both sides.
  - A bar's verdict is `handed off` when neither side ran code of its own. Against a baseline that runs its own kernels there, the size is timed as before.
  - `judge()` leaves `handed off` sizes out of a phase. A phase whose sizes are all handed off is `handed off`.
- **`bench/grader/test_hand_off.py`:**
  - checks `build()` with a toy kernel at row counts on both sides of each bound, bit for bit, and that bad bounds are refused;
  - checks `judge()` on five sets of verdicts.
  - Passed on 2026-11-04.
- **A real attempt.** Claude re-graded round 3's routing attempt-6 (`max_rows` 32) with the changed grader ([results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/](../../results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/)):
  - G2 passes;
  - decode is `faster` at 1, 8 and 32 rows, on 29, 26 and 27 wins of 30;
  - the three prefill sizes are `handed off`;
  - `beats_compiled` is true.
- **The skill, version 9.**
  - The ready check makes a passing `muse-all` a set.
  - *Ready to test* names a set's attempts together.
  - Builders and boundary agents record `min_rows` and the sizes it hands off.
- **G3 and the ready check are unchanged.** They time whole requests, so a slot's kernels count wherever they run. With 1 request every decode step has 1 row, so an attempt that hands off 1 row runs MLX's own code for the whole 1-request workload. Alone it is then no faster than its compiled bar there, and it can pass G3 only in a set whose other kernels are faster with 1 request. The brief says so.

## Consequences

- **Round 3's pair qualifies for round 4.** Under the set rule, routing attempt-6 with combine attempt-2 would have been `ready` in round 3, because its `muse-all` passed the swarm's ready check. Claude's G3 failed the same pair against the compiled bar at 32 requests of 1,024 tokens, on overlapping ranges, so the pair is still no baseline.
- **A set is judged once.** Its parts are not judged alone, so a set can carry a part that only helps together with the others. G3 still requires the whole set to be faster than both bars, and to be slower nowhere.
- **The interaction of all three slots is untested.** In rounds 1 and 2, replacing all three slots at once lost about 2.8 ms with 8 requests, for an unknown reason ([round 2](../findings/muse-round-2.md), section 4). A set with an experts attempt meets that again.

## Considered options

- **A paired test on medians for the ready check and G3,** so that one outlier repeat can't sink a candidate, as it sank combine attempt-2 in round 3. Not chosen for round 4: it changes ADR 0011's rule for Claude's G3 too, and there was too little time to check it before the deadline.
- **Hand-off by an explicit list of row counts.** More flexible, but no attempt has needed more than one range, and two bounds are simple to check.
