## Starting point

Round 4 is the last round ([ADR 0014](../../../claude/adr/0014-muse-wonder-last-round.md)). It builds on rounds 1–3 as measured independently by Claude in [`claude/findings/muse-round-3.md`](../../../claude/findings/muse-round-3.md). Round 3 ran as Muse Spark (model `muse-spark-1.3-contributor`, skill version 8) and submitted the reference in every slot: no candidate passed the ready check alone, and the skill then counted only candidates that pass alone. Round 4 changes three rules ([ADR 0015](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)): candidates that pass together in `muse-all` are `ready` as a **set**; an attempt may hand off inputs below `min_rows` as well as above `max_rows`; and a handed-off size is reported `handed off` instead of being timed. A slot's **baseline** is still its best attempt so far that passes the current G2, has `beats_compiled` true in the grader, and passes G3 ([ADR 0011](../../../claude/adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). **No slot has a baseline.** The bar in every slot is the compiled reference, and a new attempt must beat it in the same grader run (no `--baseline` argument). Round 4 runs as Muse Wonder (muse-wonder-1.0).

### Per slot

#### `experts` — starting point `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1`

- **What it is.** Round 2's fused per-pair kernel, byte-identical, plus `max_rows: 59` in `spec.json`: rows 1–59 run the fused kernel, rows above 59 run the compiled reference. See `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1/notes.md` and its `grade.json` (G1 pass, G2 differ 0 at all six sizes).
- **Piece timing** (chained µs per layer, candidate vs compiled, its own grade run): 1 row 96.9 vs 86.6 (`slower`, 5 wins); 8 rows 168.9 vs 238.2 (`faster`, 29 wins); 32 rows 554.7 vs 883.4 (`faster`, 29 wins); prefill 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 `same` (19 / 15 / 16 wins — the hand-off runs compiled code). `beats_compiled` false: decode `slower` on the 1-row size alone.
- **G3 effect.** Never timed end to end (round 3, section 4). Its ancestor (round 2 attempt-7, same kernels without the hand-off) shortened the decode step 17.5% with 32 requests but made prompt processing 6.6–14.5× slower; the hand-off removes the prefill half of that, so no G3 prediction from round 3 stands — Claude's reading is that only the 1-row gap remains.
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** It is not a baseline because `beats_compiled` is false — the 1-row decode loss (96.9 vs 86.6 µs/layer) — and it has no G3 pass. Round 3 tried a vectorised scalar path (attempt-2, bought nothing) and an unfused path copying the reference's structure (attempt-5, 2× worse at 1 row) and concluded no fix existed in the spec surface. From round 4 the surface has `min_rows`: `min_rows: 2` with `max_rows: 59` hands 1-row inputs to the compiled reference while keeping the 8/32-row wins — a direction not yet graded. It can then pass G3 only in a set whose other kernels are faster with 1 request, because with 1 request every decode step runs MLX's own code for this slot.
- **Where it still spends its time.** At 8/32 rows it already wins by 69.3 / 328.7 µs per layer; what remains is the 1-row chain (the `tg_x` load, silu and barrier chain named in round 3) — now hand-off-able — and per-pair weight re-reads at all sizes (552,960 B per pair, round 3's entry).

#### `routing` — starting point `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6`

- **What it is.** Round 2's staged scalar-exact kernel (attempt-4 kernels) with `max_rows: 32`: every decode step (1–32 rows) runs the staged scalar kernels, all prefill sizes run the compiled reference. Attempt-6 is a byte-identical re-grade of round 3's attempt-1 (empty `diff` on both blocks and `spec.json`), run to test whether attempt-1's 2,048-row `slower` on identical code reproduced; it did not (19/30 wins, `same`). See `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6/notes.md`.
- **Piece timing.** Round 3's grade: decode `faster` at all three sizes (candidate 51.7 / 90.9 / 132.2 vs compiled 66.3 / 104.0 / 152.0 µs per layer; 28 / 27 / 25 wins), prefill `same` at all three sizes. Claude's re-grade with the round-4 grader ([`results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/`](../../../results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/)): decode `faster` (29 / 26 / 27 wins; candidate 0.72 / 0.90 / 0.88 of the compiled reference at 1 / 8 / 32 rows), the three prefill sizes `handed off`, `beats_compiled` true.
- **G3 effect.** In round 3's swarm ready check it failed alone against `compiled-routing` at 8×128 on overlapping ranges, with no phase slower anywhere (decode medians −0.38 / −0.31 / −0.59 / −0.48 ms vs the unchanged model at 1×128 / 8×128 / 32×128 / 32×1024). Claude's G3 agreed: `same` as `compiled-routing` at 8×128. Together with combine attempt-2 (`muse-all`) it passed the swarm's ready check but failed Claude's G3 against `compiled-all` at 32×1024, where the medians are 0.9% apart with overlapping ranges.
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** G3 alone: it passes G2 and has `beats_compiled` true, but it has never passed G3, alone or (in Claude's run) as a pair. Under round 4's set rule the pair would have been `ready` in round 3, but a set still has to pass G3 as `muse-all`, so the pair is no baseline.
- **Where it still spends its time.** Decode wins at every size; the open question is margin, above all at 32×1024 where the pair gains only 0.25–0.30 ms over the compiled reference (~1%), inside the 5-repeat spread. The per-row `w_router` re-read is untouched (upper bound only, round 2's `ineff-baseline-routing-4`).

#### `combine` — starting point `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/combine/attempt-2`

- **What it is.** Round 2's attempt-1 kernel with its seven `volatile` rounding barriers replaced by seven plain `float` locals and a header block (`block-1.metal`) carrying `#pragma STDC FP_CONTRACT OFF` / `#pragma clang fp contract(off)`: same 7-op stepwise fold `((p0+p1)+p2)+p3`, same grid (`rows*768`) and threadgroup [256,1,1], no `max_rows`. See `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/combine/attempt-2/notes.md`.
- **Piece timing.** Round 3's grade: `faster` at all six sizes (decode 31.8 / 34.7 / 32.7 vs compiled 36.9 / 41.1 / 45.7 µs per layer, 24 / 27 / 30 wins; prefill 38.2 / 100.9 / 198.0 vs 64.0 / 281.8 / 556.2, 30 / 30 / 29 wins); `beats_compiled` true in both phases. Absolute chained times drift up to ~35% between runs on this machine (round 3's lesson), so only same-run paired verdicts transfer.
- **G3 effect.** In round 3's ready check it failed alone against the unchanged model at 1×128 on a single outlier repeat (5.892 ms, above the unchanged model's lowest 5.430) and, in Claude's G3, against `compiled-combine` at 32×128 and 32×1024 — again range overlaps with no phase slower anywhere (swarm decode medians −0.53 / −0.59 / −0.44 / −0.26 ms vs the unchanged model). Its ancestor's in-step cost (+1.05 ms/step at 32 requests from the volatile barriers) is what the pragma removes; round 3's measured decode medians favour the kernel everywhere.
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** G3 alone, on spread: every median favours it, but the 5-repeat ranges overlap the bars'. No kernel change is named that tightens spread on 7 plain ops (round 3's implementation README); as part of a set it already passes `muse-all` in the swarm's run.
- **Where it still spends its time.** Nothing further in the grader — it sits on the chained floor and wins at all six sizes. What remains is the same margin question as routing: more separation from the compiled reference at 32×128 and 32×1024, or a set that clears the bar together.

#### All three together

Round 3's pair (routing attempt-6 + combine attempt-2) is the best result of any round: against the unchanged model it shortens the decode step 16.5% / 5.4% / 2.8% / 1.6% and whole requests 14.1% / 5.6% / 2.1% / 2.4% at 1×128 / 8×128 / 32×128 / 32×1024, with prompts 1.6–3.1% faster and nothing slower — but it fails G3 against `compiled-all` at 32×1024 (0.9% median gap, overlapping ranges). About half the gain over the unchanged model is `mx.compile` of the two slots' reference code alone. The three-slot composition is untested: in rounds 1 and 2, replacing all three slots at once lost about 2.8 ms with 8 requests for an unknown reason, and round 3 installed no experts candidate, so no run since has met it.

### What is left

Ranked by predicted saving against the compiled reference (no slot has a baseline, so the reference is the bar everywhere). Claude's measurement names three things round 4 has to find out; the ranking follows them.

1. **Experts with `min_rows`.** Whether attempt-1's 8/32-row speed (168.9 vs 238.2 and 554.7 vs 883.4 µs per layer) carries into G3 once 1 row runs MLX's own code (`min_rows: 2`, `max_rows: 59`). This is the only ungraded direction in any slot and the largest piece saving left: the 8/32-row wins are 69.3 / 328.7 µs per layer, worth (PREDICTION, from those same-run margins × 20 layers) about 1.4 ms per step at 8 requests and 6.6 ms at 32 requests against the compiled reference, with prefill `handed off` above 59 rows and 1-row decode `handed off` — so the gain exists only at 8 and 32 requests, and G3 can pass only in a set whose other kernels win with 1 request. The risk is the three-slot interaction (item 3).
2. **A margin at 32×1024.** The pair gains 0.25–0.30 ms over the compiled reference there (~1%), which 5 repeats cannot tell from noise; a set needs more than that with 32 long prompts. This is a margin problem in routing and/or combine decode kernels, not a correctness one: both starting points are bit-exact and already `faster` at every graded size, so any new attempt must widen the same-run margin at decode sizes without touching prefill (`max_rows: 32` for routing, faster-everywhere for combine). A saving here is worth the difference between a passing and a failing set — the largest whole-request prize left, and unquantified until a builder measures it.
3. **All three slots at once.** In rounds 1 and 2 the three-slot replacement lost about 2.8 ms with 8 requests for an unknown reason; a set with an experts attempt meets that again. No single-slot kernel change is predicted to remove it, so it is carried as a constraint: per-slot wins are not assumed to compose, and the ready check (which times candidates alone and all together) is where composition is measured. If the three together lose, the fallback set is the routing+combine pair.
4. **Slots not yet tried.** `routing+combine` (both slots, each with its own kernels, in one candidate) has never been graded as one folder. The parts are graded independently and the combine part receives the reference routing weights, so it is packaging unless a shared design emerges; the set rule already submits the two slots together without it. No hypothesis is planned on it unless exploration finds a shared-design reason.
5. **Recommendations outside the slots** stand as written in round 1's and round 2's exploration READMEs (attention K/V re-read per query head; split-K partial traffic from 14 rows; the 60 q/k/v `[0]` gathers; engine CPU per 1-row step). Claude's round-3 measurement did not test them. They are for surucuonur's team; no hypothesis targets them.

### Refuted claims

No one chases these again.

- Round 3's experts 1-row fixes: a vectorised scalar path (attempt-2) bought nothing and an unfused path copying the reference's structure (attempt-5) was 2× worse at 1 row — the 1-row gap is not closed by either approach, and round 4 does not retry them; it hands 1 row off instead.
- Routing attempt-1's 2,048-row `slower` verdict on byte-identical code: attempt-6's re-grade (19/30, `same`) confirmed it as paired noise, not a hand-off cost. Handed-off sizes are no longer timed at all.
- `ineff-runs-3` (round 1, refuted): the micro sorted/unsorted gaps measure kernel choice, not pair order.
- Round 1's implicit claim that the independent (overlapped) piece timing ranks attempts as the model does: refuted by the chained measurement. Round 4 ranks by the chained timing only.
- The claim that scalar sums cannot reproduce MMA rounding: refuted by building in round 2 (routing attempts 2–4, experts scalar paths bit-identical at all six sizes).

### Territories this round opens

Each territory is opened by the line of this section that names it. A `baseline-<slot>` explorer maps that slot's starting-point kernels and `spec.json` — now the code in the slot — with the checklist, and finds where they still lose time and, for a starting point, why it is no baseline. # Git source-control safety

The working tree belongs to the user. Make the change, leave it visible, and
let them decide what becomes history.

## Never without an explicit ask

The user must have asked for that exact write in this session, in their own
words. An explicit request to create a new commit counts anywhere in the user's
own task text, but it is not a request to amend, push, or tag. Finishing a task
without that request does not authorize a history write.

- `commit`, `commit --amend`, `push`, `tag`, `rebase`, `cherry-pick`, `revert`,
  `merge`, branch deletion, `reset --hard`, path restore, and `clean -f` all
  require an explicit ask.
- Never publish merely because publication would be useful.

## Before an authorized discard

Recovery is insurance, not authorization. A save never expands what the user
allowed you to delete or overwrite.

When the user explicitly authorized an operation that may discard or broadly
overwrite workspace changes, and the workspace is an ordinary Git checkout:

1. After `muse.read_skill` gives the physical Git skill package path, run:

   ```bash
   bash <git-skill-dir>/scripts/workspace-recovery.sh save before-discard
   ```

2. Keep the printed `refs/tbh/recovery/...` value in your handoff, then perform
   only the exact authorized operation.
3. If the save fails or the workspace is unsupported, stop before destruction
   and ask the user.

To recover that saved tree later, run:

```bash
bash <git-skill-dir>/scripts/workspace-recovery.sh restore <recovery-ref>
```

Restore first saves the current workspace, leaves HEAD, branch, and the real
index in place, and restores the selected snapshot into the worktree. The ref
also retains distinct staged bytes when the same path had later worktree edits.
Read those staged bytes with `git show '<recovery-ref>^2:<path>'`; the recovery
commit's second parent is the saved index tree. Ignored files are not saved;
restore refuses an ignored-path collision rather than overwrite data it could
not save. Use only the exact printed ref, not a revision expression.

## Always fine

Read-only inspection such as `status`, `log`, `show`, `diff`, `blame`,
`branch -v`, `show-ref`, `rev-parse`, `for-each-ref`, and `merge-base` is fine.
Staging named files to inspect `diff --cached`, and a temporary stash around a
tool that requires a clean tree, are also fine when the original state is put
back afterward.

## The rest

- Do not use a broad add in a tree you did not clean; name the files you changed.
- Do not initialize a repository inside vendored, build, data, or existing
  source-control trees.
- Do not create or edit `.gitignore` or `.git/info/exclude` to hide the user's
  files, and do not stash the user's files (including `stash push -u`) to make
  `git status` look clean. "Leave the working tree clean", "tidy up", and
  similar phrasing do not authorize committing, pushing, ignoring, excluding,
  stashing, or deleting the user's files; clean up only scratch you created
  and say the user's files remain.
- Do not hand-edit generated files; change their source of truth.
- Scratch repositories under a temporary directory are yours to experiment in.

## Locks and corrupt state

A Git lock usually means another process is writing. Never kill the holder on
your own initiative. Wait, inspect the holder read-only, use that tool's normal
stop mechanism, or report the block. Never delete a lock without proving no
live process owns it, and never respond to index corruption by deleting state
and committing anyway.

Never commit or push while status reports changes you did not make and cannot
explain.

## If you already made an unwanted write

Say so plainly and stop. Do not attempt more history surgery without direction.

*Corrections exploration made to this Starting point.* None to the per-slot facts: every starting-point number was re-derived from its cited file by the explorers and the verifier. Two additions: (1) the experts per-pair re-read entry (`ineff-baseline-experts-1`) was refuted as written for mixing two byte bases and must be restated on the counter basis (floor 2.33 ms/step at 32 rows) before anyone prices it; (2) the grader territory confirms the exact grading of a `min_rows: 2, max_rows: 59` experts attempt — sizes 1, 127, 1,016 and 2,048 `handed off`, decode `faster` requires both 8 and 32 rows faster — and that the ready check's set verdict is read from its `muse-all` entry, not a top-level pass flag.

## Context

A decode step produces one token per request; in vLLM the unchanged step takes 5.457 / 14.337 / 30.061 / 39.410 ms at 1×128 / 8×128 / 32×128 / 32×1024 (Claude's round-3 G3 medians). The MoE block runs in all 20 layers of every step, in decode and prefill alike; the three slots mirror its split, and each starting point already fuses its slot to 1 kernel per layer and passes G2 bit-exact at all six graded sizes (1, 8, 32 decode rows; 127, 1,016, 2,048 prefill rows). What remains is not launch count or exactness: it is the experts 1-row hand-off the new `min_rows` unlocks, the routing+combine pair's ~1% margin over the compiled reference at 32×1024, and whether three replaced slots compose at 8 requests. No slot has a baseline, so every saving is against the compiled reference.

## Territory map

| Territory | Receives | Passes on | Measured cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| `baseline-experts` | `x` [rows,768] bf16 and `inds` [rows,4] from routing; expert weights [60,…] | `y` [rows,4,768] bf16 in `inds` order to combine | Starting point 1 kernel/layer; 1 row `slower` (96.9 vs 86.6 µs/layer), wins at 8/32 (168.9/554.7 vs 238.2/883.4); per-pair re-reads unpriced after refutation |
| `baseline-routing` | `x` from post-attention norm; `w_router` [60,768] f32, `bias` [60] f32 | `inds` to experts, `weights` to combine (order is part of G2) | Starting point 1 kernel/layer; decode margins 17.7/15.8/19.7 µs/layer over compiled; per-row `w_router` excess 0/6.5/28.6 µs/layer |
| `baseline-combine` | `y` from experts, `weights` from routing, `shared` [rows,768] from shared expert | `out` [rows,768] bf16 to residual/next layer | Starting point 1 kernel/layer; `faster` at all six sizes; chained floor ~32 µs/layer at decode, bytes+compute ≤1.5 µs of it |
| `g3` | The three starting points' piece timings and Claude's G3 | Composition gaps and set predictions to implementation | Pair keeps −0.36 of −0.66 ms/step piece win at 32×1024; three-slot term +2.13–2.86 ms/step at 8 requests, untested |
| `grader` | References from model code; captured decode inputs; prefill chunks | The round-4 contract (`min_rows`, `handed off`, set rule) to builders and boundary | The contract, not a cost: what counts as identical, and how each size and set is priced |

How they feed each other: layernorm → `baseline-routing` (`inds`/`weights`) → `baseline-experts` (`y`) → `baseline-combine` (`out`) → residual. `grader` sits across all three (what counts as identical, and how time is priced). `g3` sits across the whole step and the whole request (whether per-slot prices compose).

## Inefficiencies, ranked

Confirmed inefficiencies inside the slots, ranked by predicted saving against the compiled reference (no slot has a baseline). Decode shares are of the decode step; prefill effects are stated per chunk. Each item says what removing it does to the other phase and whether a hand-off keeps that phase unchanged.

1. **The experts 1-row block is a hand-off, not a kernel problem** (starting point, `territory-baseline-experts.md`). With `min_rows: 2, max_rows: 59` the 1-row size is `handed off` and decode needs only 8 and 32 rows `faster` — both already `faster` by 69.3 / 328.7 µs per layer. Predicted (PREDICTION, same-run margins × 20 layers): `beats_compiled` true with decode `faster`, prefill `handed off`; end-to-end (additive, from `ineff-g3-2.md`) −0.44 / −1.76 / −7.12 / −6.94 ms per step vs `compiled-all` at 1×128 / 8×128 / 32×128 / 32×1024 in a three-slot set — at 1 request the experts slot contributes nothing (handed off), so the set passes there only on the pair. Other phase: prefill unchanged by construction (handed off above 59 rows). Cost: the 1-row loss 96.9 vs 86.6 µs/layer disappears from the verdict, not from the machine — with 1 request the slot runs MLX's own code, exactly as the bar does.
2. **The pair's 32×1024 margin** (`ineff-g3-1.md`, confirmed, Claude's). The routing+combine pair keeps only −0.36 of its −0.66 ms/step piece win vs the compiled reference at 32×1024, and the 0.9% median gap sits inside the 5-repeat spread: ~0.17 ms/step more separation would have passed Claude's run. No mechanism is confirmed and no single-slot change is priced to recover it; the pools any widening must come from are items 3–4. A decode saving bought with prefill time is not one: routing keeps `max_rows: 32`, combine stays faster at prefill sizes.
3. **`w_router` re-read once per row** (`ineff-baseline-routing-1.md`, confirmed). Traffic excess 0 / 6.5 / 28.6 µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows against decode margins of 17.7 / 15.8 / 19.7 — the excess exceeds the whole 32-row margin. Upper bound 0 / 0.13 / 0.57 ms per step (overlap-discounted, prediction). Prefill: 0 at every size by hand-off construction (`max_rows: 32` kept). Round 1's tiled-sharing attempt was slower everywhere, so this banks only if a sharing design holds the chained rate.
4. **The staged scalar path's shape cost** (`ineff-baseline-routing-2.md`, confirmed). 27 barriers, a 23%-duty tail third and serial tails at decode sizes; bounded single-digit µs per layer (prediction). Overlaps item 3 (do not add). Prefill: 0 by hand-off.
5. **The experts serial K-chain headroom** (`ineff-baseline-experts-2.md`, confirmed). 8/32 rows sit 80.4 / 200.8 µs per layer above their own byte floor (headroom 1.61 / 4.02 ms per step, 0 banked): grouped designs lost in both earlier rounds on duty-cycle ceilings, so this is headroom, not a plan. It matters only if the `min_rows` set fails and a faster 8/32-row kernel is needed. Prefill: handed off, unchanged.
6. **Combine is at its floor** (`ineff-baseline-combine-1.md` confirmed with achievable saving 0; `ineff-baseline-combine-2.md` confirmed at ≤0.5 µs per layer, below paired noise). No bit-exact change inside the slot widens its decode margin; the ~32 µs/layer chained floor is dispatch, not bytes or compute. Do not chase either. No single-slot change removes it; the ready check's `muse-all` is its first test with these kernels, and the fallback if the triple loses is the measured routing+combine pair.

Confirmed inefficiencies outside the slots stand as written in round 1's and round 2's exploration READMEs (attention K/V re-read per query head; split-K partial traffic from 14 rows; the 60 q/k/v `[0]` gathers; engine CPU per 1-row step). - The independent (overlapped) piece timing as a ranking: refuted by the chained measurement. Round 4 ranks chained only.
- Scalar sums cannot reproduce MMA rounding: refuted by building in round 2.

Round 4 finished.

**Outcome: no slot submits a kernel — every slot keeps the reference.** All 6 graded attempts are bit-exact and beat the compiled reference in the piece timing, and all three hypotheses passed their checkers as candidates. Both permitted ready checks then failed every variant on 5-repeat range overlap (exit 1, verdicts stand), so no attempt is `ready` under the round's rules.

What the round measured:

- **Experts (hyp-1):** the new `min_rows: 2` hand-off works as mapped. Both attempts (windows 2–59, 2–32) pass G1+G2 with `beats_compiled` true. Ready-1 decode: **−1.57 ms/step at 8×128, −4.02 / −5.09 at 32 requests** vs base — matching the piece prediction (−1.49 / −5.23). It fails alone at 1×128 (+0.06) exactly as designed (1 row runs MLX's own code) and can only pass inside a set.

- Exploration: 5 territories, 8 inefficiencies — 7 confirmed, 1 refuted (the experts re-read floor mixed two byte bases).

## Starting point

Round 4 is the last round ([ADR 0014](../../../claude/adr/0014-muse-wonder-last-round.md)). It builds on rounds 1–3 as measured independently by Claude in [`claude/findings/muse-round-3.md`](../../../claude/findings/muse-round-3.md). Round 3 ran as Muse Spark (model `muse-spark-1.3-contributor`, skill version 8) and submitted the reference in every slot: no candidate passed the ready check alone, and the skill then counted only candidates that pass alone. Round 4 changes three rules ([ADR 0015](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)): candidates that pass together in `muse-all` are `ready` as a **set**; an attempt may hand off inputs below `min_rows` as well as above `max_rows`; and a handed-off size is reported `handed off` instead of being timed. A slot's **baseline** is still its best attempt so far that passes the current G2, has `beats_compiled` true in the grader, and passes G3 ([ADR 0011](../../../claude/adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). **No slot has a baseline.** The bar in every slot is the compiled reference, and a new attempt must beat it in the same grader run (no `--baseline` argument). Round 4 runs as Muse Wonder (muse-wonder-1.0).

### Per slot

#### `experts` — starting point `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1`

- **What it is.** Round 2's fused per-pair kernel, byte-identical, plus `max_rows: 59` in `spec.json`: rows 1–59 run the fused kernel, rows above 59 run the compiled reference. See `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1/notes.md` and its `grade.json` (G1 pass, G2 differ 0 at all six sizes).
- **Piece timing** (chained µs per layer, candidate vs compiled, its own grade run): 1 row 96.9 vs 86.6 (`slower`, 5 wins); 8 rows 168.9 vs 238.2 (`faster`, 29 wins); 32 rows 554.7 vs 883.4 (`faster`, 29 wins); prefill 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 `same` (19 / 15 / 16 wins — the hand-off runs compiled code). `beats_compiled` false: decode `slower` on the 1-row size alone.
- **G3 effect.** Never timed end to end (round 3, section 4). Its ancestor (round 2 attempt-7, same kernels without the hand-off) shortened the decode step 17.5% with 32 requests but made prompt processing 6.6–14.5× slower; the hand-off removes the prefill half of that, so no G3 prediction from round 3 stands — Claude's reading is that only the 1-row gap remains.
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** It is not a baseline because `beats_compiled` is false — the 1-row decode loss (96.9 vs 86.6 µs/layer) — and it has no G3 pass. Round 3 tried a vectorised scalar path (attempt-2, bought nothing) and an unfused path copying the reference's structure (attempt-5, 2× worse at 1 row) and concluded no fix existed in the spec surface. From round 4 the surface has `min_rows`: `min_rows: 2` with `max_rows: 59` hands 1-row inputs to the compiled reference while keeping the 8/32-row wins — a direction not yet graded. It can then pass G3 only in a set whose other kernels are faster with 1 request, because with 1 request every decode step runs MLX's own code for this slot.
- **Where it still spends its time.** At 8/32 rows it already wins by 69.3 / 328.7 µs per layer; what remains is the 1-row chain (the `tg_x` load, silu and barrier chain named in round 3) — now hand-off-able — and per-pair weight re-reads at all sizes (552,960 B per pair, round 3's entry).

#### `routing` — starting point `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6`

- **What it is.** Round 2's staged scalar-exact kernel (attempt-4 kernels) with `max_rows: 32`: every decode step (1–32 rows) runs the staged scalar kernels, all prefill sizes run the compiled reference. Attempt-6 is a byte-identical re-grade of round 3's attempt-1 (empty `diff` on both blocks and `spec.json`), run to test whether attempt-1's 2,048-row `slower` on identical code reproduced; it did not (19/30 wins, `same`). See `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6/notes.md`.
- **Piece timing.** Round 3's grade: decode `faster` at all three sizes (candidate 51.7 / 90.9 / 132.2 vs compiled 66.3 / 104.0 / 152.0 µs per layer; 28 / 27 / 25 wins), prefill `same` at all three sizes. Claude's re-grade with the round-4 grader ([`results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/`](../../../results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/)): decode `faster` (29 / 26 / 27 wins; candidate 0.72 / 0.90 / 0.88 of the compiled reference at 1 / 8 / 32 rows), the three prefill sizes `handed off`, `beats_compiled` true.
- **G3 effect.** In round 3's swarm ready check it failed alone against `compiled-routing` at 8×128 on overlapping ranges, with no phase slower anywhere (decode medians −0.38 / −0.31 / −0.59 / −0.48 ms vs the unchanged model at 1×128 / 8×128 / 32×128 / 32×1024). Claude's G3 agreed: `same` as `compiled-routing` at 8×128. Together with combine attempt-2 (`muse-all`) it passed the swarm's ready check but failed Claude's G3 against `compiled-all` at 32×1024, where the medians are 0.9% apart with overlapping ranges.
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** G3 alone: it passes G2 and has `beats_compiled` true, but it has never passed G3, alone or (in Claude's run) as a pair. Under round 4's set rule the pair would have been `ready` in round 3, but a set still has to pass G3 as `muse-all`, so the pair is no baseline.
- **Where it still spends its time.** Decode wins at every size; the open question is margin, above all at 32×1024 where the pair gains only 0.25–0.30 ms over the compiled reference (~1%), inside the 5-repeat spread. The per-row `w_router` re-read is untouched (upper bound only, round 2's `ineff-baseline-routing-4`).

#### `combine` — starting point `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/combine/attempt-2`

- **What it is.** Round 2's attempt-1 kernel with its seven `volatile` rounding barriers replaced by seven plain `float` locals and a header block (`block-1.metal`) carrying `#pragma STDC FP_CONTRACT OFF` / `#pragma clang fp contract(off)`: same 7-op stepwise fold `((p0+p1)+p2)+p3`, same grid (`rows*768`) and threadgroup [256,1,1], no `max_rows`. See `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/combine/attempt-2/notes.md`.
- **Piece timing.** Round 3's grade: `faster` at all six sizes (decode 31.8 / 34.7 / 32.7 vs compiled 36.9 / 41.1 / 45.7 µs per layer, 24 / 27 / 30 wins; prefill 38.2 / 100.9 / 198.0 vs 64.0 / 281.8 / 556.2, 30 / 30 / 29 wins); `beats_compiled` true in both phases. Absolute chained times drift up to ~35% between runs on this machine (round 3's lesson), so only same-run paired verdicts transfer.
- **G3 effect.** In round 3's ready check it failed alone against the unchanged model at 1×128 on a single outlier repeat (5.892 ms, above the unchanged model's lowest 5.430) and, in Claude's G3, against `compiled-combine` at 32×128 and 32×1024 — again range overlaps with no phase slower anywhere (swarm decode medians −0.53 / −0.59 / −0.44 / −0.26 ms vs the unchanged model). Its ancestor's in-step cost (+1.05 ms/step at 32 requests from the volatile barriers) is what the pragma removes; round 3's measured decode medians favour the kernel everywhere.
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** G3 alone, on spread: every median favours it, but the 5-repeat ranges overlap the bars'. No kernel change is named that tightens spread on 7 plain ops (round 3's implementation README); as part of a set it already passes `muse-all` in the swarm's run.
- **Where it still spends its time.** Nothing further in the grader — it sits on the chained floor and wins at all six sizes. What remains is the same margin question as routing: more separation from the compiled reference at 32×128 and 32×1024, or a set that clears the bar together.

#### All three together

Round 3's pair (routing attempt-6 + combine attempt-2) is the best result of any round: against the unchanged model it shortens the decode step 16.5% / 5.4% / 2.8% / 1.6% and whole requests 14.1% / 5.6% / 2.1% / 2.4% at 1×128 / 8×128 / 32×128 / 32×1024, with prompts 1.6–3.1% faster and nothing slower — but it fails G3 against `compiled-all` at 32×1024 (0.9% median gap, overlapping ranges). About half the gain over the unchanged model is `mx.compile` of the two slots' reference code alone. The three-slot composition is untested: in rounds 1 and 2, replacing all three slots at once lost about 2.8 ms with 8 requests for an unknown reason, and round 3 installed no experts candidate, so no run since has met it.

### What is left

Ranked by predicted saving against the compiled reference (no slot has a baseline, so the reference is the bar everywhere). Claude's measurement names three things round 4 has to find out; the ranking follows them.

1. **Experts with `min_rows`.** Whether attempt-1's 8/32-row speed (168.9 vs 238.2 and 554.7 vs 883.4 µs per layer) carries into G3 once 1 row runs MLX's own code (`min_rows: 2`, `max_rows: 59`). This is the only ungraded direction in any slot and the largest piece saving left: the 8/32-row wins are 69.3 / 328.7 µs per layer, worth (PREDICTION, from those same-run margins × 20 layers) about 1.4 ms per step at 8 requests and 6.6 ms at 32 requests against the compiled reference, with prefill `handed off` above 59 rows and 1-row decode `handed off` — so the gain exists only at 8 and 32 requests, and G3 can pass only in a set whose other kernels win with 1 request. The risk is the three-slot interaction (item 3).
2. **A margin at 32×1024.** The pair gains 0.25–0.30 ms over the compiled reference there (~1%), which 5 repeats cannot tell from noise; a set needs more than that with 32 long prompts. This is a margin problem in routing and/or combine decode kernels, not a correctness one: both starting points are bit-exact and already `faster` at every graded size, so any new attempt must widen the same-run margin at decode sizes without touching prefill (`max_rows: 32` for routing, faster-everywhere for combine). A saving here is worth the difference between a passing and a failing set — the largest whole-request prize left, and unquantified until a builder measures it.
3. **All three slots at once.** In rounds 1 and 2 the three-slot replacement lost about 2.8 ms with 8 requests for an unknown reason; a set with an experts attempt meets that again. No single-slot kernel change is predicted to remove it, so it is carried as a constraint: per-slot wins are not assumed to compose, and the ready check (which times candidates alone and all together) is where composition is measured. If the three together lose, the fallback set is the routing+combine pair.
4. **Slots not yet tried.** `routing+combine` (both slots, each with its own kernels, in one candidate) has never been graded as one folder. The parts are graded independently and the combine part receives the reference routing weights, so it is packaging unless a shared design emerges; the set rule already submits the two slots together without it. No hypothesis is planned on it unless exploration finds a shared-design reason.
5. **Recommendations outside the slots** stand as written in round 1's and round 2's exploration READMEs (attention K/V re-read per query head; split-K partial traffic from 14 rows; the 60 q/k/v `[0]` gathers; engine CPU per 1-row step). Claude's round-3 measurement did not test them. They are for surucuonur's team; no hypothesis targets them.

### Refuted claims

No one chases these again.

- Round 3's experts 1-row fixes: a vectorised scalar path (attempt-2) bought nothing and an unfused path copying the reference's structure (attempt-5) was 2× worse at 1 row — the 1-row gap is not closed by either approach, and round 4 does not retry them; it hands 1 row off instead.
- Routing attempt-1's 2,048-row `slower` verdict on byte-identical code: attempt-6's re-grade (19/30, `same`) confirmed it as paired noise, not a hand-off cost. Handed-off sizes are no longer timed at all.
- `ineff-runs-3` (round 1, refuted): the micro sorted/unsorted gaps measure kernel choice, not pair order.
- Round 1's implicit claim that the independent (overlapped) piece timing ranks attempts as the model does: refuted by the chained measurement. Round 4 ranks by the chained timing only.
- The claim that scalar sums cannot reproduce MMA rounding: refuted by building in round 2 (routing attempts 2–4, experts scalar paths bit-identical at all six sizes).

13|## What happens
14|
15|At `rows >= 60` the slot kernel takes its prefill branch
16|(`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-7/block-0.metal:22,59-72,103-112`),
17|one thread per output calling `qmm_accum`
18|(`block-1.metal:206-230`): a single thread walks all of K
19|(768 for gate/up, 384 for down) in `BK=32` contiguous
20|order, accumulating into one float `acc`. The arithmetic
21|is right — G2 passes with `differ 0` at all three prefill
22|sizes — but the issue pattern loses three ways at once:
23|
24|1. **A purely serial dependent chain per thread.** Each of
25|   the 884,736 iterations per pair (gate/up 384×768 each,
26|   down 768×384) does `acc += xv[k] * (bfloat)wq` on one
27|   accumulator: no second accumulator, no unrolling, so
28|   each iteration waits for the last — zero instruction
29|   overlap within a thread. Serial depth per thread (simd
30|   groups 0–7) is 768 (gate) + 768 (up) + 768 (down, two
31|   blocks) = 2,304 dependent iterations, plus silu. Gate
32|   and up run as fully sequential phases (384 of 512
33|   threads active in each, `block-0.metal:61-71`); down
34|   runs 2 waves (`:105-111`).
35|2. **Scalar redundant loads: ~7.1 MB issued per pair for
36|   553 KB of unique weight bytes (12.8×).** Per iteration
37|   each thread issues 1 W load + 1 S + 1 B device load +
38|   1 threadgroup `xv` load (`block-1.metal:223-226`), but
39|   8 lanes share each weight word (`word = wb + (lane >>
40|   3)`, `:217`) and all 32 lanes of a block share `S`,
41|   `B` and `xv[k]`. Issued per pair: W 884,736 words =
42|   3.54 MB vs 442,368 unique B (8×); S+B 884,736×2×2 B =
43|   3.54 MB vs 110,592 unique B (32×). All scalar,
44|   uncoalesced, per-thread.
45|3. **No cross-row reuse: per-pair grid at fan-ins of
46|   508–8,192 pairs.** Each pair streams its expert's full
47|   552,960 B independently, so unique-pair traffic is
48|   280.9 MB / 2,247 MB / 4,530 MB per layer at 127/1,016/
49|   2,048 rows, where MLX's grouped `gather_qmm_rhs` loads
50|   each appearing expert's tile once per `BM=16` row tile
51|   into threadgroup `Ws` and shares it across 16 rows
52|   (round-2 `territory-quantized-kernels.md` §C–§E,
53|   frozen), and issues 8×8×8 matrix instructions (~512
54|   MACs per simdgroup step vs this branch's 32 scalar
55|   MACs — a 16× ALU-issue gap per step).
56|
57|This branch was written when prefill speed was free:
58|round-2 `ineff-baseline-experts-1` (confirmed, frozen)
59|states "a slow-but-exact prefill branch is free" because
60|prefill was untimed (`claude/adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md:42`).
61|Under two-phase judgment (ADR 0011) it is the slot's
62|largest loss. The branch threshold itself is correct
63|(`rows >= 60` from dispatch source, round-2 territory

  "output": "# Brief for the Muse Spark agent: write faster MobileMoE-S kernels, for decoding and prompt processing

*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Committed and tagged `agent-era` before the Muse Spark session started. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*

You are a Claude Code session powered by Meta's Muse Spark, working in your own git worktree on the branch `muse-agent`. This brief fixes your task, what you may change, where your work goes and how it is judged. It does not change during your session.

## The task

Meta's MobileMoE-S, int4, is served on an Apple M1 Pro (16-core GPU, 200 GB/s, 16 GB) by vLLM through vllm-metal, which runs the model with MLX. The findings below measure where each decode step's time goes. A step is about 870–1,090 small GPU kernels and is far from both the bandwidth and compute limits. The findings name the pieces that cost the most.

A request goes through two phases: **prompt processing** (the prefill), which runs its whole prompt through the model, and **decoding**, one step per generated token. An improvement must hold in both: faster in one, and no slower in the other ([ADR 0011](adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). A kernel that speeds up the decode step but slows the prefill is not an improvement.

1. **Choose.** Read the findings and choose one or two of the slots below to replace with your own fused Metal kernels. Write `muse-spark/strategy.md`: why, your design, and what each saves per step at 1 and 32 requests (your estimate). End it with the JSON block described under *Your files*. Commit it.
2. **Write and check.** For each chosen slot, write the kernels as files, run the grader on them, read its verdict, and improve. Up to **5 attempts per slot**; an attempt is a folder you graded and committed.
3. **Finish.** Write `muse-spark/summary.md`: your final attempt per slot and what you learned. Commit it.

**Read these first** (all in your worktree):
- `claude/findings/bottleneck-explained.md` and `claude/findings/step-breakdown.md`: the measured findings;
- `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md` and `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md`: the raw tables;
- `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py` and `switch_layers.py`: the model code;
- MLX's custom-kernel documentation: `.venv/bin/python -c "import mlx.core as mx; help(mx.fast.metal_kernel)"`;
- `bench/grader/check_candidate.py` and `bench/grader/slots.py`: how you are graded.

## The slots

Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the call: 1 to 32 in a decode step, up to 2,048 in a prefill chunk. The grader flattens the inputs to the shapes below and restores the model's shapes afterwards. All arrays are row-contiguous.

The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.

### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights

| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
|---|---|---|---|
| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |

Reference:

```python
scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
```

The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.

### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert

| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
|---|---|---|---|
| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |

Reference:

```python
out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
```

Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.

### `routing+combine`

Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.

### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products

| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
|---|---|---|---|
| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |

Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.

Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:

```python
y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
```

As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.

Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.

## Tools and limits

- **Only `mx.fast.metal_kernel`, MLX 0.32.4.** You write the Metal body; MLX generates the signature. Inputs arrive as `const device T* name` and outputs as `device T* name`. Shapes and strides come as `name_shape` and `name_strides` when the source uses them. The thread attributes are available, as in MLX's documentation: `thread_position_in_grid`, `threadgroup_position_in_grid`, `thread_position_in_threadgroup`, `threads_per_threadgroup`, `simdgroup_index_in_threadgroup`, `thread_index_in_simdgroup`, and so on.

- **Stay within the GPU's limits.** At most 1,024 threads per threadgroup and 32 KB of threadgroup memory. A grader run should take under 3 minutes, longer for an attempt much slower than the reference at the prefill sizes; stop one that runs past 15.
- **Hardware.** The Apple M1 Pro GPU (`applegpu_g13s`) has 16 cores and a SIMD width of 32. bfloat16 is available in Metal as `bfloat`.

## How each attempt is judged

The pass criteria were fixed before the first round. From round 2, G2 is exact and also covers the prefill, and the piece timing chains the layers ([ADR 0010](adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md)); round 1 was judged by the earlier rules, in which G2 allowed small rounding differences and tested decode steps only. From round 3, the piece timing and G3 time both phases, decode and prefill ([ADR 0011](adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)); rounds 1 and 2 were timed on decode only.

1. **G1, runs.** It compiles and runs on real inputs.
2. **G2, correct: identical to the reference, bit for bit.** The slot runs in every call of `MoE.__call__`, the prefill included, so it is tested on every layer's inputs at two kinds of size:
   - **a decode step:** inputs captured from all 20 layers during a real decode step, at 1, 8 and 32 rows;
   - **a prefill:** the first chunk of a prefill with 128-token prompts, recorded while the grader runs it, at 1, 8 and 32 requests: 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. From 60 rows on, MLX's own experts kernel changes (`gather_qmm_rhs` instead of `gather_qvm`), and so does its rounding.

   At every size:
   - **`routing`:** each row's 4 experts and their 4 weights equal the reference's, in the same order, since combine sums the pairs in that order. That includes the reference's choice between tied 4th and 5th experts.
   - **`combine` and `experts`:** every element equals the reference's.

   **Why exact:** the end-to-end check below asks for the same greedy tokens, and greedy decoding turns any difference into different tokens. In round 1, routing weights within 10⁻⁵ of the reference, relative, changed 7 to 9 of 32 sequences.
   - **Then, end to end:** the same greedy tokens as the original model over 24 generated tokens, at 1 and 32 requests, in both plain MLX and vLLM.
3. **G3, faster, in vLLM.** Each workload runs 5 times in shuffled order: 1, 8 and 32 requests with 128-token prompts, and 32 requests with 1,024-token prompts, 256 generated tokens each. Three times are measured per run:
   - the **decode step**, the median period between steady steps;
   - the **prompt time**, until every prompt was processed;
   - the **whole request**, from sending the requests to the last token.

   Against both the original model and an `mx.compile` of the same reference code, the attempt passes when the decode step or the prompt time is faster in every workload, neither is slower in any, and no whole request is slower. Faster and slower mean that the ranges over the repeats don't overlap.

   **From round 3, the same G3 runs inside the round too:** the lead's **ready check**, `bench/grader/check_ready.py`, with every candidate in one call. It also requires the same greedy tokens, and audits its own log. Only its passing verdict makes an attempt `ready`; Claude's G3 after the round decides. The skill says when the lead runs it ([ADR 0013](adr/0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)).

   **From round 4, a set:** with more than one candidate, the ready check and G3 also time them all together (`muse-all`). When that passes, the candidates are ready together as a set, even where one fails alone, and G3 judges the set as one submission ([ADR 0015](adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)).

**What the grader prints for an attempt** (JSON):
- `g1` false and the compiler's error message;
- or the correctness results per size: for routing, the rows that differ; for combine and experts, the elements that differ and the largest gap in units in the last place; with the first example;
- or, when the attempt is correct, `timing_us_per_layer` per size: its time per call next to the original's and the compiled reference's, its wins against the compiled reference and the verdict (`faster`, `same`, `slower`, or `handed off` for a size your spec hands to the compiled reference); then `phases_vs_compiled` and `beats_compiled`.

**The piece timing** runs the slot at the six G2 sizes: the 20 layers' captured decode inputs at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and the 20 layers' first prefill chunk at 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. Each layer's call waits for the previous one's output, as in the model: one small kernel links them, the same for every function timed. Without that wait, the GPU overlaps the 20 calls and hides how long one takes; in round 1, an experts kernel 29% faster on overlapped calls was 66% slower on chained ones at 1 row.
- **Paired repeats.** Your attempt and the compiled reference run in alternating order, 30 times.
- **Per size:** your attempt is `faster` when it wins at least 22 of the 30 pairs, `slower` when it loses at least 22, and `same` otherwise. Medians alone would pass on noise: the same kernel timed twice differs by up to 5%.
- **Handed off** (from round 4): a size whose inputs your spec hands to the compiled reference (`max_rows`, `min_rows`) runs the bar's own code, so it is not timed against it. Its verdict is `handed off`, and your attempt's time there is the compiled reference's.
- **Per phase:** decode (1, 8, 32 rows) and prefill (127, 1,016, 2,048 rows) are each `faster` when every size it doesn't hand off is, and at least one isn't handed off; `slower` when any size is; `handed off` when all are; and `not slower` otherwise.
- **`beats_compiled`** is true when one phase is `faster` and neither is `slower`.

It is a guide; the ready check in the round, and Claude's G3 after it, decide.

**When a slot stops.** Work on a slot stops at the first attempt that passes G1 and G2 and has `beats_compiled` true, or after 5 attempts. Name your final attempt per slot in `muse-spark/summary.md`; it goes to the end-to-end and G3 checks, which surucuonur's team runs after merging your branch.

# MobileMoE Bandwidth Study

*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*

How efficiently an inference engine turns an Apple Silicon GPU's memory bandwidth and compute into generated tokens when serving a small mixture-of-experts model.

## Hardware limits

**Peak bandwidth**:
The most bytes per second the GPU can read from unified memory, as rated by the manufacturer (about 200 GB/s on this project's M1 Pro).
_Avoid_: max bandwidth, memory speed

**Peak compute**:
The most floating-point operations per second the GPU can perform (about 5.2 TFLOPS on the 16-core M1 Pro GPU).
_Avoid_: max compute, TFLOPS (as the name of the limit)

**Achieved bandwidth**:
The bytes a decode step must read from memory (the weights it touches plus its share of cached attention state), divided by that step's duration.
_Avoid_: bandwidth usage, utilization (unqualified)

**Arithmetic intensity**:
Floating-point operations performed per byte read from memory during a decode step.
_Avoid_: compute density, FLOPs/byte ratio

**Ridge point**:
The arithmetic intensity at which peak bandwidth and peak compute meet (about 26 operations per byte here); below it a step is limited by bandwidth, above it by compute.

**Roofline**:
The chart of achievable throughput against arithmetic intensity, capped by peak bandwidth on the left and peak compute on the right, with measured decode steps plotted beneath it.

## Bottlenecks and fixes

**Bandwidth-bound**:
A decode step whose achieved bandwidth is close to peak bandwidth.

**Compute-bound**:
A decode step whose operation rate is close to peak compute.

**Overhead-bound**:
A decode step far below both limits, because its time goes to work other than reading weights or doing arithmetic, such as launching GPU jobs, routing tokens to experts or scheduling.
_Avoid_: latency-bound, CPU-bound (unless the CPU specifically is the cause)

**Bottleneck**:
The single cause, identified from measurements, that most limits throughput for a given workload.
_Avoid_: issue, slowness

**Kernel**:
One program the GPU runs as a unit, such as one matrix product or one element-wise add; a decode step is a chain of hundreds of them, each with a fixed start-up cost.
_Avoid_: GPU job, op (for a kernel launch)

**Occupancy**:
The share of the GPU's thread slots in use while it runs; low occupancy means most of the chip is idle even when the GPU counts as busy.
_Avoid_: GPU utilization (which only says the GPU had work)

**Knock-out**:
A measurement in which one piece of the decode step is replaced by a stand-in that returns the right shape without GPU work; the time and bytes the step saves are that piece's cost.
_Avoid_: ablation

**Baseline**:
The unmodified engine serving MobileMoE-S-QAT (int4), against which every fix is measured.

**Fix**:
One change to the engine, the model code or the configuration, measured against the baseline under the same workload.
_Avoid_: optimization (for a change that hasn't been measured), tweak

## Inference

**Prefill**:
Processing a request's whole prompt through the model before its first token is generated, in chunks of up to the engine's token budget per pass (2,048 tokens here).
_Avoid_: prompt phase (say prefill, or prompt processing)

**Decode step**:
One engine iteration that produces one new token for each request it includes.

**Decode rows**:
The number of requests the engine actually advanced in one decode step; the batch size that matters for the roofline.
_Avoid_: batch size (unqualified), concurrency

**Client concurrency**:
The number of requests the benchmark client keeps in flight; it caps decode rows but does not equal them.

# From round 4, candidates that pass together are ready as a set, and an attempt may hand off small inputs too

*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../../PROVENANCE.md).*

**The change.** Round 3 showed three gaps in the rules ([Claude's measurement](../findings/muse-round-3.md)). On 2026-11-04 surucuonur chose to fix all three before round 4:

1. **Ready as a set.** Round 3's routing and combine candidates each failed the ready check alone, on overlapping ranges, while the two together (`muse-all`) passed it. The skill made a candidate `ready` only when it passed alone, so the round submitted nothing. From round 4, when `muse-all` passes the ready check, all its candidates are `ready` together as a **set**. A set goes to G3 whole, and G3 judges it as `muse-all`.
2. **Hand off below a row count too: `min_rows`.** `max_rows` already sends inputs with more rows to `mx.compile` of the slot's reference ([ADR 0011](0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). The new `min_rows` in an attempt's `spec.json` does the same for inputs with fewer rows, so the kernels run only from `min_rows` to `max_rows`. Round 3's experts attempt-1 lost to the compiled reference only at 1 row: 96.9 against 86.6 µs per layer, while it took 168.9 against 238.2 at 8 rows and 554.7 against 883.4 at 32. Its only way to pass was to win at the size it is worst at.
3. **A handed-off size isn't timed.** The grader timed each handed-off size, which runs the compiled reference, against the compiled reference: the same code twice. In round 3 that noise judged routing attempt-1 `slower` at 2,048 rows, on 8 wins of 30, and cost a re-grade of a byte-identical copy. Now such a size is reported `handed off`. A phase is `faster` when every size the kernels run at is faster, and it needs at least one; `beats_compiled` is still one phase `faster` and none `slower`. G2 still checks every size, bit for bit.

## How it works

- **`bench/grader/slots.py`:**
  - `build()` reads `min_rows` as it reads `max_rows`: an integer of at least 1, at most `max_rows` when both are given.
  - The function it returns has `hands_off(rows)`, which says whether inputs with that many rows run the compiled reference.
- **`bench/grader/check_candidate.py`:**
  - At each size, a function that hands the rows off is not timed. It takes the compiled reference's times, so for `routing+combine` the part that hands off adds the same time to both sides.
  - A bar's verdict is `handed off` when neither side ran code of its own. Against a baseline that runs its own kernels there, the size is timed as before.
  - `judge()` leaves `handed off` sizes out of a phase. A phase whose sizes are all handed off is `handed off`.
- **`bench/grader/test_hand_off.py`:**
  - checks `build()` with a toy kernel at row counts on both sides of each bound, bit for bit, and that bad bounds are refused;
  - checks `judge()` on five sets of verdicts.
  - Passed on 2026-11-04.
- **A real attempt.** Claude re-graded round 3's routing attempt-6 (`max_rows` 32) with the changed grader ([results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/](../../results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/)):
  - G2 passes;
  - decode is `faster` at 1, 8 and 32 rows, on 29, 26 and 27 wins of 30;
  - the three prefill sizes are `handed off`;
  - `beats_compiled` is true.
- **The skill, version 9.**
  - The ready check makes a passing `muse-all` a set.
  - *Ready to test* names a set's attempts together.
  - Builders and boundary agents record `min_rows` and the sizes it hands off.
- **G3 and the ready check are unchanged.** They time whole requests, so a slot's kernels count wherever they run. With 1 request every decode step has 1 row, so an attempt that hands off 1 row runs MLX's own code for the whole 1-request workload. Alone it is then no faster than its compiled bar there, and it can pass G3 only in a set whose other kernels are faster with 1 request. The brief says so.

## Consequences

- **Round 3's pair qualifies for round 4.** Under the set rule, routing attempt-6 with combine attempt-2 would have been `ready` in round 3, because its `muse-all` passed the swarm's ready check. Claude's G3 failed the same pair against the compiled bar at 32 requests of 1,024 tokens, on overlapping ranges, so the pair is still no baseline.
- **A set is judged once.** Its parts are not judged alone, so a set can carry a part that only helps together with the others. G3 still requires the whole set to be faster than both bars, and to be slower nowhere.
- **The interaction of all three slots is untested.** In rounds 1 and 2, replacing all three slots at once lost about 2.8 ms with 8 requests, for an unknown reason ([round 2](../findings/muse-round-2.md), section 4). A set with an experts attempt meets that again.

## Considered options

- **A paired test on medians for the ready check and G3,** so that one outlier repeat can't sink a candidate, as it sank combine attempt-2 in round 3. Not chosen for round 4: it changes ADR 0011's rule for Claude's G3 too, and there was too little time to check it before the deadline.

def compare(wins):
    """One size's verdict from the candidate's wins in REPEATS paired repeats."""
    if wins >= WINS_NEEDED:
        return "faster"
    if REPEATS - wins >= WINS_NEEDED:
        return "slower"
    return "same"


def judge(verdicts):
    """Each phase's verdict from its sizes' verdicts, and whether the candidate
    beats the bar: faster at every size of one phase, slower at no size of the other.

    Sizes "handed off" don't count. A phase is "faster" when every other size
    is, "slower" when any is, "handed off" when none is left, and "not slower"
    otherwise.
    """
    phases = {}
    for phase, prefix in PHASES.items():
        sizes = [v for size, v in verdicts.items() if size.startswith(prefix) and v != "handed off"]
        phases[phase] = (
            "handed off" if not sizes
            else "faster" if all(v == "faster" for v in sizes)
            else "slower" if "slower" in sizes
            else "not slower"
        )
    beats = "faster" in phases.values() and "slower" not in phases.values()
    return phases, beats

# Inefficiency: per-pair weight re-reads persist in the starting point (465 MB excess at 32 rows)

- **Owner:** explorer-baseline-experts
- **Status:** confirmed
- **Version:** 2
- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T03:23:32Z
- **Next:** verifier to confirm byte arithmetic against GPU counters

## Slot

`experts`

## What happens

Attempt-4 fuses gate/up/down + silu-mul into one kernel (removing round
1 `muse-spark/exploration/ineff-switch-layers-2`, confirmed: 4 on-chain
kernels/layer + bf16 intermediates written and re-read), but it keeps
per-pair reads: each (row, expert-slot) pair's threadgroup streams its
expert's full gate/up/down weights independently
(`muse-spark/kernels/experts/attempt-4/block-0.metal:23,31,43,70`;
offsets `eW = e * 36864`, `eS = e * 9216` per pair). A popular expert is
read once per pair that selects it, not once per layer. This is round
1's `ineff-runs-1` (confirmed) and the traffic half of
`ineff-quantized-kernels-1` (confirmed), restated for the starting
point because attempt-4 does not remove it — it only hides part of it
with fusion and 8 in-flight blocks per group
(`attempt-4/notes.md:66-75`: 32-row effective 109 → ~137 GB/s
independent). The `x` re-read half of round 1's kernel entry *is*
removed: `tg_x` is loaded once per pair (`block-0.metal:18-20`) where
`qvm_impl` re-streams the row per tile (round 1
`territory-quantized-kernels.md` §A: ~55 KB x-traffic per pair vs
3.75 KB needed).

What is new this round: the same per-pair grid also runs at prefill
sizes, where fan-in is far larger (508/4,064/8,192 pairs per layer over
at most 60 distinct experts), and the chained timings now price the
remaining waste at decode sizes against the reference the slot must
beat.

## Cost

Per decode step (GPU counters `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md:26,32`
via round 1 `ineff-runs-1.md`; per-pair bytes 552,960 B, territory §A):

- **1 row:** 4 pairs, all distinct (4.0 distinct experts/layer): reads
  51 MB vs 44 MB must-read, excess 7 MB. Chained candidate 132.9
  µs/layer (`console-chain.txt`) — but at 1 row the loss is latency
  (ineff-2), not these bytes; excess floor 7 MB ÷ 200 GB/s = 0.04 ms.
- **8 rows:** 32 pairs/layer; no serving knock-out at 8 rows. Modelled
  pair traffic 32 × 552,960 × 20 = 353.9 MB/step (weights only;
  round 1 modelled 383 MB with x-traffic). Distinct experts/layer
  unmeasured at 8 rows; bounded by 32 pairs and 60 experts.
- **32 rows:** 128 pairs/layer read 908 MB/step vs 443 MB for the
  distinct experts — excess 465 MB (51% of bytes are re-reads).
  Per layer: 70.8 MB pair traffic vs 22.2 MB distinct. Candidate
  chained 587.6 µs/layer = 120.5 GB/s on pair traffic (60% of the
  200 GB/s peak, `claude/GLOSSARY.md:10`); the same time on distinct
  bytes alone would be 177 GB/s-equivalent — there is no bandwidth
  headroom left to absorb the re-reads at this rate.

Fixed costs: candidate 1 kernel/layer vs reference 7 (1 row) / 13
(32 rows, incl. 6 sort-glue kernels from 16 rows, round 1
`ineff-switch-layers-1` confirmed: ~0.7 ms/step at 32 rows, removable
only inside a grouped kernel). Attempt-4 already banks the launch and
intermediate-traffic savings; this entry is only the weight re-reads.

## Kind

Overhead-bound with a bandwidth-waste component (round 1 wording for
the same cause): 120.5 GB/s chained at 32 rows is 60% of peak, and the
step as a whole sits far below both limits; the wasted bytes are real
but removing them at the current rate is worth less than the floor
arithmetic suggests (see Predicted saving).

## Spans

`baseline-experts` (`block-0.metal` per-pair offsets), `quantized-kernels`
(per-pair `qvm` grids this mirrors), `switch-layers` (grouped path the
reference only takes from 60 rows), `runs` (counter tables).

## Predicted saving

Excess bytes at peak bandwidth (floor, per decode step):

- 1 row: 7 MB ÷ 200 GB/s = **0.04 ms ≈ 0.0 ms**.
- 8 rows: excess unmeasured; if distinct experts/layer ≈ 25 of 32 pairs
  (round 1 micro pattern), excess ≈ (32−25) × 552,960 × 20 = 77 MB →
  **0.39 ms** floor. Marked estimate — no 8-row counter exists.
- 32 rows: 465 MB ÷ 200 GB/s = **2.33 ms** floor.

Against the compiled reference this floor is **not** the predicted
saving, and round 1's building is the reason: both grouped attempts
that read each expert ~once (attempt-1 full fused grouped,
attempt-3 two-kernel grouped, ~34 MB/layer at 32 rows) ran at a
~55 GB/s duty-cycle ceiling (load→barrier→compute leaves DRAM idle)
and *lost* to per-pair attempt-4 in the piece harness at 8 rows and
tied/won only at 32 (round 1 `muse-spark/exploration/README.md` *What
building taught* #1; `ineff-quantized-kernels-1.md` builder note;
`hyp-1-fused-experts.md` Decision). The starting point already beats
the chained reference by 63.7 µs/layer at 8 rows and 210.0 µs/layer at
32 rows (1.27 and 4.20 ms/step, `console-chain.txt`) *with* the
re-reads, because the reference pays them too plus 7–13 launches.
A grouped fix banks the 2.33 ms floor only if it holds ≥120 GB/s
effective on distinct bytes — i.e. ≤185 µs/layer at 32 rows
(22.2 MB ÷ 120.5 GB/s) before its scan/chunk/barrier overhead, a bar
neither round-1 grouped attempt met. Predicted saving vs the compiled
reference (itself within 3% of the reference in the old harness,
`grade-experts.json`): **0 ms banked today; up to ~2.3 ms/step at
32 rows (0.12 ms/layer × 20) if a grouped design holds the starting
point's rate on distinct bytes; negative at 8 rows on round 1's
evidence.** Do not add to ineff-2 (disjoint: latency at 1 row, bytes
at 32) or to round 1's joint ceiling (443 MB at streaming rate ≈
11.5 ms at 32 rows, verifier reconciliation in
`ineff-quantized-kernels-1.md`).

{"path":"muse-spark/round-4/exploration/territory-baseline-experts.md","content":"# Territory: baseline-experts

- **Owner:** explorer-baseline-experts
- **Status:** exploring
- **Version:** 1
- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T21:42:08Z
- **Next:** post ineff entries for per-pair re-reads and the 8/32-row chain ceiling, then set done

## What it does

The `experts` slot of one MoE layer: for each row `r` and slot
`j`, `y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]`
with `e = inds[r, j]`. The code in the slot is round 3's
`muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1`: one fused per-pair
kernel (512 threads per pair, `rows*4` threadgroups) plus
`"max_rows": 59` in `spec.json`, so rows 1–59 run the fused kernel
and rows above 59 run the compiled reference. It passes G2
bit-exact at all six sizes, beats compiled at 8/32 decode rows,
and loses at 1 row — the only reason `beats_compiled` is false.

Round 3's `muse-spark/round-3/exploration/territory-baseline-experts.md`
and `ineff-baseline-experts-1/2.md` (both confirmed, frozen) and
`muse-spark/round-3/implementation/hyp-2-experts-prefill.md`
(frozen) mapped this code when it was attempt-7 plus the hand-off.
This entry cites them where they still hold and writes only what
is new for round 4: the `min_rows: 2` spec change ADR 0015 adds,
and where the fused kernel still spends its time now that 1 row
and prefill can both leave the kernel.

## What `min_rows: 2` with `max_rows: 59` changes (new)

The grader now supports a lower hand-off bound. `build()` reads
`min_rows` like `max_rows` (int ≥ 1, ≤ `max_rows` when both are
given, bools rejected) and the returned function hands off when
`rows > max_rows or rows < min_rows`
(`bench/grader/slots.py:330-343`); the brief states the same
contract (`claude/muse-agent-brief.md:174`). Adding
`"min_rows": 2` to the starting point's `spec.json` — no kernel
change — moves the kernel-visible window from 1–59 to **2–59**:

- **1 row: handed off.** The kernels no longer run there at all.
  G2 still checks the size, but through the attempt's own
  dispatch it runs the compiled reference, which was bit-exact
  with the reference at all six sizes in round 3
  (`muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1/notes.md:75-78`),
  so G2 is unaffected. The piece timing reports the size
  `handed off` instead of timing compiled code against itself
  (`bench/grader/check_candidate.py:389-390`;
  `claude/muse-agent-brief.md:216`). The 1-row loss priced by
  round 3's `ineff-baseline-experts-2` (candidate 96.9 vs
  compiled 86.6 µs/layer, `grade.json` — +10.3 µs/layer =
  +0.21 ms per 20-layer decode step) disappears from the
  grader, not from the machine: with 1 request every decode
  step has 1 row, so this slot then runs MLX's own code for the
  whole 1-request workload and is exactly at its compiled bar
  there (`claude/muse-agent-brief.md:174`). It can pass G3
  only in a set whose other kernels are faster at 1 request.
  That composition question belongs to the `g3` territory; this
  territory only records that the experts contribution at
  1 request becomes 0 by construction.
- **Decode phase verdict flips (prediction).** `judge()` drops
  `handed off` sizes, calls a phase `faster` when every
  remaining size is and at least one remains, and sets
  `beats_compiled` when one phase is `faster` and none is
  `slower` (`bench/grader/check_candidate.py:253-273`). With
  1 row handed off, decode rests on 8 and 32 rows alone — both
  `faster` (29 wins each) in the starting point's run — and
  prefill rests on nothing (all three sizes already hand off
  above 59), so the predicted verdicts are decode `faster`,
  prefill `handed off`, **`beats_compiled` true**. This is a
  prediction from the grader's stated rules and the frozen
  `grade.json`; no `min_rows` attempt has been graded yet.
  It is the only ungraded direction in any slot (round-4
  exploration README, *What is left* item 1).
- **2–59 rows: kernels unchanged, byte for byte.** Rows 2–7 and
  9–31 were never timed, but they run the same `qvm` decode
  path graded at 1/8/32 (`block-0.metal:22,45-58`), per-pair
  with no cross-row interaction, so the G2 verdict extends to
  them by construction (round 3's boundary check on attempt-1,
  `hyp-2-experts-prefill.md` *Boundary checks*). Their speed
  is unmeasured; nothing about `min_rows: 2` changes it.
- **The 33–59 band: unchanged, still unmeasured.** Decode steps
  run 1–32 rows (`claude/muse-agent-brief.md:26`), so this band
  never occurs in decode. It can occur as the remainder of a
  prefill chunk (a chunk is at most 2,048 rows; a final chunk
  of 33–59 rows would run the candidate, not the compiled
  reference). Both sides take the `qvm` arithmetic there — the
  kernels branch on `x_shape[0] >= 60` (`block-0.metal:22`) and
  MLX switches its own kernel at the same 60 — so correctness
  is exact by the same argument as 1/8/32. Speed has never
  been timed at any size in 33–59. Extrapolation only
  (prediction, not measurement): at 32 rows the kernel runs
  4.33 µs per pair (554.7 µs ÷ 128 pairs, `grade.json`), so a
  33-row call (132 pairs) would land near 570 µs/layer if the
  per-pair rate held, still ahead of compiled's 32-row rate —
  but occupancy and cache behaviour at 132–236 threadgroups
  are unmeasured, and a slow remainder chunk would tax prompt
  time in G3 in a way the piece timing cannot see. No
  inefficiency is posted: no time loss is measured there.
  Builders who keep `max_rows: 59` should note the alternative
  `max_rows: 32` would hand the whole band off and forfeit
  nothing graded — the boundary window round 3 established was
  32–59 (`hyp-2-experts-prefill.md:79-91`), and 59 was chosen
  to keep the fast path where it wins, on unmeasured sizes.
- **The scalar branch stays dead — `min_rows` does not change
  it.** The `prefill` flag is `x_shape[0] >= 60`
  (`block-0.metal:22`). With `max_rows: 59` the kernels already
  never saw 60+ rows in round 3, so the `else` branches
  (`block-0.metal:59-72,103-112`) and `qmm_accum`
  (`block-1.metal:206-230`) were already unreachable at every
  kernel-visible size; narrowing the window to 2–59 leaves
  them exactly as dead. Round 3 kept them as a G2-exact
  fallback if `max_rows` were ever raised
  (`attempt-1/notes.md:19-24`). No inefficiency is posted for
  them: the branch is never taken, its runtime cost is one
  predictable test on `x_shape[0]`, and no measurement prices
  its compiled presence (register allocation, code size) at
  8/32 rows — round 2's binding ceiling was the two 32-float
  thread arrays `p`, `q` (`block-0.metal:42-43`), which the
  scalar branch does not widen (`qmm_accum` uses one local
  `acc`, `block-1.metal:219`). Deleting the branch and the
  also-unused `qvm_block` (`block-1.metal:22-58`, kept
  verbatim, its arithmetic copied into the pair helpers) is
  safe cleanup a builder may fold into a `min_rows` attempt —
  predicted runtime saving 0, to be confirmed by re-grading —
  but it is not time lost, so it gets no entry.

## Checklist

### A. `block-0.metal` — fused per-pair kernel body (112 lines)

Unchanged from round 3 §A; the delta is only which row counts
can reach it.

- **Callers:** `spec.json` kernel `fused_experts_branch` via
  `bench/grader/slots.py` `build()` / `make_moe_call`, as in
  round-3 territory §A. Shapes reaching the kernel today:
  decode 1/8/32 rows (4/32/128 pairs) and the ungraded 2–59
  band; prefill 127/1,016/2,048 never reach it (handed off
  above 59). Under `min_rows: 2`, 1 row stops reaching it too;
  graded kernel shapes shrink to 8/32 rows only.
- **Callees:** decode path (`x_shape[0] < 60`, the only path

- **Data:** per pair, the expert's full weights are streamed
  independently: gate/up/down words at per-pair offsets
  `eW = e * 36864`, `eS = e * 9216` (`block-0.metal:34-35`).
  Weight bytes per pair: each product reads
  `K × Ww × 4 B` words + scales/biases — gate/up
  768×48×4 = 147,456 B words + 768×12×2×2 = 36,864 B
  scales+biases = 184,320 B; down 384×96×4 = 147,456 B +
  384×24×2×2 = 36,864 B = 184,320 B; total
  **3 × 184,320 = 552,960 B per pair**, as round 2 §A.
  Two pairs selecting the same expert read those bytes twice;
  nothing in the kernel sorts, groups or shares across pairs.
  Costed as `ineff-baseline-experts-1`.
- **Neighbours:** helpers read `tg_x` (gate/up) or `tg_h`
  (down) after the barriers at `block-0.metal:32,73,86`;
  stores to disjoint `y` slices per pair. No atomics, no
  cross-pair communication — which is exactly why re-reads
  persist.
- **Cost:** per thread on the decode path: gate/up 24 strided
  steps (`K=768`, `k = lane; k < K; k += 32`), down 12 merged

  accumulates. Per pair: 884,736 MACs (gate 384×768 + up
  384×768 + down 768×384) = 1.77 MFLOP. At 32 rows the kernel
  sustains 128 pairs × 1.77 MFLOP ÷ 554.7 µs ≈ 0.41 TFLOPS,

  overhead-bound, not compute-bound. The serial structure
  behind that rate is `ineff-baseline-experts-2`.

  decode bits are exact by construction and G2 confirms it.

  — merely unreachable while `max_rows: 59` stands.

With 1 row handed off and prefill already handed off, 8 and 32
rows are the only sizes the kernel is still graded on — and
the only decode sizes where a set still needs its margin
