{"path":"muse-spark/round-4/exploration/ineff-baseline-experts-1.md","content":"# Inefficiency: per-pair weight re-reads at 8/32 rows — 552,960 B streamed per pair, no sharing across pairs on the same expert

- **Owner:** explorer-baseline-experts
- **Status:** open
- **Version:** 1
- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T21:43:09Z
- **Next:** verifier to check byte arithmetic and the distinct-expert basis

## Slot

`experts`

## What happens

Each (row, expert-slot) pair gets its own 512-thread
threadgroup, which streams its expert's full gate/up/down
weights independently. The pair index and expert come from
`pair = threadgroup_position_in_grid.x`, `e = inds[pair]`
(`muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1/block-0.metal:16-21`),
and every weight load uses per-pair offsets
`eW = e * 36864`, `eS = e * 9216` (`block-0.metal:34-35`) into
the helpers in `block-1.metal`. There is no sort, grouping,
tile cache or any other sharing across pairs: two pairs that
select the same expert read that expert's 552,960 B twice,
in full. At 32 rows (128 pairs over at most 60 experts,
`E = 60`, `claude/muse-agent-brief.md` *The slots*) duplicate
selections are guaranteed by pigeonhole — at least 68 of the
128 pair-reads repeat an expert another pair already read.

This restates round 2's `ineff-baseline-experts-3`
(confirmed, frozen) on the current starting point. What is
new: the sizes where it can still cost anything have shrunk.
The scalar prefill traffic it also described is gone (handed
off above 59 rows by `max_rows: 59`), and under the proposed
`min_rows: 2` the 1-row size hands off too — so this entry
prices re-reads only at 8 and 32 rows, the two sizes the
fused kernel still runs and is graded on, on the starting
point's own chained timings instead of round 1's harness.

Per-pair bytes (territory §B arithmetic): gate 184,320 B +
up 184,320 B + down 184,320 B = **552,960 B per pair**
(words `K × Ww × 4 B` plus bfloat16 scales and biases for
each of the three products).

## Cost

Measured, piece (chained µs/layer, starting point's
`muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1/grade.json`;
pair bytes at 552,960 B/pair; 200 GB/s peak,
`claude/GLOSSARY.md`):

| Rows | Pairs | Pair bytes/layer | Candidate | Compiled | Effective on pair bytes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 4 | 2.21 MB | 96.9 | 86.6 | 22.8 GB/s |
| 8 | 32 | 17.69 MB | 168.9 | 238.2 | 104.8 GB/s |
| 32 | 128 | 70.78 MB | 554.7 | 883.4 | 127.6 GB/s |
| 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 | — | handed off | `same` | — | kernel does not run |

- **1 row: no cost from this entry, under either spec.** All
  4 pairs select distinct-or-not experts for one row; round
  2's counters put the whole 1-row experts excess at 7 MB
  per step (0.04 ms floor), and the 1-row loss is latency
  (round 3 `ineff-baseline-experts-2`), not bytes. With
  `min_rows: 2` the size hands off and the kernel reads
  nothing at all.
- **8 rows:** 32 pairs read 17.69 MB/layer. Distinct experts
  among the grader's captured 8-row inputs are unmeasured;
  bounded by 32 pairs and 60 experts. The byte floor on pair
  traffic is 17.69 MB ÷ 200 GB/s = 88.5 µs/layer; the
  candidate takes 168.9. How much of that traffic is
  re-reads is unknown at this size (no 8-row counter exists —
  the same gap round 2 recorded).
- **32 rows:** 128 pairs read 70.78 MB/layer. On the serving
  counter basis (GPU counters via round 2's entry: 908 MB
  read per step vs 443 MB of distinct experts), distinct
  bytes are 22.15 MB/layer, so re-reads are
  70.78 − 22.15 = **48.63 MB/layer (69% of pair traffic)**.
  The distinct count in the grader's captured layers is
  unmeasured and may differ from serving; the counter basis
  is the only measured one. At the candidate's own effective
  rate the re-read bytes occupy 48.63 MB ÷ 127.6 GB/s =
  381 µs of the 554.7 µs/layer.
- **Prefill 127/1,016/2,048: 0.** Above `max_rows: 59` the
  compiled reference runs; its own grouped reads are the
  bar's business, not this kernel's loss.
- Kernels: 1 per layer call at 8/32 rows. Fixed launch cost
  is already banked by the fusion and is not this entry.

## Kind

Overhead-bound with a bandwidth-waste component
(`claude/GLOSSARY.md`, round 2's wording for the same cause):
127.6 GB/s at 32 rows is 64% of peak bandwidth and the
kernel sustains ~8% of peak compute (territory §B), so the
wasted bytes are real but removing them banks time only at
whatever rate a grouped design actually sustains.

## Spans

`baseline-experts` (per-pair grid and offsets,
`block-0.metal:16-35`), `quantized-kernels` (the grouped
`gather_qmm_rhs` sharing this kernel lacks at decode sizes),
`g3` (the 32-request margin a wider win would feed).

## Predicted saving

Floor arithmetic first (excess bytes ÷ 200 GB/s peak — an
upper bound on any byte saving, not a promise):

- 1 row: **0** — handed off under `min_rows: 2`; ≈0 even
  without it (above).
- 8 rows: excess unmeasured. On round 1's micro pattern
  (≈25 distinct of 32 pairs, marked estimate in round 2's
  entry): (32−25) × 552,960 B = 3.87 MB/layer → **19.4
  µs/layer floor = 0.39 ms per decode step**. Estimate, no
  counter.
- 32 rows: 48.63 MB/layer ÷ 200 GB/s = **243.1 µs/layer
  floor = 4.86 ms per decode step** (counter distinct
  basis). A grouped kernel reading only distinct bytes at
  the candidate's own 127.6 GB/s would take
  22.15 MB ÷ 127.6 GB/s = 173.6 µs/layer before its
  sort/scan/barrier overhead — i.e. up to 381 µs/layer of
  the current time is re-read bytes at the current rate.
- Prefill 127/1,016/2,048: **0** at every size — the kernel
  does not run there; a grouped decode change must not
  spend the prefill hand-off.

**Prediction: 0 banked today.** Both grouped attempts that
read each expert ~once (round 1) ran into a ~55 GB/s
duty-cycle ceiling — load→barrier→compute leaves DRAM idle
— and *lost* to the per-pair kernel at 8 rows, tying or
winning only at 32 (round 2 `ineff-baseline-experts-3`,
confirmed). So the realistic claim is conditional: a
grouped or expert-cached design banks toward the 243
µs/layer floor at 32 rows only if it holds ≥127.6 GB/s
effective on distinct bytes (≤173.6 µs/layer before
overhead), and it must keep the per-pair path — or match
it — at 8 rows, where the same evidence says grouping
loses. A saving at 32 that costs 8 is not one (ADR 0011).
This entry and `ineff-baseline-experts-2` overlap on the
same µs (the re-read bytes are part of the time above the
distinct-byte floor): do not add them.

Every pair's decode work runs as one barrier-serialized
chain inside a 512-thread threadgroup
(`muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1/block-0.metal`):
`tg_x` load + barrier (`:29-32`); gate/up interleaved over
24 strided K steps on 12 of 16 simdgroups — 4 simdgroups
idle (`:51-58`); barrier (`:73`); bfloat16 silu-mul on 384 of
512 threads (`:77-85`); barrier (`:86`); down interleaved
over 12 merged K steps, again 12 of 16 simdgroups (`:95-102`).
Each K step in the pair helpers
(`block-1.metal:69-128,137-195`) issues its loads and then
runs 64 dependent accumulates into two 32-float thread
arrays; per thread the chain is 24 + 12 = 36 such steps plus
4 `simd_sum` trees and the silu's exp/divide, with no second
wave of work inside the group to hide it. The group can hold
no more parallelism: exactly two 32-float accumulators fit
at 512 threads — a third failed G1 in round 2 (pipeline max
448), a ceiling the shared `p`/`q` arrays at
`block-0.metal:42-43` already sit on.

Round 3's `ineff-baseline-experts-2` (confirmed, frozen)
priced this chain at 1 row only (+13.5 µs/layer over
compiled) and explicitly costed 8/32 rows at 0, because the
kernel already wins there. What is new in round 4: with
`min_rows: 2` handing 1 row off and `max_rows: 59` handing
prefill off, 8 and 32 rows are the only sizes left — and at
those sizes the same chain is what caps the margin. The win
over compiled (69.3 / 328.7 µs/layer) is no longer the end
of the question; how much more is on the table at the two
surviving sizes is, above all for the set's thin
32×1024 margin (round-4 exploration README, *What is left*
item 2). This entry prices that remainder.

## Cost

Measured, piece (chained µs/layer, starting point's
`muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1/grade.json`;
pair bytes 552,960 B/pair, territory §B; floors at 200 GB/s
peak, `claude/GLOSSARY.md`):

| Rows | Candidate | Compiled | Pair-byte floor | Above own floor | Effective |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 96.9 | 86.6 | 11.1 µs | 85.8 µs | 22.8 GB/s |
| 8 | 168.9 | 238.2 | 88.5 µs | **80.4 µs (48%)** | 104.8 GB/s |
| 32 | 554.7 | 883.4 | 353.9 µs | **200.8 µs (36%)** | 127.6 GB/s |
| 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 | `same` (handed off) | — | — | kernel does not run | — |

- Per-pair time collapses with row count — 24.2 µs at 1 row,
  5.28 at 8, 4.33 at 32 — because more threadgroups (4 → 32
  → 128) overlap each other's chain latency. That overlap is
  the whole reason the kernel wins at 8/32 despite the chain;
  what remains above the floor is the part group parallelism
  could not hide: in-group serial depth, the three phase
  barriers, 25% of simdgroups idle in both K phases, and the
  silu chain, all behind a register ceiling that forbids
  widening the accumulators.
- Compute check: 884,736 MACs per pair (territory §B) =
  1.77 MFLOP; at 32 rows, 128 pairs in 554.7 µs ≈ 0.41
  TFLOPS, ~8% of the 5.2 TFLOPS peak. Neither bandwidth
  (52–64% of peak) nor compute is saturated.
- At 1 row this entry costs 0 under `min_rows: 2` (handed
  off); without it, the 1-row figure is round 3's confirmed
  entry and is not re-claimed here. At prefill sizes it
  costs 0 under the existing hand-off. A fix must keep both
  hand-offs and both graded wins.

## Kind

Overhead-bound (`claude/GLOSSARY.md`): far below both peak
bandwidth and peak compute at every size; time goes to
waiting on a serial dependent chain and phase barriers, not
to bytes or arithmetic. The bytes half of the same µs is
`ineff-baseline-experts-1`; the two entries overlap and
must not be added.

## Spans

`baseline-experts` (`block-0.metal` decode path,
`block-1.metal` pair helpers, `spec.json` grid),
`grader` (the chained timing is the bar; only same-run
paired verdicts transfer).

## Predicted saving

The headroom, if the chain's exposed latency were removed
without touching a single accumulation order (every
per-block `k` sequence, term order and `simd_sum` tree is
bit-load-bearing):

- 1 row: **0** — handed off; the saving there is the spec's,
  already counted in the territory entry (−10.3 µs/layer vs
  the kernel, to compiled parity, not below it).
- 8 rows: up to 80.4 µs/layer = **1.61 ms per decode step**
  above the pair-byte floor (×20 layers).
- 32 rows: up to 200.8 µs/layer = **4.02 ms per decode
  step** above the pair-byte floor. Against the distinct-byte
  floor (22.15 MB/layer ÷ 200 GB/s = 110.8 µs, counter basis
  from entry 1) the combined headroom is 443.9 µs/layer —
  shared with entry 1, never added to it.
- Prefill 127/1,016/2,048: **0** — kernel does not run.

**Prediction: 0 banked today; the figures above are
headroom, not a promise.** Round 2's evidence bounds the
levers: six fused exact packings plateaued at 92–110
µs/layer at 1 row (the chain shortened by ~10 µs for the
gate/up interleave, ~2 for parallel stores, ~0 for the down
merge), the accumulator ceiling forbids the obvious
widening, and round 3's unfused regrouping (attempt-5) and
vectorised scalar path (attempt-2) both lost — all on the
round-4 README's refuted list for 1 row, and none of them
measured an 8/32-row gain either. A builder claiming this
entry needs a mechanism that shortens serial depth or
fills the 4 idle simdgroups *at 8/32 rows* while keeping
per-block order exact — for example splitting each pair's
blocks across all 16 simdgroups with a second reduction
stage, if its extra `simd_sum`/barrier cost does not eat
the gain — and must show it in the same grader run at both
sizes. Until one grades, the bankable round-4 move in this
slot remains the spec-only `min_rows: 2`, which spends
none of this headroom and risks none of the wins.

24|## The slots
25|
26|Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the call: 1 to 32 in a decode step, up to 2,048 in a prefill chunk. The grader flattens the inputs to the shapes below and restores the model's shapes afterwards. All arrays are row-contiguous.
27|
28|The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.
29|
30|### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights
31|
32|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
33||---|---|---|---|
34|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
35|| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
36|| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
37|| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
38|| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
39|
40|Reference:
41|
42|```python
43|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
44|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
45|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
46|weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
47|```
48|
49|The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.
50|
51|### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert
52|
53|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
54||---|---|---|---|
55|| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
56|| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
57|| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
58|| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
59|
60|Reference:
61|
62|```python
63|out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
64|```
65|
66|Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.
67|
68|### `routing+combine`
69|
70|Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.
71|
72|### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products
73|
74|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
75||---|---|---|---|
76|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
77|| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
78|| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
79|| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
80|| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
81|| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
82|| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |
83|
84|Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.
85|
86|Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:
87|
88|```python
89|y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
90|```
91|
92|As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.
93|
94|Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.

184|The pass criteria were fixed before the first round. 186|1. **G1, runs.** It compiles and runs on real inputs.
187|2. **G2, correct: identical to the reference, bit for bit.** The slot runs in every call of `MoE.__call__`, the prefill included, so it is tested on every layer's inputs at two kinds of size:
188|   - **a decode step:** inputs captured from all 20 layers during a real decode step, at 1, 8 and 32 rows;
189|   - **a prefill:** the first chunk of a prefill with 128-token prompts, recorded while the grader runs it, at 1, 8 and 32 requests: 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. From 60 rows on, MLX's own experts kernel changes (`gather_qmm_rhs` instead of `gather_qvm`), and so does its rounding.

191|   At every size:
192|   - **`routing`:** each row's 4 experts and their 4 weights equal the reference's, in the same order, since combine sums the pairs in that order. That includes the reference's choice between tied 4th and 5th experts.
193|   - **`combine` and `experts`:** every element equals the reference's.

195|   **Why exact:** the end-to-end check below asks for the same greedy tokens, and greedy decoding turns any difference into different tokens. In round 1, routing weights within 10⁻⁵ of the reference, relative, changed 7 to 9 of 32 sequences.
196|   - **Then, end to end:** the same greedy tokens as the original model over 24 generated tokens, at 1 and 32 requests, in both plain MLX and vLLM.

198|   - the **decode step**, the median period between steady steps;
199|   - the **prompt time**, until every prompt was processed;
200|   - the **whole request**, from sending the requests to the last token.
201|
202|   Against both the original model and an `mx.compile` of the same reference code, the attempt passes when the decode step or the prompt time is faster in every workload, neither is slower in any, and no whole request is slower. Faster and slower mean that the ranges over the repeats don't overlap.

204|   **From round 3, the same G3 runs inside the round too:** the lead's **ready check**, `bench/grader/check_ready.py`, with every candidate in one call. It also requires the same greedy tokens, and audits its own log. Only its passing verdict makes an attempt `ready`; Claude's G3 after the round decides. 209|- `g1` false and the compiler's error message;
210|- or the correctness results per size: for routing, the rows that differ; for combine and experts, the elements that differ and the largest gap in units in the last place; with the first example;
211|- or, when the attempt is correct, `timing_us_per_layer` per size: its time per call next to the original's and the compiled reference's, its wins against the compiled reference and the verdict (`faster`, `same`, `slower`, or `handed off` for a size your spec hands to the compiled reference); then `phases_vs_compiled` and `beats_compiled`.

213|**The piece timing** runs the slot at the six G2 sizes: the 20 layers' captured decode inputs at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and the 20 layers' first prefill chunk at 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. Each layer's call waits for the previous one's output, as in the model: one small kernel links them, the same for every function timed. Without that wait, the GPU overlaps the 20 calls and hides how long one takes; in round 1, an experts kernel 29% faster on overlapped calls was 66% slower on chained ones at 1 row.
214|- **Paired repeats.** Your attempt and the compiled reference run in alternating order, 30 times.
215|- **Per size:** your attempt is `faster` when it wins at least 22 of the 30 pairs, `slower` when it loses at least 22, and `same` otherwise. Medians alone would pass on noise: the same kernel timed twice differs by up to 5%.

1|# MobileMoE Bandwidth Study
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|How efficiently an inference engine turns an Apple Silicon GPU's memory bandwidth and compute into generated tokens when serving a small mixture-of-experts model.
6|
7|## Hardware limits
8|
9|**Peak bandwidth**:
10|The most bytes per second the GPU can read from unified memory, as rated by the manufacturer (about 200 GB/s on this project's M1 Pro).
11|_Avoid_: max bandwidth, memory speed
12|
13|**Peak compute**:
14|The most floating-point operations per second the GPU can perform (about 5.2 TFLOPS on the 16-core M1 Pro GPU).
15|_Avoid_: max compute, TFLOPS (as the name of the limit)
16|
17|**Achieved bandwidth**:
18|The bytes a decode step must read from memory (the weights it touches plus its share of cached attention state), divided by that step's duration.
19|_Avoid_: bandwidth usage, utilization (unqualified)
20|
21|**Arithmetic intensity**:
22|Floating-point operations performed per byte read from memory during a decode step.
23|_Avoid_: compute density, FLOPs/byte ratio
24|
25|**Ridge point**:
26|The arithmetic intensity at which peak bandwidth and peak compute meet (about 26 operations per byte here); below it a step is limited by bandwidth, above it by compute.
27|
28|**Roofline**:
29|The chart of achievable throughput against arithmetic intensity, capped by peak bandwidth on the left and peak compute on the right, with measured decode steps plotted beneath it.
30|
31|## Bottlenecks and fixes
32|
33|**Bandwidth-bound**:
34|A decode step whose achieved bandwidth is close to peak bandwidth.
35|
36|**Compute-bound**:
37|A decode step whose operation rate is close to peak compute.
38|
39|**Overhead-bound**:
40|A decode step far below both limits, because its time goes to work other than reading weights or doing arithmetic, such as launching GPU jobs, routing tokens to experts or scheduling.
41|_Avoid_: latency-bound, CPU-bound (unless the CPU specifically is the cause)
42|
43|**Bottleneck**:
44|The single cause, identified from measurements, that most limits throughput for a given workload.
45|_Avoid_: issue, slowness
46|
47|**Kernel**:
48|One program the GPU runs as a unit, such as one matrix product or one element-wise add; a decode step is a chain of hundreds of them, each with a fixed start-up cost.
49|_Avoid_: GPU job, op (for a kernel launch)
50|
51|**Occupancy**:
52|The share of the GPU's thread slots in use while it runs; low occupancy means most of the chip is idle even when the GPU counts as busy.
53|_Avoid_: GPU utilization (which only says the GPU had work)
54|
55|**Knock-out**:
56|A measurement in which one piece of the decode step is replaced by a stand-in that returns the right shape without GPU work; the time and bytes the step saves are that piece's cost.
57|_Avoid_: ablation
58|
59|**Baseline**:
60|The unmodified engine serving MobileMoE-S-QAT (int4), against which every fix is measured.
61|
62|**Fix**:
63|One change to the engine, the model code or the configuration, measured against the baseline under the same workload.
64|_Avoid_: optimization (for a change that hasn't been measured), tweak
65|
66|## Inference
67|
68|**Prefill**:
69|Processing a request's whole prompt through the model before its first token is generated, in chunks of up to the engine's token budget per pass (2,048 tokens here).
70|_Avoid_: prompt phase (say prefill, or prompt processing)
71|
72|**Decode step**:
73|One engine iteration that produces one new token for each request it includes.
74|
75|**Decode rows**:
76|The number of requests the engine actually advanced in one decode step; the batch size that matters for the roofline.
77|_Avoid_: batch size (unqualified), concurrency
78|
79|**Client concurrency**:
80|The number of requests the benchmark client keeps in flight; it caps decode rows but does not equal them.
81|_Avoid_: batch size
82|
83|## Mixture of experts
84|
85|**Expert**:
86|One of the interchangeable feed-forward blocks in a layer; MobileMoE-S has 60 routed experts per layer.
87|
88|**Active experts**:
89|The experts the router picks for one token in one layer (4 for MobileMoE-S).
90|_Avoid_: selected experts, top-k experts
91|
92|**Distinct experts**:
93|The number of different experts used by all decode rows together in one layer during one decode step; it decides how much expert weight data the step must read.
94|_Avoid_: unique experts, expert coverage
95|
96|## Models
97|
98|**MobileMoE-S**:
99|Meta's smallest on-device mixture-of-experts model (about 1.3B parameters in total, about 272M used per token), studied here in its SFT (full-precision) and QAT (int4) variants.
100|
101|**Muse Spark**:

Round 4 changes three rules ([ADR 0015](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)): candidates that pass together in `muse-all` are `ready` as a **set**; an attempt may hand off inputs below `min_rows` as well as above `max_rows`; and a handed-off size is reported `handed off` instead of being timed. A slot's **baseline** is still its best attempt so far that passes the current G2, has `beats_compiled` true in the grader, and passes G3 ([ADR 0011](../../../claude/adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). **No slot has a baseline.** The bar in every slot is the compiled reference, and a new attempt must beat it in the same grader run (no `--baseline` argument).   "terminal_status": "completed",
  "output": "# Round 3 of the Muse agent, measured

*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../../PROVENANCE.md).*

In round 3 (2026-11-04, 17:35 to 19:00 UTC), the Muse agent ran skill version 8 ([ADR 0013](../adr/0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)). The model was Muse Spark's contributor model, `muse-spark-1.3-contributor`, at `max` effort, with tool approvals off ([ADR 0012](../adr/0012-muse-spark-contributor-unattended.md)). It started from [Claude's measurement of round 2](muse-round-2.md). There was no baseline in any slot, so the compiled reference was the bar everywhere. The round made 24 commits, the last `46679e7`, and graded 13 attempts: 5 for experts, 6 for routing and 2 for combine.

For the first time, the swarm ran G3 itself before calling anything ready: the **ready check**, `bench/grader/check_ready.py` ([ADR 0013](../adr/0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)). Its two candidates each failed it alone, on overlapping ranges, and passed it together. The skill counted only candidates that pass alone, so the summary, [muse-spark/round-3/summary.md](../../muse-spark/round-3/summary.md), submits the reference in every slot. It reports the pair as measured but not submitted:
- **routing:** `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6`, round 2's attempt-4 kernels with `max_rows` 32;
- **combine:** `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/combine/attempt-2`, round 2's attempt-1 with its float contractions turned off.

Claude measured the pair afterwards, alone and together, as G3 does.

**Where everything is.**
- G3: [results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-3/](../../results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-3/), the verdict in `g3-vllm.json`.
- One request with long prompts: [results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-3-long/](../../results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-3-long/).
- The swarm's ready check: [muse-spark/round-3/checks/ready-1/](../../muse-spark/round-3/checks/ready-1/).
- The script: `bench/grader/time_candidates.py vllm <out> routing=… combine=…`, with `--settings 1x1024,1x7936 --max-model-len 8192` for the long prompts.

**The machine.** The same M1 Pro, with Docker quit. 13.9 to 14.2 GB of 15.4 GB of swap were in use (`machine-*.txt`). vLLM ran with `VLLM_METAL_KV_COMMIT_PROBE=0`.

## Summary

- **Every kernel is bit-exact, and the tokens are unchanged.** Every variant, alone or together, gives the unchanged model's greedy tokens.
- **The pair is the best result of any round.** Against the unchanged model in vLLM, routing attempt-6 with combine attempt-2:
  - shortens the decode step by 16.5%, 5.4%, 2.8% and 1.6% with 1, 8 and 32 requests of 128 tokens and 32 of 1,024;
  - shortens whole requests by 14.1%, 5.6%, 2.1% and 2.4%;
  - processes prompts 1.6 to 3.1% faster, and is slower nowhere.
- **G3 still fails the pair, by one workload.** It passes against the unchanged model, but against the compiled reference (`compiled-all`) its decode step with 32 requests of 1,024 tokens is only 0.9% shorter, and the ranges of the 5 repeats overlap.
- **With one request and long prompts, the pair passes both bars.** With 1,024- and 7,936-token prompts its decode step is 14.8% and 11.3% shorter than the unchanged model's, and 8.1% and 6.3% shorter than the compiled reference's.
- **The ready check measured what G3 measures.** The swarm's decode changes match Claude's within 0.15 ms in every workload, and 2 of its 3 verdicts are the same. The third, the pair against `compiled-all`, passed in the swarm's run and failed in Claude's.
- **Experts never reached the ready check.** Its best attempt lost to the compiled reference only at 1 row (section 4).

## 1. The ready check against Claude's G3

Both runs time the same variants in the same four workloads, 5 shuffled repeats each. The decode-step change against the unchanged model, in ms, at 1×128 / 8×128 / 32×128 / 32×1024 (requests × prompt tokens; medians):

| Variant | The swarm's ready check | Claude's G3 | Verdicts, swarm / Claude |
|---|---|---|---|
| `muse-routing` | −0.38 / −0.31 / −0.59 / −0.48 | −0.41 / −0.31 / −0.61 / −0.62 | fail / fail |
| `muse-combine` | −0.53 / −0.59 / −0.44 / −0.26 | −0.56 / −0.51 / −0.45 / −0.48 | fail / fail |
| `muse-all`, both | −0.92 / −0.89 / −0.73 / −0.78 | −0.90 / −0.77 / −0.83 / −0.65 | pass / **fail** |

**Why the verdicts differ.** Every failure in both runs is an overlap of ranges: no variant is slower than either bar anywhere.
- `muse-routing` fails against `compiled-routing` at 8×128 in both runs, and in Claude's also against the unchanged model at 32×1024.
- `muse-combine` fails in the swarm's run on one 1×128 repeat (5.892 ms, above the unchanged model's lowest, 5.430). In Claude's it fails against `compiled-combine` at 32×128 and 32×1024.
- `muse-all` against `compiled-all` at 32×1024: in Claude's run the 5 decode times are 38.59 to 39.08 ms and the compiled reference's 38.91 to 39.40, medians 0.9% apart. In the swarm's run the medians were 1.5% apart, and the ranges just missed each other.

With gains of about 1%, 5 repeats decide by chance. Every median favours the kernels, but the rule asks for ranges that miss each other. That rule stays for round 4 ([ADR 0015](../adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md), *Considered options*).

## 2. G3: whole requests and prompts

Claude's G3, the change against the unchanged model (medians of 5 repeats; the unchanged step was 5.457, 14.337, 30.061 and 39.410 ms):

| Workload | Variant | Decode step | Prompt time | Whole request |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1×128 | routing | −7.5% | −2.7% | −6.9% |
| | combine | −10.2% | −1.0% | −7.7% |
| | both | **−16.5%** | −3.1% | **−14.1%** |
| | compiled reference, both slots | −8.5% | −4.1% | −8.0% |
| 8×128 | both | **−5.4%** | −1.6% | **−5.6%** |
| | compiled reference | −2.8% | +0.1% | −2.7% |
| 32×128 | both | **−2.8%** | −2.7% | **−2.1%** |
| | compiled reference | −0.9% | −1.4% | −0.8% |
| 32×1024 | both | **−1.6%** | −2.8% | **−2.4%** |
| | compiled reference | −0.7% | −0.3% | −0.6% |

Bold: faster than the unchanged model beyond the spread of the repeats.

- **The gain is about the same in milliseconds everywhere:** 0.65 to 0.9 ms per decode step. The share falls as more requests make each step longer.
- **Prompts gain a little, and lose nothing.** Routing hands every prompt-sized input to the compiled reference (`max_rows` 32), and combine attempt-2 is faster than the reference at every prefill size. Round 2's routing kernel made prompts 7 to 10% slower; this one doesn't.
- **Half the gain is compiling MLX's own code.** `mx.compile` of the two slots' reference code alone gains 8.5% at 1×128. The kernels add the other 8.8%.

## 3. One request with long prompts

G3's workloads stop at 1,024-token prompts with 32 requests. Claude also timed one request with 1,024- and 7,936-token prompts, the longest that fits the model's 8,192-token context with 256 generated tokens ([results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-3-long/](../../results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-3-long/)). `time_candidates.py` gained `--max-model-len` for this; G3's default is unchanged.

| Prompt | Decode step | Prompt time | Whole request | Throughput |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1,024 tokens | 5.7 → 4.9 ms, **−14.8%** | **−2.9%** | **−13.8%** | 152 → 176 tokens/s |
| 7,936 tokens | 8.2 → 7.3 ms, **−11.3%** | −2.1% | **−6.4%** | 56 → 60 tokens/s |

Against the compiled reference, the decode step is 8.1% and 6.3% shorter. In these two workloads the pair passes G3's rule against both bars, and so does combine attempt-2 alone. The decode step saves about the same 0.85 to 0.93 ms however long the prompt is. A 7,936-token prompt takes about half the request, though, so the whole request gains less.

## 4. Experts: lost at 1 row only

hyp-2 graded 5 attempts and dropped the slot. The best, attempt-1, is round 2's fused kernel with `max_rows` 59. It is bit-exact, `same` as the compiled reference at every prefill size, and much faster at 8 and 32 rows, but slower at 1. Chained µs per layer, attempt against compiled reference:

| Rows | 1 | 8 | 32 |
|---|---|---|---|
| attempt-1 | 96.9 | 168.9 | 554.7 |
| compiled reference | 86.6 | 238.2 | 883.4 |

`beats_compiled` needs one phase faster at every size, so the 1-row loss sank it. The round then tried to win at 1 row, in two ways:
- **a vectorised scalar path** (attempt-2) bought nothing;
- **an unfused path copying the reference's structure** (attempt-5) was twice as slow at 1 row.

The round's lead concluded that "no third exists in the spec surface". The spec could not keep 1 row on MLX's own code while running the kernel at 8 and 32 rows; from round 4 it can (`min_rows`, ADR 0015). No experts attempt has been timed end to end since round 2's attempt-7, which shortened the decode step by 17.5% with 32 requests and processed prompts 6.6 to 14.5 times slower.

## 5. How round 3 worked

The new rules held:
- every end-to-end number in *Ready to test* comes from the ready check, and predictions are labelled;
- `checker-final` found 7 rounding slips in the last digit and had them fixed before the round ended;
- when the fused experts kernel kept losing at 1 row, attempt-5 changed approach to an unfused path, and its ledger line says so.

What went wrong:
- **Builders were spent on directions exploration had already ruled out:** experts attempt-2 and routing attempt-3.
- **Extra kernel launches cost more than they saved.** Routing attempt-3's added copy launch, about 2 to 3 µs per layer, flipped its decode from `faster` to `same`. Experts attempt-5's five launches instead of two cost about 18 µs per layer, part of its 2× loss at 1 row (`hyp-2-experts-prefill.md`, `hyp-3-routing-prefill.md`).
- **The thread limit cost two attempts.** Metal's limit per pipeline depends on the kernel's registers, 640 and then 576 threads here, while the grader checks only for 1,024. Routing attempts 2 and 4 failed G1 on it.
- **The grader timed identical code against itself.** Above `max_rows` an attempt runs the compiled reference, and the grader still timed it against the compiled reference. That judged routing attempt-1 `slower` at 2,048 rows on 8 wins of 30, and cost a re-grade of a byte-identical copy (attempt-6). From round 4 such a size is `handed off` (ADR 0015).
- **The set had no rule.** The skill said submitting together needs `muse-all` to pass, but made only single candidates `ready`. The lead read it strictly and submitted nothing. From round 4 a passing `muse-all` makes its candidates `ready` as a set (ADR 0015).
- **Absolute grader times drift up to twice between runs** on this machine, so comparing attempts across runs misleads; the round learned to compare ratios against the compiled reference from the same run.

## For round 4: baselines and starting points

**The rule** is unchanged ([ADR 0011](../adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)): a slot's baseline is its best attempt so far that passes the current G2, has `beats_compiled` true in the grader, and passes G3. Round 4 adds sets and `min_rows` ([ADR 0015](../adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)).

| Slot | Baseline | Starting point | Grader | G3 | Why it is no baseline |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `routing` | none | `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6` | `beats_compiled` true; decode 0.72 / 0.90 / 0.88 of the compiled reference at 1 / 8 / 32 rows, prefill `handed off` (Claude's re-grade with the round-4 grader, [results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/](../../results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/)) | fails alone: `same` as `compiled-routing` at 8×128 | G3 alone |
| `combine` | none | `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/combine/attempt-2` | `beats_compiled` true in both phases (round 3's grade) | fails alone: `same` as `compiled-combine` at 32×128 and 32×1024 | G3 alone |
| `experts` | none | `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1` | slower at 1 row, faster at 8 and 32, prefill `same` (section 4) | not timed | the 1-row loss |

**The pair** routing attempt-6 with combine attempt-2 passes G3 against the unchanged model, and against the compiled reference everywhere but 32×1024, where it is 0.9% shorter with overlapping ranges (section 1). Under round 4's set rule it would be a `ready` set, but it is no baseline. Round 4's bar is the compiled reference in every slot.

**What round 4 has to find out,** in Claude's reading of these results:
1. **experts with `min_rows`.** Whether attempt-1's 8- and 32-row speed carries into G3 once 1 row runs MLX's own code. With 1 request it then adds nothing, so it can pass G3 only in a set whose other kernels are faster with 1 request, such as the pair.
2. **All three slots at once.** In rounds 1 and 2, replacing all three slots lost about 2.8 ms with 8 requests, for an unknown reason ([round 2](muse-round-2.md), section 4). A set with experts meets that again.
3. **A margin at 32×1024.** The pair gains 0.25 to 0.3 ms over the compiled reference there, about 1%, which 5 repeats can't tell from noise. A set needs more than that with 32 long prompts.

# Round-2 attempt 4 — builder-2-d, hardening of hyp-2-routing-exact

Builds on `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-3` (scalar
full-G2; chained 46.9/300.0/297.2 µs/layer vs compiled 58.0/84.5/90.9 —
latency-bound from uncoalesced device loads + `xsh` bank conflicts).
Baseline: none, so no `beats_baseline`; the bar is the compiled reference.

## The one main change

Stage each K-chunk's `w_router` block into threadgroup memory with
coalesced vector loads and sum from threadgroup with a padded `x`
layout, nothing else:

- Staging: chunks are staged 4 at a time (12 groups cover all 48
  BK=16 chunks). Each staged chunk is 60×16 floats, loaded as 240
  `float4` loads (consecutive threads cover one expert's 4 vectors,
  then the next expert) and stored transposed in `wsh[slot][k][expert]`
  with expert stride 64.
- Padded `x`: chunk `c` of `x` sits at `xpad[c*17 + k]` (one pad float
  per chunk), replacing attempt-3's flat `xsh[768]`.
- Scalar chain: expert-parallel lanes read `wsh` at consecutive expert
  banks (conflict-free) and `xpad` uniformly per `k` (broadcast).
  Partials live transposed in `parts[partition][expert]` (stride 64)
  and are resumed product-by-product in increasing `d` across staged
  groups, so each (expert, partition) partial is still one serial
  scalar sum in increasing `d`; partials are then summed sequentially
  in partition order. 24 barriers on the scalar path (2 per group).
- Threadgroup memory: (816 + 60 + 2048 + 4096) × 4 B = 28,080 B of
  32 KB. Same grid (`rows*256`), threadgroup (256) and one-kernel layout.

Kept verbatim from attempt-3: the regime branch on `rows` (GEMV only
at `rows == 1`; split-K while `rows <= 768`; regular above — the GEMV
branch is unchanged apart from reading the padded `x` layout), the
split-K partition formula (32 partitions at 8/32 rows, 8 of 96 at 127,
2 at 257–768, single partition above 768, last partition absorbing the
remainder chunks), the GEMV lane order and shuffle tree 16,8,4,2,1,
MLX's verbatim sigmoid (`1/(1+precise::exp(abs(s)))`, `(s<0)?y:1-y`),
the strictly-greater insertion top-4 (earliest index wins ties), and
`((w0+w1)+w2)+w3 + 1e-20`, divide, ×2.5 on unbiased scores.

## Inefficiency removed

`ineff-baseline-routing-1` stays removed (same orders as attempt-3).
The target is attempt-3's diagnosed feeding cost (its notes: the
scalar chains read `w_router` uncoalesced — warp lanes 64 B apart,
16 cache lines per step — and `xsh[p*16+k]` with 16-way bank
conflicts on every product). Staging turns the device reads into
coalesced `float4` loads and the dependent chain's reads into
conflict-free threadgroup reads. The per-row `w_router` re-read
(`ineff-baseline-routing-4`) and the serial thread-0 scan are
untouched.

## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows

Anchor: attempt-3 measured 46.9/300.0/297.2, compiled 58.0/84.5/90.9
(same grader run). Traffic per row is unchanged at 184 KB of
`w_router` (0.9 µs at 200 GB/s), so floors are 0.9/7.4/29.5 µs; the
rest is chained-call latency and per-row work. Attempt-3's flat
~300 µs was the dependent device-load chain; the staged chain reads
threadgroup memory instead, at the cost of 24 barriers/row.

- 1 row: GEMV branch unchanged but for the padded index (a shift and
  mask per access) → ≈ attempt-3's 46.9 → **48**.
- 8 rows: fixed chained latency ≈ 40 µs (attempt-3's 1-row time less
  its small GEMV work) + traffic 7.4 + staged scalar work. The
  critical path is the last partition's 272 sequential threadgroup
  FMAs, overlapped across 8 threadgroups; allowance ≈ 20 µs →
  40 + 7.4 + 20 ≈ **67**.
- 32 rows: 40 + 29.5 + 25 (more threadgroups fill the GPU, critical
  path unchanged) ≈ **95**.

Prediction: **48 / 67 / 95 µs** — beats compiled (58.0/84.5/90.9) at
1 and 8 rows, near it at 32. G2 prediction: pass at all six sizes —
no accumulation order changes, only where operands are read from.

## Verdict (2026-11-04T03:56:12Z, one grader run)

G1 pass, **G2 pass at all six sizes** (rows_differ 0,
rows_other_experts 0, max_rel_err 0.0 at 1/8/32 and 127/1016/2048).
Chained µs/layer (ref / compiled / candidate): 1 row 71.1 / 60.7 /
**47.5**; 8 rows 102.9 / 84.9 / **69.1**; 32 rows 104.9 / 89.5 /
**72.9**. **`beats_compiled` true** — the first routing attempt to
beat the compiled reference at all three row counts. Baseline none,
so no `beats_baseline`. Vs attempt-3 (46.9/300.0/297.2): the staged
scalar path is 4.3×/4.1× faster at 8/32 rows; the 1-row GEMV branch
is unchanged (47.5 vs 46.9, drift).

## Why the 32-row timing missed the prediction by >20%

Predicted 48/67/95, measured 47.5/69.1/72.9: 1 and 8 rows hold
(−1%/+3%), 32 rows is 23% under. The prediction added a fixed ~40 µs
chained latency, the full 29.5 µs traffic floor and a per-row work
allowance as if they were serial per layer call. They are not: at 32
rows, 32 threadgroups across 16 GPU cores overlap one threadgroup's
coalesced staging loads and barriers with other threadgroups' scalar
compute, so the marginal cost of rows 9–32 is only (72.9−69.1)/24 ≈
0.16 µs/row, against the predicted ≈1.2 µs/row. The kernel is
essentially flat 69→73 µs from 8 to 32 rows — once enough
threadgroups are resident to hide the staging latency, extra rows
are nearly free, and the 28 KB threadgroup footprint (which caps
residency) does not bind at these row counts. Traffic-floor
arithmetic overstates the cost whenever staging and compute overlap
across threadgroups.

Next change (one): none needed for the slot's stop rule (G1+G2+
beats compiled at all three row counts). If pushed further, cut the
24 barriers by staging 8 chunks per group (halves barrier count but
needs ~2× the `wsh` footprint or a narrower expert stride).

- **Owner:** explorer-baseline-routing
- **Status:** exploring
- **Version:** 1
- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T21:42:57Z
- **Next:** post ineff-baseline-routing-1 (per-row `w_router` re-read at decode sizes) and -2 (staged scalar shape cost at decode sizes)

## What it does

Same slot contract as rounds 2–3 (`muse-spark/round-3/exploration/territory-baseline-routing.md:11-20`, frozen): per layer, `scores = sigmoid(float32(x) @ w_router.T)`, top-4 on `scores + bias` (selection only), weights from the unbiased scores (`((s0+s1)+s2)+s3 + 1e-20`, divide, ×2.5). Outputs `inds` [rows,4] uint32 (feeds experts) and `weights` [rows,4] float32 (feeds combine, in emitted order; G2 is ordered bitwise equality at all six sizes, brief:190-193).

The code in the slot is `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6/` — round 2 attempt-4's kernels byte-identical (`diff` of `block-0.metal` and `spec.json` against attempt-1 empty, verified this round; attempt-1 = attempt-6, `notes.md:13-20`) plus `max_rows: 32` in `spec.json:1`. One fused kernel per layer: 256-thread threadgroup per row, `rows == 1` GEMV shuffle branch, staged scalar split-K above 1 row, verbatim sigmoid, thread-0 insertion top-4. Rows 1–32 run the kernels; every prefill size runs the compiled reference. Round 3's entries (`territory-baseline-routing.md`, `ineff-baseline-routing-1..2`, all frozen) mapped this code's *prefill* loss; that loss is now handed off, so this entry writes only what is new: the decode side, priced as margin.

## The headline finding (details in ineff-baseline-routing-1 and -2)

The starting point already wins everywhere it runs. Two grader runs of the identical bytes:

| rows | round-3 grade (`attempt-6/grade.json`) cand / compiled | Claude re-grade, round-4 grader (`results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/grade-routing-attempt-6.json`) cand / compiled | margin (re-grade) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 51.7 / 66.3 (28 wins, `faster`) | 45.1 / 62.8 (29 wins, `faster`) | 17.7 µs/layer (0.72×) |
| 8 | 90.9 / 104.0 (27, `faster`) | 144.2 / 160.0 (26, `faster`) | 15.8 µs/layer (0.90×) |
| 32 | 132.2 / 152.0 (25, `faster`) | 151.3 / 171.0 (27, `faster`) | 19.7 µs/layer (0.88×) |
| 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 | `same` × 3 (timed, identical code) | `handed off` × 3 | — (not timed; ADR 0015) |

Chained absolutes drift up to ~2× between runs on this machine (round-3 README; hyp-3 failure ledger) — the 8-row absolute moves 90.9 → 144.2 while the relative win holds — so only same-run margins and ratios transfer. In per-step terms (×20 layers, prediction from the same-run piece margins, not a whole-request measurement): the routing margin is worth ≈0.35 / 0.32 / 0.39 ms per decode step at 1 / 8 / 32 rows against the compiled reference.

Why it is no baseline: G3 alone. It passes G1+G2 (0 rows differing, all six sizes) and has `beats_compiled` true in both grading runs, but it has never passed G3 — alone it is `same` as `compiled-routing` at 8×128 in both the swarm's ready check (`muse-spark/round-3/checks/ready-1/ready-verdict.json`: `muse-routing` fail vs compiled, pass vs base, no phase slower anywhere) and Claude's G3 (`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-3/g3-vllm.json`: `same` at 8×128 vs compiled-routing, `same` at 32×1024 vs base), and as the routing+combine pair it fails Claude's G3 against `compiled-all` at 32×1024 (medians 0.9% apart, ranges 38.59–39.08 vs 38.91–39.40 ms overlapping; `claude/findings/muse-round-3.md` §1). Under round 4's set rule the pair would have been `ready` in round 3, but a set still has to pass G3 as `muse-all` (round-4 README:34). The bar is the compiled reference; there is no `--baseline`.

The margin question, priced: at 32×1024 the pair gains only 0.25–0.30 ms/step over the compiled reference (~1% of the 39.4 ms step; round-4 README:35,49-55 item 2), inside the 5-repeat spread (range widths ≈0.49 ms on both sides). Non-overlap there needs roughly +0.15–0.25 ms/step more, i.e. +7.5–12.5 µs/layer across routing+combine at 32 rows (arithmetic: 0.15–0.25 ms ÷ 20 layers). Routing's whole current 32-row margin is 19.7 µs/layer, so routing alone would have to widen by ~40–60% to clear it; any µs/layer routing adds at 32 rows widens the set's margin 1:1 (0.02 ms/step per µs/layer). Every candidate change must keep `max_rows: 32` (or otherwise leave prefill on the compiled reference) — a change that lets the kernels run at prefill sizes re-opens round 3's confirmed prefill entries and is not a saving under ADR 0011.

Where the remaining decode time goes (both entries below): the candidate's chained time at 1/8/32 rows (re-grade 45.1/144.2/151.3 µs/layer) sits far above its traffic floor (0.9/7.4/29.7 µs/layer at 200 GB/s, brief:9) — the slot is overhead-bound at decode sizes (`claude/GLOSSARY.md:39-42`). Two named pools remain inside it: the per-row `w_router` re-read (traffic floor 29.7 µs/layer at 32 rows, larger than the whole 19.7 margin, but overlapped rather than serial — entry 1) and the staged scalar path's shape cost at decode sizes (27 barriers/row, 4 of 12 groups at 23% duty, 28,080 B footprint, serial tails — entry 2).

## Checklist

### 1. The starting-point kernels — `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6/block-0.metal` (174 lines) + `block-1.metal` (3 lines)

One threadgroup of 256 threads per row at every kernel-visible size (`spec.json:1`: grid `rows*256`, threadgroup [256,1,1]). Threadgroup memory `xpad[816]` + `scores[60]` + `parts[2048]` + `wsh[4096]` floats = 28,080 B of 32 KB (85.7%, headroom 4,688 B; block-0:15,22-25). Phases per row:

- **(a) `x` staging + `parts` zeroing (block-0:27-33, 1 barrier).** `x[row]` (768 bf16 → f32) into padded `xpad[(d>>4)*17+(d&15)]` (one pad float per BK=16 chunk); `parts[2048]` zeroed (8 floats/thread). On the `rows == 1` path both `parts` and `wsh` are then never read — the zeroing is dead work at 1 row (entry 2).
- **(b) GEMV branch, `rows == 1` only (block-0:35-55).** 8 simdgroups; simdgroup `sg` takes experts `sg, sg+8, …`; each lane serially sums 24 products from padded `xpad` and `w_router` read straight from device (uncoalesced by expert), shuffle tree 16,8,4,2,1, lane 0 writes `scores[e]`. This branch carries the largest relative win (0.72× compiled).
- **(c) Staged scalar path, `rows > 1` (block-0:56-128).** Partition geometry (block-0:57-75): at every decode size 2–32, `tm = 1`, `ratio = 24`, so `partitions = 32`, `base_iters = 1`, last partition absorbing chunks 31–47 (the graded 8/32 and every ungraded 2–7/9–31 run this exact configuration — hyp-3 boundary check, frozen). 12 groups of 4 K-chunks (block-0:76-120): coalesced `float4` staging of `w_router` into transposed `wsh[slot][k][expert]` (stride 64), barrier, scalar FMAs resuming `parts[p*64+e]` in increasing `d`, barrier — 24 barriers in the loop, 27 per row total (block-0:33,94,119,129,137). Scalar duty: groups at `gbase` 0–28 run 240/256 threads (94%); the four groups at `gbase` 32–44 touch only partition 31 and run 60/256 (23%) — one third of all K-chunks (16 of 48) issue through a quarter of the lanes at every decode size (recomputed from block-0:75,96-101). Final sequential partial sum 60/256 threads (block-0:121-127). Per-row device traffic: the full 184,320 B `w_router` re-read, private to each row's threadgroup (entry 1).
- **(d) Verbatim sigmoid (block-0:131-137).** `1/(1+precise::exp(abs(s)))`, `(s<0)?y:1-y`, 60 of 256 threads. MLX's exact form; not a cost item.
- **(e) Serial thread-0 top-4 + weights (block-0:139-174).** Strictly-greater insertion over 60 biased scores (`scores[e] + bias[e]`, `bias` read from device by thread 0 alone), earliest index wins ties; `((s0+s1)+s2)+s3 + 1e-20f`, divide, ×2.5. 255 threads idle through it, after the last barrier, on every row at every size.

- **Callers:** the grader builds it via `slots.build` into one `mx.fast.metal_kernel` (`bench/grader/slots.py:303-345`) and calls it once per layer per size in G2 and in the chained two-phase piece timing; above `max_rows` (and below `min_rows` when set) `run()` dispatches to `mx.compile(ref_routing)` instead (`slots.py:338-345`). In the model it replaces the routing part of `make_moe_call` (`slots.py:97-119`). Kernel-visible shapes: rows 1–32 only (grid `rows*256`).
- **Callees:** none inside the kernels — 1 kernel/layer (20/step) where the reference launches ~12/layer (brief:49). Above 32 rows the callee is the compiled reference itself.
- **Data:** in: `x` [rows,768] bfloat16, `w_router` [60,768] float32, `bias` [60] float32; out: `inds` [rows,4] uint32, `weights` [rows,4] float32 (`spec.json:1`; brief:32-38). All row-contiguous (brief:26). Threadgroup 28,080 B, row-count independent. `w_router` is the same 184,320 B buffer for all 20 layers' calls in a step, re-read per row per layer by construction.
- **Neighbours:** before: post-attention layernorm output reshaped to [rows,768] (`mobilemoe.py` `MoE.__call__`, `slots.py:107`); after: experts gather by `inds`, combine sums `(y * weights[...,None])` in emitted order (`slots.py:51-52`). A replacement must keep shapes, dtypes, the unbiased-score rule and the reference's exact per-row order.
- **Cost:** chained µs/layer in the table above (measured, piece: `attempt-6/grade.json` and `results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/grade-routing-attempt-6.json`). Traffic per layer rows×184,320 B (`w_router`) + rows×1,536 B (`x`): floors 0.9/7.4/29.7 µs at 1/8/32 rows (200 GB/s). End to end (measured, whole request: round-3 ready check + Claude's G3): routing-alone decode medians −0.38/−0.31/−0.59/−0.48 ms vs the unchanged model at 1×128/8×128/32×128/32×1024 (swarm) and −0.41/−0.31/−0.61/−0.62 (Claude); vs the compiled reference it separates only where ranges miss (see headline).
- **Invariants:** G1+G2 pass at all six sizes in both runs (`rows_differ` 0, `max_rel_err` 0.0). Bit-exactness rests on: exact bf16→f32 cast of `x`; the `rows`-branched regime matching MLX's dispatch (GEMV at `rows == 1`, split-K while `rows <= 768`) with partition counts from the `rows`-only formula; scalar≡MMA rounding at every grouping (proven rounds 2–3); verbatim sigmoid; strictly-greater tie rule; `((s0+s1)+s2)+s3 + 1e-20` fold. Feeding changes (staging, barriers, thread mapping, cross-row sharing) that keep each row's accumulation order keep G2 — attempt-4 proved it against attempt-3, and round 3's sharing kernel (attempt-5) proved it again for a different feeding. Anything that reorders one expert's serial chain (e.g. sharding one expert's K across threads) fails G2 (hyp-3, builder-3-c, frozen).

### 2. `spec.json` (1 line) and the hand-off

- **Callers/callees/data/neighbours:** declares the single kernel `fused_routing_exact` (inputs `x`, `w_router`, `bias`; outputs `inds`, `weights`; header block 1 = `#include <metal_simdgroup>`), `"max_rows": 32`, no `min_rows`. `slots.build` validates both hand-off keys (int ≥ 1, `min_rows <= max_rows`; `slots.py:330-337`).
- **Cost:** the hand-off is the whole prefill story: at 127/1,016/2,048 rows the candidate *is* the compiled reference, reported `handed off` under the round-4 grader (no paired timing, no identical-code verdict risk — the round-3 attempt-1 8/30 `slower` noise event is retired by construction). The choice of 32 is the bottom of the boundary's 32–126 window (hyp-3 boundary, frozen): every decode step (1–32 rows, brief:26) stays on the kernels, and no graded prefill size runs them. Kernel-visible band 33–126 in real serving (chunked prefill) does not exist for this attempt — counts above 32 hand off in serving too.
- **Invariants:** `min_rows` is available in round 4 (brief:174) but this slot does not need it: the kernel wins at 1 row in both runs (0.72–0.78× compiled, 28–29 wins), the strongest relative margin of the three decode sizes. Handing 1 row off would surrender that win and, in a set with an experts `min_rows: 2` attempt, leave 1-request decode with no routing contribution. `atomic_outputs` false; grid counts threads (brief:180).

### 3. The measurement tables

- `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6/grade.json` (frozen): G2 pass ×6; decode `faster` ×3 (28/27/25 wins), prefill `same` ×3 timed against identical code; `beats_compiled` true.
- `results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/grade-routing-attempt-6.json`: Claude's re-grade with the round-4 grader — decode `faster` ×3 (29/26/27), prefill `handed off` ×3, `beats_compiled` true. The current piece-timing source for this territory.
- `muse-spark/round-3/checks/ready-1/ready-verdict.json`: the swarm's G3 — `muse-routing` fail vs compiled-routing (8×128 overlap), `muse-all` pass in that run.
- `results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-3/g3-vllm.json` + `claude/findings/muse-round-3.md` §§1–2: Claude's G3 — `muse-routing` fail vs both bars somewhere, pair fail vs `compiled-all` at 32×1024 only; decode-step medians and the 0.9% figure.
- Round-3 frozen analysis: `territory-baseline-routing.md` (the code's anatomy), `ineff-baseline-routing-1.md` (confirmed: per-row re-read priced at prefill), `ineff-baseline-routing-2.md` (confirmed: staged shape priced at prefill), `implementation/hyp-3-routing-prefill.md` (six attempts: hand-off attempts 1/6 the only `beats_compiled`; GEMM-sharing attempts 2/4 G1-fail on the per-pipeline thread cap 640→576, attempt-5 exact but 1.44/2.52/3.50× off compiled at prefill with decode `same` at 8/32; narrower-footprint attempt-3 flipped decode to `same` on a ~2–3 µs copy launch).

## Relations

- **Fed by:** the model territory (layernorm output `x`; router weight and `expert_bias`); the grader territory (`max_rows`/`min_rows` dispatch in `slots.build`, the `handed off` verdict, chained timing).
- **Feeds:** `baseline-experts` (`inds` chooses the (row, expert) pairs and their order); `baseline-combine` (`weights` multiply the experts' outputs in emitted order — the reason order is part of G2); `g3` (the pair's 32×1024 margin is the binding set constraint; routing's 32-row piece margin is the largest single routing contribution to it).
- **Shared constraint:** per-slot wins are not assumed to compose (round-4 README item 3, the three-slot interaction); both entries below price routing alone, and the set's margin is measured only by the ready check timing `muse-all`.

## Inefficiencies

- `ineff-baseline-routing-1` — the per-row `w_router` re-read at decode sizes: rows×184 KB per layer where the compiled reference reads it once; traffic excess 0/6.5/28.6 µs/layer at 1/8/32 rows against a current margin of 17.7/15.8/19.7 µs/layer. Predicted saving (upper bound, overlap-discounted in the entry): 0/0.13/0.57 ms per decode step, 0 at prefill by hand-off construction.
- `ineff-baseline-routing-2` — the staged scalar path's shape cost at decode sizes: 27 barriers/row, the last third of K-chunks at 23% thread duty, 28,080 B footprint, dead `parts` zeroing at 1 row, serial thread-0 tail. Predicted saving bounded in the entry; every µs/layer removed widens the 32-row margin 1:1.

{"path":"muse-spark/round-4/exploration/ineff-baseline-routing-1.md","content":"# Inefficiency: `w_router` re-read once per row at decode sizes — traffic excess larger than the whole 32-row margin

- **Owner:** explorer-baseline-routing
- **Status:** open
- **Version:** 1
- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T21:43:26Z
- **Next:** verifier to check the decode repricing against both grade runs; a builder needs a barrier-light sharing design proven on the chained timing

## Slot

`routing`

## What happens

Every row's threadgroup streams its own full copy of the router weight from device memory. On the staged scalar path (`rows > 1`) all 256 threads cooperatively load all 48 K-chunks × 60 experts as `float4`s into `wsh` across the 12 groups (`muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6/block-0.metal:81-93`, the code in the slot); in the GEMV branch (`rows == 1`) each lane reads `w_router` straight from device (block-0:41-45). Nothing is shared across rows: per layer the kernel reads rows × 60×768×4 B = rows × 184,320 B of `w_router`, plus rows × 1,536 B of `x`. The compiled reference's GEMM/GEMV reads `w_router` once per layer and reuses each tile across rows (round-2 `territory-baseline-routing.md` §3.1, frozen).

This is the decode slice of round 2's `ineff-baseline-routing-4` (frozen, confirmed, upper-bound-only) and round 3's `ineff-baseline-routing-1` (frozen, confirmed), repriced because the context changed twice over: (1) `max_rows: 32` in `spec.json` now hands every prefill size to the compiled reference, so the prefill side of those entries — 116.1/935.4/1,886.5 µs/layer at 127/1,016/2,048 rows — is banked and costs nothing; what remains is exactly the decode side they ranked as not worth chasing. (2) The round-4 question is no longer beating the compiled reference (the starting point does, at every decode size) but *widening the margin*, above all at 32 rows for the 32×1024 set workload (round-4 exploration README item 2). At 32 rows the re-read excess is larger than the entire margin there is to widen.

## Cost

Traffic floors at the 200 GB/s peak (brief:9), candidate per layer; measured = chained µs/layer, candidate vs compiled reference, from the two runs of the identical bytes (`muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6/grade.json`; `results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/grade-routing-attempt-6.json`):

| rows | `w_router` read | floor (w+x) | measured cand / compiled (re-grade) | margin | excess over read-once |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.18 MB | 0.9 µs | 45.1 / 62.8 | 17.7 µs | 0 µs |
| 8 | 1.47 MB | 7.4 µs | 144.2 / 160.0 | 15.8 µs | 6.5 µs |
| 32 | 5.90 MB | 29.7 µs | 151.3 / 171.0 | 19.7 µs | 28.6 µs |
| 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 | — (handed off) | — | `handed off` | — | 0 (compiled reference runs) |

The excess is (rows−1) × 184,320 B ÷ 200 GB/s. At 32 rows the excess floor (28.6 µs/layer) is 1.45× the whole measured margin over the compiled reference (19.7 µs/layer, re-grade; 19.8 in the round-3 grade) — the only pool inside this slot big enough, on its own, to supply the +7.5–12.5 µs/layer (routing+combine combined) that non-overlap at 32×1024 needs (territory entry, headline). At 8 rows the excess (6.5) is 41% of the margin (15.8); at 1 row there is no excess (a single row reads the weight once by definition).

The floor is an upper bound, not time on the clock. The kernel is overhead-bound at decode sizes, and the staging loads overlap other resident threadgroups' scalar compute: the starting point's own measurements put the marginal cost of rows 9–32 at ≈0.16 µs/row (`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-4/notes.md`, flat 69.1→72.9 µs from 8 to 32 rows), against a 0.92 µs/row traffic floor — at most ~17% of the floor appears as marginal time, and a sharing design still pays its own staging and barriers out of that. The measured counter-evidence stands: round 1's attempt-2 tiled `w_router` across 8 rows to remove this re-read and was slower at every decode size (36.3/34.9/49.0 vs 28.5/23.6/41.8 µs/layer, `muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-2/notes.md`, frozen), and round 3's sharing kernel (attempt-5) proved cross-row sharing bit-exact but ran it only above 32 rows — no sharing design has ever been timed at decode sizes 2–32.

## Kind

Overhead-bound at decode sizes with a bandwidth-waste component (`claude/GLOSSARY.md:39-42`; at 32 rows 5.90 MB in ~132–151 µs is ≈40 GB/s, a fifth of peak — the waste is real bytes but the time is not byte-limited). At prefill sizes: not applicable — the kernels do not run there.

## Spans

`baseline-routing`. The comparison point (read-once tile reuse) is MLX's GEMM dispatch behind the compiled reference; the prize lands in `g3` territory (the set's 32×1024 margin), and any design must keep the `max_rows: 32` hand-off in `grader` territory's dispatch terms.

## Predicted saving

Upper bound if each weight byte were read once per layer at peak bandwidth, per layer and per decode step (×20 layers); prefill 0 at every size by hand-off construction (the design runs only where the kernels already run, `rows <= 32`, and changes no prefill path — so it cannot cost the other phase):

| rows | per layer | per decode step |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 µs | 0 ms |
| 8 | 6.5 µs | 0.13 ms |
| 32 | 28.6 µs | 0.57 ms |
| 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 | 0 µs | 0 ms per prefill chunk |

Arithmetic: (rows−1) × 184,320 B ÷ 200 GB/s; at 32 rows 31 × 184,320 B = 5.71 MB ÷ 200 GB/s = 28.6 µs/layer × 20 = 0.57 ms/step. Confidence is low that more than a fraction is realised — the overlap account above caps the plausibly recoverable slice at roughly the 0.16 µs/row marginal (≈3.8 µs/layer ≈ 0.08 ms/step at 32 rows) unless the design also removes staging latency the current kernel hides by overlap. Label: prediction, counting only this slot's own effect; it stands beside a builder's same-run chained measurement before anyone banks it.

What a builder needs: cross-row `w_router` sharing that keeps every row's exact accumulation order (sharing bytes is free; reordering any row's serial chain fails G2 — hyp-3 boundary, frozen) without round-1 attempt-2's barrier structure. Hard constraints already measured: threadgroups of 960 and 600 threads fail G1 on a per-pipeline cap that moved 640→576 between recompiles (round-3 attempts 2/4), while 480 threads (8 rows × 60 experts) is the proven-passing band (attempt-5); attempt-5's own named next probe — stage each `w` chunk once per group while streaming 2–4 sequential row-blocks through it, cutting traffic and barriers per row 2–4× with no more threads — is untested, and untested at decode sizes in any form. A rows-conditional design (shared path only at, say, 16–32 rows where the excess exceeds ~14 µs/layer, staged path kept below) keeps the proven 1/8-row paths untouched; the branch must be on `rows` regimes, never on the graded values.

{"path":"muse-spark/round-4/exploration/ineff-baseline-routing-2.md","content":"# Inefficiency: the staged scalar path's shape cost at decode sizes — 27 barriers, a 23%-duty tail third, serial tails

- **Owner:** explorer-baseline-routing
- **Status:** open
- **Version:** 1
- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T21:43:44Z
- **Next:** verifier to check the duty/barrier counts and the residual table; builders take only the exact-preserving items listed

## Slot

`routing`

## What happens

Past the bytes in `ineff-baseline-routing-1`, the staged scalar path that runs at every decode size above 1 row pays a per-row shape cost in `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6/block-0.metal` (the code in the slot). Round 3's `ineff-baseline-routing-2` (frozen, confirmed) priced this shape at *prefill* sizes and put the decode saving at ~0 because the candidate's residual already beat the compiled reference's overhead. That verdict stands; what is new in round 4 is the question — not "reach the compiled reference's overhead" but "cut the candidate's own residual", since every µs/layer cut at 32 rows widens the set's 32×1024 margin 1:1 (territory entry, headline). The items, all inside one 256-thread threadgroup per row:

1. **27 barriers per row.** The 12 staged groups pay 2 `threadgroup_barrier`s each (stage-then-compute block-0:94, compute-then-overwrite block-0:119), plus 3 outside the loop (block-0:33,129,137). Every barrier stalls the whole threadgroup; the `rows == 1` GEMV branch pays only the 3 outside ones.
2. **The last third of K-chunks runs at 23% thread duty.** At every decode size 2–32 the partition formula (block-0:57-75) gives 32 partitions, `base_iters = 1`, the last partition absorbing chunks 31–47. Groups at `gbase` 0–28 therefore touch 4 partitions and run 240/256 threads (94%); the four groups at `gbase` 32–44 touch only partition 31 and run 60/256 threads (23.4%, block-0:99-101) — 16 of 48 chunks (33% of each row's 46,080 FMAs) issue through a quarter of the lanes, behind the same 2 barriers per group as the full groups. The final sequential partial sum also runs 60/256 (block-0:121-127). Recomputed from the formula this round; the graded 8/32 and every ungraded 2–7/9–31 share this geometry.
3. **28,080 B threadgroup footprint** (`xpad[816]` + `scores[60]` + `parts[2048]` + `wsh[4096]` floats, block-0:15,22-25) — 85.7% of the 32 KB limit, 4,688 B of headroom. At decode sizes the starting point's own account says this does not yet bind (flat 69→73 µs from 8 to 32 rows as staging/barriers overlap across resident threadgroups, `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-4/notes.md`); it is a constraint on fixes, not a measured decode cost — wider staging is already proven infeasible (6 chunks/group needs 36,272 B with `parts`, 8 chunks/group needs 32,768 B of `wsh` alone; hyp-3 builder-3-c, frozen), and the round-3 verifier flagged the residency mechanism itself as unmeasured.
4. **Dead work at `rows == 1`.** Lines 27–32 stage `xpad` and zero `parts[2048]` (8 floats per thread) before the branch; the GEMV branch (block-0:35-55) then reads neither `parts` nor `wsh`. The zeroing is pure waste on the 1-row path, in front of a barrier.
5. **Serial tails.** The sigmoid runs 60/256 threads (block-0:132-136); the top-4 + weights fold is thread 0 alone (block-0:139-174): 60 strictly-greater insertion iterations, each adding a `bias[e]` it loads from device itself, then 4 divisions — 255 threads idle after the last barrier, on every row at every size. (Unchanged since round 1; round 2's entry 3 priced it as lost in the fixed cost, which was the right call at prefill scale and is re-listed here only because the round-4 prize is single-digit µs/layer.)

Items 1–2 cannot be fixed by rebalancing accumulation: the partition grouping *is* the reference's split-K rounding order (changing partition boundaries or sharding one expert's K across threads reorders a serial chain and fails G2 — hyp-3 boundary and builder-3-c, frozen). What remains legal is feeding: let the 196 idle threads in tail groups pre-stage or pre-load instead of waiting at barriers, and delete dead work — changes that keep every row's accumulation order and so keep G2, as attempt-4 itself proved against attempt-3.

## Cost

Measured chained µs/layer (candidate) minus the traffic floor from `ineff-baseline-routing-1` (200 GB/s), both runs of the identical bytes; compiled overhead ≈ compiled total minus its own ~0.9 µs read-once floor:

| rows | measured (re-grade / round-3 grade) | traffic floor | candidate residual | compiled overhead (re-grade) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 45.1 / 51.7 | 0.9 µs | 44.2 / 50.8 µs | ~61.9 µs |
| 8 | 144.2 / 90.9 | 7.4 µs | 136.8 / 83.5 µs | ~159.1 µs |
| 32 | 151.3 / 132.2 | 29.7 µs | 121.6 / 102.5 µs | ~170.1 µs |
| 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 | `handed off` | — | 0 (kernels do not run) | — |

Kernels × fixed cost: 1 kernel/layer here against the reference's ~12 (brief:49), so the residual is not launch count — it is the chained per-call floor (shared with the compiled reference, whose overhead is larger at every decode size) plus the per-threadgroup shape above. The residual therefore *overstates* what this entry can claim: the shape-attributable slice inside it (barrier exposure, tail-group latency, serial tails, dead zeroing) has never been decomposed by measurement, and the one barrier-cost datum in the tree is inferred and confounded (round 3's sharing kernel: ~3.2 µs/group overhead against ~0.8 modelled, "barriers ~2 µs each or ~4× occupancy serialisation, inferred", hyp-3 attempt-5). At decode sizes the overlap across 8–32 resident threadgroups hides much of the barrier/staging latency the prefill pricing exposed (round-3 entry 2's residual grew with rows; the decode residual does not scale per row — 136.8 µs at 8 rows vs 121.6 at 32 in the same run, i.e. rows past the first are nearly free).

## Kind

Overhead-bound (`claude/GLOSSARY.md:39-42`): time goes to barriers, idle thread slots and the chained fixed floor, not to bytes (entry 1) or FLOPs (46,080 FMA/row ≈ 0.01 µs at peak compute). At prefill sizes: not applicable — handed off.

## Spans

`baseline-routing`; the prize lands in `g3` (set margin at 32×1024). This entry owns the per-threadgroup shape; `ineff-baseline-routing-1` owns the bytes. The two do not add beyond the candidate's measured total, and neither adds beyond the residual-plus-floor decomposition of it.

## Predicted saving

Upper bound: the shape-attributable slice of the candidate residual above — unmeasured, so no single figure is claimed. Bounded sub-items, per layer (×20 for per-step), prediction only, counting only this slot's own effect, prefill 0 at every size (nothing here runs above `max_rows: 32`, so the other phase cannot be cost):

- **Dead `parts` zeroing at 1 row** (item 4): removing 2,048 threadgroup writes in front of a barrier is worth at most their issue/mem time — sub-µs/layer; certain in direction, negligible in size. 0 at 8/32 rows (the zeroing is used there).
- **Tail-group feeding overlap** (items 1–2): if the four 23%-duty groups' exposed staging/barrier latency were fully hidden by idle-thread pre-staging, the saving is at most those groups' barrier-to-barrier time beyond their 16-FMA-per-thread scalar chain — with the tree's only barrier datum (~2 µs/barrier, inferred, prefill-confounded) as an outer envelope, ≤ ~8 barriers' worth ≈ single-digit µs/layer at 8/32 rows, 0.02 ms/step per µs/layer at 32 rows. Realised value is likely well under the envelope because cross-threadgroup overlap already hides part of it at decode sizes.
- **Serial tails** (item 5): parallelising the sigmoid is already 60-wide; the thread-0 scan could be widened only by a parallel top-4 that reproduces the strictly-greater, earliest-index-wins tie order bit-exactly (a tree reduction with index-ordered tie-breaking does, in principle) — worth at most the scan's serial latency, unmeasured, plausibly ~1 µs/layer at every decode size.

Total honest expectation: single-digit µs/layer at 32 rows — material only combined with `ineff-baseline-routing-1` and the combine slot's margin against the +7.5–12.5 µs/layer (routing+combine) that 32×1024 non-overlap needs, and each item must be proven on the same-run chained timing (round 3's lesson: a ~2–3 µs copy launch flipped decode `faster` to `same`, attempt-3). A builder who cannot decompose the residual first should treat this entry as a list of legal micro-directions, not a banked saving.

## Verdict

# Inefficiency: the routing+combine pair keeps only −0.36 of its −0.66 ms/step piece win vs the compiled reference at 32×1024, inside the repeat spread

- **Owner:** explorer-g3
- **Status:** open
- **Version:** 1
- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T21:42:54Z
- **Next:** builders widening routing/combine decode margin at 32 rows answer this; verifier to check the arithmetic

## Slot

Outside the slots — the routing+combine set as timed in `muse-all` (routing attempt-6 + combine attempt-2, `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6`, `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/combine/attempt-2`). Measurement side owned by territory `g3`; kernel-side margin owned by territories `baseline-routing` and `baseline-combine`.

## What happens

The chained piece timing prices the pair at −0.656 ms/step vs the compiled reference at 32 decode rows (routing −0.396 + combine −0.260; [territory-g3.md](territory-g3.md) piece 1). Timed whole in vLLM at 32 requests, the pair keeps −0.548 ms/step at 32×128 and only **−0.362 ms/step at 32×1024** in Claude's G3 (medians 38.765 vs 39.127 ms, **0.93% apart, 5-repeat ranges [38.589–39.080] vs [38.912–39.400] overlapping**, so `muse-all` vs `compiled-all` decode is `same` and G3 fails on this one workload). In the swarm's ready check the same workload keeps −0.588 (38.942 vs 39.530, 1.49%) and the ranges miss, so the pair passes there. The verdict flips between two runs of identical kernels while every median favours the pair. Full derivation in [territory-g3.md](territory-g3.md) gap 1.

## Cost

Shortfall = (measured, whole-request change vs `compiled-all`) − (piece-implied change vs compiled, candidate − compiled × 20 layers), ms per decode step. Piece from the two `grade.json` (routing 132.2 vs 152.0, combine 32.7 vs 45.7 µs/layer at 32 rows; at 1/8 rows routing 51.7/90.9 vs 66.3/104.0, combine 31.8/34.7 vs 36.9/41.1); measured from `results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-3/console-vllm.txt` summary medians (cross-checked in `muse-vllm.jsonl`) and `muse-spark/round-3/checks/ready-1/ready-verdict.json` `medians`.

| Workload | Piece vs compiled | Claude G3 vs compiled | Shortfall (Claude) | Swarm vs compiled | Shortfall (swarm) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1×128 (1 row) | −0.394 | −0.436 | −0.042 | −0.491 | −0.097 |
| 8×128 (8 rows) | −0.390 | −0.375 | +0.015 | −0.446 | −0.056 |
| 32×128 (32 rows) | −0.656 | −0.548 | +0.108 | −0.483 | +0.173 |
| 32×1024 (32 rows) | −0.656 | **−0.362** | **+0.294** | −0.588 | +0.068 |

Per layer at 32×1024 (÷20): +14.7 µs (Claude) / +3.4 µs (swarm); the two runs disagree by 0.226 ms/step, the same order as the larger shortfall, so the solid cost is the **margin**, not a fixed 0.294: the pair's separation from the compiled bar at 32×1024 is 0.36–0.59 ms/step (0.9–1.5%) against per-run 5-repeat spreads of ~0.49 ms (pair) and ~0.49 ms (compiled) wide. To have separated in Claude's draw the pair needed roughly a further 0.17 ms/step (its max 39.080 below the compiled min 38.912). At 1 row with long prompts the piece sum transfers fully (measured −0.428 at 1×1024, −0.487 at 1×7936 vs piece −0.394; [territory-g3.md](territory-g3.md) piece 4), so the shortfall needs 32 rows, and grows again with context at fixed 32 rows.

In kernel terms: the pair removes 280 kernels/step vs base (1087→807 at 32 rows) and 180 vs `compiled-all` (987→807), exactly additive, tokens bit-exact — kernel count and correctness are not the cost. The slots' own traffic is unchanged by context while the step grows 30.1→39.4 ms from 32×128 to 32×1024; the lost time scales with neither.

## Kind

Overhead-bound (in the terms of `claude/GLOSSARY.md`): the step is far from peak bandwidth and peak compute, and the shortfall scales with neither weight bytes nor kernel count. Ruled out: the kernels' own chained work (both `faster` at every decode size, piece 1), token divergence (exact everywhere), prompt length alone (piece 4). Not ruled out: a fixed in-step composition cost at 32 rows that the chained timing cannot see, vs machine drift across runs (swap 13.9–14.2 GB) — the two runs bound the sum at +0.07 to +0.29 ms/step without separating them.

## Spans

`g3` (measurement), `baseline-routing`, `baseline-combine` (any exact kernel change that widens the 32-row decode margin), `grader` (the 5-repeat range rule that prices a ~1% margin by chance; unchanged for round 4).

## Predicted saving

If the pair's full piece win transferred at 32 rows, the step gains back the shortfall: up to **0.29 ms/step at 32 requests in Claude's draw (0.07 in the swarm's)**, i.e. `muse-all` would measure ≈ −0.66 ms/step vs `compiled-all` at both 32-row workloads instead of −0.55 / −0.36; ~0 claimed at 1/8 requests, where G3 already meets or beats the piece sum. The decision-relevant saving is smaller and sharper: **~0.17 ms/step of extra separation at 32×1024** would have made the ranges miss in Claude's run and turned the pair's one failing workload into a pass. At prefill sizes nothing is predicted: prompts are already 1.6–3.1% faster than base and slower nowhere (routing handed off, combine `faster` at 127/1,016/2,048 rows), so no per-chunk saving exists on either basis. This is an upper bound on the prize, not a prediction that a specific kernel change recovers it: no mechanism is confirmed, any widening must hold bit-exact G2 at all six sizes, and a decode saving bought with prefill time is not one.

## Verdict

(verifier writes here)
