## Starting point

Round 4 is the last round ([ADR 0014](../../../claude/adr/0014-muse-wonder-last-round.md)). It builds on rounds 1–3 as measured independently by Claude in [`claude/findings/muse-round-3.md`](../../../claude/findings/muse-round-3.md). Round 3 ran as Muse Spark (model `muse-spark-1.3-contributor`, skill version 8) and submitted the reference in every slot: no candidate passed the ready check alone, and the skill then counted only candidates that pass alone. Round 4 changes three rules ([ADR 0015](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)): candidates that pass together in `muse-all` are `ready` as a **set**; an attempt may hand off inputs below `min_rows` as well as above `max_rows`; and a handed-off size is reported `handed off` instead of being timed. A slot's **baseline** is still its best attempt so far that passes the current G2, has `beats_compiled` true in the grader, and passes G3 ([ADR 0011](../../../claude/adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). **No slot has a baseline.** The bar in every slot is the compiled reference, and a new attempt must beat it in the same grader run (no `--baseline` argument). Round 4 runs as Muse Wonder (muse-wonder-1.0).

### Per slot

#### `experts` — starting point `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1`

- **What it is.** Round 2's fused per-pair kernel, byte-identical, plus `max_rows: 59` in `spec.json`: rows 1–59 run the fused kernel, rows above 59 run the compiled reference. See `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1/notes.md` and its `grade.json` (G1 pass, G2 differ 0 at all six sizes).
- **Piece timing** (chained µs per layer, candidate vs compiled, its own grade run): 1 row 96.9 vs 86.6 (`slower`, 5 wins); 8 rows 168.9 vs 238.2 (`faster`, 29 wins); 32 rows 554.7 vs 883.4 (`faster`, 29 wins); prefill 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 `same` (19 / 15 / 16 wins — the hand-off runs compiled code). `beats_compiled` false: decode `slower` on the 1-row size alone.
- **G3 effect.** Never timed end to end (round 3, section 4). Its ancestor (round 2 attempt-7, same kernels without the hand-off) shortened the decode step 17.5% with 32 requests but made prompt processing 6.6–14.5× slower; the hand-off removes the prefill half of that, so no G3 prediction from round 3 stands — Claude's reading is that only the 1-row gap remains.
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** It is not a baseline because `beats_compiled` is false — the 1-row decode loss (96.9 vs 86.6 µs/layer) — and it has no G3 pass. Round 3 tried a vectorised scalar path (attempt-2, bought nothing) and an unfused path copying the reference's structure (attempt-5, 2× worse at 1 row) and concluded no fix existed in the spec surface. From round 4 the surface has `min_rows`: `min_rows: 2` with `max_rows: 59` hands 1-row inputs to the compiled reference while keeping the 8/32-row wins — a direction not yet graded. It can then pass G3 only in a set whose other kernels are faster with 1 request, because with 1 request every decode step runs MLX's own code for this slot.
- **Where it still spends its time.** At 8/32 rows it already wins by 69.3 / 328.7 µs per layer; what remains is the 1-row chain (the `tg_x` load, silu and barrier chain named in round 3) — now hand-off-able — and per-pair weight re-reads at all sizes (552,960 B per pair, round 3's entry).

#### `routing` — starting point `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6`

- **What it is.** Round 2's staged scalar-exact kernel (attempt-4 kernels) with `max_rows: 32`: every decode step (1–32 rows) runs the staged scalar kernels, all prefill sizes run the compiled reference. Attempt-6 is a byte-identical re-grade of round 3's attempt-1 (empty `diff` on both blocks and `spec.json`), run to test whether attempt-1's 2,048-row `slower` on identical code reproduced; it did not (19/30 wins, `same`). See `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6/notes.md`.
- **Piece timing.** Round 3's grade: decode `faster` at all three sizes (candidate 51.7 / 90.9 / 132.2 vs compiled 66.3 / 104.0 / 152.0 µs per layer; 28 / 27 / 25 wins), prefill `same` at all three sizes. Claude's re-grade with the round-4 grader ([`results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/`](../../../results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/)): decode `faster` (29 / 26 / 27 wins; candidate 0.72 / 0.90 / 0.88 of the compiled reference at 1 / 8 / 32 rows), the three prefill sizes `handed off`, `beats_compiled` true.
- **G3 effect.** In round 3's swarm ready check it failed alone against `compiled-routing` at 8×128 on overlapping ranges, with no phase slower anywhere (decode medians −0.38 / −0.31 / −0.59 / −0.48 ms vs the unchanged model at 1×128 / 8×128 / 32×128 / 32×1024). Claude's G3 agreed: `same` as `compiled-routing` at 8×128. Together with combine attempt-2 (`muse-all`) it passed the swarm's ready check but failed Claude's G3 against `compiled-all` at 32×1024, where the medians are 0.9% apart with overlapping ranges.
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** G3 alone: it passes G2 and has `beats_compiled` true, but it has never passed G3, alone or (in Claude's run) as a pair. Under round 4's set rule the pair would have been `ready` in round 3, but a set still has to pass G3 as `muse-all`, so the pair is no baseline.
- **Where it still spends its time.** Decode wins at every size; the open question is margin, above all at 32×1024 where the pair gains only 0.25–0.30 ms over the compiled reference (~1%), inside the 5-repeat spread. The per-row `w_router` re-read is untouched (upper bound only, round 2's `ineff-baseline-routing-4`).

#### `combine` — starting point `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/combine/attempt-2`

- **What it is.** Round 2's attempt-1 kernel with its seven `volatile` rounding barriers replaced by seven plain `float` locals and a header block (`block-1.metal`) carrying `#pragma STDC FP_CONTRACT OFF` / `#pragma clang fp contract(off)`: same 7-op stepwise fold `((p0+p1)+p2)+p3`, same grid (`rows*768`) and threadgroup [256,1,1], no `max_rows`. See `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/combine/attempt-2/notes.md`.
- **Piece timing.** Round 3's grade: `faster` at all six sizes (decode 31.8 / 34.7 / 32.7 vs compiled 36.9 / 41.1 / 45.7 µs per layer, 24 / 27 / 30 wins; prefill 38.2 / 100.9 / 198.0 vs 64.0 / 281.8 / 556.2, 30 / 30 / 29 wins); `beats_compiled` true in both phases. Absolute chained times drift up to ~35% between runs on this machine (round 3's lesson), so only same-run paired verdicts transfer.
- **G3 effect.** In round 3's ready check it failed alone against the unchanged model at 1×128 on a single outlier repeat (5.892 ms, above the unchanged model's lowest 5.430) and, in Claude's G3, against `compiled-combine` at 32×128 and 32×1024 — again range overlaps with no phase slower anywhere (swarm decode medians −0.53 / −0.59 / −0.44 / −0.26 ms vs the unchanged model). Its ancestor's in-step cost (+1.05 ms/step at 32 requests from the volatile barriers) is what the pragma removes; round 3's measured decode medians favour the kernel everywhere.
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** G3 alone, on spread: every median favours it, but the 5-repeat ranges overlap the bars'. No kernel change is named that tightens spread on 7 plain ops (round 3's implementation README); as part of a set it already passes `muse-all` in the swarm's run.
- **Where it still spends its time.** Nothing further in the grader — it sits on the chained floor and wins at all six sizes. What remains is the same margin question as routing: more separation from the compiled reference at 32×128 and 32×1024, or a set that clears the bar together.

#### All three together

Round 3's pair (routing attempt-6 + combine attempt-2) is the best result of any round: against the unchanged model it shortens the decode step 16.5% / 5.4% / 2.8% / 1.6% and whole requests 14.1% / 5.6% / 2.1% / 2.4% at 1×128 / 8×128 / 32×128 / 32×1024, with prompts 1.6–3.1% faster and nothing slower — but it fails G3 against `compiled-all` at 32×1024 (0.9% median gap, overlapping ranges). About half the gain over the unchanged model is `mx.compile` of the two slots' reference code alone. The three-slot composition is untested: in rounds 1 and 2, replacing all three slots at once lost about 2.8 ms with 8 requests for an unknown reason, and round 3 installed no experts candidate, so no run since has met it.

### What is left

Ranked by predicted saving against the compiled reference (no slot has a baseline, so the reference is the bar everywhere). Claude's measurement names three things round 4 has to find out; the ranking follows them.

1. **Experts with `min_rows`.** Whether attempt-1's 8/32-row speed (168.9 vs 238.2 and 554.7 vs 883.4 µs per layer) carries into G3 once 1 row runs MLX's own code (`min_rows: 2`, `max_rows: 59`). This is the only ungraded direction in any slot and the largest piece saving left: the 8/32-row wins are 69.3 / 328.7 µs per layer, worth (PREDICTION, from those same-run margins × 20 layers) about 1.4 ms per step at 8 requests and 6.6 ms at 32 requests against the compiled reference, with prefill `handed off` above 59 rows and 1-row decode `handed off` — so the gain exists only at 8 and 32 requests, and G3 can pass only in a set whose other kernels win with 1 request. The risk is the three-slot interaction (item 3).
2. **A margin at 32×1024.** The pair gains 0.25–0.30 ms over the compiled reference there (~1%), which 5 repeats cannot tell from noise; a set needs more than that with 32 long prompts. This is a margin problem in routing and/or combine decode kernels, not a correctness one: both starting points are bit-exact and already `faster` at every graded size, so any new attempt must widen the same-run margin at decode sizes without touching prefill (`max_rows: 32` for routing, faster-everywhere for combine). A saving here is worth the difference between a passing and a failing set — the largest whole-request prize left, and unquantified until a builder measures it.
3. **All three slots at once.** In rounds 1 and 2 the three-slot replacement lost about 2.8 ms with 8 requests for an unknown reason; a set with an experts attempt meets that again. No single-slot kernel change is predicted to remove it, so it is carried as a constraint: per-slot wins are not assumed to compose, and the ready check (which times candidates alone and all together) is where composition is measured. If the three together lose, the fallback set is the routing+combine pair.
4. **Slots not yet tried.** `routing+combine` (both slots, each with its own kernels, in one candidate) has never been graded as one folder. The parts are graded independently and the combine part receives the reference routing weights, so it is packaging unless a shared design emerges; the set rule already submits the two slots together without it. No hypothesis is planned on it unless exploration finds a shared-design reason.
5. **Recommendations outside the slots** stand as written in round 1's and round 2's exploration READMEs (attention K/V re-read per query head; split-K partial traffic from 14 rows; the 60 q/k/v `[0]` gathers; engine CPU per 1-row step). Claude's round-3 measurement did not test them. They are for surucuonur's team; no hypothesis targets them.

### Refuted claims

No one chases these again.

- Round 3's experts 1-row fixes: a vectorised scalar path (attempt-2) bought nothing and an unfused path copying the reference's structure (attempt-5) was 2× worse at 1 row — the 1-row gap is not closed by either approach, and round 4 does not retry them; it hands 1 row off instead.
- Routing attempt-1's 2,048-row `slower` verdict on byte-identical code: attempt-6's re-grade (19/30, `same`) confirmed it as paired noise, not a hand-off cost. Handed-off sizes are no longer timed at all.
- `ineff-runs-3` (round 1, refuted): the micro sorted/unsorted gaps measure kernel choice, not pair order.
- Round 1's implicit claim that the independent (overlapped) piece timing ranks attempts as the model does: refuted by the chained measurement. Round 4 ranks by the chained timing only.
- The claim that scalar sums cannot reproduce MMA rounding: refuted by building in round 2 (routing attempts 2–4, experts scalar paths bit-identical at all six sizes).

## Starting point

Round 4 is the last round ([ADR 0014](../../../claude/adr/0014-muse-wonder-last-round.md)). It builds on rounds 1–3 as measured independently by Claude in [`claude/findings/muse-round-3.md`](../../../claude/findings/muse-round-3.md). Round 3 ran as Muse Spark (model `muse-spark-1.3-contributor`, skill version 8) and submitted the reference in every slot: no candidate passed the ready check alone, and the skill then counted only candidates that pass alone. Round 4 changes three rules ([ADR 0015](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)): candidates that pass together in `muse-all` are `ready` as a **set**; an attempt may hand off inputs below `min_rows` as well as above `max_rows`; and a handed-off size is reported `handed off` instead of being timed. A slot's **baseline** is still its best attempt so far that passes the current G2, has `beats_compiled` true in the grader, and passes G3 ([ADR 0011](../../../claude/adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). **No slot has a baseline.** The bar in every slot is the compiled reference, and a new attempt must beat it in the same grader run (no `--baseline` argument). Round 4 runs as Muse Wonder (muse-wonder-1.0).

### Per slot

#### `experts` — starting point `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1`

- **What it is.** Round 2's fused per-pair kernel, byte-identical, plus `max_rows: 59` in `spec.json`: rows 1–59 run the fused kernel, rows above 59 run the compiled reference. See `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1/notes.md` and its `grade.json` (G1 pass, G2 differ 0 at all six sizes).
- **Piece timing** (chained µs per layer, candidate vs compiled, its own grade run): 1 row 96.9 vs 86.6 (`slower`, 5 wins); 8 rows 168.9 vs 238.2 (`faster`, 29 wins); 32 rows 554.7 vs 883.4 (`faster`, 29 wins); prefill 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 `same` (19 / 15 / 16 wins — the hand-off runs compiled code). `beats_compiled` false: decode `slower` on the 1-row size alone.
- **G3 effect.** Never timed end to end (round 3, section 4). Its ancestor (round 2 attempt-7, same kernels without the hand-off) shortened the decode step 17.5% with 32 requests but made prompt processing 6.6–14.5× slower; the hand-off removes the prefill half of that, so no G3 prediction from round 3 stands — Claude's reading is that only the 1-row gap remains.
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** It is not a baseline because `beats_compiled` is false — the 1-row decode loss (96.9 vs 86.6 µs/layer) — and it has no G3 pass. Round 3 tried a vectorised scalar path (attempt-2, bought nothing) and an unfused path copying the reference's structure (attempt-5, 2× worse at 1 row) and concluded no fix existed in the spec surface. From round 4 the surface has `min_rows`: `min_rows: 2` with `max_rows: 59` hands 1-row inputs to the compiled reference while keeping the 8/32-row wins — a direction not yet graded. It can then pass G3 only in a set whose other kernels are faster with 1 request, because with 1 request every decode step runs MLX's own code for this slot.
- **Where it still spends its time.** At 8/32 rows it already wins by 69.3 / 328.7 µs per layer; what remains is the 1-row chain (the `tg_x` load, silu and barrier chain named in round 3) — now hand-off-able — and per-pair weight re-reads at all sizes (552,960 B per pair, round 3's entry).

#### `routing` — starting point `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6`

- **What it is.** Round 2's staged scalar-exact kernel (attempt-4 kernels) with `max_rows: 32`: every decode step (1–32 rows) runs the staged scalar kernels, all prefill sizes run the compiled reference. Attempt-6 is a byte-identical re-grade of round 3's attempt-1 (empty `diff` on both blocks and `spec.json`), run to test whether attempt-1's 2,048-row `slower` on identical code reproduced; it did not (19/30 wins, `same`). See `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6/notes.md`.
- **Piece timing.** Round 3's grade: decode `faster` at all three sizes (candidate 51.7 / 90.9 / 132.2 vs compiled 66.3 / 104.0 / 152.0 µs per layer; 28 / 27 / 25 wins), prefill `same` at all three sizes. Claude's re-grade with the round-4 grader ([`results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/`](../../../results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/)): decode `faster` (29 / 26 / 27 wins; candidate 0.72 / 0.90 / 0.88 of the compiled reference at 1 / 8 / 32 rows), the three prefill sizes `handed off`, `beats_compiled` true.
- **G3 effect.** In round 3's swarm ready check it failed alone against `compiled-routing` at 8×128 on overlapping ranges, with no phase slower anywhere (decode medians −0.38 / −0.31 / −0.59 / −0.48 ms vs the unchanged model at 1×128 / 8×128 / 32×128 / 32×1024). Claude's G3 agreed: `same` as `compiled-routing` at 8×128. Together with combine attempt-2 (`muse-all`) it passed the swarm's ready check but failed Claude's G3 against `compiled-all` at 32×1024, where the medians are 0.9% apart with overlapping ranges.
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** G3 alone: it passes G2 and has `beats_compiled` true, but it has never passed G3, alone or (in Claude's run) as a pair. Under round 4's set rule the pair would have been `ready` in round 3, but a set still has to pass G3 as `muse-all`, so the pair is no baseline.
- **Where it still spends its time.** Decode wins at every size; the open question is margin, above all at 32×1024 where the pair gains only 0.25–0.30 ms over the compiled reference (~1%), inside the 5-repeat spread. The per-row `w_router` re-read is untouched (upper bound only, round 2's `ineff-baseline-routing-4`).

#### `combine` — starting point `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/combine/attempt-2`

- **What it is.** Round 2's attempt-1 kernel with its seven `volatile` rounding barriers replaced by seven plain `float` locals and a header block (`block-1.metal`) carrying `#pragma STDC FP_CONTRACT OFF` / `#pragma clang fp contract(off)`: same 7-op stepwise fold `((p0+p1)+p2)+p3`, same grid (`rows*768`) and threadgroup [256,1,1], no `max_rows`. See `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/combine/attempt-2/notes.md`.
- **Piece timing.** Round 3's grade: `faster` at all six sizes (decode 31.8 / 34.7 / 32.7 vs compiled 36.9 / 41.1 / 45.7 µs per layer, 24 / 27 / 30 wins; prefill 38.2 / 100.9 / 198.0 vs 64.0 / 281.8 / 556.2, 30 / 30 / 29 wins); `beats_compiled` true in both phases. Absolute chained times drift up to ~35% between runs on this machine (round 3's lesson), so only same-run paired verdicts transfer.
- **G3 effect.** In round 3's ready check it failed alone against the unchanged model at 1×128 on a single outlier repeat (5.892 ms, above the unchanged model's lowest 5.430) and, in Claude's G3, against `compiled-combine` at 32×128 and 32×1024 — again range overlaps with no phase slower anywhere (swarm decode medians −0.53 / −0.59 / −0.44 / −0.26 ms vs the unchanged model). Its ancestor's in-step cost (+1.05 ms/step at 32 requests from the volatile barriers) is what the pragma removes; round 3's measured decode medians favour the kernel everywhere.
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** G3 alone, on spread: every median favours it, but the 5-repeat ranges overlap the bars'. No kernel change is named that tightens spread on 7 plain ops (round 3's implementation README); as part of a set it already passes `muse-all` in the swarm's run.
- **Where it still spends its time.** Nothing further in the grader — it sits on the chained floor and wins at all six sizes. What remains is the same margin question as routing: more separation from the compiled reference at 32×128 and 32×1024, or a set that clears the bar together.

#### All three together

Round 3's pair (routing attempt-6 + combine attempt-2) is the best result of any round: against the unchanged model it shortens the decode step 16.5% / 5.4% / 2.8% / 1.6% and whole requests 14.1% / 5.6% / 2.1% / 2.4% at 1×128 / 8×128 / 32×128 / 32×1024, with prompts 1.6–3.1% faster and nothing slower — but it fails G3 against `compiled-all` at 32×1024 (0.9% median gap, overlapping ranges). About half the gain over the unchanged model is `mx.compile` of the two slots' reference code alone. The three-slot composition is untested: in rounds 1 and 2, replacing all three slots at once lost about 2.8 ms with 8 requests for an unknown reason, and round 3 installed no experts candidate, so no run since has met it.

### What is left

Ranked by predicted saving against the compiled reference (no slot has a baseline, so the reference is the bar everywhere). Claude's measurement names three things round 4 has to find out; the ranking follows them.

1. **Experts with `min_rows`.** Whether attempt-1's 8/32-row speed (168.9 vs 238.2 and 554.7 vs 883.4 µs per layer) carries into G3 once 1 row runs MLX's own code (`min_rows: 2`, `max_rows: 59`). This is the only ungraded direction in any slot and the largest piece saving left: the 8/32-row wins are 69.3 / 328.7 µs per layer, worth (PREDICTION, from those same-run margins × 20 layers) about 1.4 ms per step at 8 requests and 6.6 ms at 32 requests against the compiled reference, with prefill `handed off` above 59 rows and 1-row decode `handed off` — so the gain exists only at 8 and 32 requests, and G3 can pass only in a set whose other kernels win with 1 request. The risk is the three-slot interaction (item 3).
2. **A margin at 32×1024.** The pair gains 0.25–0.30 ms over the compiled reference there (~1%), which 5 repeats cannot tell from noise; a set needs more than that with 32 long prompts. This is a margin problem in routing and/or combine decode kernels, not a correctness one: both starting points are bit-exact and already `faster` at every graded size, so any new attempt must widen the same-run margin at decode sizes without touching prefill (`max_rows: 32` for routing, faster-everywhere for combine). A saving here is worth the difference between a passing and a failing set — the largest whole-request prize left, and unquantified until a builder measures it.
3. **All three slots at once.** In rounds 1 and 2 the three-slot replacement lost about 2.8 ms with 8 requests for an unknown reason; a set with an experts attempt meets that again. No single-slot kernel change is predicted to remove it, so it is carried as a constraint: per-slot wins are not assumed to compose, and the ready check (which times candidates alone and all together) is where composition is measured. If the three together lose, the fallback set is the routing+combine pair.
4. **Slots not yet tried.** `routing+combine` (both slots, each with its own kernels, in one candidate) has never been graded as one folder. The parts are graded independently and the combine part receives the reference routing weights, so it is packaging unless a shared design emerges; the set rule already submits the two slots together without it. No hypothesis is planned on it unless exploration finds a shared-design reason.
5. **Recommendations outside the slots** stand as written in round 1's and round 2's exploration READMEs (attention K/V re-read per query head; split-K partial traffic from 14 rows; the 60 q/k/v `[0]` gathers; engine CPU per 1-row step). Claude's round-3 measurement did not test them. They are for surucuonur's team; no hypothesis targets them.

### Refuted claims

No one chases these again.

- Round 3's experts 1-row fixes: a vectorised scalar path (attempt-2) bought nothing and an unfused path copying the reference's structure (attempt-5) was 2× worse at 1 row — the 1-row gap is not closed by either approach, and round 4 does not retry them; it hands 1 row off instead.
- Routing attempt-1's 2,048-row `slower` verdict on byte-identical code: attempt-6's re-grade (19/30, `same`) confirmed it as paired noise, not a hand-off cost. Handed-off sizes are no longer timed at all.
- `ineff-runs-3` (round 1, refuted): the micro sorted/unsorted gaps measure kernel choice, not pair order.
- Round 1's implicit claim that the independent (overlapped) piece timing ranks attempts as the model does: refuted by the chained measurement. Round 4 ranks by the chained timing only.
- The claim that scalar sums cannot reproduce MMA rounding: refuted by building in round 2 (routing attempts 2–4, experts scalar paths bit-identical at all six sizes).

75|- **Territories** this round opens (step 2.2), each with the line of this section that reopens it.
76|
77|Commit it as exploration v1. **Done** when every slot has its baseline or starting point and every territory has its reason.
78|
79|### 2. Exploration
80|
81|1. **Set up the folder.** Write `<round>/exploration/README.md` with a heading, its version line (v1, with skill version 10), the tracker (one row per territory) and `## Versions`, and an empty `log.md`.
82|2. **Start the explorers and the verifier,** all at once.
83|   - **Round 1** starts with these territories:
84|
85|     | Territory | Covers |
86|     |---|---|
87|     | `model` | `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py`: the decoder layer, `MoE.__call__` and everything around the slots |
88|     | `switch-layers` | `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/switch_layers.py`: the routed experts' path, `gather_qmm`, the sort from 16 rows |
89|     | `quantized-kernels` | `quantized.h` and `quantized_utils.h` in `.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/mlx/include/mlx/backend/metal/kernels/`: the `affine_gather_*` kernels behind `gather_qmm` |
90|     | `other-kernels` | the other Metal kernels in the same folder that the routing and combine slots launch: sort, softmax, reductions, elementwise, copies |
91|     | `vllm-metal` | `third_party/vllm-metal/vllm_metal/`: how the engine runs a decode step and a prefill chunk around the model |
92|     | `grader` | `bench/grader/`: the slot interface, what G1, G2 and the piece timing measure, and so the boundary every solution keeps |
93|     | `findings` | `claude/findings/` and `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/` |
94|     | `runs` | `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/`, `2026-10-29-baseline/` and `2026-10-30-micro/` |
95|
96|   - **From round 2 on,** the starting point lists the territories:
97|     - `baseline-<slot>` for each slot: its baseline's kernels and `spec.json`, which are now the code in the slot, or its starting point's. Map them with the checklist, and find where they still lose time and, for a starting point, why it fails G2;
98|     - `g3`: Claude's measurement of the previous round, where the end-to-end change differs from the piece timing, and why;
99|     - of round 1's territories, only those the starting point reopens. An explorer starts from that territory's earlier entries and writes only what is new.
100|3. **Refocus as costs show up.** When an entry shows that one file holds most of a territory's cost, split it off as a territory of its own, with its own explorer. Merge or close a territory that turns out to hold nothing, and add one when an inefficiency points somewhere no one covers. Log each change and update the tracker.
101|4. **Checkpoint** each time a helper returns.
102|
103|**Done** when every territory entry is `done`, the verifier has returned, and every inefficiency is `confirmed`, `refuted` or `superseded`.
104|
105|### 3. The analysis
106|
107|Write the final `<round>/exploration/README.md`. It is the round's report on the code, for this round's builders and for future improvements:
108|
109|- **Tracker:** the final table.
110|- **Starting point** (from round 2 on), as written in step 1, with any correction exploration made.
111|- **Context:** the decode step and the prefill, the MoE block and its slots, and what the measurements say about where the time goes in each.
112|- **Territory map:** how the territories feed each other. For each territory: what it receives, what it passes on, and its measured cost.
113|- **Inefficiencies, ranked:**
114|  - the confirmed ones inside the slots, ranked by predicted saving as a share of the decode step, averaged over 1, 8 and 32 rows, or of the prefill chunk, averaged over 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows; from round 2 on, the saving is against the baseline where the slot has one;
115|  - each with what removing it does to the other phase, and whether a hand-off (`max_rows`) keeps that phase unchanged;
116|  - each with its cost, kind and entry;
117|  - Claude's findings marked as Claude's, earlier rounds' entries linked as theirs, and this round's own reading marked as yours.
118|- **Recommendations:** the confirmed inefficiencies outside the slots, with their evidence. They're for surucuonur's team.
119|- **Refuted claims,** in one line each, so no one chases them again.
120|- **Files read:** links to each territory entry's list.
121|
122|Commit it. **Done** when every ranked item links a confirmed entry and every number in the README has its source.
123|
124|### 4. Implementation
125|
126|Take the ranked inefficiencies in order, at most two at a time, in different slots so their attempts never touch. Write `<round>/implementation/README.md` with a heading, its version line, the tracker and `## Versions`, and an empty `log.md`. For each hypothesis:
127|
128|1. **Open the hypothesis.** Write `<round>/implementation/hyp-<n>-<slug>.md`, with status `boundary`, the inefficiency, the slot and, from round 2 on, the slot's baseline folder or `none`. Add its tracker row and log it.
129|2. **Draw its boundary.** Start `boundary-<n>` to write the boundary, and wait for it.
130|3. **Compete.**
131|   - Set the status to `building`.
132|   - Start 2 or 3 builders, `builder-<n>-a`, `-b` and `-c`. Give each a different direction drawn from the analysis: for example, fusing kernels, reading each weight byte once, or a different threadgroup shape. From round 2 on, a direction may start from the baseline's or starting point's kernels, or from scratch.
133|4. **Collect.** Each time a builder returns:
134|   - checkpoint, committing its attempt folder with the hypothesis entry, the README and the log;
135|   - if the attempt passed G2, start `boundary-<n>` to check it.
136|5. **Harden.**
137|   - Pick the best attempt: it passes G1, G2 and its boundary check, has `beats_compiled` true and, where the slot has a baseline, `beats_baseline`, and it is the fastest across the six sizes.
138|   - Set the status to `hardening`, and start a builder for that attempt's next single change.
139|   - Repeat while the attempt still has a cause you can name and remove.
140|   - **Change approach after three alike failures.** Keep the hypothesis entry's failure ledger at each collect: every graded attempt that lost, the size or phase it lost at, and its named cause. When three attempts have lost at the same phase for the same cause, the next one changes approach (another kernel structure, parallelisation or dataflow, not a tuning), and its `notes.md` says "approach change: from X to Y"; or you log why not. A cause renamed without a measurement that refutes the old one is the same cause.
141|6. **Close.**
142|   - **`candidate`:** the best attempt passes G1, G2 and its boundary check, has `beats_compiled` true and, where the slot has a baseline, `beats_baseline` true, and you can name no further change worth making. Write the **Decision**: the attempt, why it is best, and the change in whole requests you predict, labelled a prediction. Then start `checker-<n>` on the entry; the hypothesis is a candidate once its **Checks** section says `pass`.
143|   - **`dropped`:** say why. A slot whose hypotheses are all dropped keeps its baseline, or the reference where it has none.
144|
145|Then open the next-ranked inefficiency.
146|
147|**The ready check** ([ADR 0013](../../../claude/adr/0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)). Once no hypothesis is building or hardening and at least one is a `candidate`, run it yourself, over every candidate in one call:
148|
149|```bash
150|.venv/bin/python bench/grader/check_ready.py <round>/checks/ready-<k> <slot>=<attempt folder> [<slot>=<attempt folder> ...]
151|```
152|
153|It times the candidates in vLLM exactly as Claude's G3 will after the round, each alone and, with more than one, all together, then audits its own log and writes `ready-verdict.json`. It takes about 10 to 15 minutes per slot, more for an attempt with a slow prefill, and waits its turn for the GPU. Commit its folder at the next checkpoint.
154|- **Exit 0 or 1: a verdict, and it stands.** Cite the file.
155|  - **A set** ([ADR 0015](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)). With more than one candidate, when `muse-all` passes, all of them are `ready` together as a set, even where one fails alone. A set goes to G3 whole: all its attempts, or none.
156|  - **Alone.** Otherwise, a candidate whose `muse-<slot>` passes becomes `ready` on its own; one that fails goes back to `hardening` with the failure in its ledger, or to `dropped`. If some pass alone and `muse-all` fails, a second check may take only those.
157|  - An attempt that hands off 1 row (`min_rows`) runs MLX's own code for the whole 1-request workload, so it passes the ready check only in a set whose other kernels are faster with 1 request.
158|- **Exit 2: no verdict.** The run stopped or broke the protocol; run it again in a new folder.
159|- **At most two ready checks per round.**
160|
161|**Done** when no confirmed inefficiency is left that you judge will pay, and every candidate has a ready-check verdict. Write why in the implementation README.
162|
163|### 5. Finish
164|
165|1. **The implementation README:** the final tracker, one paragraph per hypothesis, and a **Ready to test** section. It names the attempt per slot that goes to Claude's G3: a `ready` attempt, the baseline kept, or the reference, and says which `ready` attempts go together as a set. For the `ready` ones it shows the ready check's measured change in the four workloads (the decode step, the prompt time and the whole request, against the unchanged model and the compiled reference; for a set, its `muse-all`), citing `ready-verdict.json`, with your earlier prediction beside it, labelled PREDICTION, and the **Unverified** list. Nothing else in it is an end-to-end number.
166|2. **The exploration README:** add *What building taught*, the analysis corrected by what the attempts showed.
167|3. **`<round>/summary.md`:** a `## Round N` section with:
168|   - the model, the skill version this round ran, and the final versions of both READMEs;
169|   - the final attempt per slot;
170|   - the number of graded attempts per slot, this round and over all rounds;
171|   - the ready check's measured change, citing its file;
172|   - what you'd try next;
173|   - your recommendations outside the slots.
174|4. **Check, commit, reply.** Start `checker-final` on *Ready to test* and the summary, and fix what it finds until it signs `pass`. Then commit, and reply with this round's commits and the words "Round N finished".
175|
176|## Your own rules
177|
178|- **Writes:**
179|  - you write the two READMEs, the hypothesis entries' status blocks and decisions, and `summary.md`;
180|  - every helper writes only what its card names;
181|  - all of it stays in this round's folder.
182|- **Claude's G3 after the round is the authority;** your ready check is the same measurement, made earlier. vLLM runs only through the ready check.
183|- **The rules every agent keeps** are in tracking.md.
184|
185|## Commits
186|
187|You are the only agent that commits. Commit only on `muse-agent`.
188|- **What to add:** this round's phase folders that exist so far (only `exploration` until implementation starts) and the attempt folders that came back. An attempt another builder is still writing waits for its own commit. An entry that is mid-edit is committed as it stands, and finished in a later commit.
189|- **The message:**
190|  - every subject starts with the name the first prompt gives you, then a colon;
191|  - a checkpoint's subject is `<name>: <phase> v<N>: <what changed>`, the version it records;
192|  - every message ends with the first prompt's co-author line, exactly.
193|
194|For example, in round 2 as Muse Wonder:
195|
196|```bash
197|git add muse-spark/round-2/exploration muse-spark/round-2/implementation muse-spark/round-2/kernels/<slot-folder>/attempt-<M>
198|git commit -m "Muse Wonder: implementation v4: experts attempt 3 graded, beats baseline" \
199|  -m "Co-Authored-By: Muse Wonder (Meta Model API) <muse-wonder@meta-model-api.invalid>"
200|```
201|
202|Use no other co-author. The hooks refuse a commit without a Muse agent's co-author, a commit outside `muse-spark/`, a change to a finished round's files, a new file outside this round's folder, and any merge. Push, merge, rebase, tags, git config and hook skipping stay with surucuonur.

{"path":"muse-spark/round-4/exploration/territory-grader.md","content":"# Territory: grader — round 4's three rule changes (ADR 0015)

- **Owner:** explorer-grader
- **Status:** done
- **Version:** 2
- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T21:42:57Z
- **Next:** none — checklist complete (5 pieces), 0 inefficiencies posted (grader runs no decode-step kernels; see *Inefficiencies*); held notes for `baseline-experts`, `g3` and the checker are in *Inefficiencies*; no `## From other agents` notes existed to answer at finish

## What it does

Round 3's entry ([`muse-spark/round-3/exploration/territory-grader.md`](../../round-3/exploration/territory-grader.md), frozen) mapped the grader through ADR 0011/0013: bit-exact G2 at six sizes, paired timing at all six sizes, two-phase `beats_compiled`, the `max_rows` hand-off, and the ready check that judged each `muse-*` variant on its own pass. Round 4 changes three rules ([ADR 0015](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)): an attempt may also hand off below `min_rows`; a handed-off size is reported `handed off` and is not timed against the compiled reference; and candidates that pass together as `muse-all` are `ready` as a **set**. This entry writes only that delta. G1/G2 mechanics, the spec language apart from the two bounds, `capture`, `gpu_lock`, the chained timing and the G3 range rule are cited to round 3, not re-described. The grader was not run and no GPU work was done for this entry; unit-test and re-grade results below are cited to ADR 0015, not re-measured.

## The exact boundary a round-4 solution must keep

A round-4 attempt is inside the boundary only if all five hold. This is the checklist the builders, the boundary agent and the checker grade against; each line names its source.

1. **Spec validity.** `min_rows` and `max_rows` in `spec.json` are each an integer of at least 1, booleans and floats refused, and `min_rows ≤ max_rows` when both are given — otherwise `build()` raises `ValueError` before any kernel runs and the attempt is a G1 failure ([slots.py:330-335](../../../bench/grader/slots.py); brief:174). For `routing+combine` each part's spec carries its own pair of bounds (brief:176).
2. **Inclusive kernel window.** The attempt's kernels run exactly when `min_rows ≤ rows ≤ max_rows` for the bounds it gives (a missing bound is open on that side), and run the slot's reference under `mx.compile` outside that window; `rows` is the first slot input's `shape[0]` ([slots.py:338-345](../../../bench/grader/slots.py)). Row-for-row: `hands_off(rows)` is `rows > max_rows or rows < min_rows` ([slots.py:338-339](../../../bench/grader/slots.py)), and `test_hand_off.py` pins the edges bit-for-bit: 8 and 59 run the kernel, 7 and 60 run the compiled reference, for `min_rows: 8, max_rows: 59` ([test_hand_off.py:69](../../../bench/grader/test_hand_off.py)).
3. **G2 bit-exactness at every size, handed off or not.** G2 runs the attempt's `run()` — hand-off dispatch included — on all 20 layers at 1, 8, 32, 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows and requires bit-for-bit equality with the plain reference, in order for routing (including the tied 4th/5th choice) and elementwise for combine/experts; timing runs only if G2 passes ([check_candidate.py:320-351](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py); brief:187-195,175). A handed-off size therefore tests `mx.compile(reference)` against the plain reference through the attempt's own dispatch, which is why the boundary also includes compiled==reference at the six sizes (round-3 entry §2; [ADR 0011:34](../../../claude/adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). For experts the window must also sit on the right side of MLX's 60-row kernel switch (`gather_qmm_rhs` from 60 rows, different rounding): a decode-built experts kernel may run only below 60 rows, i.e. `max_rows ≤ 59` ([slots.py:219-220](../../../bench/grader/slots.py); round-3 entry §2). Inside the window the reference still changes behaviour once: `ref_experts` sorts the pairs from 16 rows (`inds.size >= 64`, [slots.py:62](../../../bench/grader/slots.py)), so a kernel running at both 8 and 32 rows must match the unsorted and the sorted reference, both on the `gather_qvm` side of 60.
4. **Piece-timing phase rule.** At each timed size the verdict is `faster` with ≥22 wins of 30 paired repeats, `slower` with ≥22 losses, else `same` ([check_candidate.py:244-250](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)). `judge()` drops `handed off` sizes from their phase: a phase is `faster` only when **every** size the kernels run at is `faster` and at least one such size exists, `slower` when any timed size is `slower`, `handed off` when none is left, else `not slower`; `beats_compiled` is true iff one phase is `faster` and neither is `slower` ([check_candidate.py:253-271](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py); brief:217-218). One `same` at a timed size blocks the bar; one `slower` anywhere fails it.
5. **Whole-request rule, and the set.** The ready check and G3 time whole requests in vLLM at 1×128, 8×128, 32×128, 32×1024 (5 repeats, 256 tokens), require the same greedy tokens at 1 and 32 requests, and pass a variant only when decode or prompt is `faster` (non-overlapping ranges) in every workload and nothing — decode, prompt or whole request — is `slower` anywhere ([check_ready.py:47-56,131-161](../../../bench/grader/check_ready.py); [time_candidates.py:163-201](../../../bench/grader/time_candidates.py)). From round 4, when `muse-all` passes, its candidates are `ready` together as a set even where one fails alone, and G3 judges the set as one (skill step 4; brief:206; [ADR 0015:11,42](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)). The converse also binds: with 1 request every decode step has 1 row, so an attempt with `min_rows: 2` runs MLX's own code for the whole 1×128 workload and can pass G3/the ready check only inside a set whose other kernels are faster there (brief:174; [ADR 0015:37](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)).

## Checklist

### 1. `slots.py` `build()` — `min_rows`/`max_rows` and `hands_off` (slots.py:304-368)

- **Callers:** `check_candidate.load` ([check_candidate.py:70-77](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)), and through it `time_candidates.Variants`/`implementations` and the ready check — so the same dispatch, bounds included, runs in G2, the piece timing, G3 and the ready check. For `routing+combine`, `load` splits the folder spec into per-part specs and builds each part separately, so each part hands off by its own bounds ([check_candidate.py:76-77](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py); brief:176).
- **Callees:** `mx.fast.metal_kernel` per spec kernel (built once per `build` call), and `compiled = mx.compile(REFERENCE[slot])`, also built once per call whether or not the spec gives bounds ([slots.py:336](../../../bench/grader/slots.py)). `run()` calls `compiled(*inputs)` in slot-input order and re-zips to slot outputs on a hand-off ([slots.py:341-345](../../../bench/grader/slots.py)).
- **Data:** unchanged from round 3 (`SLOTS`, brief slot tables); the only new data is the two optional spec integers. `rows` is read from the first slot input's `shape[0]` for both dispatch and grid evaluation ([slots.py:342](../../../bench/grader/slots.py)).
- **Neighbours:** before it, the spec validation refuses a bad bound as a `ValueError`, which `check_candidate` reports as G1 (`result["error"]`, [check_candidate.py:401-402](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)); after it, `run.hands_off` is the attribute the timing loop consults (piece 2). The threadgroup product ≤1024 check is unchanged ([slots.py:348-350](../../../bench/grader/slots.py)); threadgroup memory is still not checked (round-3 *can't see* item 8 stands).
- **Cost:** `build` launches no kernel itself. The hand-off branch is one Python comparison per `run()` call; in G3/ready-check serving that call happens per layer per step through `make_moe_call`, and any wrapper cost there is inside the whole-request times, not the piece timing (piece 2, *can't see* item 2). No new measured number is claimed here.
- **Invariants:** the inclusive window and the refusal rules in *The exact boundary* items 1–2; validation rejects `bool` explicitly because `True` is an `int` in Python ([slots.py:331-333](../../../bench/grader/slots.py)), and `min_rows > max_rows` is refused with "the kernels would never run" ([slots.py:334-335](../../../bench/grader/slots.py)). What `build` does **not** check: that the window sits on the right side of 60 for experts, or anything about rows between the tested sizes (see *What each tool still cannot see*).

### 2. `check_candidate.py` — handed-off sizes not timed, `judge()` and `beats_compiled` (check_candidate.py:244-271, 352-400)

- **Callers:** builders, `.venv/bin/python bench/grader/check_candidate.py <attempt> <slot> [--out FILE]`; no `--baseline` this round — no slot has one (round-4 README *Starting point*), so the only bar is `compiled`. The `--baseline` path still exists and its handed-off rule differs (below), which a reader of a baseline grade must not confuse with the compiled bar.
- **What is new — exclusion, not a tie.** Per part and size, the timing loop builds `together = {candidate, compiled[, baseline]}` and then drops every function except `compiled` whose `hands_off(rows)` is true, so a handing-off function is never run in `paired_times` at that size ([check_candidate.py:372-380](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)). Its per-repeat times are then taken from the compiled function's repeats (`paired.get(name, paired["compiled"])`) and summed across parts as before ([check_candidate.py:381-384](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)). Consequences in the printed verdict: at a fully handed-off size (vs the compiled bar) there is a `vs_compiled: "handed off"` and **no** `wins_vs_compiled` key, and the candidate's reported median equals the compiled median by construction ([check_candidate.py:386-394](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)). The unpaired `reference` median is still timed at every size ([check_candidate.py:371](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)) — informational only, as in round 3. This removes round 3's defect exactly: identical code can no longer be judged `slower` on paired noise (routing attempt-1's 2,048-row verdict, re-graded `same` by attempt-6; round-4 README *Refuted claims*).
- **What is new — the `own` rule and the baseline exception.** `own[name]` records whether a function ran code of its own in **any** part at that size ([check_candidate.py:364,382](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)). A size's verdict against a bar is `handed off` only when neither the candidate nor that bar ran its own kernels there: `if not (own["candidate"] or own[bar])` ([check_candidate.py:387-390](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)). For the compiled bar `own["compiled"]` is never set, so the rule reduces to "candidate handed off in every part". Against a `--baseline` attempt that runs its own kernels at a size the candidate hands off, the size **is** timed as before — candidate repeats copied from compiled against the baseline's own repeats ([ADR 0015:22](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)). For `routing+combine` the summing is per part before wins are counted (round 3 §1 stands), so one part handing off while the other runs still times the size, on the summed repeats.
- **What is new — `judge()`.** It filters `handed off` verdicts out of each phase before judging ([check_candidate.py:262-269](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)); the phase rule and `beats_compiled` are *The exact boundary* item 4. The five synthetic cases in `test_hand_off.py` pin them (piece 4). G2 is untouched: correctness still runs at all six sizes through the dispatch, and timing still runs only when G2 passes ([check_candidate.py:349-352](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)).
- **Cost:** the timing still chains 20 layers × 30 paired repeats per timed size (round 3 §1); handed-off sizes now cost one compiled timing instead of two identical ones per part. The one real-attempt evidence that the new reporting works end to end is Claude's re-grade of round 3's routing attempt-6 (`max_rows: 32`) with this grader: G2 passes, decode `faster` at 1/8/32 on 29/26/27 wins of 30, the three prefill sizes `handed off`, `beats_compiled` true ([ADR 0015:28-32](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)).
- **Invariants:** `WINS_NEEDED` is still 22 of 30 (one-sided sign test, p < 0.01, [check_candidate.py:56-63](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)); size labels still carry the phase prefix (`rows ` / `prefill rows `) that `judge()` splits on ([check_candidate.py:57,358](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)). A phase with every size handed off can never supply the required `faster` phase: an attempt that hands off everything beats nothing (`judge` case "everything handed off", piece 4).

### 3. `check_ready.py` — the set rule (check_ready.py:98-100, 152-174; time_candidates.py:111-132, 168-201)

- **Callers:** the lead only, `.venv/bin/python bench/grader/check_ready.py <new out folder> SLOT=FOLDER...`, at most twice per round (round-3 entry §5 stands: pinned protocol, log audit, `--audit`, exit codes). What round 4 changes is only how its verdict is read.
- **Where `muse-all` comes from.** `expected_variants` requires `compiled-all`/`muse-all` exactly when more than one slot is submitted ([check_ready.py:98-100](../../../bench/grader/check_ready.py)); `time_candidates.Variants` builds them by installing every slot's attempts (resp. compiled references) into one `MoE.__call__` ([time_candidates.py:117-127](../../../bench/grader/time_candidates.py)). `g3()` judges `muse-all` against `base` and `compiled-all` with the same range rule as any variant ([time_candidates.py:177-200](../../../bench/grader/time_candidates.py)), and the audit recomputes that verdict from the log before trusting it ([check_ready.py:142-148](../../../bench/grader/check_ready.py)).
- **The set rule, precisely.** The audit fills `judged[v]` for **every** `muse-*` variant — each single slot and `muse-all` — with `pass = g3[v]["g3"] and same_tokens` ([check_ready.py:152-161](../../../bench/grader/check_ready.py)). The set rule is **not** in this file's aggregate: the file still computes `passed = all(j["pass"] for j in judged.values())` and exits 0 only then ([check_ready.py:173-174](../../../bench/grader/check_ready.py)). So a set that passes only together produces `ready-verdict.json` with `pass: false` and exit 1, alongside `variants."muse-all".pass: true`. Readiness as a set is the skill's reading of that per-variant field (skill step 4: "when `muse-all` passes, all of them are `ready` together as a set, even where one fails alone"; brief:206). Any checker, tracker or script that reads only the top-level `pass`/exit code will report a passing set as failed — the single most misreadable line in the round-4 grader. The parts are still timed alone in the same run (the variants are all required by the audit), so the set reading costs no extra GPU run; a set's parts are not required to pass alone, but `muse-all` must still pass both bars and keep the tokens (`same_tokens` for `muse-all` at 1 and 32 requests, [check_ready.py:131-140,154-157](../../../bench/grader/check_ready.py)).
- **Data:** `ready-verdict.json` gains nothing new in round 4; the set is read out of the existing per-variant `variants`, `vs` and `phases` fields (round-3 entry §5). G3 after the round judges the set as `muse-all` in the same way ([ADR 0015:11,42](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)).
- **Invariants:** G3 and the ready-check protocol are unchanged ([ADR 0015:37](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)): a slot's kernels count wherever they run in a whole request, so the hand-off that the piece timing forgives is fully visible here — in particular at 1×128, where a `min_rows: 2` slot contributes the compiled reference's code, not its kernels (boundary item 5). Claude's post-round G3 stays the authority (round-3 entry §5).

### 4. `test_hand_off.py` — the unit check for pieces 1–2 (whole file)

- **What it checks.** With a toy combine kernel that copies `shared` (`out[i] = shared[i]`), `runs()` classifies each probed row count as `"kernel"` or `"compiled"` by bit-comparing the output against the toy output and against `mx.compile(ref_combine)` ([test_hand_off.py:21-54](../../../bench/grader/test_hand_off.py)). Four bound sets pin the dispatch and `hands_off` together at rows on both sides of each edge — no bounds; `max_rows: 32` (32 kernel, 33 compiled); `min_rows: 2` (1 compiled, 2 kernel); `min_rows: 8, max_rows: 59` (7 compiled, 8/59 kernel, 60 compiled) ([test_hand_off.py:65-74](../../../bench/grader/test_hand_off.py)). Four bad bounds must raise `ValueError`: `min_rows: 0`, `True`, `2.0`, and `min_rows: 33, max_rows: 32` ([test_hand_off.py:76-82](../../../bench/grader/test_hand_off.py)). Five synthetic verdict dicts pin `judge()`: all-timed with a slower prefill size (beats false); prefill handed off (beats true); 1 row handed off with 8/32 faster (beats true); a timed `same` blocking `faster` (beats false); everything handed off (beats false) ([test_hand_off.py:84-97](../../../bench/grader/test_hand_off.py)).
- **Callers / cost:** a standalone script (`.venv/bin/python bench/grader/test_hand_off.py`) using the GPU for a few small kernels, not the model ([test_hand_off.py:1-10](../../../bench/grader/test_hand_off.py)). ADR 0015 records it passed on 2026-11-04 ([ADR 0015:24-27](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)); this entry did not re-run it.
- **What it does not check:** any real slot, kernel or rounding (the toy output is exact by construction); the timing loop's exclusion/substitution and the `--baseline` exception in piece 2 (only the pure `judge()` is imported); per-part hand-offs in a `routing+combine` grade; and the set rule in piece 3, which has no unit test here at all. See *can't see* item 5.

### 5. The brief's slot interface — what builders see (muse-agent-brief.md:173-176, 206, 211-218)

- The brief now documents `min_rows` beside `max_rows` in the launch spec: integer ≥1, at most `max_rows`, kernels run only from `min_rows` to `max_rows`, with the 1-request G3 consequence stated in the same bullet (brief:173-174). It states that a hand-off is still G2-checked bit-exact at every size and that the piece timing reports the size as `handed off` (brief:175), that `routing+combine` carries both bounds per part (brief:176), the per-size/per-phase/`beats_compiled` reading of `handed off` (brief:216-218), and the set rule for the ready check and G3 (brief:206). The grader's printed per-size verdict list gains `handed off` as a fourth value (brief:211).
- **Invariant for builders and the boundary agent:** the brief, ADR 0015 and the code agree on the window, the phase rule and the set reading; the one place the wording runs ahead of the code is the ready check's aggregate verdict (piece 3), where the brief's "when that passes, the candidates are ready together" refers to `muse-all`'s own pass, not to `ready-verdict.json`'s top-level `pass`.

## Worked example: an experts attempt with `min_rows: 2, max_rows: 59`

The round-4 README's ungraded direction (round-4 README *What is left* item 1): round 3's experts attempt-1 kernels plus this window. `hands_off(rows)` is true at 1 row (`1 < 2`) and at every row above 59 ([slots.py:338-339](../../../bench/grader/slots.py)). Graded with no `--baseline`, so the only bar is `compiled`:

| Size | Phase | Who runs | G2 | Piece verdict vs compiled |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 row | decode | compiled reference | compiled vs plain reference, bit-exact required | `handed off` — not timed; no `wins_vs_compiled`; candidate median = compiled median |
| 8 rows | decode | attempt's kernels | kernels vs `gather_qvm` reference, unsorted pairs | timed: `faster` iff ≥22/30 wins, `slower` iff ≥22 losses, else `same` |
| 32 rows | decode | attempt's kernels | kernels vs `gather_qvm` reference, sorted pairs (from 16 rows) | timed, same rule |
| 127 rows | prefill | compiled reference | compiled vs plain reference (`gather_qmm_rhs` side) | `handed off` |
| 1,016 rows | prefill | compiled reference | same | `handed off` |
| 2,048 rows | prefill | compiled reference | same | `handed off` |

Phase arithmetic ([check_candidate.py:253-271](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)): decode keeps only 8 and 32 rows, so decode is `faster` iff **both** are `faster`, `slower` iff either is `slower`, else `not slower`. Prefill has no timed size left, so it is `handed off`. `beats_compiled` is therefore true exactly when 8 and 32 rows are both `faster`; a `same` at either makes decode `not slower` and `beats_compiled` false, and a `slower` at either makes it false with decode `slower`. For scale only (prediction, not a grade): round 3's attempt-1 kernels timed 168.9 vs 238.2 µs per layer at 8 rows and 554.7 vs 883.4 at 32 in their own run, while losing 96.9 vs 86.6 at 1 row ([ADR 0015:12](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md); round-4 README *Per slot: experts*) — under the old rule that single `slower` made `beats_compiled` false; under this window the 1-row size is removed from the phase instead of having to be won. The kernels never face `gather_qmm_rhs` rounding: every row they run at is below 60, and every prefill size is handed off. Two cautions the table cannot show: rows 2–7 and 33–59 run the kernels in real serving but are graded at no size (only 8 and 32 represent the whole window), and at 1 request this attempt contributes nothing in G3 — alone it cannot be faster than its compiled bar at 1×128, so it passes whole requests only in a set whose other kernels win there (boundary item 5).

## What each tool still cannot see

Round 3's list stands except where the hand-off change retires it (its items 3 and 5c were already retired in round 3; the duplicate-timing half of its item 5 is now removed by piece 2). What round 4 adds or leaves open, per tool:

1. **`slots.build` cannot see where the window sits.** Any `max_rows` in 32..126, and any `min_rows` in 2..8, produce identical dispatch at the six G2 sizes on the far side of the tested points (32 runs the kernels, 127 hands off; 1 hands off for both `min_rows` values) — the piece grader cannot tell `max_rows: 59` (right side of the 60-row switch) from 100 (wrong side), and cannot see kernel speed or exactness at rows 2–7, 9–31 or 33–126 at all. `check_sizes.py` at 59/60/61 (round-3 entry §3) is still the only tool that places the experts hand-off, and only where the boundary agent runs it; hypotheses with kernels running above 32 rows carry the 33–59 band as **Unverified**.
2. **The piece timing cannot see the hand-off's own cost.** At a handed-off size the candidate is not run, so its reported time is the compiled bar's repeats copied over ([check_candidate.py:383](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)); the `build` wrapper's dispatch branch and its separately compiled `mx.compile(REFERENCE[slot])` instance ([slots.py:336](../../../bench/grader/slots.py)) are never compared with the bar's own `mx.compile(ref)` wrapper at that size. In whole-request serving the muse variant goes through `build`'s `run()` while the compiled variant does not, so only G3/the ready check can show a wrapper cost — aggregated into whole-request ranges, never attributed to the hand-off.
3. **`judge()`'s all-or-nothing phase.** A phase is `faster` only when every timed size is; the size of a win is invisible to the verdict (a 300 µs win and a 1 µs win at 22/30 count the same), and one noisy `same` blocks `beats_compiled` even with large wins elsewhere (pinned deliberately by `test_hand_off.py`'s "a timed size not faster" case). Builders must read `timing_us_per_layer` magnitudes, not verdicts alone.
4. **`check_ready.py` cannot say "set" in its own verdict.** Its top-level `pass` and exit code still require every `muse-*` variant, singles included, to pass ([check_ready.py:173-174](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)); the set exists only in `variants."muse-all".pass` plus the skill's reading (piece 3). It also cannot attribute a `muse-all` result to its parts beyond the separately timed singles, cannot see per-slot contributions inside the combined `MoE.__call__`, and inherits round 3's items 6–7: 1-request whole-request verdicts are mostly noise-`same`, and a wholly invented log still passes the audit — only Claude's independent G3 catches it.
5. **`test_hand_off.py` cannot see the grader it guards.** It proves dispatch edges, bound refusal and `judge()` on synthetic verdicts with an exact-by-construction toy, but never runs `check_candidate`'s timing loop, a `routing+combine` two-part grade, the `--baseline` exception, a real experts kernel across the 60-row switch, or any part of the set rule (piece 4). A regression in the timing substitution at [check_candidate.py:376-394](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py) would pass this test suite.
6. **Handed-off exactness between the six sizes** still rests on compiled==reference where `check_sizes.py` has not run the attempt: G2 shows it at 1/8/32/127/1,016/2,048, `check_sizes` extends the hand-off path to its 25 sizes where run, and no tool tests above 2,048 rows (round-3 items 3 and 5 stand). Threadgroup memory, the link-kernel caveats and host-clock limits (round-3 items 8–9) are unchanged.

## Relations

- **Fed by:** ADR 0015's three decisions and Claude's round-3 measurement behind them (the 1-row experts loss, the routing 2,048-row noise verdict, the pair that passed only together); the slot references and `make_moe_call` in `slots.py` that `build` dispatches between; `time_candidates.py`'s variant construction, without which `check_ready.py` has no `muse-all` to judge; round 3's frozen grader entry for everything this delta does not restate.
- **Feeds:** builders (the spec surface: two bounds, the inclusive window, the phase rule they must satisfy); the boundary agent (boundary items 1–5, the 60-row placement that only `check_sizes.py` proves, the 33–59 **Unverified** band); `explorer-baseline-experts` (the worked example: what `min_rows: 2, max_rows: 59` does at each of the six sizes); `explorer-g3` and the lead (the set reading of `ready-verdict.json`, and the 1×128 consequence of a 1-row hand-off); the checker (`variants."muse-all".pass`, not the top-level `pass`, is the set's verdict; `--audit` unchanged).

## Inefficiencies

None posted from this territory, and that is deliberate. The grader and the ready check run no decode-step kernels, so nothing here loses decode-step time in the sense of an inefficiency entry (cost at 1/8/32 decode rows and 127/1,016/2,048 prefill rows); round 4's changes in fact remove grader-side waste (identical code is no longer timed twice) and a false blocker (the set rule). The blind spots in *What each tool still cannot see* are contract limits, delivered here and as the held notes below instead of `ineff-grader-N` entries, as in round 3. Held for their owners to fold in when their entries land:

- `territory-baseline-experts` — the attempt's kernels run only at 2..59 rows; the piece verdict rests entirely on 8 and 32 rows, decode is `faster` only if both are `faster`, and the 33–59 band plus rows 2–7 are **Unverified** at every graded size. The hand-off's side of 60 is proved by `check_sizes.py` (59/60/61), never by the piece verdict.
- `territory-g3` / the lead — read the set from `ready-verdict.json`'s `variants."muse-all".pass`: the file's top-level `pass` and exit code still fail a set that passes only together (piece 3). A `min_rows: 2` experts attempt adds nothing at 1×128, so a set containing it must win the 1-request workload with its other slots.
- `checker` — a grade's `handed off` at a size means "not timed against this bar", and against a `--baseline` bar a candidate-handed-off size can still be timed (candidate as compiled vs the baseline's own kernels); round 4 grades use no `--baseline`, so every `handed off` in them is the compiled-bar case. Check `wins_vs_compiled` is absent, not zero, at handed-off sizes.

# Exploration: round 4 — analysis

**Version:** v1 · 2026-11-04T21:40:34Z · skill version 10

## Tracker

| Territory | Agent | Status | Inefficiencies | Updated |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `baseline-experts` | `explorer-baseline-experts` | open | — | 2026-11-04 21:40Z |
| `baseline-routing` | `explorer-baseline-routing` | open | — | 2026-11-04 21:40Z |
| `baseline-combine` | `explorer-baseline-combine` | open | — | 2026-11-04 21:40Z |
| `g3` | `explorer-g3` | open | — | 2026-11-04 21:40Z |
| `grader` | `explorer-grader` | open | — | 2026-11-04 21:40Z |

## Starting point

Round 4 is the last round ([ADR 0014](../../../claude/adr/0014-muse-wonder-last-round.md)). It builds on rounds 1–3 as measured independently by Claude in [`claude/findings/muse-round-3.md`](../../../claude/findings/muse-round-3.md). Round 3 ran as Muse Spark (model `muse-spark-1.3-contributor`, skill version 8) and submitted the reference in every slot: no candidate passed the ready check alone, and the skill then counted only candidates that pass alone. Round 4 changes three rules ([ADR 0015](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)): candidates that pass together in `muse-all` are `ready` as a **set**; an attempt may hand off inputs below `min_rows` as well as above `max_rows`; and a handed-off size is reported `handed off` instead of being timed. A slot's **baseline** is still its best attempt so far that passes the current G2, has `beats_compiled` true in the grader, and passes G3 ([ADR 0011](../../../claude/adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). **No slot has a baseline.** The bar in every slot is the compiled reference, and a new attempt must beat it in the same grader run (no `--baseline` argument). Round 4 runs as Muse Wonder (muse-wonder-1.0).

### Per slot

#### `experts` — starting point `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1`

- **What it is.** Round 2's fused per-pair kernel, byte-identical, plus `max_rows: 59` in `spec.json`: rows 1–59 run the fused kernel, rows above 59 run the compiled reference. See `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1/notes.md` and its `grade.json` (G1 pass, G2 differ 0 at all six sizes).
- **Piece timing** (chained µs per layer, candidate vs compiled, its own grade run): 1 row 96.9 vs 86.6 (`slower`, 5 wins); 8 rows 168.9 vs 238.2 (`faster`, 29 wins); 32 rows 554.7 vs 883.4 (`faster`, 29 wins); prefill 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 `same` (19 / 15 / 16 wins — the hand-off runs compiled code). `beats_compiled` false: decode `slower` on the 1-row size alone.
- **G3 effect.** Never timed end to end (round 3, section 4). Its ancestor (round 2 attempt-7, same kernels without the hand-off) shortened the decode step 17.5% with 32 requests but made prompt processing 6.6–14.5× slower; the hand-off removes the prefill half of that, so no G3 prediction from round 3 stands — Claude's reading is that only the 1-row gap remains.
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** It is not a baseline because `beats_compiled` is false — the 1-row decode loss (96.9 vs 86.6 µs/layer) — and it has no G3 pass. Round 3 tried a vectorised scalar path (attempt-2, bought nothing) and an unfused path copying the reference's structure (attempt-5, 2× worse at 1 row) and concluded no fix existed in the spec surface. From round 4 the surface has `min_rows`: `min_rows: 2` with `max_rows: 59` hands 1-row inputs to the compiled reference while keeping the 8/32-row wins — a direction not yet graded. It can then pass G3 only in a set whose other kernels are faster with 1 request, because with 1 request every decode step runs MLX's own code for this slot.
- **Where it still spends its time.** At 8/32 rows it already wins by 69.3 / 328.7 µs per layer; what remains is the 1-row chain (the `tg_x` load, silu and barrier chain named in round 3) — now hand-off-able — and per-pair weight re-reads at all sizes (552,960 B per pair, round 3's entry).

#### `routing` — starting point `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6`

- **What it is.** Round 2's staged scalar-exact kernel (attempt-4 kernels) with `max_rows: 32`: every decode step (1–32 rows) runs the staged scalar kernels, all prefill sizes run the compiled reference. Attempt-6 is a byte-identical re-grade of round 3's attempt-1 (empty `diff` on both blocks and `spec.json`), run to test whether attempt-1's 2,048-row `slower` on identical code reproduced; it did not (19/30 wins, `same`). See `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6/notes.md`.
- **Piece timing.** Round 3's grade: decode `faster` at all three sizes (candidate 51.7 / 90.9 / 132.2 vs compiled 66.3 / 104.0 / 152.0 µs per layer; 28 / 27 / 25 wins), prefill `same` at all three sizes. Claude's re-grade with the round-4 grader ([`results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/`](../../../results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/)): decode `faster` (29 / 26 / 27 wins; candidate 0.72 / 0.90 / 0.88 of the compiled reference at 1 / 8 / 32 rows), the three prefill sizes `handed off`, `beats_compiled` true.
- **G3 effect.** In round 3's swarm ready check it failed alone against `compiled-routing` at 8×128 on overlapping ranges, with no phase slower anywhere (decode medians −0.38 / −0.31 / −0.59 / −0.48 ms vs the unchanged model at 1×128 / 8×128 / 32×128 / 32×1024). Claude's G3 agreed: `same` as `compiled-routing` at 8×128. Together with combine attempt-2 (`muse-all`) it passed the swarm's ready check but failed Claude's G3 against `compiled-all` at 32×1024, where the medians are 0.9% apart with overlapping ranges.
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** G3 alone: it passes G2 and has `beats_compiled` true, but it has never passed G3, alone or (in Claude's run) as a pair. Under round 4's set rule the pair would have been `ready` in round 3, but a set still has to pass G3 as `muse-all`, so the pair is no baseline.
- **Where it still spends its time.** Decode wins at every size; the open question is margin, above all at 32×1024 where the pair gains only 0.25–0.30 ms over the compiled reference (~1%), inside the 5-repeat spread. The per-row `w_router` re-read is untouched (upper bound only, round 2's `ineff-baseline-routing-4`).

#### `combine` — starting point `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/combine/attempt-2`

- **What it is.** Round 2's attempt-1 kernel with its seven `volatile` rounding barriers replaced by seven plain `float` locals and a header block (`block-1.metal`) carrying `#pragma STDC FP_CONTRACT OFF` / `#pragma clang fp contract(off)`: same 7-op stepwise fold `((p0+p1)+p2)+p3`, same grid (`rows*768`) and threadgroup [256,1,1], no `max_rows`. See `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/combine/attempt-2/notes.md`.
- **Piece timing.** Round 3's grade: `faster` at all six sizes (decode 31.8 / 34.7 / 32.7 vs compiled 36.9 / 41.1 / 45.7 µs per layer, 24 / 27 / 30 wins; prefill 38.2 / 100.9 / 198.0 vs 64.0 / 281.8 / 556.2, 30 / 30 / 29 wins); `beats_compiled` true in both phases. Absolute chained times drift up to ~35% between runs on this machine (round 3's lesson), so only same-run paired verdicts transfer.
- **G3 effect.** In round 3's ready check it failed alone against the unchanged model at 1×128 on a single outlier repeat (5.892 ms, above the unchanged model's lowest 5.430) and, in Claude's G3, against `compiled-combine` at 32×128 and 32×1024 — again range overlaps with no phase slower anywhere (swarm decode medians −0.53 / −0.59 / −0.44 / −0.26 ms vs the unchanged model). Its ancestor's in-step cost (+1.05 ms/step at 32 requests from the volatile barriers) is what the pragma removes; round 3's measured decode medians favour the kernel everywhere.
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** G3 alone, on spread: every median favours it, but the 5-repeat ranges overlap the bars'. No kernel change is named that tightens spread on 7 plain ops (round 3's implementation README); as part of a set it already passes `muse-all` in the swarm's run.
- **Where it still spends its time.** Nothing further in the grader — it sits on the chained floor and wins at all six sizes. What remains is the same margin question as routing: more separation from the compiled reference at 32×128 and 32×1024, or a set that clears the bar together.

#### All three together

Round 3's pair (routing attempt-6 + combine attempt-2) is the best result of any round: against the unchanged model it shortens the decode step 16.5% / 5.4% / 2.8% / 1.6% and whole requests 14.1% / 5.6% / 2.1% / 2.4% at 1×128 / 8×128 / 32×128 / 32×1024, with prompts 1.6–3.1% faster and nothing slower — but it fails G3 against `compiled-all` at 32×1024 (0.9% median gap, overlapping ranges). About half the gain over the unchanged model is `mx.compile` of the two slots' reference code alone. The three-slot composition is untested: in rounds 1 and 2, replacing all three slots at once lost about 2.8 ms with 8 requests for an unknown reason, and round 3 installed no experts candidate, so no run since has met it.

### What is left

Ranked by predicted saving against the compiled reference (no slot has a baseline, so the reference is the bar everywhere). Claude's measurement names three things round 4 has to find out; the ranking follows them.

1. **Experts with `min_rows`.** Whether attempt-1's 8/32-row speed (168.9 vs 238.2 and 554.7 vs 883.4 µs per layer) carries into G3 once 1 row runs MLX's own code (`min_rows: 2`, `max_rows: 59`). This is the only ungraded direction in any slot and the largest piece saving left: the 8/32-row wins are 69.3 / 328.7 µs per layer, worth (PREDICTION, from those same-run margins × 20 layers) about 1.4 ms per step at 8 requests and 6.6 ms at 32 requests against the compiled reference, with prefill `handed off` above 59 rows and 1-row decode `handed off` — so the gain exists only at 8 and 32 requests, and G3 can pass only in a set whose other kernels win with 1 request. The risk is the three-slot interaction (item 3).
2. **A margin at 32×1024.** The pair gains 0.25–0.30 ms over the compiled reference there (~1%), which 5 repeats cannot tell from noise; a set needs more than that with 32 long prompts. This is a margin problem in routing and/or combine decode kernels, not a correctness one: both starting points are bit-exact and already `faster` at every graded size, so any new attempt must widen the same-run margin at decode sizes without touching prefill (`max_rows: 32` for routing, faster-everywhere for combine). A saving here is worth the difference between a passing and a failing set — the largest whole-request prize left, and unquantified until a builder measures it.
3. **All three slots at once.** In rounds 1 and 2 the three-slot replacement lost about 2.8 ms with 8 requests for an unknown reason; a set with an experts attempt meets that again. No single-slot kernel change is predicted to remove it, so it is carried as a constraint: per-slot wins are not assumed to compose, and the ready check (which times candidates alone and all together) is where composition is measured. If the three together lose, the fallback set is the routing+combine pair.
4. **Slots not yet tried.** `routing+combine` (both slots, each with its own kernels, in one candidate) has never been graded as one folder. The parts are graded independently and the combine part receives the reference routing weights, so it is packaging unless a shared design emerges; the set rule already submits the two slots together without it. No hypothesis is planned on it unless exploration finds a shared-design reason.
5. **Recommendations outside the slots** stand as written in round 1's and round 2's exploration READMEs (attention K/V re-read per query head; split-K partial traffic from 14 rows; the 60 q/k/v `[0]` gathers; engine CPU per 1-row step). Claude's round-3 measurement did not test them. They are for surucuonur's team; no hypothesis targets them.

### Refuted claims

No one chases these again.

- Round 3's experts 1-row fixes: a vectorised scalar path (attempt-2) bought nothing and an unfused path copying the reference's structure (attempt-5) was 2× worse at 1 row — the 1-row gap is not closed by either approach, and round 4 does not retry them; it hands 1 row off instead.
- Routing attempt-1's 2,048-row `slower` verdict on byte-identical code: attempt-6's re-grade (19/30, `same`) confirmed it as paired noise, not a hand-off cost. Handed-off sizes are no longer timed at all.
- `ineff-runs-3` (round 1, refuted): the micro sorted/unsorted gaps measure kernel choice, not pair order.
- Round 1's implicit claim that the independent (overlapped) piece timing ranks attempts as the model does: refuted by the chained measurement. Round 4 ranks by the chained timing only.
- The claim that scalar sums cannot reproduce MMA rounding: refuted by building in round 2 (routing attempts 2–4, experts scalar paths bit-identical at all six sizes).

### Territories this round opens

Each territory is opened by the line of this section that names it. A `baseline-<slot>` explorer maps that slot's starting-point kernels and `spec.json` — now the code in the slot — with the checklist, and finds where they still lose time and, for a starting point, why it is no baseline. Explorers start from the earlier rounds' entries for their territory and write only what is new.

| Territory | Opened by |
|---|---|
| `baseline-experts` | "`experts` — starting point `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1`" — its kernels and `spec.json` are now the code in the slot; what `min_rows: 2` changes (the 1-row hand-off, the 33–59 band, the dead scalar branch), and where the fused kernel still spends its time at 8/32 rows. |
| `baseline-routing` | "`routing` — starting point `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6`" — likewise; where decode margin can still be widened, above all for the 32×1024 workload (item 2 of *What is left*). |
| `baseline-combine` | "`combine` — starting point `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/combine/attempt-2`" — likewise; whether any exact change widens its decode margin, and what the pragma leaves in the compiled binary. |
| `g3` | "All three together" and items 1–3 of *What is left* — where the end-to-end change differs from the piece timing (the pair at 32×1024, the untested three-slot interaction), and why. |
| `grader` | Round 4's three rule changes (ADR 0015) — how `min_rows`, `handed off` and the set rule are implemented in `bench/grader/slots.py`, `check_candidate.py` and `check_ready.py`, and what each still can't see. |

23|tile cache or any other sharing across pairs: two pairs that
24|select the same expert read that expert's 552,960 B twice,
25|in full. At 32 rows (128 pairs over at most 60 experts,
