16|chain inside a 512-thread threadgroup
17|(`muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1/block-0.metal`):
18|`tg_x` load + barrier (`:29-32`); gate/up interleaved over
19|24 strided K steps on 12 of 16 simdgroups — 4 simdgroups
20|idle (`:51-58`); barrier (`:73`); bfloat16 silu-mul on 384 of
21|512 threads (`:77-85`); barrier (`:86`); down interleaved
22|over 12 merged K steps, again 12 of 16 simdgroups (`:95-102`).
23|Each K step in the pair helpers
24|(`block-1.metal:69-128,137-195`) issues its loads and then
25|runs 64 dependent accumulates into two 32-float thread
26|arrays; per thread the chain is 24 + 12 = 36 such steps plus
27|4 `simd_sum` trees and the silu's exp/divide, with no second
28|wave of work inside the group to hide it. The group can hold
29|no more parallelism: exactly two 32-float accumulators fit
30|at 512 threads — a third failed G1 in round 2 (pipeline max
31|448), a ceiling the shared `p`/`q` arrays at
32|`block-0.metal:42-43` already sit on.

39|prefill off, 8 and 32 rows are the only sizes left — and at
40|those sizes the same chain is what caps the margin. The win

13|## The exact boundary a round-4 solution must keep
14|
15|A round-4 attempt is inside the boundary only if all five hold. This is the checklist the builders, the boundary agent and the checker grade against; each line names its source.
16|
17|1. **Spec validity.** `min_rows` and `max_rows` in `spec.json` are each an integer of at least 1, booleans and floats refused, and `min_rows ≤ max_rows` when both are given — otherwise `build()` raises `ValueError` before any kernel runs and the attempt is a G1 failure ([slots.py:330-335](../../../bench/grader/slots.py); brief:174). For `routing+combine` each part's spec carries its own pair of bounds (brief:176).
18|2. **Inclusive kernel window.** The attempt's kernels run exactly when `min_rows ≤ rows ≤ max_rows` for the bounds it gives (a missing bound is open on that side), and run the slot's reference under `mx.compile` outside that window; `rows` is the first slot input's `shape[0]` ([slots.py:338-345](../../../bench/grader/slots.py)). Row-for-row: `hands_off(rows)` is `rows > max_rows or rows < min_rows` ([slots.py:338-339](../../../bench/grader/slots.py)), and `test_hand_off.py` pins the edges bit-for-bit: 8 and 59 run the kernel, 7 and 60 run the compiled reference, for `min_rows: 8, max_rows: 59` ([test_hand_off.py:69](../../../bench/grader/test_hand_off.py)).
19|3. **G2 bit-exactness at every size, handed off or not.** G2 runs the attempt's `run()` — hand-off dispatch included — on all 20 layers at 1, 8, 32, 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows and requires bit-for-bit equality with the plain reference, in order for routing (including the tied 4th/5th choice) and elementwise for combine/experts; timing runs only if G2 passes ([check_candidate.py:320-351](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py); brief:187-195,175). A handed-off size therefore tests `mx.compile(reference)` against the plain reference through the attempt's own dispatch, which is why the boundary also includes compiled==reference at the six sizes (round-3 entry §2; [ADR 0011:34](../../../claude/adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). For experts the window must also sit on the right side of MLX's 60-row kernel switch (`gather_qmm_rhs` from 60 rows, different rounding): a decode-built experts kernel may run only below 60 rows, i.e. `max_rows ≤ 59` ([slots.py:219-220](../../../bench/grader/slots.py); round-3 entry §2). Inside the window the reference still changes behaviour once: `ref_experts` sorts the pairs from 16 rows (`inds.size >= 64`, [slots.py:62](../../../bench/grader/slots.py)), so a kernel running at both 8 and 32 rows must match the unsorted and the sorted reference, both on the `gather_qvm` side of 60.
20|4. **Piece-timing phase rule.** At each timed size the verdict is `faster` with ≥22 wins of 30 paired repeats, `slower` with ≥22 losses, else `same` ([check_candidate.py:244-250](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)). `judge()` drops `handed off` sizes from their phase: a phase is `faster` only when **every** size the kernels run at is `faster` and at least one such size exists, `slower` when any timed size is `slower`, `handed off` when none is left, else `not slower`; `beats_compiled` is true iff one phase is `faster` and neither is `slower` ([check_candidate.py:253-271](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py); brief:217-218). One `same` at a timed size blocks the bar; one `slower` anywhere fails it.
21|5. **Whole-request rule, and the set.** The ready check and G3 time whole requests in vLLM at 1×128, 8×128, 32×128, 32×1024 (5 repeats, 256 tokens), require the same greedy tokens at 1 and 32 requests, and pass a variant only when decode or prompt is `faster` (non-overlapping ranges) in every workload and nothing — decode, prompt or whole request — is `slower` anywhere ([check_ready.py:47-56,131-161](../../../bench/grader/check_ready.py); [time_candidates.py:163-201](../../../bench/grader/time_candidates.py)). From round 4, when `muse-all` passes, its candidates are `ready` together as a set even where one fails alone, and G3 judges the set as one (skill step 4; brief:206; [ADR 0015:11,42](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)). The converse also binds: with 1 request every decode step has 1 row, so an attempt with `min_rows: 2` runs MLX's own code for the whole 1×128 workload and can pass G3/the ready check only inside a set whose other kernels are faster there (brief:174; [ADR 0015:37](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)).

No new measured number is claimed here.
32|- **Invariants:** the inclusive window and the refusal rules in *The exact boundary* items 1–2; validation rejects `bool` explicitly because `True` is an `int` in Python ([slots.py:331-333](../../../bench/grader/slots.py)), and `min_rows > max_rows` is refused with "the kernels would never run" ([slots.py:334-335](../../../bench/grader/slots.py)). What `build` does **not** check: that the window sits on the right side of 60 for experts, or anything about rows between the tested sizes (see *What each tool still cannot see*).

34|### 2. `check_candidate.py` — handed-off sizes not timed, `judge()` and `beats_compiled` (check_candidate.py:244-271, 352-400)
35|
36|- **Callers:** builders, `.venv/bin/python bench/grader/check_candidate.py <attempt> <slot> [--out FILE]`; no `--baseline` this round — no slot has one (round-4 README *Starting point*), so the only bar is `compiled`. The `--baseline` path still exists and its handed-off rule differs (below), which a reader of a baseline grade must not confuse with the compiled bar.
37|- **What is new — exclusion, not a tie.** Per part and size, the timing loop builds `together = {candidate, compiled[, baseline]}` and then drops every function except `compiled` whose `hands_off(rows)` is true, so a handing-off function is never run in `paired_times` at that size ([check_candidate.py:372-380](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)). Its per-repeat times are then taken from the compiled function's repeats (`paired.get(name, paired["compiled"])`) and summed across parts as before ([check_candidate.py:381-384](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)). Consequences in the printed verdict: at a fully handed-off size (vs the compiled bar) there is a `vs_compiled: "handed off"` and **no** `wins_vs_compiled` key, and the candidate's reported median equals the compiled median by construction ([check_candidate.py:386-394](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)). The unpaired `reference` median is still timed at every size ([check_candidate.py:371](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)) — informational only, as in round 3. This removes round 3's defect exactly: identical code can no longer be judged `slower` on paired noise (routing attempt-1's 2,048-row verdict, re-graded `same` by attempt-6; round-4 README *Refuted claims*).
38|- **What is new — the `own` rule and the baseline exception.** `own[name]` records whether a function ran code of its own in **any** part at that size ([check_candidate.py:364,382](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)). A size's verdict against a bar is `handed off` only when neither the candidate nor that bar ran its own kernels there: `if not (own["candidate"] or own[bar])` ([check_candidate.py:387-390](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)). For the compiled bar `own["compiled"]` is never set, so the rule reduces to "candidate handed off in every part". Against a `--baseline` attempt that runs its own kernels at a size the candidate hands off, the size **is** timed as before — candidate repeats copied from compiled against the baseline's own repeats ([ADR 0015:22](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)). For `routing+combine` the summing is per part before wins are counted (round 3 §1 stands), so one part handing off while the other runs still times the size, on the summed repeats.
39|- **What is new — `judge()`.** It filters `handed off` verdicts out of each phase before judging ([check_candidate.py:262-269](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)); the phase rule and `beats_compiled` are *The exact boundary* item 4. The five synthetic cases in `test_hand_off.py` pin them (piece 4). G2 is untouched: correctness still runs at all six sizes through the dispatch, and timing still runs only when G2 passes ([check_candidate.py:349-352](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)).
40|- **Cost:** the timing still chains 20 layers × 30 paired repeats per timed size (round 3 §1); handed-off sizes now cost one compiled timing instead of two identical ones per part. The one real-attempt evidence that the new reporting works end to end is Claude's re-grade of round 3's routing attempt-6 (`max_rows: 32`) with this grader: G2 passes, decode `faster` at 1/8/32 on 29/26/27 wins of 30, the three prefill sizes `handed off`, `beats_compiled` true ([ADR 0015:28-32](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)).
41|- **Invariants:** `WINS_NEEDED` is still 22 of 30 (one-sided sign test, p < 0.01, [check_candidate.py:56-63](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)); size labels still carry the phase prefix (`rows ` / `prefill rows `) that `judge()` splits on ([check_candidate.py:57,358](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)). A phase with every size handed off can never supply the required `faster` phase: an attempt that hands off everything beats nothing (`judge` case "everything handed off", piece 4).

43|### 3. `check_ready.py` — the set rule (check_ready.py:98-100, 152-174; time_candidates.py:111-132, 168-201)
44|
45|- **Callers:** the lead only, `.venv/bin/python bench/grader/check_ready.py <new out folder> SLOT=FOLDER...`, at most twice per round (round-3 entry §5 stands: pinned protocol, log audit, `--audit`, exit codes). What round 4 changes is only how its verdict is read.
46|- **Where `muse-all` comes from.** `expected_variants` requires `compiled-all`/`muse-all` exactly when more than one slot is submitted ([check_ready.py:98-100](../../../bench/grader/check_ready.py)); `time_candidates.Variants` builds them by installing every slot's attempts (resp. compiled references) into one `MoE.__call__` ([time_candidates.py:117-127](../../../bench/grader/time_candidates.py)). `g3()` judges `muse-all` against `base` and `compiled-all` with the same range rule as any variant ([time_candidates.py:177-200](../../../bench/grader/time_candidates.py)), and the audit recomputes that verdict from the log before trusting it ([check_ready.py:142-148](../../../bench/grader/check_ready.py)).
47|- **The set rule, precisely.** The audit fills `judged[v]` for **every** `muse-*` variant — each single slot and `muse-all` — with `pass = g3[v]["g3"] and same_tokens` ([check_ready.py:152-161](../../../bench/grader/check_ready.py)). The set rule is **not** in this file's aggregate: the file still computes `passed = all(j["pass"] for j in judged.values())` and exits 0 only then ([check_ready.py:173-174](../../../bench/grader/check_ready.py)). So a set that passes only together produces `ready-verdict.json` with `pass: false` and exit 1, alongside `variants."muse-all".pass: true`. Readiness as a set is the skill's reading of that per-variant field (skill step 4: "when `muse-all` passes, all of them are `ready` together as a set, even where one fails alone"; brief:206). Any checker, tracker or script that reads only the top-level `pass`/exit code will report a passing set as failed — the single most misreadable line in the round-4 grader. The parts are still timed alone in the same run (the variants are all required by the audit), so the set reading costs no extra GPU run; a set's parts are not required to pass alone, but `muse-all` must still pass both bars and keep the tokens (`same_tokens` for `muse-all` at 1 and 32 requests, [check_ready.py:131-140,154-157](../../../bench/grader/check_ready.py)).
48|- **Data:** `ready-verdict.json` gains nothing new in round 4; the set is read out of the existing per-variant `variants`, `vs` and `phases` fields (round-3 entry §5). G3 after the round judges the set as `muse-all` in the same way ([ADR 0015:11,42](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)).
49|- **Invariants:** G3 and the ready-check protocol are unchanged ([ADR 0015:37](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)): a slot's kernels count wherever they run in a whole request, so the hand-off that the piece timing forgives is fully visible here — in particular at 1×128, where a `min_rows: 2` slot contributes the compiled reference's code, not its kernels (boundary item 5). Claude's post-round G3 stays the authority (round-3 entry §5).

52|

See *can't see* item 5.

It states that a hand-off is still G2-checked bit-exact at every size and that the piece timing reports the size as `handed off` (brief:175), that `routing+combine` carries both bounds per part (brief:176), the per-size/per-phase/`beats_compiled` reading of `handed off` (brief:216-218), and the set rule for the ready check and G3 (brief:206). 62|## Worked example: an experts attempt with `min_rows: 2, max_rows: 59`
63|
64|The round-4 README's ungraded direction (round-4 README *What is left* item 1): round 3's experts attempt-1 kernels plus this window. `hands_off(rows)` is true at 1 row (`1 < 2`) and at every row above 59 ([slots.py:338-339](../../../bench/grader/slots.py)). Graded with no `--baseline`, so the only bar is `compiled`:
65|
66|| Size | Phase | Who runs | G2 | Piece verdict vs compiled |
67||---|---|---|---|---|
68|| 1 row | decode | compiled reference | compiled vs plain reference, bit-exact required | `handed off` — not timed; no `wins_vs_compiled`; candidate median = compiled median |
69|| 8 rows | decode | attempt's kernels | kernels vs `gather_qvm` reference, unsorted pairs | timed: `faster` iff ≥22/30 wins, `slower` iff ≥22 losses, else `same` |
70|| 32 rows | decode | attempt's kernels | kernels vs `gather_qvm` reference, sorted pairs (from 16 rows) | timed, same rule |
71|| 127 rows | prefill | compiled reference | compiled vs plain reference (`gather_qmm_rhs` side) | `handed off` |
72|| 1,016 rows | prefill | compiled reference | same | `handed off` |
73|| 2,048 rows | prefill | compiled reference | same | `handed off` |
74|
75|Phase arithmetic ([check_candidate.py:253-271](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)): decode keeps only 8 and 32 rows, so decode is `faster` iff **both** are `faster`, `slower` iff either is `slower`, else `not slower`. Prefill has no timed size left, so it is `handed off`. `beats_compiled` is therefore true exactly when 8 and 32 rows are both `faster`; a `same` at either makes decode `not slower` and `beats_compiled` false, and a `slower` at either makes it false with decode `slower`. For scale only (prediction, not a grade): round 3's attempt-1 kernels timed 168.9 vs 238.2 µs per layer at 8 rows and 554.7 vs 883.4 at 32 in their own run, while losing 96.9 vs 86.6 at 1 row ([ADR 0015:12](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md); round-4 README *Per slot: experts*) — under the old rule that single `slower` made `beats_compiled` false; under this window the 1-row size is removed from the phase instead of having to be won. The kernels never face `gather_qmm_rhs` rounding: every row they run at is below 60, and every prefill size is handed off. Two cautions the table cannot show: rows 2–7 and 33–59 run the kernels in real serving but are graded at no size (only 8 and 32 represent the whole window), and at 1 request this attempt contributes nothing in G3 — alone it cannot be faster than its compiled bar at 1×128, so it passes whole requests only in a set whose other kernels win there (boundary item 5).

77|## What each tool still cannot see
78|
79|Round 3's list stands except where the hand-off change retires it (its items 3 and 5c were already retired in round 3; the duplicate-timing half of its item 5 is now removed by piece 2). What round 4 adds or leaves open, per tool:
80|
81|1. **`slots.build` cannot see where the window sits.** Any `max_rows` in 32..126, and any `min_rows` in 2..8, produce identical dispatch at the six G2 sizes on the far side of the tested points (32 runs the kernels, 127 hands off; 1 hands off for both `min_rows` values) — the piece grader cannot tell `max_rows: 59` (right side of the 60-row switch) from 100 (wrong side), and cannot see kernel speed or exactness at rows 2–7, 9–31 or 33–126 at all. `check_sizes.py` at 59/60/61 (round-3 entry §3) is still the only tool that places the experts hand-off, and only where the boundary agent runs it; hypotheses with kernels running above 32 rows carry the 33–59 band as **Unverified**.

In whole-request serving the muse variant goes through `build`'s `run()` while the compiled variant does not, so only G3/the ready check can show a wrapper cost — aggregated into whole-request ranges, never attributed to the hand-off.
83|3. **`judge()`'s all-or-nothing phase.** A phase is `faster` only when every timed size is; the size of a win is invisible to the verdict (a 300 µs win and a 1 µs win at 22/30 count the same), and one noisy `same` blocks `beats_compiled` even with large wins elsewhere (pinned deliberately by `test_hand_off.py`'s "a timed size not faster" case). A regression in the timing substitution at [check_candidate.py:376-394](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py) would pass this test suite.
86|6. **Handed-off exactness between the six sizes** still rests on compiled==reference where `check_sizes.py` has not run the attempt: G2 shows it at 1/8/32/127/1,016/2,048, `check_sizes` extends the hand-off path to its 25 sizes where run, and no tool tests above 2,048 rows (round-3 items 3 and 5 stand).   "output": "# MobileMoE Bandwidth Study

*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*

How efficiently an inference engine turns an Apple Silicon GPU's memory bandwidth and compute into generated tokens when serving a small mixture-of-experts model.

## Hardware limits

**Peak bandwidth**:
The most bytes per second the GPU can read from unified memory, as rated by the manufacturer (about 200 GB/s on this project's M1 Pro).
_Avoid_: max bandwidth, memory speed

**Peak compute**:
The most floating-point operations per second the GPU can perform (about 5.2 TFLOPS on the 16-core M1 Pro GPU).
_Avoid_: max compute, TFLOPS (as the name of the limit)

**Achieved bandwidth**:
The bytes a decode step must read from memory (the weights it touches plus its share of cached attention state), divided by that step's duration.
_Avoid_: bandwidth usage, utilization (unqualified)

**Arithmetic intensity**:
Floating-point operations performed per byte read from memory during a decode step.
_Avoid_: compute density, FLOPs/byte ratio

**Ridge point**:
The arithmetic intensity at which peak bandwidth and peak compute meet (about 26 operations per byte here); below it a step is limited by bandwidth, above it by compute.

**Roofline**:
The chart of achievable throughput against arithmetic intensity, capped by peak bandwidth on the left and peak compute on the right, with measured decode steps plotted beneath it.

## Bottlenecks and fixes

**Bandwidth-bound**:
A decode step whose achieved bandwidth is close to peak bandwidth.

**Compute-bound**:
A decode step whose operation rate is close to peak compute.

**Overhead-bound**:
A decode step far below both limits, because its time goes to work other than reading weights or doing arithmetic, such as launching GPU jobs, routing tokens to experts or scheduling.
_Avoid_: latency-bound, CPU-bound (unless the CPU specifically is the cause)

**Bottleneck**:
The single cause, identified from measurements, that most limits throughput for a given workload.
_Avoid_: issue, slowness

**Kernel**:
One program the GPU runs as a unit, such as one matrix product or one element-wise add; a decode step is a chain of hundreds of them, each with a fixed start-up cost.
_Avoid_: GPU job, op (for a kernel launch)

**Occupancy**:
The share of the GPU's thread slots in use while it runs; low occupancy means most of the chip is idle even when the GPU counts as busy.
_Avoid_: GPU utilization (which only says the GPU had work)

**Knock-out**:
A measurement in which one piece of the decode step is replaced by a stand-in that returns the right shape without GPU work; the time and bytes the step saves are that piece's cost.
_Avoid_: ablation

**Baseline**:
The unmodified engine serving MobileMoE-S-QAT (int4), against which every fix is measured.

**Fix**:
One change to the engine, the model code or the configuration, measured against the baseline under the same workload.
_Avoid_: optimization (for a change that hasn't been measured), tweak

## Inference

**Prefill**:
Processing a request's whole prompt through the model before its first token is generated, in chunks of up to the engine's token budget per pass (2,048 tokens here).
_Avoid_: prompt phase (say prefill, or prompt processing)

**Decode step**:
One engine iteration that produces one new token for each request it includes.

**Decode rows**:
The number of requests the engine actually advanced in one decode step; the batch size that matters for the roofline.
_Avoid_: batch size (unqualified), concurrency

**Client concurrency**:
The number of requests the benchmark client keeps in flight; it caps decode rows but does not equal them.

# Inefficiency: per-pair weight re-reads persist in the starting point (465 MB excess at 32 rows)

- **Owner:** explorer-baseline-experts
- **Status:** confirmed
- **Version:** 2
- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T03:23:32Z
- **Next:** verifier to confirm byte arithmetic against GPU counters

## Slot

`experts`

## What happens

Attempt-4 fuses gate/up/down + silu-mul into one kernel (removing round
1 `muse-spark/exploration/ineff-switch-layers-2`, confirmed: 4 on-chain
kernels/layer + bf16 intermediates written and re-read), but it keeps
per-pair reads: each (row, expert-slot) pair's threadgroup streams its
expert's full gate/up/down weights independently
(`muse-spark/kernels/experts/attempt-4/block-0.metal:23,31,43,70`;
offsets `eW = e * 36864`, `eS = e * 9216` per pair). A popular expert is
read once per pair that selects it, not once per layer. This is round
1's `ineff-runs-1` (confirmed) and the traffic half of
`ineff-quantized-kernels-1` (confirmed), restated for the starting
point because attempt-4 does not remove it — it only hides part of it
with fusion and 8 in-flight blocks per group
(`attempt-4/notes.md:66-75`: 32-row effective 109 → ~137 GB/s
independent). The `x` re-read half of round 1's kernel entry *is*
removed: `tg_x` is loaded once per pair (`block-0.metal:18-20`) where
`qvm_impl` re-streams the row per tile (round 1
`territory-quantized-kernels.md` §A: ~55 KB x-traffic per pair vs
3.75 KB needed).

What is new this round: the same per-pair grid also runs at prefill
sizes, where fan-in is far larger (508/4,064/8,192 pairs per layer over
at most 60 distinct experts), and the chained timings now price the
remaining waste at decode sizes against the reference the slot must
beat.

## Cost

Per decode step (GPU counters `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md:26,32`
via round 1 `ineff-runs-1.md`; per-pair bytes 552,960 B, territory §A):

- **1 row:** 4 pairs, all distinct (4.0 distinct experts/layer): reads
  51 MB vs 44 MB must-read, excess 7 MB. Chained candidate 132.9
  µs/layer (`console-chain.txt`) — but at 1 row the loss is latency
  (ineff-2), not these bytes; excess floor 7 MB ÷ 200 GB/s = 0.04 ms.
- **8 rows:** 32 pairs/layer; no serving knock-out at 8 rows. Modelled
  pair traffic 32 × 552,960 × 20 = 353.9 MB/step (weights only;
  round 1 modelled 383 MB with x-traffic). Distinct experts/layer
  unmeasured at 8 rows; bounded by 32 pairs and 60 experts.
- **32 rows:** 128 pairs/layer read 908 MB/step vs 443 MB for the
  distinct experts — excess 465 MB (51% of bytes are re-reads).
  Per layer: 70.8 MB pair traffic vs 22.2 MB distinct. Candidate
  chained 587.6 µs/layer = 120.5 GB/s on pair traffic (60% of the
  200 GB/s peak, `claude/GLOSSARY.md:10`); the same time on distinct
  bytes alone would be 177 GB/s-equivalent — there is no bandwidth
  headroom left to absorb the re-reads at this rate.

Fixed costs: candidate 1 kernel/layer vs reference 7 (1 row) / 13
(32 rows, incl. 6 sort-glue kernels from 16 rows, round 1
`ineff-switch-layers-1` confirmed: ~0.7 ms/step at 32 rows, removable
only inside a grouped kernel). Attempt-4 already banks the launch and
intermediate-traffic savings; this entry is only the weight re-reads.

## Kind

Overhead-bound with a bandwidth-waste component (round 1 wording for
the same cause): 120.5 GB/s chained at 32 rows is 60% of peak, and the
step as a whole sits far below both limits; the wasted bytes are real
but removing them at the current rate is worth less than the floor
arithmetic suggests (see Predicted saving).

## Spans

`baseline-experts` (`block-0.metal` per-pair offsets), `quantized-kernels`
(per-pair `qvm` grids this mirrors), `switch-layers` (grouped path the
reference only takes from 60 rows), `runs` (counter tables).

## Predicted saving

Excess bytes at peak bandwidth (floor, per decode step):

- 1 row: 7 MB ÷ 200 GB/s = **0.04 ms ≈ 0.0 ms**.
- 8 rows: excess unmeasured; if distinct experts/layer ≈ 25 of 32 pairs
  (round 1 micro pattern), excess ≈ (32−25) × 552,960 × 20 = 77 MB →
  **0.39 ms** floor. Marked estimate — no 8-row counter exists.
- 32 rows: 465 MB ÷ 200 GB/s = **2.33 ms** floor.

Against the compiled reference this floor is **not** the predicted
saving, and round 1's building is the reason: both grouped attempts
that read each expert ~once (attempt-1 full fused grouped,
attempt-3 two-kernel grouped, ~34 MB/layer at 32 rows) ran at a
~55 GB/s duty-cycle ceiling (load→barrier→compute leaves DRAM idle)
and *lost* to per-pair attempt-4 in the piece harness at 8 rows and
tied/won only at 32 (round 1 `muse-spark/exploration/README.md` *What
building taught* #1; `ineff-quantized-kernels-1.md` builder note;
`hyp-1-fused-experts.md` Decision). The starting point already beats
the chained reference by 63.7 µs/layer at 8 rows and 210.0 µs/layer at
32 rows (1.27 and 4.20 ms/step, `console-chain.txt`) *with* the
re-reads, because the reference pays them too plus 7–13 launches.
A grouped fix banks the 2.33 ms floor only if it holds ≥120 GB/s
effective on distinct bytes — i.e. ≤185 µs/layer at 32 rows
(22.2 MB ÷ 120.5 GB/s) before its scan/chunk/barrier overhead, a bar
neither round-1 grouped attempt met. Predicted saving vs the compiled
reference (itself within 3% of the reference in the old harness,
`grade-experts.json`): **0 ms banked today; up to ~2.3 ms/step at
32 rows (0.12 ms/layer × 20) if a grouped design holds the starting
point's rate on distinct bytes; negative at 8 rows on round 1's
evidence.** Do not add to ineff-2 (disjoint: latency at 1 row, bytes
at 32) or to round 1's joint ceiling (443 MB at streaming rate ≈
11.5 ms at 32 rows, verifier reconciliation in
`ineff-quantized-kernels-1.md`).

## Slot

`routing` + `combine` + `experts` — the cause, whatever it is, only appears when all three slot replacements are installed together; each pair behaves as its parts predict. Spans territory `g3` and, kernel-side, `baseline-experts`, `baseline-routing`, `baseline-combine`. New instance for round-2 kernels of frozen round-2 [ineff-g3-1](../../round-2/exploration/ineff-g3-1.md) (round-1 kernels, confirmed); the pairs measurement it asked for is now run.

## What happens

The G3 runs install each round-2 kernel alone and all three at once and time the decode step (median of 3 shuffled repeats; [territory-g3.md](territory-g3.md) pieces 4–6). At 8 requests the combined variant is slower than the sum of the three single-slot changes by **+2.1 to +2.9 ms/step in all four runs**, while in the pairs run every pair comes within ±0.35 ms of its parts' sum. At 1 request the three-way term is within the spread (not claimed); at 32 it is +0.19 ms — real but 15× smaller than at 8, and round 1's +2.8/+3.3 ms 32-request interaction is gone. Full derivation in [territory-g3.md](territory-g3.md) gap 2.

## Cost

Three-way interaction = (change of all-three) − (sum of the three alone changes), ms per decode step, against the unchanged model.

## Kind

Overhead-bound (`claude/GLOSSARY.md`): the step is far from peak bandwidth and peak compute, and the lost time scales with neither weight bytes (unchanged per slot, shape-fixed grids) nor kernel count (reduced, additively). Two exact kernel sets (rounds 1 and 2) show the 8-request three-way term, so the cause is likely in how the step runs with all three slots replaced at that size, not in one kernel — while the 32-request term vanished with the round-1 kernels, so that one was a round-1-kernel property. `g3` (measurement), `baseline-experts`, `baseline-routing`, `baseline-combine` (the three kernels as installed), `grader` (the ready check must time the 8-request all-together step or round 3 re-learns this from Claude).

If the three-way interaction were removed while keeping each slot's alone change, the step gains back the interaction term: up to **2.86 ms/step at 8 requests in plain MLX** (2.13 vLLM), i.e. all-three would measure ≈ −1.86 ms instead of +0.94/+0.28 ms. # Attempt 2: two-kernel split (direction b)

First attempt in direction (b): kernel 1 fuses router scores (dense matmul +
sigmoid + bias add), kernel 2 fuses top-4 selection plus weight
normalize/scale. The dense matmul keeps a regular GEMM shape (one thread per
(row, expert), k tiled through threadgroup memory); the 11 bookkeeping kernels
around it collapse into the two fused kernels.

Removes `ineff-runs-2`: 12 kernels/layer of pure launch overhead become 2.
Kernel 1 additionally avoids re-reading the 184 KB router weight once per row
by staging k-chunks in threadgroup memory shared across 8 rows (17.4 KB <
32 KB limit; 480 threads/group < 1024).

## Predicted µs per layer (piece timing)

Fixed cost: 2 kernels x 6.81 µs (step_parts.txt:2) = 13.6 µs. Traffic at
200 GB/s peak:

- 1 row: w 184 KB (1 group) + x 1.5 KB + intermediates ~1 KB = ~187 KB ~= 0.9 µs.
  Total ~= 14.5 -> **15 µs/layer** (original 51).
- 8 rows: w 184 KB (1 group) + x 12 KB + intermediates ~8 KB = ~204 KB ~= 1.0 µs.
  Total ~= 14.6 -> **15 µs/layer** (original ~59, interpolated).
- 32 rows: w 737 KB (4 groups) + x 49 KB + intermediates ~32 KB = ~818 KB ~= 4.1 µs.
  Total ~= 17.7 -> **18 µs/layer** (original 84).

Predicted saving per step (x20 layers): 0.72 / 0.88 / 1.32 ms at 1/8/32 rows.

## Verdict

G1 pass. G2 pass: 0 wrong-expert rows, 0 near-tie rows at all row counts,
worst max_rel_err 2.6e-6 (40x inside the 1e-4 tolerance).

| rows | candidate | reference | compiled | beats compiled |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 36.3 | 36.3 | 29.3 | no |
| 8 | 34.9 | 56.9 | 42.9 | yes |
| 32 | 49.0 | 51.7 | 46.6 | no |

`beats_compiled: false`. Attempt-1 (direction a, single kernel) measured
28.5 / 23.6 / 41.8 against compiled 30.5 / 42.0 / 49.1 on its run and stops
the slot; this attempt is slower than it at every row count.

## Why the prediction missed (predicted 15 / 15 / 18, off by 142 / 133 / 172%)

1. Wrong fixed-cost model. I charged 2 x 6.81 µs = 13.6 µs from
   step_parts.txt. The piece harness shows a ~24-28 µs floor even for one
   fused kernel (attempt-1: 28.5 at 1 row), while the reference's 12 kernels
   cost only ~3 µs each when pipelined 20 layers deep. A heavy fused kernel
   costs a dispatch floor plus low-occupancy ramp, not one microbench launch.
2. Two launches, each under-occupied. Kernel 1 runs 60 threads (2 simdgroups,
   1 of 16 cores) at 1 row with 24 threadgroup barriers; kernel 2 runs a
   single thread at 1 row -- a whole launch for ~100 ns of ALU.
3. Sub-peak bandwidth. Kernel 1's w reads are 3 KB apart across SIMD lanes,
   far from the assumed 200 GB/s, and the two [rows,60] intermediates add a
   write-plus-reread round trip the single-kernel design avoids.
4. Attempt-1 is the control: re-reading w once per row (no tiling) still wins
   at 32 rows, so my barrier-heavy tiling bought traffic savings that never
   mattered and paid overhead that did.

One change I would make next (staying in direction b): delete the
threadgroup tiling in kernel 1 -- stream each expert's w column from device
memory with zero barriers -- since traffic is not the binding constraint.
Honestly, direction (a) dominates this split: one launch and no intermediates
beats two launches at all three row counts.

@mx.compile
def link(a, prev):
    """*a* unchanged, computed after *prev*: one small fused kernel."""
    return a + (prev.reshape(-1)[:1] * 0).astype(a.dtype)


def chained(fn, layers, names):
    """All 20 layers' calls, each one waiting for the one before, as in a decode step.

    A call's smallest input is linked to the previous call's last output, the
    same for every function timed. Without the wait, the GPU overlaps the
    calls and hides a slow call's latency; mx.depends orders only the graph.
    """
    small = min(names, key=lambda n: layers[0][n].size)
    outs = []
    for layer in layers:
        args = {n: layer[n] for n in names}
        if outs:
            args[small] = link(args[small], outs[-1][-1])
        out = fn(**args)
        if isinstance(out, dict):
            out = list(out.values())
        outs.append(list(out) if isinstance(out, (tuple, list)) else [out])
    return outs


def timed(fn, layers, names):
    """Median µs per layer: the 20 layers' chained calls, then one wait for the GPU."""
    for _ in range(3):
        mx.eval(chained(fn, layers, names))

# Inefficiency: `w_router` is re-read once per row instead of once per layer

- **Owner:** explorer-baseline-routing
- **Status:** confirmed
- **Version:** 2
- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T03:24:18Z
- **Next:** verifier to weigh the attempt-2 counter-evidence before confirming any saving

## Slot

`routing`

## What happens

Each row's threadgroup streams the full router weight for its own experts
straight from device memory (`muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-1/block-0.metal:30-34`):
60×768 float32 = 184 KB per row per layer, with no sharing across rows. The
reference's GEMM reads `w_router` once per layer and reuses each tile across
all rows in the tile (steel GEMM/GEMV dispatches, territory section 3.1).
Per layer the starting point therefore reads rows×184 KB where the reference
reads 184 KB: 0.18 MB at 1 row, 1.47 MB at 8 rows, 5.90 MB at 32 rows (and
377 MB at the 2,048-row prefill size, where only correctness is graded —
ADR 0010:42 — so that figure costs grader time, not step time).

## Cost

Traffic floor at the 200 GB/s peak (brief:9): candidate 0.9 / 7.4 / 29.5 µs
per layer at 1/8/32 rows vs the reference's 0.9 µs at every row count. At 32
rows the excess (5.90−0.18 MB ≈ 5.7 MB/layer ≈ 28.6 µs at peak, 0.57 ms/step
over 20 layers) is ~43% of the candidate's measured 68.9 µs/layer
(independent timing, `claude/findings/muse-round-1.md:47`) — the one place
in this slot where bytes, not launches, are a large share. At 1 and 8 rows
the excess is 0 and ~6.4 µs/layer respectively.

## Kind

Bandwidth-bound at 32 rows only; overhead-bound at 1/8 rows (the slot's
usual regime, `ineff-runs-2`).

## Spans

`baseline-routing`

## Predicted saving

Upper bound if each weight byte were read once per layer at peak bandwidth:
**~0 ms/step at 1 row, ~0.13 ms/step at 8 rows (6.4 µs/layer), ~0.57 ms/step
at 32 rows (28.6 µs/layer)**. Confidence is low at decode sizes, on measured
counter-evidence from round 1: attempt-2 tiled `w_router` through
threadgroup memory shared across 8 rows precisely to remove this re-read
and was *slower* at every row count (36.3/34.9/49.0 vs attempt-1's
28.5/23.6/41.8 µs/layer, `muse-spark/kernels/routing/attempt-2/notes.md`) —
barriers and sub-peak strided reads ate the traffic saving. A builder
claiming this saving needs a design that shares weights without
attempt-2's barrier structure (e.g. one threadgroup spanning several rows
in the steel-GEMM shape the exactness fix already pushes toward), and must
prove it on the chained timing, not the traffic arithmetic.

## Slot

`experts`

## What happens

At 1 row the slot kernel (`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-7/block-0.metal`,
`!prefill` path) launches 4 threadgroups of 512 threads —
one per pair — each running a barrier-serialized chain:
`tg_x` load + barrier (`:29-32`); gate/up interleaved, 24
strided steps (`K=768`) over 12 of 16 simdgroups
(`:51-58`); barrier (`:73`); full-bfloat16 silu-mul, 384
of 512 threads (`:77-85`); barrier (`:86`); down
interleaved, 12 merged steps (`K=384`) over 12 of 16
simdgroups (`:95-102`). That is 36 heavy K steps per
thread — each ~2×(2 scale/bias + 4 weight words) plus 64
dependent accumulates — with 4 of 16 simdgroups idle in
every phase, 4 `simd_sum` trees per thread, and an
exp/divide silu between two of the three barriers.

Why the gap survives everything round 2 tried (six fused
exact packings plateaued at 92–110 µs/layer chained:
104.3 / 103.6 / 109.5 / 94.0 / 92.1 / 93.8 — attempts
1–5, 7 own runs, per the builder notes on round-2
`ineff-baseline-experts-2.md:120-251`, frozen):

1. **The chain is at the register ceiling.** Widening
   threads/pair bought ~29 µs (132.9 → 104.3) and the
   gate/up interleave ~10 µs (104.3 → 94.0, cross-run),
   but attempt-6 proved a third 32-float accumulator
   fails G1 at 512 threads (pipeline max 448); exactly
   two fit (`attempt-7/notes.md:10-15, 227-240`). The
   per-thread chain cannot be widened further in this
   packing.
2. **Merging spent the available parallelism.** The down
   interleave is latency-neutral at 1 row (93.8 vs 92.1
   cross-run, +1.8%): down's blocks already overlapped
   across the 16-simdgroup wave, so merging trades
   cross-simdgroup parallelism for in-step parallelism
   while each step doubles its loads
   (`attempt-7/notes.md:237-255`). Group count past 4
   is not the lever either — 4, 48+96 and 12+24 groups
   all plateaued at 103.6–109.5 before the interleave
   (attempt-3 builder note). What remains is chain
   depth: 24 merged gate/up steps + 12 merged down
   steps that no packing shortens.
3. **The structural remainder is fixed.** `tg_x` load,
   silu (serial exp + divide per element), three
   barriers, and the chained launch/link cost sit
   outside every K-loop change; attempt-1 priced that
   block at ~20 µs of the 1-row layer time
   (`attempt-1/notes.md:46`, cross-harness model,
   indicative). Parallel stores saved only ~2 µs at 1
   row (94.0 → 92.1): stores were never the 1-row
   bottleneck.

Meanwhile the compiled reference runs 7 short kernels
per layer at 1 row (3×(Arange+GatherQMM) + silu-mul,
round-2 territory §E, frozen) with 24/24/48
threadgroups per product (`(M,(N+63)/64,B)` 64-thread
groups, round-2 territory §F) and no cross-phase
barriers inside any kernel — each kernel short, each
latency hidden across dozens of groups — totalling
78.6 µs/layer including the `link`. The candidate's one
kernel does less launching but one long chain: 92.1.

## Cost

Measured, piece (chained median µs/layer,
`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-2/grade-phases-experts-attempt-7.json`):

- **1 row:** candidate 92.1 vs compiled 78.6 (gap
  **+13.5**, +17.2%; 1/30 wins, `slower`) and vs
  reference 84.0 (+8.1). Own run
  (`attempt-7/notes.md:203-209`): 93.8 vs 74.8 (+19.0)
  — the task's "~19 µs" is the own-run gap; +13.5 is
  the operative re-grade bar. Per decode step: +13.5 ×
  20 = **270 µs ≈ 0.27 ms** (own-run basis 0.38 ms),
  reproducing the G3 effect of +0.29 ms with 1 request
  (`console-vllm.txt`, via round-3 README) to within
  run shift — no second in-step cause needed.
- Bytes: 4 pairs × 552,960 B = 2.21 MB/layer → floor
  11.1 µs at 200 GB/s peak (`claude/GLOSSARY.md:10`).
  Effective: candidate 24.0 GB/s chained (12% of peak)
  vs compiled 28.1 GB/s on the same pair model.
  Kernels: candidate 1 + `link` vs compiled 7 + `link`
  per layer per call.
- **8 rows:** 162.8 vs 235.5 (ahead 72.7, −30.9%,
  30/30 wins). 32 pairs, 17.69 MB → 108.7 GB/s. No
  loss; the win must be kept.
- **32 rows:** 515.3 vs 797.8 (ahead 282.5, −35.4%,
  30/30). 128 pairs, 70.78 MB → 137.3 GB/s. No loss.
- **Prefill 127/1,016/2,048 rows:** this entry costs
  0 there — the loss at those sizes is the scalar
  branch (`ineff-baseline-experts-1`), a disjoint
  cause. A decode-path change must leave the prefill
  branch (and its G2) intact.

Decomposition of the 92.1 (prediction from static
structure + cross-run attempt deltas, not measured):
~20 µs structural (launch/link, `tg_x`, silu,
barriers — attempt-1 model) + ~60 µs exposed K-chain
latency (36 merged steps, serial accumulates,
`simd_sum` trees) + ~11 µs byte floor, overlapped.
The ordering evidence: interleave moved 1 row by ~10,
stores by ~2, down-merge by ~0 — the serial gate/up
chain and the structural block are what is left.

## Kind

of peak bandwidth and a small fraction of peak compute

Builds on `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-4` (direction (b),
G1 fail: kernel 1 asks 600 threads/group against the pipeline max 576;
no G2, no timing). Baseline: none, so no `beats_baseline`; the bar is the
compiled reference in both phases.

## The one main change

8 rows per threadgroup instead of 10 in kernel 1 (the GEMM-shaped
prefill kernel), exactly the fix attempt-4's notes prescribe — nothing else:

- `spec.json`: kernel 1 `threadgroup` 600 → 480; grid stays `rows*60`.
  60 still divides 480, so every threadgroup covers whole rows (the last
  possibly fewer than 8) and no bounds checks are needed — edge groups
  clip to whole rows exactly as in attempt-4's 10-row design.
- `block-2.metal`: `xst`/`sc` 640 → 512 floats (8 rows × 64 stride);
  `wsh[4096]` unchanged (4 K-chunks × 16 k × 64-expert stride is
  row-count independent); row stride `g * 10u` → `g * 8u` in `r`, `Rg`
  and `rr`; `Rg` cap 10 → 8. The `w`-staging loop bound stays 960
  (4 slots × 240 elements of total work, independent of rows/group);
  every remaining `16u` is K-chunk geometry (16 d-values per chunk,
  `part[16]`), correctly untouched.
- `block-0.metal`, `block-1.metal`: byte-identical to attempt-4
  (`diff` empty) — decode path untouched.

Threadgroup: (4096 + 512 + 512) × 4 B = 20,480 B of 32 KB (was 21,504 B).
480 threads sits inside round-1 attempt-2's proven-passing band and 96
threads under attempt-4's reported 576 cap — but attempt-4 proved the cap
moves with the kernel, so G1 passing is a measurement, not a certainty.

## Inefficiency removed

Same as attempt-2/attempt-4: `ineff-baseline-routing-1` (per-row `w_router`
re-read) and `ineff-baseline-routing-2` (per-row shape cost) together.
`w_router` device traffic falls from rows × 184,320 B to
ceil(rows/8) × 184,320 B (~8× at full groups, was 10×), barriers from
24/row to 25 per group of 8 rows (~3.1/row amortised, was ~2.5),
duty from 23% to 100% in the single-partition regime, footprint from
28,080 B to 20,480 B.

## Predicted us per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 / 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows

Anchor: the round-3 re-grade of attempt-4
(`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-2/grade-phases-routing-attempt-4.json`):
ref / compiled / candidate = 68.4/65.1/49.8 at 1 row,
169.2/135.7/113.5 at 8, 159.3/145.2/121.3 at 32,
102.3/87.3/227.1 at 127, 231.3/221.1/1298.8 at 1,016,
310.0/290.4/2513.0 at 2,048. Decode margins: 15.3/22.2/23.9.

- Decode (1/8/32): kernel 0 is attempt-4 plus a never-taken branch
  (~0); kernel 1 adds one copy launch (grid rows*60 threads, rows*4
  elements × 8 B copied). Allowance 3 us: **53 / 117 / 124** vs
  compiled 65.1/135.7/145.2 — still `faster`, spending ~3 of 15–24 us
  of margin. Unchanged from attempt-4 (decode code is byte-identical).
- Prefill traffic floors at 200 GB/s (`w` staged once per 8 rows):
  - 127 rows: 16 groups × 184,320 B (w) + 127 × 1,536 B (x) + 127 × 32 B
    (out) = 3,148,256 B → 15.7 us. 16 groups fit 16 cores → 1 wave ×
    25 barriers × 0.5 us = 12.5 + idle kernel-0 launch 4 + chained
    fixed cost 25 → **~57** vs compiled 87.3 (`faster`).
  - 1,016 rows: 127 × 184,320 + 1,016 × 1,536 + 1,016 × 32 =
    25,001,728 B → 125 us. ceil(127/16) = 8 waves × 12.5 = 100 +
    idle launch 6 + fixed 25 → **~256** vs compiled 221.1 —
    `slower` under this barrier model.
  - 2,048 rows: 256 × 184,320 + 2,048 × 1,536 + 2,048 × 32 =
    50,397,184 B → 252 us. 256/16 = 16 waves × 12.5 = 200 +
    idle launch 8 + fixed 25 → **~485** vs compiled 290.4 —
    `slower` under this barrier model.

Prediction: **53 / 117 / 124 / 57 / 256 / 485 us**. G1 prediction: pass
(480 < 576 with 96 threads of headroom, inside the proven-passing band;
20,480 B < 32 KB; grid divisible along whole rows). G2
prediction: pass at all six sizes — every accumulation order is copied
op-for-op from attempt-4 (via attempt-2/attempt-4, which this copies), and
only the grouping changed, never any row's order. `beats_compiled`
prediction: false under the 0.5-us/barrier guess (1,016/2,048 rows slower)
— but the barrier cost is a guess, and barriers may
overlap across resident groups; the chained timing decides whether
prefill-big is `same`-or-better. The decode `faster` × 3 is the firm
half of the prediction.

24|## The slots
25|
26|Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the call: 1 to 32 in a decode step, up to 2,048 in a prefill chunk. The grader flattens the inputs to the shapes below and restores the model's shapes afterwards. All arrays are row-contiguous.
27|
28|The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.
29|
30|### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights
31|
32|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
33||---|---|---|---|
34|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
35|| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
36|| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
37|| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
38|| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
39|
40|Reference:
41|
42|```python
43|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
44|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
45|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
46|weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
47|```
48|
49|The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.
50|
51|### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert
52|
53|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
54||---|---|---|---|
55|| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
56|| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
57|| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
58|| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
59|
60|Reference:
61|
62|```python
63|out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
64|```
65|
66|Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.

69|
70|Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.

72|### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products
73|
74|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
75||---|---|---|---|
76|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
77|| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
78|| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
79|| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
80|| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
81|| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
82|| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |
83|
84|Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.
85|
86|Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:
87|
88|```python
89|y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
90|```
91|
92|As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.
93|
94|Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.

184|The pass criteria were fixed before the first round. From round 2, G2 is exact and also covers the prefill, and the piece timing chains the layers ([ADR 0010](adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md)); round 1 was judged by the earlier rules, in which G2 allowed small rounding differences and tested decode steps only. 186|1. **G1, runs.** It compiles and runs on real inputs.
187|2. **G2, correct: identical to the reference, bit for bit.** The slot runs in every call of `MoE.__call__`, the prefill included, so it is tested on every layer's inputs at two kinds of size:
188|   - **a decode step:** inputs captured from all 20 layers during a real decode step, at 1, 8 and 32 rows;
189|   - **a prefill:** the first chunk of a prefill with 128-token prompts, recorded while the grader runs it, at 1, 8 and 32 requests: 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. From 60 rows on, MLX's own experts kernel changes (`gather_qmm_rhs` instead of `gather_qvm`), and so does its rounding.
190|
191|   At every size:
192|   - **`routing`:** each row's 4 experts and their 4 weights equal the reference's, in the same order, since combine sums the pairs in that order. That includes the reference's choice between tied 4th and 5th experts.
193|   - **`combine` and `experts`:** every element equals the reference's.

195|   **Why exact:** the end-to-end check below asks for the same greedy tokens, and greedy decoding turns any difference into different tokens. In round 1, routing weights within 10⁻⁵ of the reference, relative, changed 7 to 9 of 32 sequences.
196|   - **Then, end to end:** the same greedy tokens as the original model over 24 generated tokens, at 1 and 32 requests, in both plain MLX and vLLM.
197|3. **G3, faster, in vLLM.** Each workload runs 5 times in shuffled order: 1, 8 and 32 requests with 128-token prompts, and 32 requests with 1,024-token prompts, 256 generated tokens each. Three times are measured per run:
198|   - the **decode step**, the median period between steady steps;
199|   - the **prompt time**, until every prompt was processed;
200|   - the **whole request**, from sending the requests to the last token.
201|
202|   Against both the original model and an `mx.compile` of the same reference code, the attempt passes when the decode step or the prompt time is faster in every workload, neither is slower in any, and no whole request is slower. Faster and slower mean that the ranges over the repeats don't overlap.

204|   **From round 3, the same G3 runs inside the round too:** the lead's **ready check**, `bench/grader/check_ready.py`, with every candidate in one call. It also requires the same greedy tokens, and audits its own log. Only its passing verdict makes an attempt `ready`; Claude's G3 after the round decides. 209|- `g1` false and the compiler's error message;
210|- or the correctness results per size: for routing, the rows that differ; for combine and experts, the elements that differ and the largest gap in units in the last place; with the first example;
211|- or, when the attempt is correct, `timing_us_per_layer` per size: its time per call next to the original's and the compiled reference's, its wins against the compiled reference and the verdict (`faster`, `same`, `slower`, or `handed off` for a size your spec hands to the compiled reference); then `phases_vs_compiled` and `beats_compiled`.

213|**The piece timing** runs the slot at the six G2 sizes: the 20 layers' captured decode inputs at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and the 20 layers' first prefill chunk at 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. Each layer's call waits for the previous one's output, as in the model: one small kernel links them, the same for every function timed. Without that wait, the GPU overlaps the 20 calls and hides how long one takes; in round 1, an experts kernel 29% faster on overlapped calls was 66% slower on chained ones at 1 row.
214|- **Paired repeats.** Your attempt and the compiled reference run in alternating order, 30 times.
215|- **Per size:** your attempt is `faster` when it wins at least 22 of the 30 pairs, `slower` when it loses at least 22, and `same` otherwise. Medians alone would pass on noise: the same kernel timed twice differs by up to 5%.

44|def ref_routing(x, w_router, bias):
45|    scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)
46|    inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=K - 1, axis=-1)[:, :K]
47|    w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)
48|    return inds, w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * SCALE

55|def ref_experts(x, inds, *weights):
56|    """The port's SwitchGLU on flat rows: [rows, D] and [rows, K] -> [rows, K, D]."""
57|    from mlx_lm.models.activations import swiglu
58|    from mlx_lm.models.switch_layers import _gather_sort, _scatter_unsort
59|
60|    gate, up, down = weights[0:3], weights[3:6], weights[6:9]
61|    xx = mx.expand_dims(x, (-2, -3))
62|    do_sort = inds.size >= 64
63|    idx, inv = inds, None
64|    if do_sort:
65|        xx, idx, inv = _gather_sort(xx, inds)
66|
67|    def qmm(a, w):
68|        return mx.gather_qmm(
69|            a,
70|            *w,
71|            rhs_indices=idx,
72|            transpose=False,
73|            group_size=32,
74|            bits=4,
75|            mode="affine",
76|            sorted_indices=do_sort,
77|        )

79|    y = qmm(swiglu(qmm(xx, gate), qmm(xx, up)), down)
80|    if do_sort:
81|        y = _scatter_unsort(y, inv, inds.shape)

304|def build(spec, sources, slot):
305|    """A function slot_inputs -> slot_outputs from Muse Spark's spec and Metal blocks.
306|
307|    With "max_rows" in the spec, inputs with more rows than that run the slot's
308|    reference under mx.compile instead of the kernels, so an attempt can keep
309|    prompt-sized inputs on MLX's own code (claude/adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md);
310|    with "min_rows", so do inputs with fewer rows than that
311|    (claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md). The function's hands_off(rows)
312|    says whether inputs of that many rows run the compiled reference.
313|    """
314|    slot_in, slot_out = SLOTS[slot]
315|    kernels = []
316|    for k in spec["kernels"]:
317|        header = "" if k.get("header_block") is None else sources[k["header_block"]]
318|        fn = mx.fast.metal_kernel(
319|            name=re.sub(r"\W", "_", str(k["name"])),
320|            input_names=list(k["inputs"]),
321|            output_names=[o["name"] for o in k["outputs"]],
322|            source=sources[k["source_block"]],
323|            header=header,
324|            atomic_outputs=bool(k.get("atomic_outputs", False)),
325|        )
326|        kernels.append((k, fn))
327|    missing = set(slot_out) - set(spec["slot_outputs"])
328|    if missing:
329|        raise ValueError(f"slot_outputs is missing {sorted(missing)}")
330|    min_rows, max_rows = spec.get("min_rows"), spec.get("max_rows")
331|    for key, v in (("min_rows", min_rows), ("max_rows", max_rows)):
332|        if v is not None and (isinstance(v, bool) or not isinstance(v, int) or v < 1):
333|            raise ValueError(f"bad {key} {v!r}")
334|    if min_rows is not None and max_rows is not None and min_rows > max_rows:
335|        raise ValueError(f"min_rows {min_rows} is above max_rows {max_rows}: the kernels would never run")
336|    compiled = mx.compile(REFERENCE[slot])
337|
338|    def hands_off(rows):
339|        return (max_rows is not None and rows > max_rows) or (min_rows is not None and rows < min_rows)
340|
341|    def run(**inputs):
342|        rows = inputs[slot_in[0]].shape[0]
343|        if hands_off(rows):  # the compiled reference takes over
344|            out = compiled(*[inputs[n] for n in slot_in])
345|            return dict(zip(slot_out, out if isinstance(out, (tuple, list)) else [out]))
346|        env = dict(inputs)
347|        for k, fn in kernels:
348|            tg = [int(t) for t in k["threadgroup"]]
349|            if any(t < 1 for t in tg) or tg[0] * tg[1] * tg[2] > 1024:
350|                raise ValueError(f"bad threadgroup {tg}")
351|            outs = fn(
352|                inputs=[env[n] for n in k["inputs"]],
353|                template=[
354|                    (n, template_value(v)) for n, v in (k.get("template") or {}).items()
355|                ],
356|                grid=tuple(dim(g, rows) for g in k["grid"]),
357|                threadgroup=tuple(tg),
358|                output_shapes=[
359|                    tuple(dim(s, rows) for s in o["shape"]) for o in k["outputs"]
360|                ],
361|                output_dtypes=[DTYPES[o["dtype"]] for o in k["outputs"]],
362|                init_value=k.get("init_value"),
363|            )
364|            env.update(zip([o["name"] for o in k["outputs"]], outs))
365|        return {name: env[src] for name, src in spec["slot_outputs"].items()}
366|
367|    run.hands_off = hands_off
368|    return run

434|- **Row counts on each side of 60.** The branch is on the dispatch threshold itself, not the tested sizes: both kernels read `rows` from `inds_shape[0]` and take `qvm_block` below 60 and `qmm_block` at/above (`block-0.metal:11,26,49`; `block-1.metal:9,21,34`). This matches `B = rows*4 >= 240 ⇔ B/E >= 4` at exactly 60 rows; 33–59 therefore stay on `gather_qvm` and 60–126 on `gather_qmm_rhs`, as the Boundary requires. The sort threshold (rows ≥ 16) is correctly ignored — the kernel is positional in `inds` order (`block-0.metal:12-15`; `block-1.metal:10-11`), so reference-internal sorting cannot affect its bits at 16–59 rows either. Nothing in the kernel depends on the row count beyond this branch and the linear grids (`rows*1536` / `rows*3072` threads = `rows*48` / `rows*96` groups of 32, `spec.json:1`): pair/block decomposition (`tg/12`, `tg%12`; `tg/24`, `tg%24`) covers every `rows >= 1`, including untested 2–7, 9–31, 61–126, 128–1,015 and >2,048, and prefill chunks other than the first. Per-pair independence (no offsets, no cross-pair grouping) means chunk position and prompt length cannot change a row's arithmetic.
435|- **Unwritten threadgroup reads.** None. Decode: `tg_x[768]` is fully written (`i = lane; i < 768; i += 32`) and barriered before `qvm_block` reads it, and `tg_gate`/`tg_up[32]` are fully written by lane 0 and barriered before the silu read (`block-0.metal:19-21,27-48`); `tg_h[384]` likewise (`block-1.metal:16,22-25`). 5|# From round 4, candidates that pass together are ready as a set, and an attempt may hand off small inputs too
6|
7|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../../PROVENANCE.md).*
8|
9|**The change.** Round 3 showed three gaps in the rules ([Claude's measurement](../findings/muse-round-3.md)). On 2026-11-04 surucuonur chose to fix all three before round 4:
10|
11|1. **Ready as a set.** Round 3's routing and combine candidates each failed the ready check alone, on overlapping ranges, while the two together (`muse-all`) passed it. The skill made a candidate `ready` only when it passed alone, so the round submitted nothing. From round 4, when `muse-all` passes the ready check, all its candidates are `ready` together as a **set**. A set goes to G3 whole, and G3 judges it as `muse-all`.
12|2. **Hand off below a row count too: `min_rows`.** `max_rows` already sends inputs with more rows to `mx.compile` of the slot's reference ([ADR 0011](0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). The new `min_rows` in an attempt's `spec.json` does the same for inputs with fewer rows, so the kernels run only from `min_rows` to `max_rows`. Round 3's experts attempt-1 lost to the compiled reference only at 1 row: 96.9 against 86.6 µs per layer, while it took 168.9 against 238.2 at 8 rows and 554.7 against 883.4 at 32. Its only way to pass was to win at the size it is worst at.
13|3. **A handed-off size isn't timed.** The grader timed each handed-off size, which runs the compiled reference, against the compiled reference: the same code twice. In round 3 that noise judged routing attempt-1 `slower` at 2,048 rows, on 8 wins of 30, and cost a re-grade of a byte-identical copy. Now such a size is reported `handed off`. A phase is `faster` when every size the kernels run at is faster, and it needs at least one; `beats_compiled` is still one phase `faster` and none `slower`. G2 still checks every size, bit for bit.
14|
15|## How it works
16|
17|- **`bench/grader/slots.py`:**
18|  - `build()` reads `min_rows` as it reads `max_rows`: an integer of at least 1, at most `max_rows` when both are given.
19|  - The function it returns has `hands_off(rows)`, which says whether inputs with that many rows run the compiled reference.
20|- **`bench/grader/check_candidate.py`:**
21|  - At each size, a function that hands the rows off is not timed. It takes the compiled reference's times, so for `routing+combine` the part that hands off adds the same time to both sides.
22|  - A bar's verdict is `handed off` when neither side ran code of its own. Against a baseline that runs its own kernels there, the size is timed as before.
23|  - `judge()` leaves `handed off` sizes out of a phase. A phase whose sizes are all handed off is `handed off`.
24|- **`bench/grader/test_hand_off.py`:**
25|  - checks `build()` with a toy kernel at row counts on both sides of each bound, bit for bit, and that bad bounds are refused;
26|  - checks `judge()` on five sets of verdicts.
27|  - Passed on 2026-11-04.
28|- **A real attempt.** Claude re-graded round 3's routing attempt-6 (`max_rows` 32) with the changed grader ([results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/](../../results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/)):
29|  - G2 passes;
30|  - decode is `faster` at 1, 8 and 32 rows, on 29, 26 and 27 wins of 30;
31|  - the three prefill sizes are `handed off`;
32|  - `beats_compiled` is true.
33|- **The skill, version 9.**
34|  - The ready check makes a passing `muse-all` a set.
35|  - *Ready to test* names a set's attempts together.
36|  - Builders and boundary agents record `min_rows` and the sizes it hands off.
37|- **G3 and the ready check are unchanged.** They time whole requests, so a slot's kernels count wherever they run. With 1 request every decode step has 1 row, so an attempt that hands off 1 row runs MLX's own code for the whole 1-request workload. Alone it is then no faster than its compiled bar there, and it can pass G3 only in a set whose other kernels are faster with 1 request. The brief says so.
38|
39|## Consequences
40|
41|- **Round 3's pair qualifies for round 4.** Under the set rule, routing attempt-6 with combine attempt-2 would have been `ready` in round 3, because its `muse-all` passed the swarm's ready check. Claude's G3 failed the same pair against the compiled bar at 32 requests of 1,024 tokens, on overlapping ranges, so the pair is still no baseline.
42|- **A set is judged once.** Its parts are not judged alone, so a set can carry a part that only helps together with the others. G3 still requires the whole set to be faster than both bars, and to be slower nowhere.
43|- **The interaction of all three slots is untested.** In rounds 1 and 2, replacing all three slots at once lost about 2.8 ms with 8 requests, for an unknown reason ([round 2](../findings/muse-round-2.md), section 4). A set with an experts attempt meets that again.
44|
45|## Considered options
46|
47|- **A paired test on medians for the ready check and G3,** so that one outlier repeat can't sink a candidate, as it sank combine attempt-2 in round 3. Not chosen for round 4: it changes ADR 0011's rule for Claude's G3 too, and there was too little time to check it before the deadline.
48|- **Hand-off by an explicit list of row counts.** More flexible, but no attempt has needed more than one range, and two bounds are simple to check.

5|# From round 3, an improvement must hold in both phases, decode and prefill, and an attempt may hand prefill-sized inputs to the compiled reference
6|
7|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../../PROVENANCE.md).*
8|
9|**The change.** Claude's comparison of every engine version over whole requests ([findings](../findings/muse-round-2.md), section 5) found that the grader and G3 timed only the decode step. They never timed the prefill, the phase in which a request's whole prompt runs through the model:
10|- **Experts attempt-7** looked like round 2's largest gain, a 19% shorter decode step at 32 requests. It processed prompts 6.6 to 14.5 times slower and cut throughput by 10% to 83%.
11|- **Routing attempt-4,** round 2's only baseline, processed prompts 7% to 10% slower. At 32 requests with 1,024-token prompts it cost 3.5% of throughput.
12|
13|The Muse agent never saw either effect: its piece timing ran decode sizes only, and G3 measured the decode step only.
14|
15|On 2026-11-04 surucuonur set the rule: "The improvement should be in the two phases of it: decode and prefill. Then, we can consider it as an improvement." surucuonur chose:
16|- **faster in one phase, slower in neither;**
17|- **the hand-off:** an attempt may leave prefill-sized inputs to the compiled reference. This replaces the part of [ADR 0010](0010-exact-at-every-size.md) that required the kernels to run in every call.
18|
19|## How it works
20|
21|- **The piece timing runs at the six G2 sizes** (`bench/grader/check_candidate.py`): decode at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and the first prefill chunk at 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. The layers are still chained.
22|- **The verdict at each size comes from paired repeats.** The candidate and the compiled reference run in alternating order, 30 times, and so does the baseline when one is given.
23|  - The candidate is `faster` when it wins at least 22 of the 30 pairs, a one-sided sign test at p < 0.01.
24|  - It is `slower` when it loses at least 22, and `same` otherwise.
25|
26|  This replaces the comparison of medians for the decode sizes too, since the same kernel timed twice differs by up to 5%.
27|- **The verdict per phase:**
28|  - a phase is `faster` when every one of its sizes is;
29|  - it is `slower` when any size is;
30|  - otherwise it is `not slower`.
31|
32|  `beats_compiled`, and `beats_baseline` against a baseline, are true when one phase is `faster` and neither is `slower`.
33|- **The hand-off** (`max_rows` in `spec.json`, `bench/grader/slots.py`). Inputs with more rows than `max_rows` run the slot's reference under `mx.compile`. G2 still checks every size.
34|  - On 2026-11-04 the compiled reference of each slot was bit-exact with the reference at all six sizes (`bench/micro/compiled_exact.py`, `results/runs/2026-11-04-handoff-check/`).
35|  - Above `max_rows` a hand-off runs the compiled reference itself, so it times `same` as the bar there, never better.
36|- **G3** (`bench/grader/time_candidates.py`, which writes `g3-vllm.json`):
37|  - **Workloads:** 1, 8 and 32 requests with 128-token prompts, and 32 requests with 1,024-token prompts.
38|  - **Measurements per run:** the decode step period, the prompt time and the whole-request time, over 5 shuffled repeats, up from 3.
39|  - **Faster and slower:** the two ranges over the repeats don't overlap.
40|  - **Why 5 repeats:** with 3 each, two identical engines' ranges miss each other by chance 1 time in 20 per direction. "Never slower" checks a phase 8 times (4 workloads, 2 bars), so a phase that changed nothing would fail about a third of the time. The first run under these rules showed it. A copy of experts attempt-7 with a hand-off at 59 rows came out `slower` on prompt time at 32 × 1,024, by 0.5% with ranges 16 ms apart, although above 59 rows it runs the compiled reference, whose own range overlapped the unchanged engine's (`results/runs/2026-11-04-handoff-check/`). With 5 repeats the chance is 1 in 252 per check, about 3% over 8.
41|  - **The pass rule:** against both the original model and the compiled reference, the decode step or the prompt time must be faster in every workload, neither may be slower in any, and no whole request may be slower.
42|- **The unchanged engine is vLLM's own.** The original model in G3 runs with Claude's step hooks, and with vLLM's engine inside the script's process. On 2026-11-04, alternating runs found it within −0.2% to +1.9% of vLLM with neither, inside the spread between repeats in every workload (`bench/micro/clean_vllm.py`, `results/runs/2026-11-04-clean-vllm/`).
43|
44|## Consequences
45|
46|- **Round 3 starts with no baseline.** Routing attempt-4 is `slower` at all three prefill sizes, 2.6 to 8.7 times the compiled reference's time. It fails G3 on prompt time at 8 and 32 requests. It becomes a starting point, so round 3's bar in every slot is the compiled reference.
47|- **A decode kernel no longer has to win at prefill sizes,** only to hand them off or not lose there. The attempt chooses the row count, so the boundary agent checks that the hand-off sits on the right side of 60 rows for the experts slot.
48|- **At prefill sizes, a slot with a hand-off is MLX's code, not the Muse agent's.** The claim for such an attempt is "faster decode, unchanged prefill".
49|- **Grader runs and G3 take longer.** Every attempt is now timed at three more sizes. G3 runs 5 repeats instead of 3, and its 32 × 1,024 workload adds at least 16 s per variant per repeat.
50|- **The decode verdict is stricter.** An attempt whose median beat the compiled reference by noise is now `same`.
51|- **Not covered:** prefill chunks of other sizes, and decode steps with other row counts. The boundary agent reports them; G3's four workloads are the end-to-end check. Not covered means not measured: from round 3 the swarm lists these as **Unverified**, never as free ([ADR 0013](0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)); round 2 read ADR 0010's line like this one as leave to slow the prefill.
52|- **At 1 request the whole-request time is noisy.** On 2026-11-04 its repeats spread 6% to 41%, so G3 there mostly says `same`, which passes the "never slower" test without showing a gain.
53|
54|## Considered options
55|
56|- **Faster in both phases.** The higher bar. A decode kernel would also have to beat MLX's large matrix kernels at 2,048 rows, which is not where the decode step loses its time. Not chosen.
57|- **Whole-request throughput alone.** Simple, but it lets a slower phase be traded for a faster one. surucuonur ruled that out.
58|- **Hand off to the uncompiled reference.** The prefill could then come out `slower` than the compiled reference wherever compiling helps; at 127 rows, routing's compiled reference takes 87 µs per layer against 102 µs uncompiled.
59|- **Keep the kernels in every call** (ADR 0010). The kernels could still branch on the row count inside themselves, but they couldn't use MLX's large-size kernels. surucuonur chose the hand-off.

1|"""Grade one kernel attempt: compile it, test it on captured inputs, time it.
2|
3|The independent grader for the Muse agent's kernels (claude/muse-agent-brief.md).
4|G2 tests it on the inputs `slots.py capture` recorded from a real decode step
5|(1, 8 and 32 rows), and on every layer's inputs in a prefill, recorded as
6|it runs (127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows): every output must be identical to the
7|reference's, bit for bit, since only then are the model's tokens identical
8|(claude/adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md). The timing runs at the same six
9|sizes and chains the 20 layers, so each call waits for the one before, as in
10|the model. The grader prints its verdict as JSON, and writes it to --out when
11|given. It writes into an attempt folder only when --out points there, as
12|the Muse agent's builders do with grade.json; load() reads only spec.json and
13|the block-N.metal files.
14|
15|  .venv/bin/python bench/grader/check_candidate.py <attempt folder> <slot> [--out FILE]
16|      [--baseline [SLOT=]FOLDER ...]
17|
18|The candidate and the compiled reference are timed in alternating repeats, so
19|drift in the GPU's clocks reaches both alike. At each size the candidate is
20|"faster" when it wins at least WINS_NEEDED of the REPEATS paired repeats (a
21|one-sided sign test at p < 0.01), "slower" when it loses that many, and
22|"same" otherwise; the same kernel timed twice differs by up to 5% between
23|medians, so comparing medians alone would pass on noise. `beats_compiled`
24|needs both phases, decode and prefill: faster at every size of one, slower
25|at none of the other (claude/adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md).
26|
27|A size whose inputs the attempt hands to the compiled reference (`max_rows`,
28|`min_rows`) runs the bar's own code, so it is "handed off", not timed against
29|it: a phase is faster when every size the kernels run is, and needs one such
30|size (claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md). G2 still checks it.
31|
32|--baseline times an earlier, already graded attempt in the same run and adds
33|`beats_baseline`, judged the same way. From round 2 on, the bar is the
34|previous round's final attempt for the slot
35|(claude/adr/0009-rounds-build-on-each-other.md). FOLDER alone is an attempt
36|for the same slot. For routing+combine, give either one routing+combine
37|attempt or `routing=FOLDER` and `combine=FOLDER`.

97|def ulp_bf16(r):
98|    """bfloat16's unit in the last place at |r|, floored at |r| = 0.001 (brief, G2)."""
99|    exp = np.floor(np.log2(np.maximum(np.abs(r), 1e-3)))
100|    return 2.0 ** (exp - 7)

103|def differences(g, r):
104|    """Elements of *g* that aren't *r*'s bit for bit, and the largest gap in units
105|    in the last place (floored at |r| = 0.001); "at" is the flat index of it."""
106|    differ = (g != r) & ~(np.isnan(g) & np.isnan(r))
107|    out = {"differ": int(differ.sum()), "max_ulp": 0.0}
108|    if out["differ"]:
109|        with np.errstate(over="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
110|            over = np.nan_to_num(np.abs(g - r) / ulp_bf16(r), nan=1e9, posinf=1e9)
111|        out |= {"max_ulp": float(min(over.max(), 1e9)), "at": int(over.argmax())}
112|    return out

115|def check_routing(fn, layer):
116|    ref_inds, ref_w = slots.ref_routing(layer["x"], layer["w_router"], layer["bias"])
117|    got = fn(x=layer["x"], w_router=layer["w_router"], bias=layer["bias"])
118|    inds, w = got["inds"], got["weights"]
119|    rows = layer["x"].shape[0]
120|    if inds.shape != (rows, slots.K) or w.shape != (rows, slots.K):
121|        return {
122|            "error": f"shapes inds {inds.shape}, weights {w.shape}; want ({rows}, 4)"
123|        }
124|    if inds.dtype != mx.uint32 or w.dtype != mx.float32:
125|        return {
126|            "error": f"dtypes inds {inds.dtype}, weights {w.dtype}; want uint32, float32"
127|        }
128|    inds, w = np.array(inds), np.array(w)
129|    ref_inds, ref_w = np.array(ref_inds), np.array(ref_w)
130|    if inds.max() >= slots.E:
131|        return {"error": f"expert index {int(inds.max())} out of range (60 experts)"}
132|    # Exact, in order: combine sums the 4 pairs in this order.
133|    differ = (inds != ref_inds).any(axis=1) | (w != ref_w).any(axis=1)
134|    same_order = (inds == ref_inds).all(axis=1)

138|        "rows_other_experts": int(

140|        ),

192|def link(a, prev):
193|    """*a* unchanged, computed after *prev*: one small fused kernel."""
194|    return a + (prev.reshape(-1)[:1] * 0).astype(a.dtype)

197|def chained(fn, layers, names):
198|    """All 20 layers' calls, each one waiting for the one before, as in a decode step.
199|
200|    A call's smallest input is linked to the previous call's last output, the
201|    same for every function timed. Without the wait, the GPU overlaps the
202|    calls and hides a slow call's latency; mx.depends orders only the graph.
203|    """
204|    small = min(names, key=lambda n: layers[0][n].size)
205|    outs = []
206|    for layer in layers:
207|        args = {n: layer[n] for n in names}
208|        if outs:
209|            args[small] = link(args[small], outs[-1][-1])
210|        out = fn(**args)
211|        if isinstance(out, dict):
212|            out = list(out.values())
213|        outs.append(list(out) if isinstance(out, (tuple, list)) else [out])
214|    return outs

217|def timed(fn, layers, names):
218|    """Median µs per layer: the 20 layers' chained calls, then one wait for the GPU."""
219|    for _ in range(3):
220|        mx.eval(chained(fn, layers, names))
221|    times = []
222|    for _ in range(REPEATS):
223|        t0 = time.perf_counter()
224|        mx.eval(chained(fn, layers, names))
225|        times.append((time.perf_counter() - t0) / len(layers))
226|    return round(statistics.median(times) * 1e6, 1)

229|def paired_times(fns, layers, names):
230|    """Per-repeat µs per layer of each function, in rotating order within each repeat."""
231|    calls = [lambda f=f: mx.eval(chained(f, layers, names)) for f in fns]
232|    for _ in range(3):
233|        for call in calls:
234|            call()
235|    times = [[] for _ in fns]
236|    for i in range(REPEATS):
237|        for j in [(i + k) % len(fns) for k in range(len(fns))]:
238|            t0 = time.perf_counter()
239|            calls[j]()
240|            times[j].append((time.perf_counter() - t0) / len(layers) * 1e6)
241|    return times

244|def compare(wins):
245|    """One size's verdict from the candidate's wins in REPEATS paired repeats."""
246|    if wins >= WINS_NEEDED:
247|        return "faster"
248|    if REPEATS - wins >= WINS_NEEDED:
249|        return "slower"
250|    return "same"
