253|def judge(verdicts):
254|    """Each phase's verdict from its sizes' verdicts, and whether the candidate
255|    beats the bar: faster at every size of one phase, slower at no size of the other.
256|
257|    Sizes "handed off" don't count. A phase is "faster" when every other size
258|    is, "slower" when any is, "handed off" when none is left, and "not slower"
259|    otherwise.
260|    """
261|    phases = {}
262|    for phase, prefix in PHASES.items():
263|        sizes = [v for size, v in verdicts.items() if size.startswith(prefix) and v != "handed off"]
264|        phases[phase] = (
265|            "handed off" if not sizes
266|            else "faster" if all(v == "faster" for v in sizes)
267|            else "slower" if "slower" in sizes
268|            else "not slower"
269|        )
270|    beats = "faster" in phases.values() and "slower" not in phases.values()
271|    return phases, beats

# Exploration: round 4 — analysis

**Version:** v2 · 2026-11-04T21:48:45Z · skill version 10

## Tracker

|---|---|---|---|---|
| `baseline-experts` | `explorer-baseline-experts` | done | `ineff-baseline-experts-1` (refuted), `-2` (confirmed) | 2026-11-04 21:48Z |

Verdicts: 7 confirmed, 1 refuted, 0 superseded, 0 open. All 5 territory entries `done`.

## Starting point

Round 4 is the last round ([ADR 0014](../../../claude/adr/0014-muse-wonder-last-round.md)). It builds on rounds 1–3 as measured independently by Claude in [`claude/findings/muse-round-3.md`](../../../claude/findings/muse-round-3.md). Round 3 ran as Muse Spark (model `muse-spark-1.3-contributor`, skill version 8) and submitted the reference in every slot: no candidate passed the ready check alone, and the skill then counted only candidates that pass alone. Round 4 changes three rules ([ADR 0015](../../../claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)): candidates that pass together in `muse-all` are `ready` as a **set**; an attempt may hand off inputs below `min_rows` as well as above `max_rows`; and a handed-off size is reported `handed off` instead of being timed. A slot's **baseline** is still its best attempt so far that passes the current G2, has `beats_compiled` true in the grader, and passes G3 ([ADR 0011](../../../claude/adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). **No slot has a baseline.** The bar in every slot is the compiled reference, and a new attempt must beat it in the same grader run (no `--baseline` argument). Round 4 runs as Muse Wonder (muse-wonder-1.0).

### Per slot

#### `experts` — starting point `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1`

- **What it is.** Round 2's fused per-pair kernel, byte-identical, plus `max_rows: 59` in `spec.json`: rows 1–59 run the fused kernel, rows above 59 run the compiled reference. See `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1/notes.md` and its `grade.json` (G1 pass, G2 differ 0 at all six sizes).
- **Piece timing** (chained µs per layer, candidate vs compiled, its own grade run): 1 row 96.9 vs 86.6 (`slower`, 5 wins); 8 rows 168.9 vs 238.2 (`faster`, 29 wins); 32 rows 554.7 vs 883.4 (`faster`, 29 wins); prefill 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 `same` (19 / 15 / 16 wins — the hand-off runs compiled code). `beats_compiled` false: decode `slower` on the 1-row size alone.
- **G3 effect.** Never timed end to end (round 3, section 4). Its ancestor (round 2 attempt-7, same kernels without the hand-off) shortened the decode step 17.5% with 32 requests but made prompt processing 6.6–14.5× slower; the hand-off removes the prefill half of that, so no G3 prediction from round 3 stands — Claude's reading is that only the 1-row gap remains.
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** It is not a baseline because `beats_compiled` is false — the 1-row decode loss (96.9 vs 86.6 µs/layer) — and it has no G3 pass. Round 3 tried a vectorised scalar path (attempt-2, bought nothing) and an unfused path copying the reference's structure (attempt-5, 2× worse at 1 row) and concluded no fix existed in the spec surface. From round 4 the surface has `min_rows`: `min_rows: 2` with `max_rows: 59` hands 1-row inputs to the compiled reference while keeping the 8/32-row wins — a direction not yet graded. It can then pass G3 only in a set whose other kernels are faster with 1 request, because with 1 request every decode step runs MLX's own code for this slot.
- **Where it still spends its time.** At 8/32 rows it already wins by 69.3 / 328.7 µs per layer; what remains is the 1-row chain (the `tg_x` load, silu and barrier chain named in round 3) — now hand-off-able — and per-pair weight re-reads at all sizes (552,960 B per pair, round 3's entry).

#### `routing` — starting point `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6`

- **What it is.** Round 2's staged scalar-exact kernel (attempt-4 kernels) with `max_rows: 32`: every decode step (1–32 rows) runs the staged scalar kernels, all prefill sizes run the compiled reference. Attempt-6 is a byte-identical re-grade of round 3's attempt-1 (empty `diff` on both blocks and `spec.json`), run to test whether attempt-1's 2,048-row `slower` on identical code reproduced; it did not (19/30 wins, `same`). See `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6/notes.md`.
- **Piece timing.** Round 3's grade: decode `faster` at all three sizes (candidate 51.7 / 90.9 / 132.2 vs compiled 66.3 / 104.0 / 152.0 µs per layer; 28 / 27 / 25 wins), prefill `same` at all three sizes. Claude's re-grade with the round-4 grader ([`results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/`](../../../results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/)): decode `faster` (29 / 26 / 27 wins; candidate 0.72 / 0.90 / 0.88 of the compiled reference at 1 / 8 / 32 rows), the three prefill sizes `handed off`, `beats_compiled` true.
- **G3 effect.** In round 3's swarm ready check it failed alone against `compiled-routing` at 8×128 on overlapping ranges, with no phase slower anywhere (decode medians −0.38 / −0.31 / −0.59 / −0.48 ms vs the unchanged model at 1×128 / 8×128 / 32×128 / 32×1024). Claude's G3 agreed: `same` as `compiled-routing` at 8×128. Together with combine attempt-2 (`muse-all`) it passed the swarm's ready check but failed Claude's G3 against `compiled-all` at 32×1024, where the medians are 0.9% apart with overlapping ranges.
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** G3 alone: it passes G2 and has `beats_compiled` true, but it has never passed G3, alone or (in Claude's run) as a pair. Under round 4's set rule the pair would have been `ready` in round 3, but a set still has to pass G3 as `muse-all`, so the pair is no baseline.
- **Where it still spends its time.** Decode wins at every size; the open question is margin, above all at 32×1024 where the pair gains only 0.25–0.30 ms over the compiled reference (~1%), inside the 5-repeat spread. The per-row `w_router` re-read is untouched (upper bound only, round 2's `ineff-baseline-routing-4`).

#### `combine` — starting point `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/combine/attempt-2`

- **What it is.** Round 2's attempt-1 kernel with its seven `volatile` rounding barriers replaced by seven plain `float` locals and a header block (`block-1.metal`) carrying `#pragma STDC FP_CONTRACT OFF` / `#pragma clang fp contract(off)`: same 7-op stepwise fold `((p0+p1)+p2)+p3`, same grid (`rows*768`) and threadgroup [256,1,1], no `max_rows`. See `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/combine/attempt-2/notes.md`.
- **Piece timing.** Round 3's grade: `faster` at all six sizes (decode 31.8 / 34.7 / 32.7 vs compiled 36.9 / 41.1 / 45.7 µs per layer, 24 / 27 / 30 wins; prefill 38.2 / 100.9 / 198.0 vs 64.0 / 281.8 / 556.2, 30 / 30 / 29 wins); `beats_compiled` true in both phases. Absolute chained times drift up to ~35% between runs on this machine (round 3's lesson), so only same-run paired verdicts transfer.
- **G3 effect.** In round 3's ready check it failed alone against the unchanged model at 1×128 on a single outlier repeat (5.892 ms, above the unchanged model's lowest 5.430) and, in Claude's G3, against `compiled-combine` at 32×128 and 32×1024 — again range overlaps with no phase slower anywhere (swarm decode medians −0.53 / −0.59 / −0.44 / −0.26 ms vs the unchanged model). Its ancestor's in-step cost (+1.05 ms/step at 32 requests from the volatile barriers) is what the pragma removes; round 3's measured decode medians favour the kernel everywhere.
- **What keeps it from being a baseline.** G3 alone, on spread: every median favours it, but the 5-repeat ranges overlap the bars'. No kernel change is named that tightens spread on 7 plain ops (round 3's implementation README); as part of a set it already passes `muse-all` in the swarm's run.
- **Where it still spends its time.** Nothing further in the grader — it sits on the chained floor and wins at all six sizes. What remains is the same margin question as routing: more separation from the compiled reference at 32×128 and 32×1024, or a set that clears the bar together.

#### All three together

Round 3's pair (routing attempt-6 + combine attempt-2) is the best result of any round: against the unchanged model it shortens the decode step 16.5% / 5.4% / 2.8% / 1.6% and whole requests 14.1% / 5.6% / 2.1% / 2.4% at 1×128 / 8×128 / 32×128 / 32×1024, with prompts 1.6–3.1% faster and nothing slower — but it fails G3 against `compiled-all` at 32×1024 (0.9% median gap, overlapping ranges). About half the gain over the unchanged model is `mx.compile` of the two slots' reference code alone. The three-slot composition is untested: in rounds 1 and 2, replacing all three slots at once lost about 2.8 ms with 8 requests for an unknown reason, and round 3 installed no experts candidate, so no run since has met it.

### What is left

Ranked by predicted saving against the compiled reference (no slot has a baseline, so the reference is the bar everywhere). Claude's measurement names three things round 4 has to find out; the ranking follows them.

1. **Experts with `min_rows`.** Whether attempt-1's 8/32-row speed (168.9 vs 238.2 and 554.7 vs 883.4 µs per layer) carries into G3 once 1 row runs MLX's own code (`min_rows: 2`, `max_rows: 59`). This is the only ungraded direction in any slot and the largest piece saving left: the 8/32-row wins are 69.3 / 328.7 µs per layer, worth (PREDICTION, from those same-run margins × 20 layers) about 1.4 ms per step at 8 requests and 6.6 ms at 32 requests against the compiled reference, with prefill `handed off` above 59 rows and 1-row decode `handed off` — so the gain exists only at 8 and 32 requests, and G3 can pass only in a set whose other kernels win with 1 request. The risk is the three-slot interaction (item 3).
2. **A margin at 32×1024.** The pair gains 0.25–0.30 ms over the compiled reference there (~1%), which 5 repeats cannot tell from noise; a set needs more than that with 32 long prompts. This is a margin problem in routing and/or combine decode kernels, not a correctness one: both starting points are bit-exact and already `faster` at every graded size, so any new attempt must widen the same-run margin at decode sizes without touching prefill (`max_rows: 32` for routing, faster-everywhere for combine). A saving here is worth the difference between a passing and a failing set — the largest whole-request prize left, and unquantified until a builder measures it.
3. **All three slots at once.** In rounds 1 and 2 the three-slot replacement lost about 2.8 ms with 8 requests for an unknown reason; a set with an experts attempt meets that again. No single-slot kernel change is predicted to remove it, so it is carried as a constraint: per-slot wins are not assumed to compose, and the ready check (which times candidates alone and all together) is where composition is measured. If the three together lose, the fallback set is the routing+combine pair.
4. **Slots not yet tried.** `routing+combine` (both slots, each with its own kernels, in one candidate) has never been graded as one folder. The parts are graded independently and the combine part receives the reference routing weights, so it is packaging unless a shared design emerges; the set rule already submits the two slots together without it. No hypothesis is planned on it unless exploration finds a shared-design reason.
5. **Recommendations outside the slots** stand as written in round 1's and round 2's exploration READMEs (attention K/V re-read per query head; split-K partial traffic from 14 rows; the 60 q/k/v `[0]` gathers; engine CPU per 1-row step). Claude's round-3 measurement did not test them. They are for surucuonur's team; no hypothesis targets them.

### Refuted claims

No one chases these again.

- Round 3's experts 1-row fixes: a vectorised scalar path (attempt-2) bought nothing and an unfused path copying the reference's structure (attempt-5) was 2× worse at 1 row — the 1-row gap is not closed by either approach, and round 4 does not retry them; it hands 1 row off instead.
- Routing attempt-1's 2,048-row `slower` verdict on byte-identical code: attempt-6's re-grade (19/30, `same`) confirmed it as paired noise, not a hand-off cost. Handed-off sizes are no longer timed at all.
- `ineff-runs-3` (round 1, refuted): the micro sorted/unsorted gaps measure kernel choice, not pair order.
- Round 1's implicit claim that the independent (overlapped) piece timing ranks attempts as the model does: refuted by the chained measurement. Round 4 ranks by the chained timing only.
- The claim that scalar sums cannot reproduce MMA rounding: refuted by building in round 2 (routing attempts 2–4, experts scalar paths bit-identical at all six sizes).

### Territories this round opens

Each territory is opened by the line of this section that names it. A `baseline-<slot>` explorer maps that slot's starting-point kernels and `spec.json` — now the code in the slot — with the checklist, and finds where they still lose time and, for a starting point, why it is no baseline. Explorers start from the earlier rounds' entries for their territory and write only what is new.

| `baseline-routing` | "`routing` — starting point `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6`" — likewise; where decode margin can still be widened, above all for the 32×1024 workload (item 2 of *What is left*). |

| `g3` | "All three together" and items 1–3 of *What is left* — where the end-to-end change differs from the piece timing (the pair at 32×1024, the untested three-slot interaction), and why. |

24|## The slots
25|
26|Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the call: 1 to 32 in a decode step, up to 2,048 in a prefill chunk. The grader flattens the inputs to the shapes below and restores the model's shapes afterwards. All arrays are row-contiguous.
27|
28|The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.
29|
30|### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights
31|
32|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
33||---|---|---|---|
34|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
35|| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
36|| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
37|| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
38|| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
39|
40|Reference:
41|
42|```python
43|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
44|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
45|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
46|weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
47|```
48|
49|The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.
50|
51|### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert
52|
53|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
54||---|---|---|---|
55|| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
56|| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
57|| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
58|| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
59|
60|Reference:
61|
62|```python
63|out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
64|```
65|
66|Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.
67|
68|### `routing+combine`
69|
70|Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.
71|
72|### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products
73|
74|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
75||---|---|---|---|
76|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
77|| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
78|| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
79|| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
80|| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
81|| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
82|| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |
83|
84|Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.
85|
86|Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:
87|
88|```python
89|y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
90|```
91|
92|As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.
93|
94|Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.
95|
96|## Tools and limits
97|
98|- **Only `mx.fast.metal_kernel`, MLX 0.32.4.** You write the Metal body; MLX generates the signature. Inputs arrive as `const device T* name` and outputs as `device T* name`. Shapes and strides come as `name_shape` and `name_strides` when the source uses them. The thread attributes are available, as in MLX's documentation: `thread_position_in_grid`, `threadgroup_position_in_grid`, `thread_position_in_threadgroup`, `threads_per_threadgroup`, `simdgroup_index_in_threadgroup`, `thread_index_in_simdgroup`, and so on.
99|- **The grader runs no Python of yours.** It reads your launch spec as data and compiles only your Metal.
100|- **Stay within the GPU's limits.** At most 1,024 threads per threadgroup and 32 KB of threadgroup memory. A grader run should take under 3 minutes, longer for an attempt much slower than the reference at the prefill sizes; stop one that runs past 15.
101|- **Hardware.** The Apple M1 Pro GPU (`applegpu_g13s`) has 16 cores and a SIMD width of 32. bfloat16 is available in Metal as `bfloat`.

182|## How each attempt is judged
183|
184|The pass criteria were fixed before the first round. From round 2, G2 is exact and also covers the prefill, and the piece timing chains the layers ([ADR 0010](adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md)); round 1 was judged by the earlier rules, in which G2 allowed small rounding differences and tested decode steps only. From round 3, the piece timing and G3 time both phases, decode and prefill ([ADR 0011](adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)); rounds 1 and 2 were timed on decode only.
185|
186|1. **G1, runs.** It compiles and runs on real inputs.
187|2. **G2, correct: identical to the reference, bit for bit.** The slot runs in every call of `MoE.__call__`, the prefill included, so it is tested on every layer's inputs at two kinds of size:
188|   - **a decode step:** inputs captured from all 20 layers during a real decode step, at 1, 8 and 32 rows;
189|   - **a prefill:** the first chunk of a prefill with 128-token prompts, recorded while the grader runs it, at 1, 8 and 32 requests: 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. From 60 rows on, MLX's own experts kernel changes (`gather_qmm_rhs` instead of `gather_qvm`), and so does its rounding.
190|
191|   At every size:
192|   - **`routing`:** each row's 4 experts and their 4 weights equal the reference's, in the same order, since combine sums the pairs in that order. That includes the reference's choice between tied 4th and 5th experts.
193|   - **`combine` and `experts`:** every element equals the reference's.
194|
195|   **Why exact:** the end-to-end check below asks for the same greedy tokens, and greedy decoding turns any difference into different tokens. In round 1, routing weights within 10⁻⁵ of the reference, relative, changed 7 to 9 of 32 sequences.
196|   - **Then, end to end:** the same greedy tokens as the original model over 24 generated tokens, at 1 and 32 requests, in both plain MLX and vLLM.
197|3. **G3, faster, in vLLM.** Each workload runs 5 times in shuffled order: 1, 8 and 32 requests with 128-token prompts, and 32 requests with 1,024-token prompts, 256 generated tokens each. Three times are measured per run:
198|   - the **decode step**, the median period between steady steps;
199|   - the **prompt time**, until every prompt was processed;
200|   - the **whole request**, from sending the requests to the last token.
201|
202|   Against both the original model and an `mx.compile` of the same reference code, the attempt passes when the decode step or the prompt time is faster in every workload, neither is slower in any, and no whole request is slower. Faster and slower mean that the ranges over the repeats don't overlap.
203|
204|   **From round 3, the same G3 runs inside the round too:** the lead's **ready check**, `bench/grader/check_ready.py`, with every candidate in one call. It also requires the same greedy tokens, and audits its own log. Only its passing verdict makes an attempt `ready`; Claude's G3 after the round decides. The skill says when the lead runs it ([ADR 0013](adr/0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)).
205|
206|   **From round 4, a set:** with more than one candidate, the ready check and G3 also time them all together (`muse-all`). When that passes, the candidates are ready together as a set, even where one fails alone, and G3 judges the set as one submission ([ADR 0015](adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)).
207|
208|**What the grader prints for an attempt** (JSON):
209|- `g1` false and the compiler's error message;
210|- or the correctness results per size: for routing, the rows that differ; for combine and experts, the elements that differ and the largest gap in units in the last place; with the first example;
211|- or, when the attempt is correct, `timing_us_per_layer` per size: its time per call next to the original's and the compiled reference's, its wins against the compiled reference and the verdict (`faster`, `same`, `slower`, or `handed off` for a size your spec hands to the compiled reference); then `phases_vs_compiled` and `beats_compiled`.
212|
213|**The piece timing** runs the slot at the six G2 sizes: the 20 layers' captured decode inputs at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and the 20 layers' first prefill chunk at 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. Each layer's call waits for the previous one's output, as in the model: one small kernel links them, the same for every function timed. Without that wait, the GPU overlaps the 20 calls and hides how long one takes; in round 1, an experts kernel 29% faster on overlapped calls was 66% slower on chained ones at 1 row.
214|- **Paired repeats.** Your attempt and the compiled reference run in alternating order, 30 times.
215|- **Per size:** your attempt is `faster` when it wins at least 22 of the 30 pairs, `slower` when it loses at least 22, and `same` otherwise. Medians alone would pass on noise: the same kernel timed twice differs by up to 5%.
216|- **Handed off** (from round 4): a size whose inputs your spec hands to the compiled reference (`max_rows`, `min_rows`) runs the bar's own code, so it is not timed against it. Its verdict is `handed off`, and your attempt's time there is the compiled reference's.
217|- **Per phase:** decode (1, 8, 32 rows) and prefill (127, 1,016, 2,048 rows) are each `faster` when every size it doesn't hand off is, and at least one isn't handed off; `slower` when any size is; `handed off` when all are; and `not slower` otherwise.
218|- **`beats_compiled`** is true when one phase is `faster` and neither is `slower`.
219|
220|It is a guide; the ready check in the round, and Claude's G3 after it, decide.
221|
222|**When a slot stops.** Work on a slot stops at the first attempt that passes G1 and G2 and has `beats_compiled` true, or after 5 attempts. Name your final attempt per slot in `muse-spark/summary.md`; it goes to the end-to-end and G3 checks, which surucuonur's team runs after merging your branch.

44|def ref_routing(x, w_router, bias):
45|    scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)
46|    inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=K - 1, axis=-1)[:, :K]

55|def ref_experts(x, inds, *weights):
56|    """The port's SwitchGLU on flat rows: [rows, D] and [rows, K] -> [rows, K, D]."""
57|    from mlx_lm.models.activations import swiglu
58|    from mlx_lm.models.switch_layers import _gather_sort, _scatter_unsort
59|
60|    gate, up, down = weights[0:3], weights[3:6], weights[6:9]
61|    xx = mx.expand_dims(x, (-2, -3))
62|    do_sort = inds.size >= 64
63|    idx, inv = inds, None
64|    if do_sort:
65|        xx, idx, inv = _gather_sort(xx, inds)
66|
67|    def qmm(a, w):
68|        return mx.gather_qmm(
69|            a,
70|            *w,
71|            rhs_indices=idx,
72|            transpose=False,
73|            group_size=32,
74|            bits=4,
75|            mode="affine",
76|            sorted_indices=do_sort,
77|        )
78|
79|    y = qmm(swiglu(qmm(xx, gate), qmm(xx, up)), down)
80|    if do_sort:
81|        y = _scatter_unsort(y, inv, inds.shape)
82|    return y.squeeze(-2)

304|def build(spec, sources, slot):
305|    """A function slot_inputs -> slot_outputs from Muse Spark's spec and Metal blocks.
306|
307|    With "max_rows" in the spec, inputs with more rows than that run the slot's
308|    reference under mx.compile instead of the kernels, so an attempt can keep
309|    prompt-sized inputs on MLX's own code (claude/adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md);
310|    with "min_rows", so do inputs with fewer rows than that
311|    (claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md). The function's hands_off(rows)
312|    says whether inputs of that many rows run the compiled reference.
313|    """
314|    slot_in, slot_out = SLOTS[slot]
315|    kernels = []
316|    for k in spec["kernels"]:
317|        header = "" if k.get("header_block") is None else sources[k["header_block"]]
318|        fn = mx.fast.metal_kernel(
319|            name=re.sub(r"\W", "_", str(k["name"])),
320|            input_names=list(k["inputs"]),
321|            output_names=[o["name"] for o in k["outputs"]],
322|            source=sources[k["source_block"]],
323|            header=header,
324|            atomic_outputs=bool(k.get("atomic_outputs", False)),
325|        )
326|        kernels.append((k, fn))
327|    missing = set(slot_out) - set(spec["slot_outputs"])
328|    if missing:
329|        raise ValueError(f"slot_outputs is missing {sorted(missing)}")
330|    min_rows, max_rows = spec.get("min_rows"), spec.get("max_rows")
331|    for key, v in (("min_rows", min_rows), ("max_rows", max_rows)):
332|        if v is not None and (isinstance(v, bool) or not isinstance(v, int) or v < 1):
333|            raise ValueError(f"bad {key} {v!r}")
334|    if min_rows is not None and max_rows is not None and min_rows > max_rows:
335|        raise ValueError(f"min_rows {min_rows} is above max_rows {max_rows}: the kernels would never run")
336|    compiled = mx.compile(REFERENCE[slot])
337|
338|    def hands_off(rows):
339|        return (max_rows is not None and rows > max_rows) or (min_rows is not None and rows < min_rows)
340|
341|    def run(**inputs):
342|        rows = inputs[slot_in[0]].shape[0]
343|        if hands_off(rows):  # the compiled reference takes over
344|            out = compiled(*[inputs[n] for n in slot_in])
345|            return dict(zip(slot_out, out if isinstance(out, (tuple, list)) else [out]))
346|        env = dict(inputs)
347|        for k, fn in kernels:
348|            tg = [int(t) for t in k["threadgroup"]]
349|            if any(t < 1 for t in tg) or tg[0] * tg[1] * tg[2] > 1024:
350|                raise ValueError(f"bad threadgroup {tg}")
351|            outs = fn(
352|                inputs=[env[n] for n in k["inputs"]],
353|                template=[
354|                    (n, template_value(v)) for n, v in (k.get("template") or {}).items()
355|                ],
356|                grid=tuple(dim(g, rows) for g in k["grid"]),
357|                threadgroup=tuple(tg),
358|                output_shapes=[
359|                    tuple(dim(s, rows) for s in o["shape"]) for o in k["outputs"]
360|                ],
361|                output_dtypes=[DTYPES[o["dtype"]] for o in k["outputs"]],
362|                init_value=k.get("init_value"),
363|            )
364|            env.update(zip([o["name"] for o in k["outputs"]], outs))
365|        return {name: env[src] for name, src in spec["slot_outputs"].items()}
366|
367|    run.hands_off = hands_off
368|    return run

2|
3|The independent grader for the Muse agent's kernels (claude/muse-agent-brief.md).
4|G2 tests it on the inputs `slots.py capture` recorded from a real decode step
5|(1, 8 and 32 rows), and on every layer's inputs in a prefill, recorded as
6|it runs (127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows): every output must be identical to the
7|reference's, bit for bit, since only then are the model's tokens identical
8|(claude/adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md). The timing runs at the same six
9|sizes and chains the 20 layers, so each call waits for the one before, as in
10|the model. The grader prints its verdict as JSON, and writes it to --out when
11|given. It writes into an attempt folder only when --out points there, as
12|the Muse agent's builders do with grade.json; load() reads only spec.json and
13|the block-N.metal files.
14|
15|  .venv/bin/python bench/grader/check_candidate.py <attempt folder> <slot> [--out FILE]
16|      [--baseline [SLOT=]FOLDER ...]
17|
18|The candidate and the compiled reference are timed in alternating repeats, so
19|drift in the GPU's clocks reaches both alike. At each size the candidate is
20|"faster" when it wins at least WINS_NEEDED of the REPEATS paired repeats (a
21|one-sided sign test at p < 0.01), "slower" when it loses that many, and
22|"same" otherwise; the same kernel timed twice differs by up to 5% between
23|medians, so comparing medians alone would pass on noise. `beats_compiled`
24|needs both phases, decode and prefill: faster at every size of one, slower
25|at none of the other (claude/adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md).
26|
27|A size whose inputs the attempt hands to the compiled reference (`max_rows`,
28|`min_rows`) runs the bar's own code, so it is "handed off", not timed against
29|it: a phase is faster when every size the kernels run is, and needs one such
30|size (claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md). G2 still checks it.
31|
32|--baseline times an earlier, already graded attempt in the same run and adds
33|`beats_baseline`, judged the same way. From round 2 on, the bar is the
34|previous round's final attempt for the slot
35|(claude/adr/0009-rounds-build-on-each-other.md). FOLDER alone is an attempt

197|def chained(fn, layers, names):
198|    """All 20 layers' calls, each one waiting for the one before, as in a decode step.
199|
200|    A call's smallest input is linked to the previous call's last output, the
201|    same for every function timed. Without the wait, the GPU overlaps the
202|    calls and hides a slow call's latency; mx.depends orders only the graph.
203|    """
204|    small = min(names, key=lambda n: layers[0][n].size)
205|    outs = []
206|    for layer in layers:
207|        args = {n: layer[n] for n in names}
208|        if outs:
209|            args[small] = link(args[small], outs[-1][-1])
210|        out = fn(**args)
211|        if isinstance(out, dict):
212|            out = list(out.values())
213|        outs.append(list(out) if isinstance(out, (tuple, list)) else [out])
214|    return outs

217|def timed(fn, layers, names):
218|    """Median µs per layer: the 20 layers' chained calls, then one wait for the GPU."""
219|    for _ in range(3):
220|        mx.eval(chained(fn, layers, names))
221|    times = []
222|    for _ in range(REPEATS):
223|        t0 = time.perf_counter()
224|        mx.eval(chained(fn, layers, names))
225|        times.append((time.perf_counter() - t0) / len(layers))
226|    return round(statistics.median(times) * 1e6, 1)

229|def paired_times(fns, layers, names):
230|    """Per-repeat µs per layer of each function, in rotating order within each repeat."""
231|    calls = [lambda f=f: mx.eval(chained(f, layers, names)) for f in fns]
232|    for _ in range(3):
233|        for call in calls:
234|            call()
235|    times = [[] for _ in fns]
236|    for i in range(REPEATS):
237|        for j in [(i + k) % len(fns) for k in range(len(fns))]:
238|            t0 = time.perf_counter()
239|            calls[j]()
240|            times[j].append((time.perf_counter() - t0) / len(layers) * 1e6)
241|    return times

253|def judge(verdicts):
254|    """Each phase's verdict from its sizes' verdicts, and whether the candidate
255|    beats the bar: faster at every size of one phase, slower at no size of the other.
256|
257|    Sizes "handed off" don't count. A phase is "faster" when every other size
258|    is, "slower" when any is, "handed off" when none is left, and "not slower"
259|    otherwise.

261|    phases = {}

263|        sizes = [v for size, v in verdicts.items() if size.startswith(prefix) and v != "handed off"]
264|        phases[phase] = (
265|            "handed off" if not sizes
266|            else "faster" if all(v == "faster" for v in sizes)
267|            else "slower" if "slower" in sizes
268|            else "not slower"
269|        )
270|    beats = "faster" in phases.values() and "slower" not in phases.values()
271|    return phases, beats

142|class TransposedQuantizedSwitchLinear(nn.Module):
143|    """Quantized expert weights in [E, in, out] layout, grouped along out."""
144|
145|    def __init__(
146|        self,

187|class MoE(nn.Module):
188|    def __init__(self, args: ModelArgs):
189|        super().__init__()
190|        dim = args.hidden_size
191|        hidden = args.intermediate_size
192|        num_experts = args.num_local_experts
193|        self.top_k = args.num_experts_per_tok
194|        self.norm_topk_prob = args.norm_topk_prob
195|        self.routed_scaling_factor = args.routed_scaling_factor
196|
197|        self.router = nn.Linear(dim, num_experts, bias=False)
198|        self.expert_bias = mx.zeros((num_experts,))
199|        self.experts = SwitchGLU(dim, hidden, num_experts)
200|        if args.transposed_experts:
201|            q = args.quantization
202|            for name, dims in (
203|                ("gate_proj", (dim, hidden)),
204|                ("up_proj", (dim, hidden)),
205|                ("down_proj", (hidden, dim)),
206|            ):
207|                proj = TransposedQuantizedSwitchLinear(
208|                    *dims,
209|                    num_experts,
210|                    q["group_size"],
211|                    q["bits"],
212|                    q.get("mode", "affine"),
213|                )
214|                setattr(self.experts, name, proj)
215|        self.shared_expert = MLP(dim, args.intermediate_size_mlp)
216|
217|    def __call__(self, x: mx.array) -> mx.array:
218|        # The reference computes the router in float32.
219|        scores = mx.sigmoid(self.router(x.astype(mx.float32)))
220|
221|        # The bias changes which experts are selected, not their weights.
222|        k = self.top_k
223|        biased = scores + self.expert_bias
224|        inds = mx.argpartition(-biased, kth=k - 1, axis=-1)[..., :k]
225|        scores = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)
226|        if self.norm_topk_prob:
227|            scores = scores / (scores.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20)
228|        scores = scores * self.routed_scaling_factor
229|
230|        y = self.experts(x, inds)
231|        y = (y * scores[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(x.dtype)
232|        return y + self.shared_expert(x)

5|# From round 3, an improvement must hold in both phases, decode and prefill, and an attempt may hand prefill-sized inputs to the compiled reference
6|
7|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../../PROVENANCE.md).*
8|
9|**The change.** Claude's comparison of every engine version over whole requests ([findings](../findings/muse-round-2.md), section 5) found that the grader and G3 timed only the decode step. They never timed the prefill, the phase in which a request's whole prompt runs through the model:
10|- **Experts attempt-7** looked like round 2's largest gain, a 19% shorter decode step at 32 requests. It processed prompts 6.6 to 14.5 times slower and cut throughput by 10% to 83%.
11|- **Routing attempt-4,** round 2's only baseline, processed prompts 7% to 10% slower. At 32 requests with 1,024-token prompts it cost 3.5% of throughput.
12|
13|The Muse agent never saw either effect: its piece timing ran decode sizes only, and G3 measured the decode step only.
14|
15|On 2026-11-04 surucuonur set the rule: "The improvement should be in the two phases of it: decode and prefill. Then, we can consider it as an improvement." surucuonur chose:
16|- **faster in one phase, slower in neither;**
17|- **the hand-off:** an attempt may leave prefill-sized inputs to the compiled reference. This replaces the part of [ADR 0010](0010-exact-at-every-size.md) that required the kernels to run in every call.
18|
19|## How it works
20|
21|- **The piece timing runs at the six G2 sizes** (`bench/grader/check_candidate.py`): decode at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and the first prefill chunk at 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. The layers are still chained.
22|- **The verdict at each size comes from paired repeats.** The candidate and the compiled reference run in alternating order, 30 times, and so does the baseline when one is given.
23|  - The candidate is `faster` when it wins at least 22 of the 30 pairs, a one-sided sign test at p < 0.01.
24|  - It is `slower` when it loses at least 22, and `same` otherwise.
25|
26|  This replaces the comparison of medians for the decode sizes too, since the same kernel timed twice differs by up to 5%.
27|- **The verdict per phase:**
28|  - a phase is `faster` when every one of its sizes is;
29|  - it is `slower` when any size is;
30|  - otherwise it is `not slower`.
31|

33|- **The hand-off** (`max_rows` in `spec.json`, `bench/grader/slots.py`). Inputs with more rows than `max_rows` run the slot's reference under `mx.compile`. G2 still checks every size.
34|  - On 2026-11-04 the compiled reference of each slot was bit-exact with the reference at all six sizes (`bench/micro/compiled_exact.py`, `results/runs/2026-11-04-handoff-check/`).

36|- **G3** (`bench/grader/time_candidates.py`, which writes `g3-vllm.json`):
37|  - **Workloads:** 1, 8 and 32 requests with 128-token prompts, and 32 requests with 1,024-token prompts.
38|  - **Measurements per run:** the decode step period, the prompt time and the whole-request time, over 5 shuffled repeats, up from 3.
39|  - **Faster and slower:** the two ranges over the repeats don't overlap.
40|  - **Why 5 repeats:** with 3 each, two identical engines' ranges miss each other by chance 1 time in 20 per direction. "Never slower" checks a phase 8 times (4 workloads, 2 bars), so a phase that changed nothing would fail about a third of the time. The first run under these rules showed it. A copy of experts attempt-7 with a hand-off at 59 rows came out `slower` on prompt time at 32 × 1,024, by 0.5% with ranges 16 ms apart, although above 59 rows it runs the compiled reference, whose own range overlapped the unchanged engine's (`results/runs/2026-11-04-handoff-check/`). With 5 repeats the chance is 1 in 252 per check, about 3% over 8.
41|  - **The pass rule:** against both the original model and the compiled reference, the decode step or the prompt time must be faster in every workload, neither may be slower in any, and no whole request may be slower.
42|- **The unchanged engine is vLLM's own.** The original model in G3 runs with Claude's step hooks, and with vLLM's engine inside the script's process. On 2026-11-04, alternating runs found it within −0.2% to +1.9% of vLLM with neither, inside the spread between repeats in every workload (`bench/micro/clean_vllm.py`, `results/runs/2026-11-04-clean-vllm/`).

45|
46|- **Round 3 starts with no baseline.** Routing attempt-4 is `slower` at all three prefill sizes, 2.6 to 8.7 times the compiled reference's time. It fails G3 on prompt time at 8 and 32 requests. It becomes a starting point, so round 3's bar in every slot is the compiled reference.
47|- **A decode kernel no longer has to win at prefill sizes,** only to hand them off or not lose there. The attempt chooses the row count, so the boundary agent checks that the hand-off sits on the right side of 60 rows for the experts slot.
48|- **At prefill sizes, a slot with a hand-off is MLX's code, not the Muse agent's.** The claim for such an attempt is "faster decode, unchanged prefill".
49|- **Grader runs and G3 take longer.** Every attempt is now timed at three more sizes. G3 runs 5 repeats instead of 3, and its 32 × 1,024 workload adds at least 16 s per variant per repeat.
50|- **The decode verdict is stricter.** An attempt whose median beat the compiled reference by noise is now `same`.
51|- **Not covered:** prefill chunks of other sizes, and decode steps with other row counts. The boundary agent reports them; G3's four workloads are the end-to-end check. Not covered means not measured: from round 3 the swarm lists these as **Unverified**, never as free ([ADR 0013](0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)); round 2 read ADR 0010's line like this one as leave to slow the prefill.
52|- **At 1 request the whole-request time is noisy.** On 2026-11-04 its repeats spread 6% to 41%, so G3 there mostly says `same`, which passes the "never slower" test without showing a gain.

54|## Considered options
55|
56|- **Faster in both phases.** The higher bar. A decode kernel would also have to beat MLX's large matrix kernels at 2,048 rows, which is not where the decode step loses its time. Not chosen.
57|- **Whole-request throughput alone.** Simple, but it lets a slower phase be traded for a faster one. surucuonur ruled that out.
58|- **Hand off to the uncompiled reference.** The prefill could then come out `slower` than the compiled reference wherever compiling helps; at 127 rows, routing's compiled reference takes 87 µs per layer against 102 µs uncompiled.
59|- **Keep the kernels in every call** (ADR 0010). The kernels could still branch on the row count inside themselves, but they couldn't use MLX's large-size kernels. surucuonur chose the hand-off.

5|# From round 4, candidates that pass together are ready as a set, and an attempt may hand off small inputs too
6|
7|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../../PROVENANCE.md).*
8|
9|**The change.** Round 3 showed three gaps in the rules ([Claude's measurement](../findings/muse-round-3.md)). On 2026-11-04 surucuonur chose to fix all three before round 4:
10|
11|1. **Ready as a set.** Round 3's routing and combine candidates each failed the ready check alone, on overlapping ranges, while the two together (`muse-all`) passed it. The skill made a candidate `ready` only when it passed alone, so the round submitted nothing. From round 4, when `muse-all` passes the ready check, all its candidates are `ready` together as a **set**. A set goes to G3 whole, and G3 judges it as `muse-all`.
12|2. **Hand off below a row count too: `min_rows`.** `max_rows` already sends inputs with more rows to `mx.compile` of the slot's reference ([ADR 0011](0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). The new `min_rows` in an attempt's `spec.json` does the same for inputs with fewer rows, so the kernels run only from `min_rows` to `max_rows`. Round 3's experts attempt-1 lost to the compiled reference only at 1 row: 96.9 against 86.6 µs per layer, while it took 168.9 against 238.2 at 8 rows and 554.7 against 883.4 at 32. Its only way to pass was to win at the size it is worst at.
13|3. **A handed-off size isn't timed.** The grader timed each handed-off size, which runs the compiled reference, against the compiled reference: the same code twice. In round 3 that noise judged routing attempt-1 `slower` at 2,048 rows, on 8 wins of 30, and cost a re-grade of a byte-identical copy. Now such a size is reported `handed off`. A phase is `faster` when every size the kernels run at is faster, and it needs at least one; `beats_compiled` is still one phase `faster` and none `slower`. G2 still checks every size, bit for bit.
14|
15|## How it works
16|
17|- **`bench/grader/slots.py`:**
18|  - `build()` reads `min_rows` as it reads `max_rows`: an integer of at least 1, at most `max_rows` when both are given.
19|  - The function it returns has `hands_off(rows)`, which says whether inputs with that many rows run the compiled reference.
20|- **`bench/grader/check_candidate.py`:**
21|  - At each size, a function that hands the rows off is not timed. It takes the compiled reference's times, so for `routing+combine` the part that hands off adds the same time to both sides.
22|  - A bar's verdict is `handed off` when neither side ran code of its own. Against a baseline that runs its own kernels there, the size is timed as before.
23|  - `judge()` leaves `handed off` sizes out of a phase. A phase whose sizes are all handed off is `handed off`.
24|- **`bench/grader/test_hand_off.py`:**
25|  - checks `build()` with a toy kernel at row counts on both sides of each bound, bit for bit, and that bad bounds are refused;
26|  - checks `judge()` on five sets of verdicts.
27|  - Passed on 2026-11-04.
28|- **A real attempt.** Claude re-graded round 3's routing attempt-6 (`max_rows` 32) with the changed grader ([results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/](../../results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/)):
29|  - G2 passes;
30|  - decode is `faster` at 1, 8 and 32 rows, on 29, 26 and 27 wins of 30;

33|- **The skill, version 9.**
34|  - The ready check makes a passing `muse-all` a set.
35|  - *Ready to test* names a set's attempts together.
36|  - Builders and boundary agents record `min_rows` and the sizes it hands off.
37|- **G3 and the ready check are unchanged.** They time whole requests, so a slot's kernels count wherever they run. With 1 request every decode step has 1 row, so an attempt that hands off 1 row runs MLX's own code for the whole 1-request workload. Alone it is then no faster than its compiled bar there, and it can pass G3 only in a set whose other kernels are faster with 1 request. The brief says so.

41|- **Round 3's pair qualifies for round 4.** Under the set rule, routing attempt-6 with combine attempt-2 would have been `ready` in round 3, because its `muse-all` passed the swarm's ready check. # Inefficiency: the routing+combine pair keeps only −0.36 of its −0.66 ms/step piece win vs the compiled reference at 32×1024, inside the repeat spread

- **Owner:** explorer-g3
- **Status:** confirmed
- **Version:** 2
- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T21:47:11Z
- **Next:** builders widening routing/combine decode margin at 32 rows answer this; verifier to check the arithmetic

## Slot

Outside the slots — the routing+combine set as timed in `muse-all` (routing attempt-6 + combine attempt-2, `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6`, `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/combine/attempt-2`). Measurement side owned by territory `g3`; kernel-side margin owned by territories `baseline-routing` and `baseline-combine`.

## What happens

The chained piece timing prices the pair at −0.656 ms/step vs the compiled reference at 32 decode rows (routing −0.396 + combine −0.260; [territory-g3.md](territory-g3.md) piece 1). Timed whole in vLLM at 32 requests, the pair keeps −0.548 ms/step at 32×128 and only **−0.362 ms/step at 32×1024** in Claude's G3 (medians 38.765 vs 39.127 ms, **0.93% apart, 5-repeat ranges [38.589–39.080] vs [38.912–39.400] overlapping**, so `muse-all` vs `compiled-all` decode is `same` and G3 fails on this one workload). In the swarm's ready check the same workload keeps −0.588 (38.942 vs 39.530, 1.49%) and the ranges miss, so the pair passes there. The verdict flips between two runs of identical kernels while every median favours the pair. Full derivation in [territory-g3.md](territory-g3.md) gap 1.

## Cost

Shortfall = (measured, whole-request change vs `compiled-all`) − (piece-implied change vs compiled, candidate − compiled × 20 layers), ms per decode step. Piece from the two `grade.json` (routing 132.2 vs 152.0, combine 32.7 vs 45.7 µs/layer at 32 rows; at 1/8 rows routing 51.7/90.9 vs 66.3/104.0, combine 31.8/34.7 vs 36.9/41.1); measured from `results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-3/console-vllm.txt` summary medians (cross-checked in `muse-vllm.jsonl`) and `muse-spark/round-3/checks/ready-1/ready-verdict.json` `medians`.

| Workload | Piece vs compiled | Claude G3 vs compiled | Shortfall (Claude) | Swarm vs compiled | Shortfall (swarm) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1×128 (1 row) | −0.394 | −0.436 | −0.042 | −0.491 | −0.097 |
| 8×128 (8 rows) | −0.390 | −0.375 | +0.015 | −0.446 | −0.056 |
| 32×128 (32 rows) | −0.656 | −0.548 | +0.108 | −0.483 | +0.173 |
| 32×1024 (32 rows) | −0.656 | **−0.362** | **+0.294** | −0.588 | +0.068 |

Per layer at 32×1024 (÷20): +14.7 µs (Claude) / +3.4 µs (swarm); the two runs disagree by 0.226 ms/step, the same order as the larger shortfall, so the solid cost is the **margin**, not a fixed 0.294: the pair's separation from the compiled bar at 32×1024 is 0.36–0.59 ms/step (0.9–1.5%) against per-run 5-repeat spreads of ~0.49 ms (pair) and ~0.49 ms (compiled) wide. To have separated in Claude's draw the pair needed roughly a further 0.17 ms/step (its max 39.080 below the compiled min 38.912). At 1 row with long prompts the piece sum transfers fully (measured −0.428 at 1×1024, −0.487 at 1×7936 vs piece −0.394; [territory-g3.md](territory-g3.md) piece 4), so the shortfall needs 32 rows, and grows again with context at fixed 32 rows.

In kernel terms: the pair removes 280 kernels/step vs base (1087→807 at 32 rows) and 180 vs `compiled-all` (987→807), exactly additive, tokens bit-exact — kernel count and correctness are not the cost. The slots' own traffic is unchanged by context while the step grows 30.1→39.4 ms from 32×128 to 32×1024; the lost time scales with neither.

## Kind

Overhead-bound (in the terms of `claude/GLOSSARY.md`): the step is far from peak bandwidth and peak compute, and the shortfall scales with neither weight bytes nor kernel count. Ruled out: the kernels' own chained work (both `faster` at every decode size, piece 1), token divergence (exact everywhere), prompt length alone (piece 4). Not ruled out: a fixed in-step composition cost at 32 rows that the chained timing cannot see, vs machine drift across runs (swap 13.9–14.2 GB) — the two runs bound the sum at +0.07 to +0.29 ms/step without separating them.

## Spans

`g3` (measurement), `baseline-routing`, `baseline-combine` (any exact kernel change that widens the 32-row decode margin), `grader` (the 5-repeat range rule that prices a ~1% margin by chance; unchanged for round 4).

## Predicted saving

If the pair's full piece win transferred at 32 rows, the step gains back the shortfall: up to **0.29 ms/step at 32 requests in Claude's draw (0.07 in the swarm's)**, i.e. `muse-all` would measure ≈ −0.66 ms/step vs `compiled-all` at both 32-row workloads instead of −0.55 / −0.36; ~0 claimed at 1/8 requests, where G3 already meets or beats the piece sum. The decision-relevant saving is smaller and sharper: **~0.17 ms/step of extra separation at 32×1024** would have made the ranges miss in Claude's run and turned the pair's one failing workload into a pass. At prefill sizes nothing is predicted: prompts are already 1.6–3.1% faster than base and slower nowhere (routing handed off, combine `faster` at 127/1,016/2,048 rows), so no per-chunk saving exists on either basis. This is an upper bound on the prize, not a prediction that a specific kernel change recovers it: no mechanism is confirmed, any widening must hold bit-exact G2 at all six sizes, and a decode saving bought with prefill time is not one.

## Verdict

Nothing is shared across rows: per layer the kernel reads rows × 60×768×4 B = rows × 184,320 B of `w_router`, plus rows × 1,536 B of `x`. The compiled reference's GEMM/GEMV reads `w_router` once per layer and reuses each tile across rows (round-2 `territory-baseline-routing.md` §3.1, frozen).

This is the decode slice of round 2's `ineff-baseline-routing-4` (frozen, confirmed, upper-bound-only) and round 3's `ineff-baseline-routing-1` (frozen, confirmed), repriced because the context changed twice over: (1) `max_rows: 32` in `spec.json` now hands every prefill size to the compiled reference, so the prefill side of those entries — 116.1/935.4/1,886.5 µs/layer at 127/1,016/2,048 rows — is banked and costs nothing; what remains is exactly the decode side they ranked as not worth chasing. (2) The round-4 question is no longer beating the compiled reference (the starting point does, at every decode size) but *widening the margin*, above all at 32 rows for the 32×1024 set workload (round-4 exploration README item 2). At 32 rows the re-read excess is larger than the entire margin there is to widen.

## Cost

| rows | `w_router` read | floor (w+x) | measured cand / compiled (re-grade) | margin | excess over read-once |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.18 MB | 0.9 µs | 45.1 / 62.8 | 17.7 µs | 0 µs |
| 8 | 1.47 MB | 7.4 µs | 144.2 / 160.0 | 15.8 µs | 6.5 µs |
| 32 | 5.90 MB | 29.7 µs | 151.3 / 171.0 | 19.7 µs | 28.6 µs |
| 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 | — (handed off) | — | `handed off` | — | 0 (compiled reference runs) |

The excess is (rows−1) × 184,320 B ÷ 200 GB/s. At 32 rows the excess floor (28.6 µs/layer) is 1.45× the whole measured margin over the compiled reference (19.7 µs/layer, re-grade; 19.8 in the round-3 grade) — the only pool inside this slot big enough, on its own, to supply the +7.5–12.5 µs/layer (routing+combine combined) that non-overlap at 32×1024 needs (territory entry, headline). At 8 rows the excess (6.5) is 41% of the margin (15.8); at 1 row there is no excess (a single row reads the weight once by definition).

The floor is an upper bound, not time on the clock. The kernel is overhead-bound at decode sizes, and the staging loads overlap other resident threadgroups' scalar compute: the starting point's own measurements put the marginal cost of rows 9–32 at ≈0.16 µs/row (`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-4/notes.md`, flat 69.1→72.9 µs from 8 to 32 rows), against a 0.92 µs/row traffic floor — at most ~17% of the floor appears as marginal time, and a sharing design still pays its own staging and barriers out of that. ## Kind

Overhead-bound at decode sizes with a bandwidth-waste component (`claude/GLOSSARY.md:39-42`; at 32 rows 5.90 MB in ~132–151 µs is ≈40 GB/s, a fifth of peak — the waste is real bytes but the time is not byte-limited). At prefill sizes: not applicable — the kernels do not run there.

## Spans

`baseline-routing`. The comparison point (read-once tile reuse) is MLX's GEMM dispatch behind the compiled reference; the prize lands in `g3` territory (the set's 32×1024 margin), and any design must keep the `max_rows: 32` hand-off in `grader` territory's dispatch terms.

## Predicted saving

Upper bound if each weight byte were read once per layer at peak bandwidth, per layer and per decode step (×20 layers); prefill 0 at every size by hand-off construction (the design runs only where the kernels already run, `rows <= 32`, and changes no prefill path — so it cannot cost the other phase):

| rows | per layer | per decode step |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 µs | 0 ms |
| 8 | 6.5 µs | 0.13 ms |
| 32 | 28.6 µs | 0.57 ms |
| 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 | 0 µs | 0 ms per prefill chunk |

Arithmetic: (rows−1) × 184,320 B ÷ 200 GB/s; at 32 rows 31 × 184,320 B = 5.71 MB ÷ 200 GB/s = 28.6 µs/layer × 20 = 0.57 ms/step. Confidence is low that more than a fraction is realised — the overlap account above caps the plausibly recoverable slice at roughly the 0.16 µs/row marginal (≈3.8 µs/layer ≈ 0.08 ms/step at 32 rows) unless the design also removes staging latency the current kernel hides by overlap. Label: prediction, counting only this slot's own effect; it stands beside a builder's same-run chained measurement before anyone banks it.

What a builder needs: cross-row `w_router` sharing that keeps every row's exact accumulation order (sharing bytes is free; reordering any row's serial chain fails G2 — hyp-3 boundary, frozen) without round-1 attempt-2's barrier structure. Hard constraints already measured: threadgroups of 960 and 600 threads fail G1 on a per-pipeline cap that moved 640→576 between recompiles (round-3 attempts 2/4), while 480 threads (8 rows × 60 experts) is the proven-passing band (attempt-5); attempt-5's own named next probe — stage each `w` chunk once per group while streaming 2–4 sequential row-blocks through it, cutting traffic and barriers per row 2–4× with no more threads — is untested, and untested at decode sizes in any form. A rows-conditional design (shared path only at, say, 16–32 rows where the excess exceeds ~14 µs/layer, staged path kept below) keeps the proven 1/8-row paths untouched; the branch must be on `rows` regimes, never on the graded values.

- **Owner:** explorer-baseline-routing
- **Status:** confirmed
- **Version:** 2
- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T21:47:11Z

## Slot

`routing`

## What happens

Past the bytes in `ineff-baseline-routing-1`, the staged scalar path that runs at every decode size above 1 row pays a per-row shape cost in `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6/block-0.metal` (the code in the slot). Round 3's `ineff-baseline-routing-2` (frozen, confirmed) priced this shape at *prefill* sizes and put the decode saving at ~0 because the candidate's residual already beat the compiled reference's overhead. That verdict stands; what is new in round 4 is the question — not "reach the compiled reference's overhead" but "cut the candidate's own residual", since every µs/layer cut at 32 rows widens the set's 32×1024 margin 1:1 (territory entry, headline). The items, all inside one 256-thread threadgroup per row:

1. **27 barriers per row.** The 12 staged groups pay 2 `threadgroup_barrier`s each (stage-then-compute block-0:94, compute-then-overwrite block-0:119), plus 3 outside the loop (block-0:33,129,137). Every barrier stalls the whole threadgroup; the `rows == 1` GEMV branch pays only the 3 outside ones.
2. **The last third of K-chunks runs at 23% thread duty.** At every decode size 2–32 the partition formula (block-0:57-75) gives 32 partitions, `base_iters = 1`, the last partition absorbing chunks 31–47. Groups at `gbase` 0–28 therefore touch 4 partitions and run 240/256 threads (94%); the four groups at `gbase` 32–44 touch only partition 31 and run 60/256 threads (23.4%, block-0:99-101) — 16 of 48 chunks (33% of each row's 46,080 FMAs) issue through a quarter of the lanes, behind the same 2 barriers per group as the full groups. The final sequential partial sum also runs 60/256 (block-0:121-127). Recomputed from the formula this round; the graded 8/32 and every ungraded 2–7/9–31 share this geometry.
3. **28,080 B threadgroup footprint** (`xpad[816]` + `scores[60]` + `parts[2048]` + `wsh[4096]` floats, block-0:15,22-25) — 85.7% of the 32 KB limit, 4,688 B of headroom. 18:2. **Inclusive kernel window.** The attempt's kernels run exactly when `min_rows ≤ rows ≤ max_rows` for the bounds it gives (a missing bound is open on that side), and run the slot's reference under `mx.compile` outside that window; `rows` is the first slot input's `shape[0]` ([slots.py:338-345](../../../bench/grader/slots.py)). Row-for-row: `hands_off(rows)` is `rows > max_rows or rows < min_rows` ([slots.py:338-339](../../../bench/grader/slots.py)), and `test_hand_off.py` pins the edges bit-for-bit: 8 and 59 run the kernel, 7 and 60 run the compiled reference, for `min_rows: 8, max_rows: 59` ([test_hand_off.py:69](../../../bench/grader/test_hand_off.py)).
19:3. **G2 bit-exactness at every size, handed off or not.** G2 runs the attempt's `run()` — hand-off dispatch included — on all 20 layers at 1, 8, 32, 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows and requires bit-for-bit equality with the plain reference, in order for routing (including the tied 4th/5th choice) and elementwise for combine/experts; timing runs only if G2 passes ([check_candidate.py:320-351](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py); brief:187-195,175). A handed-off size therefore tests `mx.compile(reference)` against the plain reference through the attempt's own dispatch, which is why the boundary also includes compiled==reference at the six sizes (round-3 entry §2; [ADR 0011:34](../../../claude/adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). For experts the window must also sit on the right side of MLX's 60-row kernel switch (`gather_qmm_rhs` from 60 rows, different rounding): a decode-built experts kernel may run only below 60 rows, i.e. `max_rows ≤ 59` ([slots.py:219-220](../../../bench/grader/slots.py); round-3 entry §2). Inside the window the reference still changes behaviour once: `ref_experts` sorts the pairs from 16 rows (`inds.size >= 64`, [slots.py:62](../../../bench/grader/slots.py)), so a kernel running at both 8 and 32 rows must match the unsorted and the sorted reference, both on the `gather_qvm` side of 60.
20:4. **Piece-timing phase rule.** At each timed size the verdict is `faster` with ≥22 wins of 30 paired repeats, `slower` with ≥22 losses, else `same` ([check_candidate.py:244-250](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py)). `judge()` drops `handed off` sizes from their phase: a phase is `faster` only when **every** size the kernels run at is `faster` and at least one such size exists, `slower` when any timed size is `slower`, `handed off` when none is left, else `not slower`; `beats_compiled` is true iff one phase is `faster` and neither is `slower` ([check_candidate.py:253-271](../../../bench/grader/check_candidate.py); brief:217-218). One `same` at a timed size blocks the bar; one `slower` anywhere fails it.

# Territory: baseline-routing — round 3 attempt-6 (staged scalar, `max_rows: 32`) under the set rule

- **Owner:** explorer-baseline-routing
- **Status:** done
- **Version:** 2
- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T21:44:34Z
- **Next:** none — checklist filled for all pieces, ineff-baseline-routing-1..2 posted, grader note folded

## What it does

Same slot contract as rounds 2–3 (`muse-spark/round-3/exploration/territory-baseline-routing.md:11-20`, frozen): per layer, `scores = sigmoid(float32(x) @ w_router.T)`, top-4 on `scores + bias` (selection only), weights from the unbiased scores (`((s0+s1)+s2)+s3 + 1e-20`, divide, ×2.5). Outputs `inds` [rows,4] uint32 (feeds experts) and `weights` [rows,4] float32 (feeds combine, in emitted order; G2 is ordered bitwise equality at all six sizes, brief:190-193).

The code in the slot is `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6/` — round 2 attempt-4's kernels byte-identical (`diff` of `block-0.metal` and `spec.json` against attempt-1 empty, verified this round; attempt-1 = attempt-6, `notes.md:13-20`) plus `max_rows: 32` in `spec.json:1`. One fused kernel per layer: 256-thread threadgroup per row, `rows == 1` GEMV shuffle branch, staged scalar split-K above 1 row, verbatim sigmoid, thread-0 insertion top-4. Rows 1–32 run the kernels; every prefill size runs the compiled reference. Round 3's entries (`territory-baseline-routing.md`, `ineff-baseline-routing-1..2`, all frozen) mapped this code's *prefill* loss; that loss is now handed off, so this entry writes only what is new: the decode side, priced as margin.

## The headline finding (details in ineff-baseline-routing-1 and -2)

The starting point already wins everywhere it runs. Two grader runs of the identical bytes:

| rows | round-3 grade (`attempt-6/grade.json`) cand / compiled | Claude re-grade, round-4 grader (`results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/grade-routing-attempt-6.json`) cand / compiled | margin (re-grade) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 51.7 / 66.3 (28 wins, `faster`) | 45.1 / 62.8 (29 wins, `faster`) | 17.7 µs/layer (0.72×) |
| 8 | 90.9 / 104.0 (27, `faster`) | 144.2 / 160.0 (26, `faster`) | 15.8 µs/layer (0.90×) |
| 32 | 132.2 / 152.0 (25, `faster`) | 151.3 / 171.0 (27, `faster`) | 19.7 µs/layer (0.88×) |
| 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 | `same` × 3 (timed, identical code) | `handed off` × 3 | — (not timed; ADR 0015) |

Chained absolutes drift up to ~2× between runs on this machine (round-3 README; hyp-3 failure ledger) — the 8-row absolute moves 90.9 → 144.2 while the relative win holds — so only same-run margins and ratios transfer. In per-step terms (×20 layers, prediction from the same-run piece margins, not a whole-request measurement): the routing margin is worth ≈0.35 / 0.32 / 0.39 ms per decode step at 1 / 8 / 32 rows against the compiled reference.

Why it is no baseline: G3 alone. It passes G1+G2 (0 rows differing, all six sizes) and has `beats_compiled` true in both grading runs, but it has never passed G3 — alone it is `same` as `compiled-routing` at 8×128 in both the swarm's ready check (`muse-spark/round-3/checks/ready-1/ready-verdict.json`: `muse-routing` fail vs compiled, pass vs base, no phase slower anywhere) and Claude's G3 (`results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-3/g3-vllm.json`: `same` at 8×128 vs compiled-routing, `same` at 32×1024 vs base), and as the routing+combine pair it fails Claude's G3 against `compiled-all` at 32×1024 (medians 0.9% apart, ranges 38.59–39.08 vs 38.91–39.40 ms overlapping; `claude/findings/muse-round-3.md` §1). Under round 4's set rule the pair would have been `ready` in round 3, but a set still has to pass G3 as `muse-all` (round-4 README:34). The bar is the compiled reference; there is no `--baseline`.

The margin question, priced: at 32×1024 the pair gains only 0.25–0.30 ms/step over the compiled reference (~1% of the 39.4 ms step; round-4 README:35,49-55 item 2), inside the 5-repeat spread (range widths ≈0.49 ms on both sides; `ineff-g3-1.md`: the pair keeps −0.362 of its −0.656 piece win in Claude's draw). Non-overlap in Claude's draw needed roughly a further 0.17 ms/step (`ineff-g3-1.md`), i.e. +7.5–12.5 µs/layer across routing+combine at 32 rows (arithmetic: 0.15–0.25 ms ÷ 20 layers). Routing's whole current 32-row margin is 19.7 µs/layer, so routing alone would have to widen by ~40–60% to clear it; any µs/layer routing adds at 32 rows widens the set's margin 1:1 (0.02 ms/step per µs/layer). Every candidate change must keep `max_rows: 32` (or otherwise leave prefill on the compiled reference) — a change that lets the kernels run at prefill sizes re-opens round 3's confirmed prefill entries and is not a saving under ADR 0011.

Where the remaining decode time goes (both entries below): the candidate's chained time at 1/8/32 rows (re-grade 45.1/144.2/151.3 µs/layer) sits far above its traffic floor (0.9/7.4/29.7 µs/layer at 200 GB/s, brief:9) — the slot is overhead-bound at decode sizes (`claude/GLOSSARY.md:39-42`). Two named pools remain inside it: the per-row `w_router` re-read (traffic floor 29.7 µs/layer at 32 rows, larger than the whole 19.7 margin, but overlapped rather than serial — entry 1) and the staged scalar path's shape cost at decode sizes (27 barriers/row, 4 of 12 groups at 23% duty, 28,080 B footprint, serial tails — entry 2).

## Checklist

### 1. The starting-point kernels — `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6/block-0.metal` (174 lines) + `block-1.metal` (3 lines)

One threadgroup of 256 threads per row at every kernel-visible size (`spec.json:1`: grid `rows*256`, threadgroup [256,1,1]). Threadgroup memory `xpad[816]` + `scores[60]` + `parts[2048]` + `wsh[4096]` floats = 28,080 B of 32 KB (85.7%, headroom 4,688 B; block-0:15,22-25). Phases per row:

- **(a) `x` staging + `parts` zeroing (block-0:27-33, 1 barrier).** `x[row]` (768 bf16 → f32) into padded `xpad[(d>>4)*17+(d&15)]` (one pad float per BK=16 chunk); `parts[2048]` zeroed (8 floats/thread). On the `rows == 1` path both `parts` and `wsh` are then never read — the zeroing is dead work at 1 row (entry 2).
- **(b) GEMV branch, `rows == 1` only (block-0:35-55).** 8 simdgroups; simdgroup `sg` takes experts `sg, sg+8, …`; each lane serially sums 24 products from padded `xpad` and `w_router` read straight from device (uncoalesced by expert), shuffle tree 16,8,4,2,1, lane 0 writes `scores[e]`. This branch carries the largest relative win (0.72× compiled).

1|# Brief for the Muse Spark agent: write faster MobileMoE-S kernels, for decoding and prompt processing
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Committed and tagged `agent-era` before the Muse Spark session started. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|You are a Claude Code session powered by Meta's Muse Spark, working in your own git worktree on the branch `muse-agent`. This brief fixes your task, what you may change, where your work goes and how it is judged. It does not change during your session.
6|
7|## The task
8|
9|Meta's MobileMoE-S, int4, is served on an Apple M1 Pro (16-core GPU, 200 GB/s, 16 GB) by vLLM through vllm-metal, which runs the model with MLX. The findings below measure where each decode step's time goes. A step is about 870–1,090 small GPU kernels and is far from both the bandwidth and compute limits. The findings name the pieces that cost the most.
10|
11|A request goes through two phases: **prompt processing** (the prefill), which runs its whole prompt through the model, and **decoding**, one step per generated token. An improvement must hold in both: faster in one, and no slower in the other ([ADR 0011](adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). A kernel that speeds up the decode step but slows the prefill is not an improvement.
12|
13|1. **Choose.** Read the findings and choose one or two of the slots below to replace with your own fused Metal kernels. Write `muse-spark/strategy.md`: why, your design, and what each saves per step at 1 and 32 requests (your estimate). End it with the JSON block described under *Your files*. Commit it.
14|2. **Write and check.** For each chosen slot, write the kernels as files, run the grader on them, read its verdict, and improve. Up to **5 attempts per slot**; an attempt is a folder you graded and committed.
15|3. **Finish.** Write `muse-spark/summary.md`: your final attempt per slot and what you learned. Commit it.
16|
17|**Read these first** (all in your worktree):
18|- `claude/findings/bottleneck-explained.md` and `claude/findings/step-breakdown.md`: the measured findings;
19|- `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md` and `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md`: the raw tables;
20|- `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py` and `switch_layers.py`: the model code;
21|- MLX's custom-kernel documentation: `.venv/bin/python -c "import mlx.core as mx; help(mx.fast.metal_kernel)"`;
22|- `bench/grader/check_candidate.py` and `bench/grader/slots.py`: how you are graded.
23|
24|## The slots
25|
26|Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the call: 1 to 32 in a decode step, up to 2,048 in a prefill chunk. The grader flattens the inputs to the shapes below and restores the model's shapes afterwards. All arrays are row-contiguous.
27|
28|The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.
29|
30|### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights
31|
32|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
33||---|---|---|---|
34|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
35|| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
36|| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
37|| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
38|| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
39|
40|Reference:
41|
42|```python
43|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
44|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
45|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
46|weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
47|```
48|
49|The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.
50|
51|### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert
52|
53|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
54||---|---|---|---|
55|| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
56|| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
57|| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
58|| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
59|
60|Reference:
61|
62|```python
63|out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
64|```
65|
66|Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.
67|
68|### `routing+combine`
69|
70|Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.
71|
72|### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products
73|
74|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
75||---|---|---|---|
76|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
77|| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
78|| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
79|| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
80|| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
81|| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
82|| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |
83|
84|Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.
85|
86|Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:
87|
88|```python
89|y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
90|```
91|
92|As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.
93|
94|Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.
95|
96|## Tools and limits
97|
98|- **Only `mx.fast.metal_kernel`, MLX 0.32.4.** You write the Metal body; MLX generates the signature. Inputs arrive as `const device T* name` and outputs as `device T* name`. Shapes and strides come as `name_shape` and `name_strides` when the source uses them. The thread attributes are available, as in MLX's documentation: `thread_position_in_grid`, `threadgroup_position_in_grid`, `thread_position_in_threadgroup`, `threads_per_threadgroup`, `simdgroup_index_in_threadgroup`, `thread_index_in_simdgroup`, and so on.
99|- **The grader runs no Python of yours.** It reads your launch spec as data and compiles only your Metal.
100|- **Stay within the GPU's limits.** At most 1,024 threads per threadgroup and 32 KB of threadgroup memory. A grader run should take under 3 minutes, longer for an attempt much slower than the reference at the prefill sizes; stop one that runs past 15.
101|- **Hardware.** The Apple M1 Pro GPU (`applegpu_g13s`) has 16 cores and a SIMD width of 32. bfloat16 is available in Metal as `bfloat`.
102|
103|## Rules of this session
104|
105|These keep your work apart from everyone else's. Git hooks and an audit script enforce them, and a commit that breaks them is refused.
106|
107|- **Write only inside `muse-spark/`.** Never change `bench/`, `claude/`, `results/`, `tools/`, `third_party/`, or any other file. A copy of the grader you edit is never used.
108|- **Commit only on `muse-agent`,** with the co-author trailer your settings add: `Co-Authored-By: Muse Spark (Meta Model API) <muse-spark@meta-model-api.invalid>`. Start each subject with `Muse Spark:`. No other co-author.
109|- **Never push, merge, rebase, change git config, or skip hooks.**
110|- **Don't read `.env`** or any credentials file.
111|- One commit per attempt, after you've run the grader on it, so the history shows every attempt in order.
112|
113|## Your files
114|
115|```
116|muse-spark/
117|  strategy.md                                your choice and design, ending with the targets JSON
118|  kernels/<slot-folder>/attempt-<N>/
119|    block-0.metal, block-1.metal, ...        Metal kernel bodies (and headers), numbered from 0
120|    spec.json                                the launch spec
