122|  summary.md                                 your final attempt per slot
123|```
124|
125|`<slot-folder>` is `routing`, `combine`, `routing-combine` or `experts`. Grade an attempt with:
126|
127|```bash
128|.venv/bin/python bench/grader/check_candidate.py muse-spark/kernels/<slot-folder>/attempt-<N> <slot>
129|```
130|
131|where `<slot>` is `routing`, `combine`, `routing+combine` or `experts`.
132|
133|**The targets JSON** at the end of `strategy.md`:
134|
135|```json
136|{
137|  "targets": [
138|    {"slot": "routing+combine", "why": "...", "expected_saving_ms": {"rows_1": 0.0, "rows_32": 0.0}, "design": "..."}
139|  ]
140|}
141|```
142|
143|List one or two targets, in the order you work on them.
144|
145|**The launch spec** (`spec.json`):
146|
147|```json
148|{
149|  "kernels": [
150|    {
151|      "name": "fused_routing",
152|      "source_block": 0,
153|      "header_block": null,
154|      "inputs": ["x", "w_router", "bias"],
155|      "outputs": [
156|        {"name": "inds", "shape": ["rows", 4], "dtype": "uint32"},
157|        {"name": "weights", "shape": ["rows", 4], "dtype": "float32"}
158|      ],
159|      "grid": ["rows*32", 1, 1],
160|      "threadgroup": [32, 1, 1],
161|      "template": {"T": "bfloat16"},
162|      "init_value": null,
163|      "atomic_outputs": false
164|    }
165|  ],
166|  "slot_outputs": {"inds": "inds", "weights": "weights"}
167|}
168|```
169|
170|- **`source_block` and `header_block`** are the numbers of your `block-N.metal` files.
171|- **Kernels run in list order.** A kernel's `inputs` may name slot inputs or outputs of earlier kernels.
172|- **`slot_outputs`** maps each output of the slot to the kernel output that provides it.
173|- **`max_rows`** (optional, an integer of at least 1): inputs with more rows than this skip your kernels and run the slot's reference under `mx.compile`. Use it to keep prefill-sized inputs on MLX's own code when your kernels are built for decode sizes; MLX switches its own experts kernel at 60 rows.
174|- **`min_rows`** (optional, from round 4; an integer of at least 1, at most `max_rows` when both are given): inputs with fewer rows than this run the compiled reference too, so your kernels run only from `min_rows` to `max_rows`. Use it when your kernels lose at the smallest decode sizes, such as 1 row ([ADR 0015](adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)). G3 times whole requests: with 1 request every decode step has 1 row, so an attempt that hands off 1 row runs MLX's own code for the whole 1-request workload, and can pass G3 only in a set whose other kernels are faster there.
175|- **A hand-off is checked like the rest:** bit-exact at every G2 size. The piece timing reports a size it hands off as `handed off` instead of timing it (*The piece timing*, below).
176|- **For `routing+combine`,** `spec.json` holds two specs, each in the format above for its own slot, `max_rows` and `min_rows` included: `{"routing": {"kernels": [...], "slot_outputs": {...}}, "combine": {"kernels": [...], "slot_outputs": {...}}}`. The original experts and shared expert run between the two parts. The grader tests each part on its own, and the combine part receives the reference routing weights.
177|- **Shape and grid entries** are integers, or products of integers and the names `rows`, `D`, `E`, `K` and `H`, such as `"rows*32"`. Nothing else is evaluated.
178|- **dtypes** are `float32`, `bfloat16`, `float16`, `uint32` or `int32`.
179|- **Template values** are one of those dtypes, an integer or a boolean.
180|- **`grid`** counts threads, not threadgroups, as in `mx.fast.metal_kernel`.
181|
182|## How each attempt is judged
183|
184|The pass criteria were fixed before the first round. From round 2, G2 is exact and also covers the prefill, and the piece timing chains the layers ([ADR 0010](adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md)); round 1 was judged by the earlier rules, in which G2 allowed small rounding differences and tested decode steps only. From round 3, the piece timing and G3 time both phases, decode and prefill ([ADR 0011](adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)); rounds 1 and 2 were timed on decode only.
185|
186|1. **G1, runs.** It compiles and runs on real inputs.
187|2. **G2, correct: identical to the reference, bit for bit.** The slot runs in every call of `MoE.__call__`, the prefill included, so it is tested on every layer's inputs at two kinds of size:
188|   - **a decode step:** inputs captured from all 20 layers during a real decode step, at 1, 8 and 32 rows;
189|   - **a prefill:** the first chunk of a prefill with 128-token prompts, recorded while the grader runs it, at 1, 8 and 32 requests: 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. From 60 rows on, MLX's own experts kernel changes (`gather_qmm_rhs` instead of `gather_qvm`), and so does its rounding.
190|
191|   At every size:
192|   - **`routing`:** each row's 4 experts and their 4 weights equal the reference's, in the same order, since combine sums the pairs in that order. That includes the reference's choice between tied 4th and 5th experts.
193|   - **`combine` and `experts`:** every element equals the reference's.
194|
195|   **Why exact:** the end-to-end check below asks for the same greedy tokens, and greedy decoding turns any difference into different tokens. In round 1, routing weights within 10⁻⁵ of the reference, relative, changed 7 to 9 of 32 sequences.
196|   - **Then, end to end:** the same greedy tokens as the original model over 24 generated tokens, at 1 and 32 requests, in both plain MLX and vLLM.
197|3. **G3, faster, in vLLM.** Each workload runs 5 times in shuffled order: 1, 8 and 32 requests with 128-token prompts, and 32 requests with 1,024-token prompts, 256 generated tokens each. Three times are measured per run:
198|   - the **decode step**, the median period between steady steps;
199|   - the **prompt time**, until every prompt was processed;
200|   - the **whole request**, from sending the requests to the last token.
201|
202|   Against both the original model and an `mx.compile` of the same reference code, the attempt passes when the decode step or the prompt time is faster in every workload, neither is slower in any, and no whole request is slower. Faster and slower mean that the ranges over the repeats don't overlap.
203|
204|   **From round 3, the same G3 runs inside the round too:** the lead's **ready check**, `bench/grader/check_ready.py`, with every candidate in one call. It also requires the same greedy tokens, and audits its own log. Only its passing verdict makes an attempt `ready`; Claude's G3 after the round decides. The skill says when the lead runs it ([ADR 0013](adr/0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)).
205|
206|   **From round 4, a set:** with more than one candidate, the ready check and G3 also time them all together (`muse-all`). When that passes, the candidates are ready together as a set, even where one fails alone, and G3 judges the set as one submission ([ADR 0015](adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)).
207|
208|**What the grader prints for an attempt** (JSON):
209|- `g1` false and the compiler's error message;
210|- or the correctness results per size: for routing, the rows that differ; for combine and experts, the elements that differ and the largest gap in units in the last place; with the first example;
211|- or, when the attempt is correct, `timing_us_per_layer` per size: its time per call next to the original's and the compiled reference's, its wins against the compiled reference and the verdict (`faster`, `same`, `slower`, or `handed off` for a size your spec hands to the compiled reference); then `phases_vs_compiled` and `beats_compiled`.
212|
213|**The piece timing** runs the slot at the six G2 sizes: the 20 layers' captured decode inputs at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and the 20 layers' first prefill chunk at 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. Each layer's call waits for the previous one's output, as in the model: one small kernel links them, the same for every function timed. Without that wait, the GPU overlaps the 20 calls and hides how long one takes; in round 1, an experts kernel 29% faster on overlapped calls was 66% slower on chained ones at 1 row.
214|- **Paired repeats.** Your attempt and the compiled reference run in alternating order, 30 times.
215|- **Per size:** your attempt is `faster` when it wins at least 22 of the 30 pairs, `slower` when it loses at least 22, and `same` otherwise. Medians alone would pass on noise: the same kernel timed twice differs by up to 5%.
216|- **Handed off** (from round 4): a size whose inputs your spec hands to the compiled reference (`max_rows`, `min_rows`) runs the bar's own code, so it is not timed against it. Its verdict is `handed off`, and your attempt's time there is the compiled reference's.
217|- **Per phase:** decode (1, 8, 32 rows) and prefill (127, 1,016, 2,048 rows) are each `faster` when every size it doesn't hand off is, and at least one isn't handed off; `slower` when any size is; `handed off` when all are; and `not slower` otherwise.
218|- **`beats_compiled`** is true when one phase is `faster` and neither is `slower`.
219|
220|It is a guide; the ready check in the round, and Claude's G3 after it, decide.
221|
222|**When a slot stops.** Work on a slot stops at the first attempt that passes G1 and G2 and has `beats_compiled` true, or after 5 attempts. Name your final attempt per slot in `muse-spark/summary.md`; it goes to the end-to-end and G3 checks, which surucuonur's team runs after merging your branch.

# attempt-1 (round 3): max_rows hand-off on round-2 attempt-7 (builder-2-a)

Hypothesis `hyp-2-experts-prefill` (slot `experts`, baseline `none`),
direction (a): the `max_rows` hand-off. Starting point
`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-7` (fused decode path +
G2-exact scalar prefill branch; G1+G2 pass, `slower` at 1 row and at
every prefill size).

## The one main change

`block-0.metal` and `block-1.metal` are byte copies of the starting
point's (verify: `diff` against
`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-7/`). `spec.json` is the
starting point's plus one key: `"max_rows": 59`.

Rows 1–59 run the candidate kernels; rows above 59 run the slot's
reference under `mx.compile` through the attempt's own dispatch
(`bench/grader/slots.py:327-337`). The fused decode path, the
`x_shape[0] >= 60` dispatch threshold (`block-0.metal:22`), the scalar
`qmm_accum` prefill branch, grids, and all four bfloat16 rounding
points are untouched — the scalar branch is now dead code at every
graded size (it can only trigger at rows ≥ 60, which all hand off),
kept as fallback so the kernels stay valid if `max_rows` is ever
raised.

## Which inefficiency it removes, and how

`ineff-baseline-experts-1` (confirmed): the `rows >= 60` scalar
`qmm_accum` branch runs 15.8/27.7/20.1× slower than compiled
(15,220/119,154/240,681 vs 961/4,306/11,999 µs/layer) — ~29.5
µs/pair serial issue at 18.8 GB/s. This attempt removes the whole
branch from the graded path: every prefill size (127/1,016/2,048
rows) runs the compiled reference, so prefill times `same` as
compiled by construction. Decode is untouched, so the 8/32-row wins
(ahead 72.7/282.5 µs/layer per the hypothesis entry) are kept.

## max_rows: 59, and why

The boundary's hand-off window is 32 ≤ `max_rows` ≤ 59:
decode steps run 1–32 rows and must stay on the fused path
(`max_rows >= 32`), while MLX switches its own experts kernel at 60
rows (`gather_qvm` below, `gather_qmm_rhs` at/above), so `qvm`-only
kernels must never see rows ≥ 60 (`max_rows <= 59`). This attempt's
kernels replicate both arithmetics (the scalar branch is G2-exact),
but decode rows 33–59 take the `qvm` decode path in both the kernels
(`block-0.metal:22`) and the reference, so keeping them on the
candidate is exact and keeps the fast path where it wins. 59 is the
top of the window: every decode-size input (≤ 32, plus 33–59) stays
on the candidate, every prefill-size input hands off. Round 2's

Hypothesis `hyp-1-experts-minrows` (slot `experts`, baseline `none`),
direction (a): pure spec change. Starting point
`muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1` (byte-identical round-2
attempt-7 kernels, `max_rows: 59`; G1 pass, G2 differ 0 at all six sizes,
1 row `slower` 96.9 vs 86.6 µs/layer, 8/32 rows `faster`).

## The one main change

`block-0.metal` and `block-1.metal` are byte copies of the starting
point's (MD5 `a1e95fc49844f714afd1a1e377967dae` /
`631e710f5dd343427667a2270a166e6d`; `diff` clean against
`muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1/`). `spec.json` is the
starting point's plus one key: `"min_rows": 2` (`"max_rows": 59` kept).
No kernel byte, grid, threadgroup (512 threads), accumulation order or
bfloat16 rounding point changes.

Rows 2–59 run the candidate kernels; rows < 2 (exactly `rows == 1`)
and rows > 59 run the slot's compiled reference through the attempt's
own dispatch (`bench/grader/slots.py:330-345`). At the six graded
sizes: 1 row handed off, 8/32 rows on the kernels, 127/1,016/2,048
rows handed off (all > 59, as before).

## Which inefficiency it removes, and how

The starting point loses `beats_compiled` on the 1-row decode size
alone: 96.9 vs 86.6 µs/layer `slower` (5 wins), while winning at 8/32
rows by 69.3 / 328.7 µs/layer (round-3 `grade.json`). Round 3's kernel
fixes for 1 row bought nothing (vectorised scalar) or 2× worse
(unfused), both refuted. This attempt removes the 1-row loss from the
verdict, not from the machine: with `min_rows: 2` the 1-row size runs
the compiled reference itself, so it reports `handed off` and decode
is judged on 8 and 32 rows alone — both already `faster`. Prefill is
unchanged by construction (handed off above 59 rows, as in the
starting point). The claim is "faster at 8/32-row decode, unchanged
everywhere else" (boundary, *What must stay identical*).

## min_rows: 2 and max_rows: 59, and why

- **`min_rows: 2` (required exactly).** `rows < 2` is exactly
  `rows == 1` (`rows` ≥ 1). Among graded decode sizes only 1 row
  hands off; 8/32 rows run the kernels; in serving every 1-row decode
  step hands off and every 2–32-row step runs the kernels.
  `min_rows: 1` would hand off nothing and leave the 1-row loss;
  `min_rows ≥ 3` would also hand off serving counts 2…`min_rows−1`,
  which neither direction proposes. With 1 request every decode step
  has 1 row, so this slot then runs MLX's own code for the whole
  1-request workload and can pass G3 only in a set whose other
  kernels are faster there (boundary; ADR 0015) — a whole-request
  fact the piece timing shows only as `handed off` at 1 row.
- **`max_rows: 59` (kept).** MLX switches its experts kernel at 60
  rows (`gather_qvm` below, `gather_qmm_rhs` at/above). 59 is the
  last `gather_qvm` count; the first handed-off count above, 60, is
  exactly MLX's first `gather_qmm_rhs` count. The kernels therefore
  run only on 2–59 rows and never need `qmm_rhs` arithmetic; the
  in-kernel `x_shape[0] >= 60` dispatch and scalar `qmm_accum`
  prefill branch stay as unreachable fallback. Valid window per the
  boundary is 32 ≤ `max_rows` ≤ 59 with `min_rows: 2`; direction (a)
  keeps the top of it (direction (b) takes 32).

Baseline `none`: predictions are against the starting point's
measured times in its own grade run
(`muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1/grade.json`:
candidate / compiled 96.9/86.6, 168.9/238.2, 554.7/883.4,

  the attempt runs literally the compiled reference, so its time is

  value. The starting point's 96.9 candidate time and its `slower`
  verdict (5 wins) disappear as `handed off`, not as a win. Saving
  vs the starting candidate: 96.9 − 86.6 = 10.3 µs/layer of loss
  removed from the verdict (the machine still pays the compiled

  point's prefill (`same` 1,053.5/4,106.9/7,557.0 — same code, run

  kernel-run size, 8 and 32, `faster`; at least one such size),
  prefill `handed off`, neither phase `slower`
  (`bench/grader/check_candidate.py:253-271`). Baseline `none`, so
  no `beats_baseline`.

## What this attempt leaves unmeasured

- Kernel speed and correctness at decode counts 2–7 and 9–31 and at
  33–59 rows (kernel-run in serving; the grader times/tests only
  1/8/32 there). Correctness there rests on the per-pair,
  rows-independent construction.

Read text file `claude/muse-agent-brief.md`.
1|# Brief for the Muse Spark agent: write faster MobileMoE-S kernels, for decoding and prompt processing
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Committed and tagged `agent-era` before the Muse Spark session started. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|You are a Claude Code session powered by Meta's Muse Spark, working in your own git worktree on the branch `muse-agent`. This brief fixes your task, what you may change, where your work goes and how it is judged. It does not change during your session.
6|
7|## The task
8|
9|Meta's MobileMoE-S, int4, is served on an Apple M1 Pro (16-core GPU, 200 GB/s, 16 GB) by vLLM through vllm-metal, which runs the model with MLX. The findings below measure where each decode step's time goes. A step is about 870–1,090 small GPU kernels and is far from both the bandwidth and compute limits. The findings name the pieces that cost the most.
10|
11|A request goes through two phases: **prompt processing** (the prefill), which runs its whole prompt through the model, and **decoding**, one step per generated token. An improvement must hold in both: faster in one, and no slower in the other ([ADR 0011](adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). A kernel that speeds up the decode step but slows the prefill is not an improvement.
12|
13|1. **Choose.** Read the findings and choose one or two of the slots below to replace with your own fused Metal kernels. Write `muse-spark/strategy.md`: why, your design, and what each saves per step at 1 and 32 requests (your estimate). End it with the JSON block described under *Your files*. Commit it.
14|2. **Write and check.** For each chosen slot, write the kernels as files, run the grader on them, read its verdict, and improve. Up to **5 attempts per slot**; an attempt is a folder you graded and committed.
15|3. **Finish.** Write `muse-spark/summary.md`: your final attempt per slot and what you learned. Commit it.
16|
17|**Read these first** (all in your worktree):
18|- `claude/findings/bottleneck-explained.md` and `claude/findings/step-breakdown.md`: the measured findings;
19|- `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md` and `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md`: the raw tables;
20|- `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py` and `switch_layers.py`: the model code;
21|- MLX's custom-kernel documentation: `.venv/bin/python -c "import mlx.core as mx; help(mx.fast.metal_kernel)"`;
22|- `bench/grader/check_candidate.py` and `bench/grader/slots.py`: how you are graded.
23|
24|## The slots
25|
26|Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the call: 1 to 32 in a decode step, up to 2,048 in a prefill chunk. The grader flattens the inputs to the shapes below and restores the model's shapes afterwards. All arrays are row-contiguous.
27|
28|The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.
29|
30|### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights
31|
32|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
33||---|---|---|---|
34|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
35|| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
36|| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
37|| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
38|| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
39|
40|Reference:
41|
42|```python
43|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
44|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
45|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
46|weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
47|```
48|
49|The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.
50|
51|### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert
52|
53|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
54||---|---|---|---|
55|| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
56|| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
57|| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
58|| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
59|
60|Reference:
61|
62|```python
63|out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
64|```
65|
66|Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.
67|
68|### `routing+combine`
69|
70|Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.
71|
72|### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products
73|
74|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
75||---|---|---|---|
76|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
77|| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
78|| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
79|| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
80|| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
81|| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
82|| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |
83|
84|Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.
85|
86|Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:
87|
88|```python
89|y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
90|```
91|
92|As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.
93|
94|Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.
95|
96|## Tools and limits
97|
98|- **Only `mx.fast.metal_kernel`, MLX 0.32.4.** You write the Metal body; MLX generates the signature. Inputs arrive as `const device T* name` and outputs as `device T* name`. Shapes and strides come as `name_shape` and `name_strides` when the source uses them. The thread attributes are available, as in MLX's documentation: `thread_position_in_grid`, `threadgroup_position_in_grid`, `thread_position_in_threadgroup`, `threads_per_threadgroup`, `simdgroup_index_in_threadgroup`, `thread_index_in_simdgroup`, and so on.
99|- **The grader runs no Python of yours.** It reads your launch spec as data and compiles only your Metal.
100|- **Stay within the GPU's limits.** At most 1,024 threads per threadgroup and 32 KB of threadgroup memory. A grader run should take under 3 minutes, longer for an attempt much slower than the reference at the prefill sizes; stop one that runs past 15.
101|- **Hardware.** The Apple M1 Pro GPU (`applegpu_g13s`) has 16 cores and a SIMD width of 32. bfloat16 is available in Metal as `bfloat`.
102|
103|## Rules of this session
104|
105|These keep your work apart from everyone else's. Git hooks and an audit script enforce them, and a commit that breaks them is refused.
106|
107|- **Write only inside `muse-spark/`.** Never change `bench/`, `claude/`, `results/`, `tools/`, `third_party/`, or any other file. A copy of the grader you edit is never used.
108|- **Commit only on `muse-agent`,** with the co-author trailer your settings add: `Co-Authored-By: Muse Spark (Meta Model API) <muse-spark@meta-model-api.invalid>`. Start each subject with `Muse Spark:`. No other co-author.
109|- **Never push, merge, rebase, change git config, or skip hooks.**
110|- **Don't read `.env`** or any credentials file.
111|- One commit per attempt, after you've run the grader on it, so the history shows every attempt in order.

118|  kernels/<slot-folder>/attempt-<N>/

120|    spec.json                                the launch spec

146|

150|    {
151|      "name": "fused_routing",
152|      "source_block": 0,
153|      "header_block": null,
154|      "inputs": ["x", "w_router", "bias"],
155|      "outputs": [
156|        {"name": "inds", "shape": ["rows", 4], "dtype": "uint32"},

169|
170|- **`source_block` and `header_block`** are the numbers of your `block-N.metal` files.
171|- **Kernels run in list order.** A kernel's `inputs` may name slot inputs or outputs of earlier kernels.
172|- **`slot_outputs`** maps each output of the slot to the kernel output that provides it.
173|- **`max_rows`** (optional, an integer of at least 1): inputs with more rows than this skip your kernels and run the slot's reference under `mx.compile`. Use it to keep prefill-sized inputs on MLX's own code when your kernels are built for decode sizes; MLX switches its own experts kernel at 60 rows.

G3 times whole requests: with 1 request every decode step has 1 row, so an attempt that hands off 1 row runs MLX's own code for the whole 1-request workload, and can pass G3 only in a set whose other kernels are faster there.
175|- **A hand-off is checked like the rest:** bit-exact at every G2 size. The piece timing reports a size it hands off as `handed off` instead of timing it (*The piece timing*, below).
176|- **For `routing+combine`,** `spec.json` holds two specs, each in the format above for its own slot, `max_rows` and `min_rows` included: `{"routing": {"kernels": [...], "slot_outputs": {...}}, "combine": {"kernels": [...], "slot_outputs": {...}}}`. The original experts and shared expert run between the two parts. The grader tests each part on its own, and the combine part receives the reference routing weights.
177|- **Shape and grid entries** are integers, or products of integers and the names `rows`, `D`, `E`, `K` and `H`, such as `"rows*32"`. Nothing else is evaluated.
178|- **dtypes** are `float32`, `bfloat16`, `float16`, `uint32` or `int32`.
179|- **Template values** are one of those dtypes, an integer or a boolean.
180|- **`grid`** counts threads, not threadgroups, as in `mx.fast.metal_kernel`.
181|
182|## How each attempt is judged
183|
184|The pass criteria were fixed before the first round. From round 2, G2 is exact and also covers the prefill, and the piece timing chains the layers ([ADR 0010](adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md)); round 1 was judged by the earlier rules, in which G2 allowed small rounding differences and tested decode steps only. From round 3, the piece timing and G3 time both phases, decode and prefill ([ADR 0011](adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)); rounds 1 and 2 were timed on decode only.
185|
186|1. **G1, runs.** It compiles and runs on real inputs.
187|2. **G2, correct: identical to the reference, bit for bit.** The slot runs in every call of `MoE.__call__`, the prefill included, so it is tested on every layer's inputs at two kinds of size:
188|   - **a decode step:** inputs captured from all 20 layers during a real decode step, at 1, 8 and 32 rows;
189|   - **a prefill:** the first chunk of a prefill with 128-token prompts, recorded while the grader runs it, at 1, 8 and 32 requests: 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. From 60 rows on, MLX's own experts kernel changes (`gather_qmm_rhs` instead of `gather_qvm`), and so does its rounding.
190|
191|   At every size:
192|   - **`routing`:** each row's 4 experts and their 4 weights equal the reference's, in the same order, since combine sums the pairs in that order. That includes the reference's choice between tied 4th and 5th experts.
193|   - **`combine` and `experts`:** every element equals the reference's.
194|
195|   **Why exact:** the end-to-end check below asks for the same greedy tokens, and greedy decoding turns any difference into different tokens. In round 1, routing weights within 10⁻⁵ of the reference, relative, changed 7 to 9 of 32 sequences.
196|   - **Then, end to end:** the same greedy tokens as the original model over 24 generated tokens, at 1 and 32 requests, in both plain MLX and vLLM.
197|3. **G3, faster, in vLLM.** Each workload runs 5 times in shuffled order: 1, 8 and 32 requests with 128-token prompts, and 32 requests with 1,024-token prompts, 256 generated tokens each. Three times are measured per run:
198|   - the **decode step**, the median period between steady steps;
199|   - the **prompt time**, until every prompt was processed;
200|   - the **whole request**, from sending the requests to the last token.
201|
202|   Against both the original model and an `mx.compile` of the same reference code, the attempt passes when the decode step or the prompt time is faster in every workload, neither is slower in any, and no whole request is slower. Faster and slower mean that the ranges over the repeats don't overlap.
203|
204|   **From round 3, the same G3 runs inside the round too:** the lead's **ready check**, `bench/grader/check_ready.py`, with every candidate in one call. It also requires the same greedy tokens, and audits its own log. Only its passing verdict makes an attempt `ready`; Claude's G3 after the round decides. The skill says when the lead runs it ([ADR 0013](adr/0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)).
205|
206|   **From round 4, a set:** with more than one candidate, the ready check and G3 also time them all together (`muse-all`). When that passes, the candidates are ready together as a set, even where one fails alone, and G3 judges the set as one submission ([ADR 0015](adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)).
207|
208|**What the grader prints for an attempt** (JSON):
209|- `g1` false and the compiler's error message;
210|- or the correctness results per size: for routing, the rows that differ; for combine and experts, the elements that differ and the largest gap in units in the last place; with the first example;
211|- or, when the attempt is correct, `timing_us_per_layer` per size: its time per call next to the original's and the compiled reference's, its wins against the compiled reference and the verdict (`faster`, `same`, `slower`, or `handed off` for a size your spec hands to the compiled reference); then `phases_vs_compiled` and `beats_compiled`.
212|
213|**The piece timing** runs the slot at the six G2 sizes: the 20 layers' captured decode inputs at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and the 20 layers' first prefill chunk at 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. Each layer's call waits for the previous one's output, as in the model: one small kernel links them, the same for every function timed. Without that wait, the GPU overlaps the 20 calls and hides how long one takes; in round 1, an experts kernel 29% faster on overlapped calls was 66% slower on chained ones at 1 row.
214|- **Paired repeats.** Your attempt and the compiled reference run in alternating order, 30 times.
215|- **Per size:** your attempt is `faster` when it wins at least 22 of the 30 pairs, `slower` when it loses at least 22, and `same` otherwise. Medians alone would pass on noise: the same kernel timed twice differs by up to 5%.
216|- **Handed off** (from round 4): a size whose inputs your spec hands to the compiled reference (`max_rows`, `min_rows`) runs the bar's own code, so it is not timed against it. Its verdict is `handed off`, and your attempt's time there is the compiled reference's.
217|- **Per phase:** decode (1, 8, 32 rows) and prefill (127, 1,016, 2,048 rows) are each `faster` when every size it doesn't hand off is, and at least one isn't handed off; `slower` when any size is; `handed off` when all are; and `not slower` otherwise.
218|- **`beats_compiled`** is true when one phase is `faster` and neither is `slower`.
219|
220|It is a guide; the ready check in the round, and Claude's G3 after it, decide.
221|
222|**When a slot stops.** Work on a slot stops at the first attempt that passes G1 and G2 and has `beats_compiled` true, or after 5 attempts. Name your final attempt per slot in `muse-spark/summary.md`; it goes to the end-to-end and G3 checks, which surucuonur's team runs after merging your branch.

## Inefficiency

[ineff-baseline-experts-1.md](../exploration/ineff-baseline-experts-1.md) (confirmed): the starting point's `rows >= 60` scalar `qmm_accum` prefill branch runs 15.8/27.7/20.1× slower than the compiled reference (15,220/119,154/240,681 vs 961/4,306/11,999 µs/layer) — constant ~29.5 µs/pair serial issue at 18.8 GB/s — making prompt processing 6.63–14.50× slower and costing −10.0% to −82.5% of whole-request throughput. Slot: `experts`. Baseline: `none` (starting point `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-7`, which passes G1+G2 but is `slower` at 1 row and at every prefill size).

Predicted effect if the prefill path matches compiled speed at equal bits: save 14,259/114,848/228,682 µs/layer = 285 ms / 2.30 s / 4.57 s per chunk, recovering the throughput loss to whatever the decode phase then gives (decode wins at 8/32 rows must be kept: ahead 72.7/282.5 µs/layer). Fix shapes: (a) vectorized per-pair scalar (one thread per word's 8 outputs, 8 accumulators, each output keeping contiguous `BK=32` order); (b) grouped/tiled replica of `qmm_rhs` issue (takes the tile-waste and offsets prizes, ranked prefill items 7–8, for free); (c) `max_rows` hand-off (Claude checked 59 bit-exact; decode stays on the fused path). The 1-row decode gap ([ineff-baseline-experts-2.md](../exploration/ineff-baseline-experts-2.md)) is a disjoint cause and a later hypothesis (hyp-4) built on this one's winner; a prefill fix that slows decode, or vice versa, is not an improvement (ADR 0011).

## Boundary

(written by boundary-2; delta only — every line carries its source)

[`muse-spark/round-2/implementation/hyp-1-experts-exact.md`](../../round-2/implementation/hyp-1-experts-exact.md)
*Boundary* (itself a delta on round 1's
[`muse-spark/implementation/hyp-1-fused-experts.md`](../../implementation/hyp-1-fused-experts.md)).
I checked each line against the starting point
`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/experts/attempt-7` (`block-0.metal`, `block-1.metal`,
`spec.json`) and against the current G2 plus the two-phase judgment
(`claude/muse-agent-brief.md:173,185-187,209-213`;
`claude/adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md:21-35`;
`bench/grader/check_candidate.py:224-264,308-378`;
`bench/grader/slots.py:304-337`). Still holding, not rewritten below:
input/output names, dtypes, layouts and weight shapes/bytes at all six sizes;
`y[r,j]` positional in `inds` order; neighbour contracts; the four bfloat16
rounding points in kind; the two reference arithmetics and the kernel switch at
60 rows; launch-spec surface; GPU limits. Baseline is `none` — no slot has one
this round, so the bar is the compiled reference everywhere
(`claude/adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md:46`). Only what changed follows.

### Inputs and outputs — unchanged

Shapes, dtypes and layouts are round 2's verbatim (`x` [rows,768] bfloat16,
`inds` [rows,4] uint32, `y` [rows,4,768] bfloat16 at 1/8/32 and 127/1,016/2,048
rows; `claude/muse-agent-brief.md:74-82`). Rechecked against the starting
point: its `spec.json` input list is the slot's full 11 inputs and its output
`y` is `["rows",4,768]` bfloat16; it reads `rows` from `x_shape[0]`
(`block-0.metal:22`), the same value the grader reads from the first slot
input's `shape[0]` (`bench/grader/slots.py:334`).

Neighbour code and contracts are round 2's verbatim (post-attention layernorm
→ `x`; router → `inds`, `weights`; `experts(x, inds)` → `y`; combine pairs
`y[r,j]` with `weights[r,j]` positionally;
`third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py:217-232`;
`bench/grader/slots.py:97-119`). The starting point's changes vs its own

`block-0.metal:42-43,95-102`) are internal to the slot; nothing crosses a
neighbour boundary.

### What must stay identical — changed: the `max_rows` hand-off is allowed

- **Bit-exactness unchanged.** G2 still requires `differ == 0` in all 20 layers

  accumulation). The starting point still branches on the dispatch threshold
  itself, `x_shape[0] >= 60` (`block-0.metal:22`), so 33–59 stay `qvm`.
- **New: rows above `max_rows` run the compiled reference, not the kernels.**
  With `"max_rows"` in `spec.json` (int ≥ 1, bools rejected),
  `slots.build` sends inputs with `rows > max_rows` to the slot's reference
  under `mx.compile` (`bench/grader/slots.py:327-337`;
  `claude/muse-agent-brief.md:173`; `claude/adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md:33-35`).

  through the attempt's own dispatch; the compiled reference was bit-exact with
  the reference at all six sizes on 2026-11-04 (`bench/micro/compiled_exact.py`,

  rows (`claude/muse-agent-brief.md:26`); every decode step up to 32 rows must

### What the grader checks, and what it can't see — changed: two-phase timing

Checks (`bench/grader/check_candidate.py`): G1/G2 mechanics unchanged — G1 is
true only after the whole six-size correctness loop completes without
exception (`:342`); per-layer shape/dtype faults fail G2 with G1 true

per phase, `faster` iff every size is, `slower` iff any size is, else

because the starting point is `slower` at every prefill size. No `--baseline`
bar exists this round (no baselines; `territory-grader.md` §1).
What it still can't see (checked by hand later — *check an attempt*; full list
`muse-spark/round-3/exploration/territory-grader.md` §*What the grader still

Hypothesis `hyp-1-experts-minrows` (slot `experts`, baseline `none`),
direction (a): pure spec change. Starting point
`muse-spark/round-3/kernels/experts/attempt-1` (byte-identical round-2
attempt-7 kernels, `max_rows: 59`; G1 pass, G2 differ 0 at all six sizes,
1 row `slower` 96.9 vs 86.6 µs/layer, 8/32 rows `faster`).

## The one main change

`block-0.metal` and `block-1.metal` are byte copies of the starting
point's (MD5 `a1e95fc49844f714afd1a1e377967dae` /
`631e710f5dd343427667a2270a166e6d`; `diff` clean against

starting point's plus one key: `"min_rows": 2` (`"max_rows": 59` kept).
No kernel byte, grid, threadgroup (512 threads), accumulation order or
bfloat16 rounding point changes.

Rows 2–59 run the candidate kernels; rows < 2 (exactly `rows == 1`)
and rows > 59 run the slot's compiled reference through the attempt's
own dispatch (`bench/grader/slots.py:330-345`). At the six graded
sizes: 1 row handed off, 8/32 rows on the kernels, 127/1,016/2,048
rows handed off (all > 59, as before).

## Which inefficiency it removes, and how

The starting point loses `beats_compiled` on the 1-row decode size
alone: 96.9 vs 86.6 µs/layer `slower` (5 wins), while winning at 8/32
rows by 69.3 / 328.7 µs/layer (round-3 `grade.json`). Round 3's kernel

## min_rows: 2 and max_rows: 59, and why

- **`min_rows: 2` (required exactly).** `rows < 2` is exactly

10|
11|`routing`
12|
13|## What happens
14|
15|Every row's threadgroup streams its own full copy of the router weight from device memory. On the staged scalar path (`rows > 1`) all 256 threads cooperatively load all 48 K-chunks × 60 experts as `float4`s into `wsh` across the 12 groups (`muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6/block-0.metal:81-93`, the code in the slot); in the GEMV branch (`rows == 1`) each lane reads `w_router` straight from device (block-0:41-45). Nothing is shared across rows: per layer the kernel reads rows × 60×768×4 B = rows × 184,320 B of `w_router`, plus rows × 1,536 B of `x`. The compiled reference's GEMM/GEMV reads `w_router` once per layer and reuses each tile across rows (round-2 `territory-baseline-routing.md` §3.1, frozen).
16|
17|This is the decode slice of round 2's `ineff-baseline-routing-4` (frozen, confirmed, upper-bound-only) and round 3's `ineff-baseline-routing-1` (frozen, confirmed), repriced because the context changed twice over: (1) `max_rows: 32` in `spec.json` now hands every prefill size to the compiled reference, so the prefill side of those entries — 116.1/935.4/1,886.5 µs/layer at 127/1,016/2,048 rows — is banked and costs nothing; what remains is exactly the decode side they ranked as not worth chasing. (2) The round-4 question is no longer beating the compiled reference (the starting point does, at every decode size) but *widening the margin*, above all at 32 rows for the 32×1024 set workload (round-4 exploration README item 2). At 32 rows the re-read excess is larger than the entire margin there is to widen.
18|
19|## Cost
20|
21|Traffic floors at the 200 GB/s peak (brief:9), candidate per layer; measured = chained µs/layer, candidate vs compiled reference, from the two runs of the identical bytes (`muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6/grade.json`; `results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/grade-routing-attempt-6.json`):
22|
23|| rows | `w_router` read | floor (w+x) | measured cand / compiled (re-grade) | margin | excess over read-once |
24||---|---|---|---|---|---|
25|| 1 | 0.18 MB | 0.9 µs | 45.1 / 62.8 | 17.7 µs | 0 µs |
26|| 8 | 1.47 MB | 7.4 µs | 144.2 / 160.0 | 15.8 µs | 6.5 µs |
27|| 32 | 5.90 MB | 29.7 µs | 151.3 / 171.0 | 19.7 µs | 28.6 µs |
28|| 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 | — (handed off) | — | `handed off` | — | 0 (compiled reference runs) |

30|The excess is (rows−1) × 184,320 B ÷ 200 GB/s. At 32 rows the excess floor (28.6 µs/layer) is 1.45× the whole measured margin over the compiled reference (19.7 µs/layer, re-grade; 19.8 in the round-3 grade) — the only pool inside this slot big enough, on its own, to supply the +7.5–12.5 µs/layer (routing+combine combined) that non-overlap at 32×1024 needs (territory entry, headline). At 8 rows the excess (6.5) is 41% of the margin (15.8); at 1 row there is no excess (a single row reads the weight once by definition).

24|## The slots
25|
26|Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the call: 1 to 32 in a decode step, up to 2,048 in a prefill chunk. The grader flattens the inputs to the shapes below and restores the model's shapes afterwards. All arrays are row-contiguous.
27|
28|The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.
29|
30|### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights
31|
32|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
33||---|---|---|---|
34|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
35|| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
36|| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
37|| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
38|| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
39|
40|Reference:
41|
42|```python
43|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
44|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
45|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
46|weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
47|```
48|
49|The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.
50|
51|### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert
52|
53|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
54||---|---|---|---|
55|| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
56|| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
57|| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
58|| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
59|
60|Reference:
61|
62|```python
63|out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
64|```
65|
66|Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.
67|
68|### `routing+combine`
69|
70|Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.
71|
72|### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products
73|
74|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
75||---|---|---|---|
76|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
77|| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
78|| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
79|| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
80|| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
81|| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
82|| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |
83|
84|Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.
85|
86|Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:
87|
88|```python
89|y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
90|```
91|
92|As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.
93|
94|Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.

184|The pass criteria were fixed before the first round. From round 2, G2 is exact and also covers the prefill, and the piece timing chains the layers ([ADR 0010](adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md)); round 1 was judged by the earlier rules, in which G2 allowed small rounding differences and tested decode steps only. 186|1. **G1, runs.** It compiles and runs on real inputs.
187|2. **G2, correct: identical to the reference, bit for bit.** The slot runs in every call of `MoE.__call__`, the prefill included, so it is tested on every layer's inputs at two kinds of size:
188|   - **a decode step:** inputs captured from all 20 layers during a real decode step, at 1, 8 and 32 rows;
189|   - **a prefill:** the first chunk of a prefill with 128-token prompts, recorded while the grader runs it, at 1, 8 and 32 requests: 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. From 60 rows on, MLX's own experts kernel changes (`gather_qmm_rhs` instead of `gather_qvm`), and so does its rounding.
190|
191|   At every size:
192|   - **`routing`:** each row's 4 experts and their 4 weights equal the reference's, in the same order, since combine sums the pairs in that order. That includes the reference's choice between tied 4th and 5th experts.
193|   - **`combine` and `experts`:** every element equals the reference's.

195|   **Why exact:** the end-to-end check below asks for the same greedy tokens, and greedy decoding turns any difference into different tokens. In round 1, routing weights within 10⁻⁵ of the reference, relative, changed 7 to 9 of 32 sequences.
196|   - **Then, end to end:** the same greedy tokens as the original model over 24 generated tokens, at 1 and 32 requests, in both plain MLX and vLLM.

198|   - the **decode step**, the median period between steady steps;
199|   - the **prompt time**, until every prompt was processed;
200|   - the **whole request**, from sending the requests to the last token.
201|
202|   Against both the original model and an `mx.compile` of the same reference code, the attempt passes when the decode step or the prompt time is faster in every workload, neither is slower in any, and no whole request is slower. Faster and slower mean that the ranges over the repeats don't overlap.

204|   **From round 3, the same G3 runs inside the round too:** the lead's **ready check**, `bench/grader/check_ready.py`, with every candidate in one call. It also requires the same greedy tokens, and audits its own log. Only its passing verdict makes an attempt `ready`; Claude's G3 after the round decides. 211|- or, when the attempt is correct, `timing_us_per_layer` per size: its time per call next to the original's and the compiled reference's, its wins against the compiled reference and the verdict (`faster`, `same`, `slower`, or `handed off` for a size your spec hands to the compiled reference); then `phases_vs_compiled` and `beats_compiled`.

213|**The piece timing** runs the slot at the six G2 sizes: the 20 layers' captured decode inputs at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and the 20 layers' first prefill chunk at 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. Each layer's call waits for the previous one's output, as in the model: one small kernel links them, the same for every function timed. Without that wait, the GPU overlaps the 20 calls and hides how long one takes; in round 1, an experts kernel 29% faster on overlapped calls was 66% slower on chained ones at 1 row.

1|# Round-2 attempt 4 — builder-2-d, hardening of hyp-2-routing-exact
2|
3|Builds on `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-3` (scalar
4|full-G2; chained 46.9/300.0/297.2 µs/layer vs compiled 58.0/84.5/90.9 —
5|latency-bound from uncoalesced device loads + `xsh` bank conflicts).
6|Baseline: none, so no `beats_baseline`; the bar is the compiled reference.
7|
8|## The one main change
9|
10|Stage each K-chunk's `w_router` block into threadgroup memory with
11|coalesced vector loads and sum from threadgroup with a padded `x`
12|layout, nothing else:
13|
14|- Staging: chunks are staged 4 at a time (12 groups cover all 48
15|  BK=16 chunks). Each staged chunk is 60×16 floats, loaded as 240
16|  `float4` loads (consecutive threads cover one expert's 4 vectors,
17|  then the next expert) and stored transposed in `wsh[slot][k][expert]`
18|  with expert stride 64.
19|- Padded `x`: chunk `c` of `x` sits at `xpad[c*17 + k]` (one pad float
20|  per chunk), replacing attempt-3's flat `xsh[768]`.
21|- Scalar chain: expert-parallel lanes read `wsh` at consecutive expert
22|  banks (conflict-free) and `xpad` uniformly per `k` (broadcast).
23|  Partials live transposed in `parts[partition][expert]` (stride 64)
24|  and are resumed product-by-product in increasing `d` across staged
25|  groups, so each (expert, partition) partial is still one serial
26|  scalar sum in increasing `d`; partials are then summed sequentially
27|  in partition order. 24 barriers on the scalar path (2 per group).
28|- Threadgroup memory: (816 + 60 + 2048 + 4096) × 4 B = 28,080 B of
29|  32 KB. Same grid (`rows*256`), threadgroup (256) and one-kernel layout.
30|
31|Kept verbatim from attempt-3: the regime branch on `rows` (GEMV only
32|at `rows == 1`; split-K while `rows <= 768`; regular above — the GEMV
33|branch is unchanged apart from reading the padded `x` layout), the
34|split-K partition formula (32 partitions at 8/32 rows, 8 of 96 at 127,
35|2 at 257–768, single partition above 768, last partition absorbing the
36|remainder chunks), the GEMV lane order and shuffle tree 16,8,4,2,1,
37|MLX's verbatim sigmoid (`1/(1+precise::exp(abs(s)))`, `(s<0)?y:1-y`),
38|the strictly-greater insertion top-4 (earliest index wins ties), and
39|`((w0+w1)+w2)+w3 + 1e-20`, divide, ×2.5 on unbiased scores.
40|
41|## Inefficiency removed
42|
43|`ineff-baseline-routing-1` stays removed (same orders as attempt-3).
44|The target is attempt-3's diagnosed feeding cost (its notes: the
45|scalar chains read `w_router` uncoalesced — warp lanes 64 B apart,
46|16 cache lines per step — and `xsh[p*16+k]` with 16-way bank
47|conflicts on every product). Staging turns the device reads into
48|coalesced `float4` loads and the dependent chain's reads into
49|conflict-free threadgroup reads. The per-row `w_router` re-read
50|(`ineff-baseline-routing-4`) and the serial thread-0 scan are
51|untouched.
52|
53|## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows
54|
55|Anchor: attempt-3 measured 46.9/300.0/297.2, compiled 58.0/84.5/90.9
56|(same grader run). Traffic per row is unchanged at 184 KB of
57|`w_router` (0.9 µs at 200 GB/s), so floors are 0.9/7.4/29.5 µs; the
58|rest is chained-call latency and per-row work. Attempt-3's flat
59|~300 µs was the dependent device-load chain; the staged chain reads
60|threadgroup memory instead, at the cost of 24 barriers/row.
61|
62|- 1 row: GEMV branch unchanged but for the padded index (a shift and
63|  mask per access) → ≈ attempt-3's 46.9 → **48**.
64|- 8 rows: fixed chained latency ≈ 40 µs (attempt-3's 1-row time less
65|  its small GEMV work) + traffic 7.4 + staged scalar work. The
66|  critical path is the last partition's 272 sequential threadgroup
67|  FMAs, overlapped across 8 threadgroups; allowance ≈ 20 µs →
68|  40 + 7.4 + 20 ≈ **67**.
69|- 32 rows: 40 + 29.5 + 25 (more threadgroups fill the GPU, critical
70|  path unchanged) ≈ **95**.
71|
72|Prediction: **48 / 67 / 95 µs** — beats compiled (58.0/84.5/90.9) at
73|1 and 8 rows, near it at 32. G2 prediction: pass at all six sizes —
74|no accumulation order changes, only where operands are read from.
75|
76|## Verdict (2026-11-04T03:56:12Z, one grader run)
77|
78|G1 pass, **G2 pass at all six sizes** (rows_differ 0,
79|rows_other_experts 0, max_rel_err 0.0 at 1/8/32 and 127/1016/2048).
80|Chained µs/layer (ref / compiled / candidate): 1 row 71.1 / 60.7 /
81|**47.5**; 8 rows 102.9 / 84.9 / **69.1**; 32 rows 104.9 / 89.5 /
82|**72.9**. **`beats_compiled` true** — the first routing attempt to
83|beat the compiled reference at all three row counts. Baseline none,
84|so no `beats_baseline`. Vs attempt-3 (46.9/300.0/297.2): the staged
85|scalar path is 4.3×/4.1× faster at 8/32 rows; the 1-row GEMV branch
86|is unchanged (47.5 vs 46.9, drift).
87|
88|## Why the 32-row timing missed the prediction by >20%
89|
90|Predicted 48/67/95, measured 47.5/69.1/72.9: 1 and 8 rows hold
91|(−1%/+3%), 32 rows is 23% under. The prediction added a fixed ~40 µs
92|chained latency, the full 29.5 µs traffic floor and a per-row work
93|allowance as if they were serial per layer call. They are not: at 32
94|rows, 32 threadgroups across 16 GPU cores overlap one threadgroup's
95|coalesced staging loads and barriers with other threadgroups' scalar
96|compute, so the marginal cost of rows 9–32 is only (72.9−69.1)/24 ≈
97|0.16 µs/row, against the predicted ≈1.2 µs/row. The kernel is
98|essentially flat 69→73 µs from 8 to 32 rows — once enough
99|threadgroups are resident to hide the staging latency, extra rows
100|are nearly free, and the 28 KB threadgroup footprint (which caps
101|residency) does not bind at these row counts. Traffic-floor
102|arithmetic overstates the cost whenever staging and compute overlap
103|across threadgroups.
104|
105|Next change (one): none needed for the slot's stop rule (G1+G2+
106|beats compiled at all three row counts). If pushed further, cut the
107|24 barriers by staging 8 chunks per group (halves barrier count but
108|needs ~2× the `wsh` footprint or a narrower expert stride).

1|# Round-3 attempt 5 — builder-3-e, hyp-3-routing-prefill direction (b)
2|
3|Builds on `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-4` (direction (b),

5|no G2, no timing). Baseline: none, so no `beats_baseline`; the bar is the

7|
8|## The one main change
9|
10|8 rows per threadgroup instead of 10 in kernel 1 (the GEMM-shaped
11|prefill kernel), exactly the fix attempt-4's notes prescribe — nothing else:
12|
13|- `spec.json`: kernel 1 `threadgroup` 600 → 480; grid stays `rows*60`.
14|  60 still divides 480, so every threadgroup covers whole rows (the last
15|  possibly fewer than 8) and no bounds checks are needed — edge groups
16|  clip to whole rows exactly as in attempt-4's 10-row design.
17|- `block-2.metal`: `xst`/`sc` 640 → 512 floats (8 rows × 64 stride);
18|  `wsh[4096]` unchanged (4 K-chunks × 16 k × 64-expert stride is
19|  row-count independent); row stride `g * 10u` → `g * 8u` in `r`, `Rg`
20|  and `rr`; `Rg` cap 10 → 8. The `w`-staging loop bound stays 960
21|  (4 slots × 240 elements of total work, independent of rows/group);
22|  every remaining `16u` is K-chunk geometry (16 d-values per chunk,
23|  `part[16]`), correctly untouched.
24|- `block-0.metal`, `block-1.metal`: byte-identical to attempt-4

27|Threadgroup: (4096 + 512 + 512) × 4 B = 20,480 B of 32 KB (was 21,504 B).

29|threads under attempt-4's reported 576 cap — but attempt-4 proved the cap
30|moves with the kernel, so G1 passing is a measurement, not a certainty.

33|
34|Same as attempt-2/attempt-4: `ineff-baseline-routing-1` (per-row `w_router`
35|re-read) and `ineff-baseline-routing-2` (per-row shape cost) together.
36|`w_router` device traffic falls from rows × 184,320 B to
37|ceil(rows/8) × 184,320 B (~8× at full groups, was 10×), barriers from
38|24/row to 25 per group of 8 rows (~3.1/row amortised, was ~2.5),
39|duty from 23% to 100% in the single-partition regime, footprint from

47|169.2/135.7/113.5 at 8, 159.3/145.2/121.3 at 32,
48|102.3/87.3/227.1 at 127, 231.3/221.1/1298.8 at 1,016,

52|  (~0); kernel 1 adds one copy launch (grid rows*60 threads, rows*4
53|  elements × 8 B copied). Allowance 3 us: **53 / 117 / 124** vs

57|  - 127 rows: 16 groups × 184,320 B (w) + 127 × 1,536 B (x) + 127 × 32 B

109|## Why the prefill missed the prediction (and what decode says)
110|
111|Predicted 53 / 117 / 124 / 57 / 256 / 485 us; measured 72.6 / 123.3 /
112|111.9 / 147.3 / 561.6 / 1,052.7 — decode within drift (+37/+5/−10%),
113|prefill 2.2–2.6× over at every size (+158/+119/+117%).

# Attempt 2: two-kernel split (direction b)

First attempt in direction (b): kernel 1 fuses router scores (dense matmul +
sigmoid + bias add), kernel 2 fuses top-4 selection plus weight
normalize/scale. The dense matmul keeps a regular GEMM shape (one thread per
(row, expert), k tiled through threadgroup memory); the 11 bookkeeping kernels
around it collapse into the two fused kernels.

Removes `ineff-runs-2`: 12 kernels/layer of pure launch overhead become 2.
Kernel 1 additionally avoids re-reading the 184 KB router weight once per row
by staging k-chunks in threadgroup memory shared across 8 rows (17.4 KB <
32 KB limit; 480 threads/group < 1024).

## Predicted µs per layer (piece timing)

Fixed cost: 2 kernels x 6.81 µs (step_parts.txt:2) = 13.6 µs. Traffic at
200 GB/s peak:

- 1 row: w 184 KB (1 group) + x 1.5 KB + intermediates ~1 KB = ~187 KB ~= 0.9 µs.
  Total ~= 14.5 -> **15 µs/layer** (original 51).
- 8 rows: w 184 KB (1 group) + x 12 KB + intermediates ~8 KB = ~204 KB ~= 1.0 µs.
  Total ~= 14.6 -> **15 µs/layer** (original ~59, interpolated).
- 32 rows: w 737 KB (4 groups) + x 49 KB + intermediates ~32 KB = ~818 KB ~= 4.1 µs.
  Total ~= 17.7 -> **18 µs/layer** (original 84).

Predicted saving per step (x20 layers): 0.72 / 0.88 / 1.32 ms at 1/8/32 rows.

## Verdict

G1 pass. G2 pass: 0 wrong-expert rows, 0 near-tie rows at all row counts,
worst max_rel_err 2.6e-6 (40x inside the 1e-4 tolerance).

| rows | candidate | reference | compiled | beats compiled |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 36.3 | 36.3 | 29.3 | no |
| 8 | 34.9 | 56.9 | 42.9 | yes |
| 32 | 49.0 | 51.7 | 46.6 | no |

`beats_compiled: false`. Attempt-1 (direction a, single kernel) measured
28.5 / 23.6 / 41.8 against compiled 30.5 / 42.0 / 49.1 on its run and stops
the slot; this attempt is slower than it at every row count.

## Why the prediction missed (predicted 15 / 15 / 18, off by 142 / 133 / 172%)

1. Wrong fixed-cost model. I charged 2 x 6.81 µs = 13.6 µs from
   step_parts.txt. The piece harness shows a ~24-28 µs floor even for one
   fused kernel (attempt-1: 28.5 at 1 row), while the reference's 12 kernels
   cost only ~3 µs each when pipelined 20 layers deep. A heavy fused kernel
   costs a dispatch floor plus low-occupancy ramp, not one microbench launch.
2. Two launches, each under-occupied. Kernel 1 runs 60 threads (2 simdgroups,
   1 of 16 cores) at 1 row with 24 threadgroup barriers; kernel 2 runs a
   single thread at 1 row -- a whole launch for ~100 ns of ALU.
3. Sub-peak bandwidth. Kernel 1's w reads are 3 KB apart across SIMD lanes,
   far from the assumed 200 GB/s, and the two [rows,60] intermediates add a
   write-plus-reread round trip the single-kernel design avoids.
4. Attempt-1 is the control: re-reading w once per row (no tiling) still wins
   at 32 rows, so my barrier-heavy tiling bought traffic savings that never
   mattered and paid overhead that did.

One change I would make next (staying in direction b): delete the
threadgroup tiling in kernel 1 -- stream each expert's w column from device
memory with zero barriers -- since traffic is not the binding constraint.
Honestly, direction (a) dominates this split: one launch and no intermediates
beats two launches at all three row counts.

{"path":"muse-spark/round-4/kernels/routing/attempt-2/notes.md","content":"# attempt-2 (round 4): share w_router across 4 rows at rows > 16 (builder-2-a, direction a)

Hypothesis `hyp-2-routing-margin` (slot `routing`, baseline `none`).
Starting point `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6`
(byte-identical round-2 attempt-4 staged scalar kernels,
`max_rows: 32`; G2 exact, decode `faster` x3, prefill handed off;
round-4 re-grade margins 17.7 / 15.8 / 19.7 µs/layer over compiled at
1 / 8 / 32 rows). Attempt-1 in this round's folder is builder-2-b's
direction (b); this is the first attempt in direction (a).

## The one main change

At `rows > 16` only, share each `w_router` byte across 4 rows; every
other size runs the starting point's path verbatim. One kernel,
threadgroup 256, grid `rows*256` as before:

- A threadgroup covers 4 rows: 240 `(row, expert)` compute threads
  (`lr = tid/60`, `e = tid%60`) plus 16 staging helpers. Threadgroups
  with `gpos*4 >= rows` return immediately, so at 32 rows 8 groups
  compute and 24 exit; at 17 rows 5 compute.
- `w_router` chunks are staged once per 4-row group with the starting
  point's exact coalesced `float4` loads and transposed
  `wsh[slot][k][expert]` layout (expert stride 64), then reused for
  all 4 rows. Device `w_router` traffic at 32 rows falls from
  32 x 184,320 B = 5.90 MB/layer to 8 x 184,320 B = 1.47 MB/layer.
- Each compute thread holds its `(row, expert)` partition partial in
  a register (`pacc`), flushing it into `tot` (`tot += pacc`) when
  the partition index advances and once at the end. A partition's
  products are added in increasing `d` (chunk, then `k`), partitions
  fold in increasing order — the same addition sequence as the staged
  path's `parts[]` store/resume plus sequential fold, so the scalar
  accumulation order is bit-identical. No `parts[]` array is kept on
  this path.
- The 4 rows' `x` are preloaded once into the same padded layout
  (`lr*816 + c*17 + k`), one initial barrier; then 12 staged groups x
  2 barriers + 1 sigmoid barrier = 26 barriers per 4-row group
  (vs 27 per row on the staged path).
- Sigmoid (verbatim `1/(1+precise::exp(abs(s)))`, `(s<0)?y:1-y`),
  the strictly-greater insertion top-4 in ascending expert order
  (earliest index wins ties; per-row scan by the `e == 0` thread),
  and the `(((s0+s1)+s2)+s3)+1e-20`, divide, `x2.5` fold in emitted
  order are copied op-for-op.

At `rows <= 16` the kernel is the starting point remapped onto one
threadgroup buffer `tg[7616]` (staged: `xpad` at 0, `scores` at 816,
`parts` at 876, `wsh` at 2924; shared: 4-row `xpad` at 0, scores at
3264, `wsh` at 3520 — the two layouts never live at once). The GEMV
branch (`rows == 1`), split-K partition formula, staged loops,
sigmoid, top-4 and fold are otherwise verbatim, so 1- and 8-row
behaviour (code and timing, one extra `rows > 16` compare aside) is
inherited, not re-proven. `block-1.metal` and `spec.json` are byte
copies of the starting point (`diff` empty, checked).

Threadgroup memory: `7616 x 4 B = 30,464 B` of 32 KB (starting point
28,080 B); 256 threads, inside the 512 thread cap the task sets and
the proven 480-thread passing band — no pipeline-cap risk of the
round-3 600/960-thread kind.

## Which inefficiency it removes, and how

`ineff-baseline-routing-1` (confirmed): every row's threadgroup
streams its own full copy of `w_router` — excess over read-once
0 / 6.5 / 28.6 µs/layer (floor at 200 GB/s) at 1 / 8 / 32 rows. The
shared path reads each weight byte once per 4 rows at rows > 16, so
at 32 rows the excess falls to (8-1) x 184,320 B / 200 GB/s =
6.4 µs/layer floor. The staged path below the threshold keeps
re-reading per row, deliberately: at 8 rows the excess (6.5 µs
floor, ~1.1 µs at the measured 17% overlap rate) does not pay for
dropping from 8 parallel row-groups to 2 four-row groups.

## max_rows: 32, and why

Inherited from the starting point's `spec.json`, unchanged (byte
copy): every decode step (1-32 rows) stays on the kernels, all three
graded prefill sizes (127 / 1,016 / 2,048) hand off to the compiled
reference and report `handed off`. No `min_rows`: the 1-row GEMV
path, where the relative win is strongest, stays on the kernel.

## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 / 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows (chained)

Anchor: the round-4 re-grade of the identical starting-point bytes
(`results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/grade-routing-attempt-6.json`):
candidate / compiled 45.1 / 62.8 at 1 row, 144.2 / 160.0 at 8,
151.3 / 171.0 at 32; compiled 85.7 / 213.1 / 282.0 at the prefill
sizes. Chained absolutes drift between runs (the round-3 grade of
the same bytes read 51.7 / 90.9 / 132.2), so the firm predictions
are the verdicts and margins; absolutes are the anchor's.

- **1 row: ~45 µs, `faster`.** GEMV path verbatim; no sharing is
  possible or needed (excess 0). One extra compare.
- **8 rows: ~144 µs, `faster`.** Staged path verbatim (threshold
  keeps it); excess 6.5 µs floor left in place by design.
- **32 rows: ~147 µs, `faster`, margin widening 19.7 -> ~24 µs.**
  Arithmetic: traffic floor saved (32-8) x 184,320 B / 200 GB/s =
  22.1 µs; at the measured overlap rate (marginal 0.16 µs/row vs
  0.92 µs/row floor, ~17%, round-2 attempt-4 notes) the realised
  slice is 24 rows x 0.16 µs = 3.8 µs, so 151.3 - 3.8 = 147.5.
  Barrier cost is already in that marginal rate's staging term;
  the risk is occupancy (8 groups on 16 cores vs 32), which the
  chained timing decides.
- **127 / 1,016 / 2,048: `handed off`** (= compiled,
  ~86 / 213 / 282 on the anchor run); the kernels never run there.

Prediction: G1 pass (256 threads, 30,464 B); G2 pass at all six
sizes (no accumulation order changes anywhere — sharing changes
where operands are read from, never the order); decode `faster` x3,
prefill `handed off` x3, `beats_compiled` true (baseline `none`, so
no `beats_baseline`).

## What this attempt leaves unmeasured (for the hypothesis entry's Unverified list)

Ungraded decode counts 17-31 on the new shared path (graded 32 runs
the same `Rg = 4` full groups; 17-31 add a partial last group) and
2-7 / 9-16 on the staged path in-kind; the 33-126 band (empty by
construction under `max_rows: 32`); sizes above 2,048; prefill past
the first chunk; hand-off exactness above `max_rows` at untested
sizes; unseen exact 4th/5th ties; the 30,464 B threadgroup sum
(unchecked by `slots.build`); unwritten threadgroup reads and
thread-timing dependence (one equality run per layer cannot expose
them); whole-request composition (ready check only).

## Why the prediction missed by >20%

Predicted ~45 / 144 / 147 µs; measured 44.4 / 71.6 / 83.8
(-2% / -50% / -43%). Two separate misses:

1. **Absolutes (all sizes): chained drift, as documented.** The
   anchor re-grade ran on a slow machine state: in this run the
   compiled bar itself moved 62.8 -> 59.2, 160.0 -> 87.6 and
   171.0 -> 92.1 µs, and the candidate moved with it. The 8-row
   absolute halved while its margin (16.0 vs 15.8 predicted-held)
   and its 30/30 wins held exactly — the code at 8 rows is
   byte-equivalent to the anchor's, so this is the drift the
   starting point's notes already document, not a code effect.
2. **The 32-row margin (the real miss): sharing traded away
   per-row parallelism the staged path was using.** The staged
   path spreads one row's 768 products over 32 partition threads
   (256 threads/row, 32 groups at 32 rows); the shared path gives
   each `(row, expert)` one thread holding a serial 768-product
   chain (60 threads/row, 8 compute groups on 16 cores, 24 groups
   launched only to exit). The traffic saved is real (5.90 ->
   1.47 MB/layer staged loads) but, as the inefficiency entry's
   overlap account warned, only ~17% of that floor was ever time;
   the parallelism given up costs more than the ~3.8 µs/layer the
   saving was priced at. Net: at the one size where sharing runs,
   the margin is ~11 µs/layer below the starting point's
   cross-run-stable ~19.7 (inferred from the two prior grades of
   identical bytes, not a same-run measurement).

Next change (one): keep the staged path's partition parallelism
and share `w_router` across rows *inside* it — e.g. one threadgroup
staging `w` once for 2 rows with both rows' `parts` interleaved in
the existing 2,048-float layout budget — instead of collapsing
each row to 60 serial threads; if that cannot fit the 32 KB
budget, direction (a) should be dropped in favour of (b)."}

25|
26|Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the call: 1 to 32 in a decode step, up to 2,048 in a prefill chunk. 28|The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.

30|### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights
31|
32|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
33||---|---|---|---|
34|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
35|| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
36|| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
37|| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
38|| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
39|
40|Reference:
41|
42|```python
43|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
44|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
45|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
46|weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
47|```
48|
49|The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.

52|
53|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
54||---|---|---|---|
55|| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
56|| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
57|| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
58|| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
59|
60|Reference:
61|
62|```python
63|out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
64|```

73|
74|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
75||---|---|---|---|
76|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
77|| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
78|| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
79|| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |

84|Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.

88|```python

# Round-2 attempt 4 — builder-2-d, hardening of hyp-2-routing-exact

Builds on `muse-spark/round-2/kernels/routing/attempt-3` (scalar
full-G2; chained 46.9/300.0/297.2 µs/layer vs compiled 58.0/84.5/90.9 —
latency-bound from uncoalesced device loads + `xsh` bank conflicts).
Baseline: none, so no `beats_baseline`; the bar is the compiled reference.

## The one main change

Stage each K-chunk's `w_router` block into threadgroup memory with
coalesced vector loads and sum from threadgroup with a padded `x`
layout, nothing else:

- Staging: chunks are staged 4 at a time (12 groups cover all 48
  BK=16 chunks). Each staged chunk is 60×16 floats, loaded as 240
  `float4` loads (consecutive threads cover one expert's 4 vectors,
  then the next expert) and stored transposed in `wsh[slot][k][expert]`
  with expert stride 64.
- Padded `x`: chunk `c` of `x` sits at `xpad[c*17 + k]` (one pad float
  per chunk), replacing attempt-3's flat `xsh[768]`.
- Scalar chain: expert-parallel lanes read `wsh` at consecutive expert
  banks (conflict-free) and `xpad` uniformly per `k` (broadcast).
  Partials live transposed in `parts[partition][expert]` (stride 64)
  and are resumed product-by-product in increasing `d` across staged
  groups, so each (expert, partition) partial is still one serial
  scalar sum in increasing `d`; partials are then summed sequentially
  in partition order. 24 barriers on the scalar path (2 per group).
- Threadgroup memory: (816 + 60 + 2048 + 4096) × 4 B = 28,080 B of
  32 KB. Same grid (`rows*256`), threadgroup (256) and one-kernel layout.

Kept verbatim from attempt-3: the regime branch on `rows` (GEMV only
at `rows == 1`; split-K while `rows <= 768`; regular above — the GEMV
branch is unchanged apart from reading the padded `x` layout), the
split-K partition formula (32 partitions at 8/32 rows, 8 of 96 at 127,
2 at 257–768, single partition above 768, last partition absorbing the
remainder chunks), the GEMV lane order and shuffle tree 16,8,4,2,1,
MLX's verbatim sigmoid (`1/(1+precise::exp(abs(s)))`, `(s<0)?y:1-y`),
the strictly-greater insertion top-4 (earliest index wins ties), and
`((w0+w1)+w2)+w3 + 1e-20`, divide, ×2.5 on unbiased scores.

## Inefficiency removed

`ineff-baseline-routing-1` stays removed (same orders as attempt-3).
The target is attempt-3's diagnosed feeding cost (its notes: the
scalar chains read `w_router` uncoalesced — warp lanes 64 B apart,
16 cache lines per step — and `xsh[p*16+k]` with 16-way bank
conflicts on every product). Staging turns the device reads into
coalesced `float4` loads and the dependent chain's reads into
conflict-free threadgroup reads. The per-row `w_router` re-read
(`ineff-baseline-routing-4`) and the serial thread-0 scan are
untouched.

## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows

Anchor: attempt-3 measured 46.9/300.0/297.2, compiled 58.0/84.5/90.9
(same grader run). Traffic per row is unchanged at 184 KB of
`w_router` (0.9 µs at 200 GB/s), so floors are 0.9/7.4/29.5 µs; the
rest is chained-call latency and per-row work. Attempt-3's flat
~300 µs was the dependent device-load chain; the staged chain reads
threadgroup memory instead, at the cost of 24 barriers/row.

- 1 row: GEMV branch unchanged but for the padded index (a shift and
  mask per access) → ≈ attempt-3's 46.9 → **48**.
- 8 rows: fixed chained latency ≈ 40 µs (attempt-3's 1-row time less
  its small GEMV work) + traffic 7.4 + staged scalar work. The
  critical path is the last partition's 272 sequential threadgroup
  FMAs, overlapped across 8 threadgroups; allowance ≈ 20 µs →
  40 + 7.4 + 20 ≈ **67**.
- 32 rows: 40 + 29.5 + 25 (more threadgroups fill the GPU, critical
  path unchanged) ≈ **95**.

Prediction: **48 / 67 / 95 µs** — beats compiled (58.0/84.5/90.9) at
1 and 8 rows, near it at 32. G2 prediction: pass at all six sizes —
no accumulation order changes, only where operands are read from.

## Verdict (2026-11-04T03:56:12Z, one grader run)

G1 pass, **G2 pass at all six sizes** (rows_differ 0,
rows_other_experts 0, max_rel_err 0.0 at 1/8/32 and 127/1016/2048).
Chained µs/layer (ref / compiled / candidate): 1 row 71.1 / 60.7 /
**47.5**; 8 rows 102.9 / 84.9 / **69.1**; 32 rows 104.9 / 89.5 /
**72.9**. **`beats_compiled` true** — the first routing attempt to
beat the compiled reference at all three row counts. Baseline none,
so no `beats_baseline`. Vs attempt-3 (46.9/300.0/297.2): the staged
scalar path is 4.3×/4.1× faster at 8/32 rows; the 1-row GEMV branch
is unchanged (47.5 vs 46.9, drift).

## Why the 32-row timing missed the prediction by >20%

Predicted 48/67/95, measured 47.5/69.1/72.9: 1 and 8 rows hold
(−1%/+3%), 32 rows is 23% under. The prediction added a fixed ~40 µs
chained latency, the full 29.5 µs traffic floor and a per-row work
allowance as if they were serial per layer call. They are not: at 32
rows, 32 threadgroups across 16 GPU cores overlap one threadgroup's
coalesced staging loads and barriers with other threadgroups' scalar
compute, so the marginal cost of rows 9–32 is only (72.9−69.1)/24 ≈
