{"path":"muse-spark/round-4/kernels/routing/attempt-1/notes.md","content":"# attempt-1 (round 4): first-touch partial init — dead `parts` zeroing removed (builder-2-b)

Hypothesis `hyp-2-routing-margin` (slot `routing`, baseline `none`),
direction (b): trim the staged scalar path's shape cost without
touching the per-row `w_router` re-read. Starting point is
`muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6` (byte-identical
round-2 attempt-4 staged scalar kernels plus `"max_rows": 32`;
G2 exact, decode `faster` ×3; round-4 re-grade margins
17.7 / 15.8 / 19.7 µs/layer over compiled at 1 / 8 / 32 rows).

## The one main change

Delete the 2,048-write `parts[]` zeroing loop and initialise each
(partition, expert) partial on first touch instead:

- Removed (was starting-point lines 30–32): `for (i = tid; i < 2048;
  i += 256) parts[i] = 0.0f;` before the first barrier.
- In the scalar compute, `acc = parts[p*64+e]` becomes
  `acc = (c_lo == pc0) ? 0.0f : parts[p*64+e]`: the first staged group
  covering a partition starts from the same `0.0f` the zero loop
  stored; later groups resume the stored partial exactly as before.

Nothing else changes: `block-1.metal` and `spec.json` are byte copies
of the starting point; grid `rows*256`, threadgroup 256 (unchanged,
inside Metal's real per-pipeline cap — no thread-count change to
re-prove), one kernel, no added launch (round 3 attempt-3's lesson),
threadgroup footprint unchanged at (816 + 60 + 2048 + 4096) × 4 B =
28,080 B, staging, partition formula, barrier count (27/row),
sigmoid, strictly-greater top-4 and weights fold all verbatim.

## Which inefficiency it removes, and how

`ineff-baseline-routing-2` item 4 (dead work at `rows == 1`) and the
used-but-avoidable half of the same zeroing at 2–32 rows. At
`rows == 1` the GEMV branch reads neither `parts` nor `wsh`, so the
2,048 threadgroup writes (8 per thread) in front of the first barrier
were pure waste. At 2–32 rows the zeroing was load-bearing only as
the partials' initial value; first-touch initialisation supplies the
identical `0.0f` at the identical point in each accumulator's life,
so the writes are dead there too. Items 1–2 (27 barriers, 23%-duty
tail groups) and item 5 (serial tails) are deliberately untouched:
this is the one change that is certain in direction, per the entry's
own bound (dead zeroing: sub-µs/layer at 1 row, certain).

## Why this is bit-exact

Every (partition, expert) accumulator still starts at `0.0f` and adds
the same chunks in the same increasing-`d` order (group iteration,
`c_lo..c_hi` clamp and partition formula unchanged); a threadgroup
store/load of a float is exact, so resuming from `parts` vs starting
from the literal `0.0f` cannot change any rounding. The GEMV branch,
the final partition-order sum, the verbatim sigmoid, the
strictly-greater earliest-index-wins top-4 and the
`(((s0+s1)+s2)+s3)+1e-20`, divide, ×2.5 fold are untouched. No
accumulation is reordered, sharded or regrouped; the per-row
`w_router` re-read (`ineff-baseline-routing-1`) is not touched.

## max_rows: 32, and why

Kept from the starting point. Decode steps have 1–32 rows, so every
decode step stays on these kernels; 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows run the
compiled reference and are reported `handed off` (not timed). No
`min_rows`: handing off 1 row would run MLX's own code for a whole
1-request workload. Sizes above `max_rows` and (no `min_rows`) below
it: none below; all above run the reference.

## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 / 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows (chained)

Anchor: the starting point's round-4 re-grade candidate times
45.1 / 144.2 / 151.3 µs/layer at 1 / 8 / 32 rows (compiled
62.8 / 160.0 / 171.0 by the margins 17.7 / 15.8 / 19.7;
`ineff-baseline-routing-2` cost table). Saving arithmetic: 2,048
threadgroup writes removed per row = 8 stores per thread; even at
8 cycles per store that is ~64 cycles ≈ 0.05 µs at ~1.3 GHz, plus
the loop's index/branch overhead — bound the saving at ≤0.5 µs/layer
at 1 row and ≤0.3 µs/layer at 8/32 rows (more threadgroups resident,
more overlap). Prediction is therefore the anchor minus ≤ the bound:

- 1 row: **≈45 µs/layer** (45.1 − ≤0.5), verdict `faster` (margin 17.7).
- 8 rows: **≈144 µs/layer** (144.2 − ≤0.3), verdict `faster` (margin 15.8).
- 32 rows: **≈151 µs/layer** (151.3 − ≤0.3), verdict `faster` (margin 19.7).
- 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows: `handed off` — not timed; the attempt's
  time there is the compiled reference's by construction.

Chained absolutes drift with machine state (identical starting-point
bytes measured 51.7 / 90.9 / 132.2 in round 3's quieter run), so the
load-bearing prediction is the verdicts: G1 pass, G2 pass at all six
sizes, decode `faster` ×3, prefill `handed off` ×3,
`beats_compiled` true. The deleted writes are far too small to flip
any verdict either way; any measured delta beyond ~1 µs/layer vs the
same-run starting point would be machine drift, not this change.

## What this attempt leaves unmeasured (for the hypothesis entry's Unverified list)

Everything the starting point left: ungraded decode counts 2–7 and
9–31 (same `tm = 1, partitions = 32, base_iters = 1` geometry, now
also exercising first-touch init — reasoned bit-exact, not graded);
the 33–126 band (empty by construction under `max_rows: 32`);
hand-off exactness above `max_rows` at untested sizes; sizes above
2,048; later prefill chunks; other prompts and later decode steps;
unseen exact 4th/5th ties; the barrier/tail-duty costs (items 1–2,
5) themselves, still undecomposed; whether the sub-µs saving is
resolvable at all inside paired-repeat noise; whole-request (G3)
effect, which only the ready check measures as a set.

## Verdict

*(filled after the grader run.)*
"}

The prefill prize is fully banked by attempt-1 (`max_rows` 59: prefill `same` × 3, G1+G2 pass, boundary pass, decode wins at 8/32 rows) — but decode at 1 row misses (96.9 vs 86.6, 5/30 wins), so `beats_compiled` is false and the attempt cannot close as a candidate. The 1-row gap now survives two approaches: six fused exact packings plateaued at 92–110 µs/layer (round 2), and the reference-shaped unfused path (attempt-5) came out nearly 2× worse (234.3 vs 118.4, 0/30 wins) — the reference's speed comes from one `mx.compile` dispatch, not just its shape. Per the approach rule, the next attempt would need a third approach; none exists in the spec surface (there is no hand-off below a row count, only `max_rows` above it). The slot keeps the reference. Durable gains: the `max_rows`-59 design (bit-exact, prefill `same`) and the bit-exact grouped prefill path (attempt-4, 2.3× off) stand as the next round's starting material.

19|  `acc = (c_lo == pc0) ? 0.0f : parts[p*64+e]`: the first staged group

21|  stored; later groups resume the stored partial exactly as before.

34|used-but-avoidable half of the same zeroing at 2–32 rows. At
35|`rows == 1` the GEMV branch reads neither `parts` nor `wsh`, so the
36|2,048 threadgroup writes (8 per thread) in front of the first barrier

38|the partials' initial value; first-touch initialisation supplies the
39|identical `0.0f` at the identical point in each accumulator's life,
40|so the writes are dead there too. Items 1–2 (27 barriers, 23%-duty

# Simulate threadgroup index write->read ordering in block-0.metal for rows 1..32
# Barriers make groups sequential; ternary logical read only when c_lo != pc0.
def check(rows):
    written_parts=set(); written_wsh=set(); first_touch=set(); resumed=set()
    # xpad: written d 0..767 -> c*17+k k<16 ; read patterns checked separately
    xpad_w={(d//16)*17+(d%16) for d in range(768)}
    assert all((c*17+k) in xpad_w for c in range(48) for k in range(16))
    assert all((( (i*128+lane*4)//16)*17+((i*128+lane*4)%16)+t) in xpad_w for i in range(6) for lane in range(32) for t in range(4))
    if rows==1:
        scores_w={e for sg in range(8) for e in range(sg,60,8)}
        assert scores_w==set(range(60))
        return "GEMV: parts/wsh never read; scores 0..59 written"
    tm=(rows+31)//32; ratio=48//(tm*2); np_=1
    while np_<ratio: np_*=2
    if np_<2: np_=2
    partitions=min(np_,32); base=48//partitions or 1
    assert (tm,partitions,base)==(1,32,1), (rows,tm,partitions,base)
    thr=(partitions-1)*base
    for gbase in range(0,48,4):
        gn=min(4,48-gbase); clast=gbase+gn-1
        # wsh staged this group
        wsh_w=set()
        for s in range(gn):
            for e in range(60):
                for kv in range(4):
                    dst=(s*16+kv*4)*64+e
                    for off in (0,64,128,192): wsh_w.add(dst+off)
        p_first=(gbase//base if gbase<thr else partitions-1)
        p_last=(clast//base if clast<thr else partitions-1)
        for dp,p in enumerate(range(p_first,p_last+1)):
            pc0=p*base; pc1=48 if p+1==partitions else (p+1)*base
            c_lo=max(pc0,gbase); c_hi=min(pc1,gbase+gn)
            assert c_lo<c_hi, (rows,gbase,p,c_lo,c_hi)
            for e in range(60):
                idx=p*64+e
                if c_lo==pc0:
                    assert idx not in written_parts or p==31 and False, (rows,gbase,p,e)
                    first_touch.add(idx)
                else:
                    assert idx in written_parts, f"UNWRITTEN parts read rows={rows} gbase={gbase} p={p} e={e}"
                    resumed.add(idx)
                for c in range(c_lo,c_hi):
                    s=c-gbase
                    for k in range(16):
                        assert s*1024+e+k*64 in wsh_w, (rows,gbase,c,k,e)
                written_parts.add(idx)
        # barrier: wsh overwritten next group, parts retained
    assert written_parts=={p*64+e for p in range(32) for e in range(60)}
    assert first_touch=={p*64+e for p in range(31) for e in range(60)} | {31*64+e for e in range(60)}
    # final sum reads all written
    return f"partitions={partitions} base={base} first-touch={len(first_touch)} resumed-reads-ok final parts written={len(written_parts)}"

for r in range(1,33):
    print(r, check(r))
print("ALL ROWS 1..32 PASS")

1|# Brief for the Muse Spark agent: write faster MobileMoE-S kernels, for decoding and prompt processing
2|
3|*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. Committed and tagged `agent-era` before the Muse Spark session started. [Who made what](../PROVENANCE.md).*
4|
5|You are a Claude Code session powered by Meta's Muse Spark, working in your own git worktree on the branch `muse-agent`. This brief fixes your task, what you may change, where your work goes and how it is judged. It does not change during your session.
6|
7|## The task
8|
9|Meta's MobileMoE-S, int4, is served on an Apple M1 Pro (16-core GPU, 200 GB/s, 16 GB) by vLLM through vllm-metal, which runs the model with MLX. The findings below measure where each decode step's time goes. A step is about 870–1,090 small GPU kernels and is far from both the bandwidth and compute limits. The findings name the pieces that cost the most.
10|
11|A request goes through two phases: **prompt processing** (the prefill), which runs its whole prompt through the model, and **decoding**, one step per generated token. An improvement must hold in both: faster in one, and no slower in the other ([ADR 0011](adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). A kernel that speeds up the decode step but slows the prefill is not an improvement.
12|
13|1. **Choose.** Read the findings and choose one or two of the slots below to replace with your own fused Metal kernels. Write `muse-spark/strategy.md`: why, your design, and what each saves per step at 1 and 32 requests (your estimate). End it with the JSON block described under *Your files*. Commit it.
14|2. **Write and check.** For each chosen slot, write the kernels as files, run the grader on them, read its verdict, and improve. Up to **5 attempts per slot**; an attempt is a folder you graded and committed.
15|3. **Finish.** Write `muse-spark/summary.md`: your final attempt per slot and what you learned. Commit it.
16|
17|**Read these first** (all in your worktree):
18|- `claude/findings/bottleneck-explained.md` and `claude/findings/step-breakdown.md`: the measured findings;
19|- `results/runs/2026-11-01-breakdown/tables.md` and `results/runs/2026-11-02-gpu-counters/tables.md`: the raw tables;
20|- `third_party/mlx-lm/mlx_lm/models/mobilemoe.py` and `switch_layers.py`: the model code;
21|- MLX's custom-kernel documentation: `.venv/bin/python -c "import mlx.core as mx; help(mx.fast.metal_kernel)"`;
22|- `bench/grader/check_candidate.py` and `bench/grader/slots.py`: how you are graded.
23|
24|## The slots
25|
26|Each slot is a piece of the mixture-of-experts block, `MoE.__call__` in `mobilemoe.py`, which runs in all 20 layers of every step. `rows` is the number of tokens in the call: 1 to 32 in a decode step, up to 2,048 in a prefill chunk. The grader flattens the inputs to the shapes below and restores the model's shapes afterwards. All arrays are row-contiguous.
27|
28|The model's constants: hidden size `D = 768`, experts `E = 60`, experts per token `K = 4`, expert hidden size `H = 384`, `routed_scaling_factor = 2.5`, `norm_topk_prob = true`.
29|
30|### `routing`: router, top-4 selection and weights
31|
32|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
33||---|---|---|---|
34|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
35|| input | `w_router` | [60, 768] | float32 |
36|| input | `bias` | [60] | float32 (the model's bfloat16 `expert_bias`, converted exactly) |
37|| output | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
38|| output | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
39|
40|Reference:
41|
42|```python
43|scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)          # [rows, 60]
44|inds = mx.argpartition(-(scores + bias), kth=3, axis=-1)[:, :4]  # the 4 largest biased scores
45|w = mx.take_along_axis(scores, inds, axis=-1)                    # unbiased scores of those 4
46|weights = w / (w.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + 1e-20) * 2.5
47|```
48|
49|The order of the 4 experts within a row is free, as long as `weights[r, j]` belongs to `inds[r, j]`. Today this slot is about 12 kernels per layer, 240 per step. It costs 1.02 ms of a 4.75 ms step at 1 request and 1.68 ms at 32 requests.
50|
51|### `combine`: weighting the routed experts' outputs and adding the shared expert
52|
53|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
54||---|---|---|---|
55|| input | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 (the 4 experts' outputs, in `inds` order) |
56|| input | `weights` | [rows, 4] | float32 |
57|| input | `shared` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 (the shared expert's output) |
58|| output | `out` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
59|
60|Reference:
61|
62|```python
63|out = (y * weights[..., None]).sum(axis=-2).astype(mx.bfloat16) + shared
64|```
65|
66|Today this slot is 5 kernels per layer, 100 per step. It costs 0.61 ms at 1 request and 0.33 ms at 32 requests.
67|
68|### `routing+combine`
69|
70|Both slots above, each with its own kernels, in one candidate.
71|
72|### `experts`: the routed experts' three quantized products
73|
74|| | Name | Shape | Dtype |
75||---|---|---|---|
76|| input | `x` | [rows, 768] | bfloat16 |
77|| input | `inds` | [rows, 4] | uint32 |
78|| input | `gate_w`, `up_w` | [60, 768, 48] | uint32 (4-bit weights in [expert, in, out] layout, 8 per word along out) |
79|| input | `gate_scales`, `gate_biases`, `up_scales`, `up_biases` | [60, 768, 12] | bfloat16 (one scale and bias per 32 outputs) |
80|| input | `down_w` | [60, 384, 96] | uint32 |
81|| input | `down_scales`, `down_biases` | [60, 384, 24] | bfloat16 |
82|| output | `y` | [rows, 4, 768] | bfloat16 |
83|
84|Each weight is `w = scale * q + bias`, with `q` the 4-bit value. In MLX's affine quantization, the value for output column `o` sits in word `o / 8` at bits `4 * (o % 8)`.
85|
86|Reference: for each row `r` and each `j`, with `e = inds[r, j]`:
87|
88|```python
89|y[r, j] = (silu(x[r] @ Wgate[e]) * (x[r] @ Wup[e])) @ Wdown[e]
90|```
91|
92|As in MLX's `gather_qmm(..., transpose=False)`, each product accumulates in float32 and rounds its output to bfloat16. `silu(gate) * up` is computed on those bfloat16 values, and its result is rounded to bfloat16 before the down product.
93|
94|Today this slot is 7 kernels per layer at 1 request and 13 at 32 requests (from 16 rows, MLX also sorts the pairs by expert). It costs 0.92 ms at 1 request and 14.67 ms of a 28.19 ms step at 32 requests, half the step. It reads each expert once per (token, expert) pair.
95|
96|## Tools and limits
97|
98|- **Only `mx.fast.metal_kernel`, MLX 0.32.4.** You write the Metal body; MLX generates the signature. Inputs arrive as `const device T* name` and outputs as `device T* name`. Shapes and strides come as `name_shape` and `name_strides` when the source uses them. The thread attributes are available, as in MLX's documentation: `thread_position_in_grid`, `threadgroup_position_in_grid`, `thread_position_in_threadgroup`, `threads_per_threadgroup`, `simdgroup_index_in_threadgroup`, `thread_index_in_simdgroup`, and so on.
99|- **The grader runs no Python of yours.** It reads your launch spec as data and compiles only your Metal.
100|- **Stay within the GPU's limits.** At most 1,024 threads per threadgroup and 32 KB of threadgroup memory. A grader run should take under 3 minutes, longer for an attempt much slower than the reference at the prefill sizes; stop one that runs past 15.
101|- **Hardware.** The Apple M1 Pro GPU (`applegpu_g13s`) has 16 cores and a SIMD width of 32. bfloat16 is available in Metal as `bfloat`.
102|
103|## Rules of this session
104|
105|These keep your work apart from everyone else's. Git hooks and an audit script enforce them, and a commit that breaks them is refused.
106|
107|- **Write only inside `muse-spark/`.** Never change `bench/`, `claude/`, `results/`, `tools/`, `third_party/`, or any other file. A copy of the grader you edit is never used.
108|- **Commit only on `muse-agent`,** with the co-author trailer your settings add: `Co-Authored-By: Muse Spark (Meta Model API) <muse-spark@meta-model-api.invalid>`. Start each subject with `Muse Spark:`. No other co-author.
109|- **Never push, merge, rebase, change git config, or skip hooks.**
110|- **Don't read `.env`** or any credentials file.

146|

150|    {
151|      "name": "fused_routing",
152|      "source_block": 0,
153|      "header_block": null,
154|      "inputs": ["x", "w_router", "bias"],
155|      "outputs": [
156|        {"name": "inds", "shape": ["rows", 4], "dtype": "uint32"},
157|        {"name": "weights", "shape": ["rows", 4], "dtype": "float32"}
158|      ],

160|      "threadgroup": [32, 1, 1],

164|    }

169|
170|- **`source_block` and `header_block`** are the numbers of your `block-N.metal` files.
171|- **Kernels run in list order.** A kernel's `inputs` may name slot inputs or outputs of earlier kernels.
172|- **`slot_outputs`** maps each output of the slot to the kernel output that provides it.
173|- **`max_rows`** (optional, an integer of at least 1): inputs with more rows than this skip your kernels and run the slot's reference under `mx.compile`. Use it to keep prefill-sized inputs on MLX's own code when your kernels are built for decode sizes; MLX switches its own experts kernel at 60 rows.
174|- **`min_rows`** (optional, from round 4; an integer of at least 1, at most `max_rows` when both are given): inputs with fewer rows than this run the compiled reference too, so your kernels run only from `min_rows` to `max_rows`. Use it when your kernels lose at the smallest decode sizes, such as 1 row ([ADR 0015](adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)). G3 times whole requests: with 1 request every decode step has 1 row, so an attempt that hands off 1 row runs MLX's own code for the whole 1-request workload, and can pass G3 only in a set whose other kernels are faster there.

177|- **Shape and grid entries** are integers, or products of integers and the names `rows`, `D`, `E`, `K` and `H`, such as `"rows*32"`. Nothing else is evaluated.

188|   - **a decode step:** inputs captured from all 20 layers during a real decode step, at 1, 8 and 32 rows;

208|**What the grader prints for an attempt** (JSON):
209|- `g1` false and the compiler's error message;
210|- or the correctness results per size: for routing, the rows that differ; for combine and experts, the elements that differ and the largest gap in units in the last place; with the first example;
211|- or, when the attempt is correct, `timing_us_per_layer` per size: its time per call next to the original's and the compiled reference's, its wins against the compiled reference and the verdict (`faster`, `same`, `slower`, or `handed off` for a size your spec hands to the compiled reference); then `phases_vs_compiled` and `beats_compiled`.
212|
213|**The piece timing** runs the slot at the six G2 sizes: the 20 layers' captured decode inputs at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and the 20 layers' first prefill chunk at 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. Each layer's call waits for the previous one's output, as in the model: one small kernel links them, the same for every function timed. Without that wait, the GPU overlaps the 20 calls and hides how long one takes; in round 1, an experts kernel 29% faster on overlapped calls was 66% slower on chained ones at 1 row.
214|- **Paired repeats.** Your attempt and the compiled reference run in alternating order, 30 times.
215|- **Per size:** your attempt is `faster` when it wins at least 22 of the 30 pairs, `slower` when it loses at least 22, and `same` otherwise. Medians alone would pass on noise: the same kernel timed twice differs by up to 5%.

# attempt-1 (round 4): first-touch partial init — dead `parts` zeroing removed (builder-2-b)

Hypothesis `hyp-2-routing-margin` (slot `routing`, baseline `none`),
direction (b): trim the staged scalar path's shape cost without
touching the per-row `w_router` re-read. Starting point is
`muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6` (byte-identical
round-2 attempt-4 staged scalar kernels plus `"max_rows": 32`;
G2 exact, decode `faster` ×3; round-4 re-grade margins
17.7 / 15.8 / 19.7 µs/layer over compiled at 1 / 8 / 32 rows).

## The one main change

Delete the 2,048-write `parts[]` zeroing loop and initialise each
(partition, expert) partial on first touch instead:

- Removed (was starting-point lines 30–32): `for (i = tid; i < 2048;
  i += 256) parts[i] = 0.0f;` before the first barrier.
- In the scalar compute, `acc = parts[p*64+e]` becomes
  `acc = (c_lo == pc0) ? 0.0f : parts[p*64+e]`: the first staged group
  covering a partition starts from the same `0.0f` the zero loop
  stored; later groups resume the stored partial exactly as before.

Nothing else changes: `block-1.metal` and `spec.json` are byte copies
of the starting point; grid `rows*256`, threadgroup 256 (unchanged,
inside Metal's real per-pipeline cap — no thread-count change to
re-prove), one kernel, no added launch (round 3 attempt-3's lesson),
threadgroup footprint unchanged at (816 + 60 + 2048 + 4096) × 4 B =
28,080 B, staging, partition formula, barrier count (27/row),
sigmoid, strictly-greater top-4 and weights fold all verbatim.

{"path":"muse-spark/round-4/kernels/routing/attempt-3/notes.md","content":"# attempt-3 (round 4): tail-group feeding — idle tail threads pre-stage the next `w_router` group (builder-2-c)

Hypothesis `hyp-2-routing-margin` (slot `routing`, baseline `none`),
direction (b) hardening of `muse-spark/round-4/kernels/routing/attempt-1`
(first-touch `parts[]` init, dead zeroing removed; G1+G2 pass at all six
sizes, decode `faster` ×3, margins 27.6 / 20.4 / 17.4 µs/layer over
compiled at 1 / 8 / 32 rows in its own grade). This is the next single
change named by attempt-1's builder: tail-group feeding against
`ineff-baseline-routing-2` items 1–2.

## The one main change

In the staged scalar path only, and only at the decode geometry
(`partitions == 32`, `base_iters == 1`, which every scalar-path decode
size 2–32 takes), the four tail staged groups (`gbase` = 32 / 36 /
40 / 44) compute a single partition on 60 of 256 threads (23.4%
duty). In the first three of those groups the 196 otherwise-idle
threads (`tid >= 60`) now pre-load the *next* staged group's
`w_router` block during the compute phase:

- Each idle thread holds up to 5 `float4`s in registers (`pre[5]`),
  covering the next group's 960 `float4` staging items exactly once
  (`lv = (tid - 60) + j * 196`, `j` = 0..4; same `(s, e, kv)` mapping
  and same coalesced `float4` device loads as the normal staging
  loop, so the bytes landing in `wsh` are identical).
- The next group then fills `wsh` from those registers with
  threadgroup stores only (same transposed `(s * 16 + kv * 4) * 64
  + e` destinations), instead of issuing fresh device loads between
  its two barriers. Device-load latency for groups 36 / 40 / 44 is
  moved behind the preceding tail group's compute phase.

Nothing else changes. `block-1.metal` and `spec.json` are byte
copies of attempt-1 (`diff` empty, checked); grid `rows*256`,
threadgroup 256, one kernel, no added launch, no added threadgroup
memory (registers only; footprint still (816 + 60 + 2048 + 4096) ×
4 B = 28,080 B), barrier count still 27 per row (2 per staged group
+ 3 outside), partition formula, first-touch `parts[]` init,
per-row `w_router` re-read structure, sigmoid, strictly-greater
top-4 and weights fold all verbatim from attempt-1. The `rows == 1`
GEMV path is untouched (the feeding state is declared inside the
scalar branch). Groups outside the tail (`gbase` < 32), the last
group (`gbase == 44`, no next group), and any non-decode geometry
(`partitions != 32` or `base_iters != 1`, unreachable under
`max_rows: 32`) run attempt-1's staging loop verbatim.

## Which inefficiency it removes, and how

`ineff-baseline-routing-2` items 1–2: 27 barriers per row and the
tail third of K-chunks running at 23% thread duty — in each tail
group 196 threads wait at the compute barrier while 60 threads run
the partition-31 chain, and the next group's device loads are then
issued cold between barriers. Feeding puts those idle threads to
work issuing the next group's `w_router` loads concurrently with
the tail compute, so the next group's staging phase shrinks to
register-to-threadgroup stores. This is the entry's legal
"feeding" fix: it touches no partition boundary, no chunk's
accumulator, and no add order (see below), so it cannot reorder
any row's accumulation the way rebalancing would.

## Why this is bit-exact

`wsh` contents for every group are bit-identical to attempt-1:
the prefetch reads the same `float4`s from the same device
addresses and stores them to the same transposed `wsh`
destinations; a device load into a register and back out to
threadgroup memory is exact for float32. Every (partition,
expert) accumulator still starts at `0.0f` on first touch
(attempt-1's init, kept) and adds the same chunks in the same
increasing-`d` order; partials are stored and resumed exactly as
before, then summed in partition order. The verbatim sigmoid,
the strictly-greater earliest-index-wins top-4 and the
`(((s0+s1)+s2)+s3)+1e-20`, divide, ×2.5 fold are untouched. No
accumulation is reordered, sharded or regrouped; the per-row
`w_router` re-read (`ineff-baseline-routing-1`) is deliberately
not touched — pre-staged bytes are still loaded once per row.

## max_rows: 32, and why

Kept from attempt-1 (byte-identical `spec.json`). Decode steps
have 1–32 rows, so every decode step stays on these kernels;
127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows run the compiled reference and are
reported `handed off` (not timed). No `min_rows`: handing off
1 row would run MLX's own code for a whole 1-request workload.
Sizes above `max_rows` run the reference; none below (no
`min_rows`).

## Predicted µs per layer at 1 / 8 / 32 / 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows (chained)

Anchor: attempt-1's own measured grade — candidate
58.5 / 136.9 / 74.7 µs/layer against compiled 86.1 / 157.3 /
92.1 at 1 / 8 / 32 rows (margins 27.6 / 20.4 / 17.4).

Saving arithmetic. Feeding pre-stages 3 of the 12 staged groups
(36 / 40 / 44) at every scalar-path row. Each such group
otherwise issues 960 `float4` device loads = 15,360 B per row
(0.077 µs at the 200 GB/s floor — bytes are not the prize) plus
their exposed latency between two barriers. No barrier is
removed, so the inefficiency entry's outer envelope (its
inferred ~2 µs/barrier datum) does not apply; the realised
saving is only the load-issue + latency slice that overlaps
the preceding tail group's compute phase, minus the cost of
holding 5 extra `float4`s (20 floats) in registers. The tail
compute phase itself is short (60 threads × 4 chunks × 16
FMAs), and cross-threadgroup overlap at 8–32 rows already hid
part of this latency in attempt-1, so the honest expectation
is 0–2 µs/layer at 8 / 32 rows and exactly 0 at 1 row (GEMV
path, code untouched — any 1-row delta is machine drift).
Prediction, attempt-1 anchor minus ~1 µs/layer at 8/32:

- 1 row: **≈58 µs/layer** (58.5 − 0), verdict `faster` (margin 27.6).
- 8 rows: **≈136 µs/layer** (136.9 − ~1), verdict `faster` (margin 20.4).
- 32 rows: **≈74 µs/layer** (74.7 − ~1), verdict `faster` (margin 17.4).
- 127 / 1,016 / 2,048 rows: `handed off` — not timed; the attempt's
  time there is the compiled reference's by construction.

Chained absolutes drift with machine state (attempt-1's own
notes: identical starting-point bytes measured 51.7 / 90.9 /
132.2 in round 3 vs 45.1 / 144.2 / 151.3 at re-grade, with the
same run's compiled bar moving +37% / −46% at 1 / 32 rows), so
the load-bearing prediction is the verdicts: G1 pass, G2 pass
at all six sizes, decode `faster` ×3, prefill `handed off` ×3,
`beats_compiled` true. A measured delta beyond ~2 µs/layer
against attempt-1's absolutes is expected to be drift, not
this change, and will be judged against the same run's
compiled bar and margins.

## What this attempt leaves unmeasured (for the hypothesis entry's Unverified list)

Everything attempt-1 left, plus: whether the tail-feeding
overlap is resolvable at all inside paired-repeat noise (the
tail compute phase may be too short to hide 960 loads, and the
register cost may eat the saving); ungraded decode counts 2–7
and 9–31 (same `partitions = 32, base_iters = 1` geometry, so
feeding is reasoned to run there in-kind, not graded); the
33–126 band (empty under `max_rows: 32`); hand-off exactness
above `max_rows` at untested sizes; sizes above 2,048; later
prefill chunks; other prompts and later decode steps; unseen
exact 4th/5th ties; the barrier cost itself (items 1–2's
barrier count is unchanged and still undecomposed); the
serial tails (item 5, untouched); whole-request (G3) effect,
which only the ready check measures as a set.

## Verdict

*(graded once below; this section is filled from `grade.json`.)*

# attempt-2 (round 4): share w_router across 4 rows at rows > 16 (builder-2-a, direction a)

Hypothesis `hyp-2-routing-margin` (slot `routing`, baseline `none`).
Starting point `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6`
(byte-identical round-2 attempt-4 staged scalar kernels,
`max_rows: 32`; G2 exact, decode `faster` x3, prefill handed off;
round-4 re-grade margins 17.7 / 15.8 / 19.7 µs/layer over compiled at
1 / 8 / 32 rows). Attempt-1 in this round's folder is builder-2-b's
direction (b); this is the first attempt in direction (a).

## The one main change

At `rows > 16` only, share each `w_router` byte across 4 rows; every
other size runs the starting point's path verbatim. One kernel,
threadgroup 256, grid `rows*256` as before:

- A threadgroup covers 4 rows: 240 `(row, expert)` compute threads
  (`lr = tid/60`, `e = tid%60`) plus 16 staging helpers. Threadgroups
  with `gpos*4 >= rows` return immediately, so at 32 rows 8 groups
  compute and 24 exit; at 17 rows 5 compute.
- `w_router` chunks are staged once per 4-row group with the starting
  point's exact coalesced `float4` loads and transposed
  `wsh[slot][k][expert]` layout (expert stride 64), then reused for
  all 4 rows. Device `w_router` traffic at 32 rows falls from
  32 x 184,320 B = 5.90 MB/layer to 8 x 184,320 B = 1.47 MB/layer.
- Each compute thread holds its `(row, expert)` partition partial in
  a register (`pacc`), flushing it into `tot` (`tot += pacc`) when
  the partition index advances and once at the end. A partition's
  products are added in increasing `d` (chunk, then `k`), partitions
  fold in increasing order — the same addition sequence as the staged
  path's `parts[]` store/resume plus sequential fold, so the scalar
  accumulation order is bit-identical. No `parts[]` array is kept on
  this path.
- The 4 rows' `x` are preloaded once into the same padded layout
  (`lr*816 + c*17 + k`), one initial barrier; then 12 staged groups x
  2 barriers + 1 sigmoid barrier = 26 barriers per 4-row group
  (vs 27 per row on the staged path).
- Sigmoid (verbatim `1/(1+precise::exp(abs(s)))`, `(s<0)?y:1-y`),
  the strictly-greater insertion top-4 in ascending expert order
  (earliest index wins ties; per-row scan by the `e == 0` thread),
  and the `(((s0+s1)+s2)+s3)+1e-20`, divide, `x2.5` fold in emitted
  order are copied op-for-op.

At `rows <= 16` the kernel is the starting point remapped onto one
threadgroup buffer `tg[7616]` (staged: `xpad` at 0, `scores` at 816,
`parts` at 876, `wsh` at 2924; shared: 4-row `xpad` at 0, scores at
3264, `wsh` at 3520 — the two layouts never live at once). The GEMV
branch (`rows == 1`), split-K partition formula, staged loops,
sigmoid, top-4 and fold are otherwise verbatim, so 1- and 8-row
behaviour (code and timing, one extra `rows > 16` compare aside) is
inherited, not re-proven. `block-1.metal` and `spec.json` are byte
copies of the starting point (`diff` empty, checked).

Threadgroup memory: `7616 x 4 B = 30,464 B` of 32 KB (starting point
28,080 B); 256 threads, inside the 512 thread cap the task sets and
the proven 480-thread passing band — no pipeline-cap risk of the
round-3 600/960-thread kind.

## Which inefficiency it removes, and how

`ineff-baseline-routing-1` (confirmed): every row's threadgroup
streams its own full copy of `w_router` — excess over read-once
0 / 6.5 / 28.6 µs/layer (floor at 200 GB/s) at 1 / 8 / 32 rows. The
shared path reads each weight byte once per 4 rows at rows > 16, so
at 32 rows the excess falls to (8-1) x 184,320 B / 200 GB/s =
6.4 µs/layer floor. The staged path below the threshold keeps
re-reading per row, deliberately: at 8 rows the excess (6.5 µs
floor, ~1.1 µs at the measured 17% overlap rate) does not pay for
dropping from 8 parallel row-groups to 2 four-row groups.

## max_rows: 32, and why

Inherited from the starting point's `spec.json`, unchanged (byte
copy): every decode step (1-32 rows) stays on the kernels, all three
graded prefill sizes (127 / 1,016 / 2,048) hand off to the compiled
reference and report `handed off`. No `min_rows`: the 1-row GEMV
path, where the relative win is strongest, stays on the kernel.

318|## Decision
319|
320|**Best attempt: `muse-spark/round-4/kernels/experts/attempt-1`** (`min_rows: 2`, `max_rows: 59`, kernels byte-identical to the starting point). It passes G1, G2 (differ 0 at all six sizes) and its boundary check (`pass`), with `beats_compiled` true: decode `faster` at 8 and 32 rows (157.6 / 571.1 vs compiled 232.1 / 832.6 µs per layer, 30 wins each), 1-row and all prefill sizes `handed off`. Attempt-2 (`max_rows: 32`) also passes everything and is faster at 32 rows (538.1) but slower at 8 (170.5 vs 157.6); attempt-1 is picked because the 8-request workload is where the untested three-slot interaction (+2.13 to +2.86 ms/step, `ineff-g3-2`) bites, and because it keeps the starting point's full 2–59 kernel window. 1|# Inefficiency: the routing+combine pair keeps only −0.36 of its −0.66 ms/step piece win vs the compiled reference at 32×1024, inside the repeat spread
2|
3|- **Owner:** explorer-g3
4|- **Status:** confirmed
5|- **Version:** 2
6|- **Updated:** 2026-11-04T21:47:11Z
7|- **Next:** builders widening routing/combine decode margin at 32 rows answer this; verifier to check the arithmetic
8|
9|## Slot
10|
11|Outside the slots — the routing+combine set as timed in `muse-all` (routing attempt-6 + combine attempt-2, `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/routing/attempt-6`, `muse-spark/round-3/kernels/combine/attempt-2`). Measurement side owned by territory `g3`; kernel-side margin owned by territories `baseline-routing` and `baseline-combine`.
12|
13|## What happens
14|
15|The chained piece timing prices the pair at −0.656 ms/step vs the compiled reference at 32 decode rows (routing −0.396 + combine −0.260; [territory-g3.md](territory-g3.md) piece 1). Timed whole in vLLM at 32 requests, the pair keeps −0.548 ms/step at 32×128 and only **−0.362 ms/step at 32×1024** in Claude's G3 (medians 38.765 vs 39.127 ms, **0.93% apart, 5-repeat ranges [38.589–39.080] vs [38.912–39.400] overlapping**, so `muse-all` vs `compiled-all` decode is `same` and G3 fails on this one workload). In the swarm's ready check the same workload keeps −0.588 (38.942 vs 39.530, 1.49%) and the ranges miss, so the pair passes there. The verdict flips between two runs of identical kernels while every median favours the pair. Full derivation in [territory-g3.md](territory-g3.md) gap 1.
16|
17|## Cost
18|
19|Shortfall = (measured, whole-request change vs `compiled-all`) − (piece-implied change vs compiled, candidate − compiled × 20 layers), ms per decode step. Piece from the two `grade.json` (routing 132.2 vs 152.0, combine 32.7 vs 45.7 µs/layer at 32 rows; at 1/8 rows routing 51.7/90.9 vs 66.3/104.0, combine 31.8/34.7 vs 36.9/41.1); measured from `results/runs/2026-11-04-muse-round-3/console-vllm.txt` summary medians (cross-checked in `muse-vllm.jsonl`) and `muse-spark/round-3/checks/ready-1/ready-verdict.json` `medians`.
20|
21|| Workload | Piece vs compiled | Claude G3 vs compiled | Shortfall (Claude) | Swarm vs compiled | Shortfall (swarm) |
22||---|---|---|---|---|---|
23|| 1×128 (1 row) | −0.394 | −0.436 | −0.042 | −0.491 | −0.097 |
24|| 8×128 (8 rows) | −0.390 | −0.375 | +0.015 | −0.446 | −0.056 |
25|| 32×128 (32 rows) | −0.656 | −0.548 | +0.108 | −0.483 | +0.173 |
26|| 32×1024 (32 rows) | −0.656 | **−0.362** | **+0.294** | −0.588 | +0.068 |
27|
28|Per layer at 32×1024 (÷20): +14.7 µs (Claude) / +3.4 µs (swarm); the two runs disagree by 0.226 ms/step, the same order as the larger shortfall, so the solid cost is the **margin**, not a fixed 0.294: the pair's separation from the compiled bar at 32×1024 is 0.36–0.59 ms/step (0.9–1.5%) against per-run 5-repeat spreads of ~0.49 ms (pair) and ~0.49 ms (compiled) wide. To have separated in Claude's draw the pair needed roughly a further 0.17 ms/step (its max 39.080 below the compiled min 38.912). At 1 row with long prompts the piece sum transfers fully (measured −0.428 at 1×1024, −0.487 at 1×7936 vs piece −0.394; [territory-g3.md](territory-g3.md) piece 4), so the shortfall needs 32 rows, and grows again with context at fixed 32 rows.
29|
30|In kernel terms: the pair removes 280 kernels/step vs base (1087→807 at 32 rows) and 180 vs `compiled-all` (987→807), exactly additive, tokens bit-exact — kernel count and correctness are not the cost. The slots' own traffic is unchanged by context while the step grows 30.1→39.4 ms from 32×128 to 32×1024; the lost time scales with neither.
31|
32|## Kind
33|
34|Overhead-bound (in the terms of `claude/GLOSSARY.md`): the step is far from peak bandwidth and peak compute, and the shortfall scales with neither weight bytes nor kernel count. Ruled out: the kernels' own chained work (both `faster` at every decode size, piece 1), token divergence (exact everywhere), prompt length alone (piece 4). Not ruled out: a fixed in-step composition cost at 32 rows that the chained timing cannot see, vs machine drift across runs (swap 13.9–14.2 GB) — the two runs bound the sum at +0.07 to +0.29 ms/step without separating them.
35|
36|## Spans
37|
38|`g3` (measurement), `baseline-routing`, `baseline-combine` (any exact kernel change that widens the 32-row decode margin), `grader` (the 5-repeat range rule that prices a ~1% margin by chance; unchanged for round 4).
39|
40|## Predicted saving
41|
42|If the pair's full piece win transferred at 32 rows, the step gains back the shortfall: up to **0.29 ms/step at 32 requests in Claude's draw (0.07 in the swarm's)**, i.e. `muse-all` would measure ≈ −0.66 ms/step vs `compiled-all` at both 32-row workloads instead of −0.55 / −0.36; ~0 claimed at 1/8 requests, where G3 already meets or beats the piece sum. The decision-relevant saving is smaller and sharper: **~0.17 ms/step of extra separation at 32×1024** would have made the ranges miss in Claude's run and turned the pair's one failing workload into a pass. At prefill sizes nothing is predicted: prompts are already 1.6–3.1% faster than base and slower nowhere (routing handed off, combine `faster` at 127/1,016/2,048 rows), so no per-chunk saving exists on either basis. This is an upper bound on the prize, not a prediction that a specific kernel change recovers it: no mechanism is confirmed, any widening must hold bit-exact G2 at all six sizes, and a decode saving bought with prefill time is not one.
43|

# From round 4, candidates that pass together are ready as a set, and an attempt may hand off small inputs too

*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../../PROVENANCE.md).*

**The change.** Round 3 showed three gaps in the rules ([Claude's measurement](../findings/muse-round-3.md)). On 2026-11-04 surucuonur chose to fix all three before round 4:

1. **Ready as a set.** Round 3's routing and combine candidates each failed the ready check alone, on overlapping ranges, while the two together (`muse-all`) passed it. The skill made a candidate `ready` only when it passed alone, so the round submitted nothing. From round 4, when `muse-all` passes the ready check, all its candidates are `ready` together as a **set**. A set goes to G3 whole, and G3 judges it as `muse-all`.
2. **Hand off below a row count too: `min_rows`.** `max_rows` already sends inputs with more rows to `mx.compile` of the slot's reference ([ADR 0011](0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). The new `min_rows` in an attempt's `spec.json` does the same for inputs with fewer rows, so the kernels run only from `min_rows` to `max_rows`. Round 3's experts attempt-1 lost to the compiled reference only at 1 row: 96.9 against 86.6 µs per layer, while it took 168.9 against 238.2 at 8 rows and 554.7 against 883.4 at 32. Its only way to pass was to win at the size it is worst at.
3. **A handed-off size isn't timed.** The grader timed each handed-off size, which runs the compiled reference, against the compiled reference: the same code twice. In round 3 that noise judged routing attempt-1 `slower` at 2,048 rows, on 8 wins of 30, and cost a re-grade of a byte-identical copy. Now such a size is reported `handed off`. A phase is `faster` when every size the kernels run at is faster, and it needs at least one; `beats_compiled` is still one phase `faster` and none `slower`. G2 still checks every size, bit for bit.

## How it works

- **`bench/grader/slots.py`:**
  - `build()` reads `min_rows` as it reads `max_rows`: an integer of at least 1, at most `max_rows` when both are given.
  - The function it returns has `hands_off(rows)`, which says whether inputs with that many rows run the compiled reference.
- **`bench/grader/check_candidate.py`:**
  - At each size, a function that hands the rows off is not timed. It takes the compiled reference's times, so for `routing+combine` the part that hands off adds the same time to both sides.
  - A bar's verdict is `handed off` when neither side ran code of its own. Against a baseline that runs its own kernels there, the size is timed as before.
  - `judge()` leaves `handed off` sizes out of a phase. A phase whose sizes are all handed off is `handed off`.
- **`bench/grader/test_hand_off.py`:**
  - checks `build()` with a toy kernel at row counts on both sides of each bound, bit for bit, and that bad bounds are refused;
  - checks `judge()` on five sets of verdicts.
  - Passed on 2026-11-04.
- **A real attempt.** Claude re-graded round 3's routing attempt-6 (`max_rows` 32) with the changed grader ([results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/](../../results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/)):
  - G2 passes;
  - decode is `faster` at 1, 8 and 32 rows, on 29, 26 and 27 wins of 30;
  - the three prefill sizes are `handed off`;
  - `beats_compiled` is true.
- **The skill, version 9.**
  - The ready check makes a passing `muse-all` a set.
  - *Ready to test* names a set's attempts together.
  - Builders and boundary agents record `min_rows` and the sizes it hands off.
- **G3 and the ready check are unchanged.** They time whole requests, so a slot's kernels count wherever they run. With 1 request every decode step has 1 row, so an attempt that hands off 1 row runs MLX's own code for the whole 1-request workload. Alone it is then no faster than its compiled bar there, and it can pass G3 only in a set whose other kernels are faster with 1 request. The brief says so.

## Consequences

- **Round 3's pair qualifies for round 4.** Under the set rule, routing attempt-6 with combine attempt-2 would have been `ready` in round 3, because its `muse-all` passed the swarm's ready check. Claude's G3 failed the same pair against the compiled bar at 32 requests of 1,024 tokens, on overlapping ranges, so the pair is still no baseline.
- **A set is judged once.** Its parts are not judged alone, so a set can carry a part that only helps together with the others. G3 still requires the whole set to be faster than both bars, and to be slower nowhere.
- **The interaction of all three slots is untested.** In rounds 1 and 2, replacing all three slots at once lost about 2.8 ms with 8 requests, for an unknown reason ([round 2](../findings/muse-round-2.md), section 4). A set with an experts attempt meets that again.

## Considered options

- **A paired test on medians for the ready check and G3,** so that one outlier repeat can't sink a candidate, as it sank combine attempt-2 in round 3. Not chosen for round 4: it changes ADR 0011's rule for Claude's G3 too, and there was too little time to check it before the deadline.
- **Hand-off by an explicit list of row counts.** More flexible, but no attempt has needed more than one range, and two bounds are simple to check.

# Attempt 2 — builder-1-b, direction (b): FP-contract-off pragma barrier

First attempt in this direction (round 3, `hyp-1-combine-devolatilize`,
slot `combine`, baseline `none`). Builds on the starting point
`muse-spark/round-2/kernels/combine/attempt-1`, which passes G1+G2 and
`beats_compiled` but fails G3 (+1.051 ms/step in vLLM at 32 requests).

## What changed

Only the barrier mechanism. Grid (`rows*768`), threadgroup [256,1,1],
index/base lines, inputs/outputs and the final
`bfloat(acc) + shared[sbase]` line are verbatim from the starting
point. The seven `volatile float` locals (`p0..p3`, `s01`, `s012`,
`acc`) become seven plain `float` locals with the identical 7-op
sequence, and a new header block (`block-1.metal`, wired via
`"header_block": 1` — the only `spec.json` delta) disables FP
contraction for the kernel:

```metal
#pragma STDC FP_CONTRACT OFF
#pragma clang fp contract(off)
```

MLX emits `header` before the main function, so the pragmas precede the
kernel definition, which is where FP-option pragmas take effect. No
`volatile` anywhere in code, no `__attribute__((noinline))` helpers,
no extra functions, calls, or memory traffic of any kind.

Why this is contraction-proof: with contract(off) the backend may not
fuse any fmul+fadd into an fma — this is the compiler's own
contraction switch, so there is no transform left that can keep a
product unrounded into its consumer add. Each of the 7 statements is
then one rounded f32 op on register values: the same 7 materialisation
points, same fold order `((p0+p1)+p2)+p3`, same two bfloat16 roundings
as the starting point. Reassociation needs no pragma: it is off without
fast-math flags, and the grader sets none. The proof is G2 itself: any
surviving contraction shows the starting point's old signature (decode
0/2/2, prefill 6/50/130 differ).

## Inefficiency removed

`ineff-baseline-combine-1` (confirmed): the seven volatiles' 7 stores +
7 loads per output (56 B/thread of thread-private traffic, 43,008
B/row/layer) stall the decode step (+7.1/+25.4/+72.1 µs/layer vLLM)
and the 32×128 prompt (+1,501.7 ms twin). The pragmas keep every value
in registers — ~10 live floats, no spill pressure — so the barrier
costs zero bytes and zero instructions. Same fix covers both phases:
both run these identical lines.

## Prediction (µs per layer, chained paired basis)

Starting point (re-grade `grade-phases-combine-attempt-1.json`, via
`ineff-g3-1`): decode reference/candidate 52.8/45.7 @1, 71.2/47.9 @8,
87.0/64.6 @32; compiled 53.4/56.4/69.1. Prefill candidate
62.8/226.5/273.0 vs compiled 66.1/271.6/520.4.

Arithmetic:

- Slot traffic unchanged: 9,232 B/row ÷ 200 GB/s = 0.05 / 0.37 / 1.48
  µs decode, 5.9 / 46.9 / 94.5 µs prefill. Floor dominates decode.
- Spill floor removed: 43,008 B/row ÷ 200 GB/s = 0.22 / 1.7 / 6.9 µs
  decode, 27 / 218 / 440 µs prefill — an upper bound the quiet grader
  chain mostly does not price (the inefficiency entry), so decode is
  predicted at the starting point ±5% paired noise, prefill
  same-or-slightly-better.
- Predicted candidate: **45 / 47 / 63** decode, **61 / 220 / 265**
  prefill. Margins to compiled (≈8/9/6 decode, ≈5/50/255 prefill)

  sizes, both phases `faster`, `beats_compiled` true.
- G1 pass, G2 differ 0 / max ULP 0.0 at all six sizes.

The piece prize is keeping `beats_compiled`; the real prize (vLLM
≈0.5 ms/step at 8 requests, ≈1.4 ms/step at 32; order-1-s prompt
recovery) is invisible to the piece timing by construction and needs

## max_rows

None. The kernel runs identical lines at all sizes, combine has no
MLX kernel switch underneath, and the boundary's grader note says no
hand-off is needed for this hypothesis's direction.

## What this attempt leaves unmeasured

For the hypothesis entry's **Unverified** list: the in-step stall
recovery (only the ready check / G3 at 32 requests shows it);
exactness at row counts other than the six graded ones (boundary tool
`check_sizes.py` can probe 25 sizes incl. 59/60/61); the 33–126 band;

## Verdict

G1 pass, G2 pass at all six sizes, `beats_compiled` true. Baseline is
`none`, so there is no `beats_baseline` bar. Single grade run,
2026-11-04T18:05:21Z, verdict in `grade.json`.

def build(spec, sources, slot):
    """A function slot_inputs -> slot_outputs from Muse Spark's spec and Metal blocks.

    With "max_rows" in the spec, inputs with more rows than that run the slot's
    reference under mx.compile instead of the kernels, so an attempt can keep
    prompt-sized inputs on MLX's own code (claude/adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md);
    with "min_rows", so do inputs with fewer rows than that
    (claude/adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md). The function's hands_off(rows)
    says whether inputs of that many rows run the compiled reference.
    """
    slot_in, slot_out = SLOTS[slot]
    kernels = []
    for k in spec["kernels"]:
        header = "" if k.get("header_block") is None else sources[k["header_block"]]
        fn = mx.fast.metal_kernel(
            name=re.sub(r"\W", "_", str(k["name"])),
            input_names=list(k["inputs"]),
            output_names=[o["name"] for o in k["outputs"]],
            source=sources[k["source_block"]],
            header=header,
            atomic_outputs=bool(k.get("atomic_outputs", False)),
        )
        kernels.append((k, fn))
    missing = set(slot_out) - set(spec["slot_outputs"])
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(f"slot_outputs is missing {sorted(missing)}")
    min_rows, max_rows = spec.get("min_rows"), spec.get("max_rows")
    for key, v in (("min_rows", min_rows), ("max_rows", max_rows)):
        if v is not None and (isinstance(v, bool) or not isinstance(v, int) or v < 1):
            raise ValueError(f"bad {key} {v!r}")
    if min_rows is not None and max_rows is not None and min_rows > max_rows:
        raise ValueError(f"min_rows {min_rows} is above max_rows {max_rows}: the kernels would never run")
    compiled = mx.compile(REFERENCE[slot])

    def hands_off(rows):
        return (max_rows is not None and rows > max_rows) or (min_rows is not None and rows < min_rows)

    def run(**inputs):
        rows = inputs[slot_in[0]].shape[0]
        if hands_off(rows):  # the compiled reference takes over
            out = compiled(*[inputs[n] for n in slot_in])
            return dict(zip(slot_out, out if isinstance(out, (tuple, list)) else [out]))
        env = dict(inputs)
        for k, fn in kernels:
            tg = [int(t) for t in k["threadgroup"]]
            if any(t < 1 for t in tg) or tg[0] * tg[1] * tg[2] > 1024:
                raise ValueError(f"bad threadgroup {tg}")
            outs = fn(
                inputs=[env[n] for n in k["inputs"]],
                template=[
                    (n, template_value(v)) for n, v in (k.get("template") or {}).items()
                ],
                grid=tuple(dim(g, rows) for g in k["grid"]),
                threadgroup=tuple(tg),
                output_shapes=[
                    tuple(dim(s, rows) for s in o["shape"]) for o in k["outputs"]
                ],
                output_dtypes=[DTYPES[o["dtype"]] for o in k["outputs"]],
                init_value=k.get("init_value"),
            )
            env.update(zip([o["name"] for o in k["outputs"]], outs))
        return {name: env[src] for name, src in spec["slot_outputs"].items()}

    run.hands_off = hands_off
    return run

def ref_routing(x, w_router, bias):
    scores = mx.sigmoid(x.astype(mx.float32) @ w_router.T)

def compare(wins):
    """One size's verdict from the candidate's wins in REPEATS paired repeats."""
    if wins >= WINS_NEEDED:
        return "faster"
    if REPEATS - wins >= WINS_NEEDED:

def judge(verdicts):
    """Each phase's verdict from its sizes' verdicts, and whether the candidate
    beats the bar: faster at every size of one phase, slower at no size of the other.

    Sizes "handed off" don't count. A phase is "faster" when every other size
    is, "slower" when any is, "handed off" when none is left, and "not slower"
    otherwise.
    """
    phases = {}
    for phase, prefix in PHASES.items():
        sizes = [v for size, v in verdicts.items() if size.startswith(prefix) and v != "handed off"]
        phases[phase] = (
            "handed off" if not sizes
            else "faster" if all(v == "faster" for v in sizes)
            else "slower" if "slower" in sizes
            else "not slower"
        )
    beats = "faster" in phases.values() and "slower" not in phases.values()
    return phases, beats

- **`source_block` and `header_block`** are the numbers of your `block-N.metal` files.
- **Kernels run in list order.** A kernel's `inputs` may name slot inputs or outputs of earlier kernels.
- **`slot_outputs`** maps each output of the slot to the kernel output that provides it.
- **`max_rows`** (optional, an integer of at least 1): inputs with more rows than this skip your kernels and run the slot's reference under `mx.compile`. Use it to keep prefill-sized inputs on MLX's own code when your kernels are built for decode sizes; MLX switches its own experts kernel at 60 rows.
- **`min_rows`** (optional, from round 4; an integer of at least 1, at most `max_rows` when both are given): inputs with fewer rows than this run the compiled reference too, so your kernels run only from `min_rows` to `max_rows`. Use it when your kernels lose at the smallest decode sizes, such as 1 row ([ADR 0015](adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)). G3 times whole requests: with 1 request every decode step has 1 row, so an attempt that hands off 1 row runs MLX's own code for the whole 1-request workload, and can pass G3 only in a set whose other kernels are faster there.
- **A hand-off is checked like the rest:** bit-exact at every G2 size. The piece timing reports a size it hands off as `handed off` instead of timing it (*The piece timing*, below).
- **For `routing+combine`,** `spec.json` holds two specs, each in the format above for its own slot, `max_rows` and `min_rows` included: `{"routing": {"kernels": [...], "slot_outputs": {...}}, "combine": {"kernels": [...], "slot_outputs": {...}}}`. The original experts and shared expert run between the two parts. The grader tests each part on its own, and the combine part receives the reference routing weights.
- **Shape and grid entries** are integers, or products of integers and the names `rows`, `D`, `E`, `K` and `H`, such as `"rows*32"`. Nothing else is evaluated.
- **dtypes** are `float32`, `bfloat16`, `float16`, `uint32` or `int32`.
- **Template values** are one of those dtypes, an integer or a boolean.
- **`grid`** counts threads, not threadgroups, as in `mx.fast.metal_kernel`.

## How each attempt is judged

The pass criteria were fixed before the first round. From round 2, G2 is exact and also covers the prefill, and the piece timing chains the layers ([ADR 0010](adr/0010-exact-at-every-size.md)); round 1 was judged by the earlier rules, in which G2 allowed small rounding differences and tested decode steps only. From round 3, the piece timing and G3 time both phases, decode and prefill ([ADR 0011](adr/0011-decode-and-prefill.md)); rounds 1 and 2 were timed on decode only.

1. **G1, runs.** It compiles and runs on real inputs.
2. **G2, correct: identical to the reference, bit for bit.** The slot runs in every call of `MoE.__call__`, the prefill included, so it is tested on every layer's inputs at two kinds of size:
   - **a decode step:** inputs captured from all 20 layers during a real decode step, at 1, 8 and 32 rows;
   - **a prefill:** the first chunk of a prefill with 128-token prompts, recorded while the grader runs it, at 1, 8 and 32 requests: 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. From 60 rows on, MLX's own experts kernel changes (`gather_qmm_rhs` instead of `gather_qvm`), and so does its rounding.

   At every size:
   - **`routing`:** each row's 4 experts and their 4 weights equal the reference's, in the same order, since combine sums the pairs in that order. That includes the reference's choice between tied 4th and 5th experts.
   - **`combine` and `experts`:** every element equals the reference's.

   **Why exact:** the end-to-end check below asks for the same greedy tokens, and greedy decoding turns any difference into different tokens. In round 1, routing weights within 10⁻⁵ of the reference, relative, changed 7 to 9 of 32 sequences.
   - **Then, end to end:** the same greedy tokens as the original model over 24 generated tokens, at 1 and 32 requests, in both plain MLX and vLLM.
3. **G3, faster, in vLLM.** Each workload runs 5 times in shuffled order: 1, 8 and 32 requests with 128-token prompts, and 32 requests with 1,024-token prompts, 256 generated tokens each. Three times are measured per run:
   - the **decode step**, the median period between steady steps;
   - the **prompt time**, until every prompt was processed;
   - the **whole request**, from sending the requests to the last token.

   Against both the original model and an `mx.compile` of the same reference code, the attempt passes when the decode step or the prompt time is faster in every workload, neither is slower in any, and no whole request is slower. Faster and slower mean that the ranges over the repeats don't overlap.

   **From round 3, the same G3 runs inside the round too:** the lead's **ready check**, `bench/grader/check_ready.py`, with every candidate in one call. It also requires the same greedy tokens, and audits its own log. Only its passing verdict makes an attempt `ready`; Claude's G3 after the round decides. The skill says when the lead runs it ([ADR 0013](adr/0013-measure-what-you-claim.md)).

   **From round 4, a set:** with more than one candidate, the ready check and G3 also time them all together (`muse-all`). When that passes, the candidates are ready together as a set, even where one fails alone, and G3 judges the set as one submission ([ADR 0015](adr/0015-sets-and-hand-off-below.md)).

**What the grader prints for an attempt** (JSON):
- `g1` false and the compiler's error message;
- or the correctness results per size: for routing, the rows that differ; for combine and experts, the elements that differ and the largest gap in units in the last place; with the first example;
- or, when the attempt is correct, `timing_us_per_layer` per size: its time per call next to the original's and the compiled reference's, its wins against the compiled reference and the verdict (`faster`, `same`, `slower`, or `handed off` for a size your spec hands to the compiled reference); then `phases_vs_compiled` and `beats_compiled`.

**The piece timing** runs the slot at the six G2 sizes: the 20 layers' captured decode inputs at 1, 8 and 32 rows, and the 20 layers' first prefill chunk at 127, 1,016 and 2,048 rows. Each layer's call waits for the previous one's output, as in the model: one small kernel links them, the same for every function timed. Without that wait, the GPU overlaps the 20 calls and hides how long one takes; in round 1, an experts kernel 29% faster on overlapped calls was 66% slower on chained ones at 1 row.
- **Paired repeats.** Your attempt and the compiled reference run in alternating order, 30 times.
- **Per size:** your attempt is `faster` when it wins at least 22 of the 30 pairs, `slower` when it loses at least 22, and `same` otherwise. Medians alone would pass on noise: the same kernel timed twice differs by up to 5%.
- **Handed off** (from round 4): a size whose inputs your spec hands to the compiled reference (`max_rows`, `min_rows`) runs the bar's own code, so it is not timed against it. Its verdict is `handed off`, and your attempt's time there is the compiled reference's.
- **Per phase:** decode (1, 8, 32 rows) and prefill (127, 1,016, 2,048 rows) are each `faster` when every size it doesn't hand off is, and at least one isn't handed off; `slower` when any size is; `handed off` when all are; and `not slower` otherwise.
- **`beats_compiled`** is true when one phase is `faster` and neither is `slower`.

It is a guide; the ready check in the round, and Claude's G3 after it, decide.

**When a slot stops.** Work on a slot stops at the first attempt that passes G1 and G2 and has `beats_compiled` true, or after 5 attempts. Name your final attempt per slot in `muse-spark/summary.md`; it goes to the end-to-end and G3 checks, which surucuonur's team runs after merging your branch.

# From round 4, candidates that pass together are ready as a set, and an attempt may hand off small inputs too

*Written by Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5), directed by surucuonur. [Who made what](../../PROVENANCE.md).*

**The change.** Round 3 showed three gaps in the rules ([Claude's measurement](../findings/muse-round-3.md)). On 2026-11-04 surucuonur chose to fix all three before round 4:

1. **Ready as a set.** Round 3's routing and combine candidates each failed the ready check alone, on overlapping ranges, while the two together (`muse-all`) passed it. The skill made a candidate `ready` only when it passed alone, so the round submitted nothing. From round 4, when `muse-all` passes the ready check, all its candidates are `ready` together as a **set**. A set goes to G3 whole, and G3 judges it as `muse-all`.
2. **Hand off below a row count too: `min_rows`.** `max_rows` already sends inputs with more rows to `mx.compile` of the slot's reference ([ADR 0011](0011-decode-and-prefill.md)). The new `min_rows` in an attempt's `spec.json` does the same for inputs with fewer rows, so the kernels run only from `min_rows` to `max_rows`. Round 3's experts attempt-1 lost to the compiled reference only at 1 row: 96.9 against 86.6 µs per layer, while it took 168.9 against 238.2 at 8 rows and 554.7 against 883.4 at 32. Its only way to pass was to win at the size it is worst at.
3. **A handed-off size isn't timed.** The grader timed each handed-off size, which runs the compiled reference, against the compiled reference: the same code twice. In round 3 that noise judged routing attempt-1 `slower` at 2,048 rows, on 8 wins of 30, and cost a re-grade of a byte-identical copy. Now such a size is reported `handed off`. A phase is `faster` when every size the kernels run at is faster, and it needs at least one; `beats_compiled` is still one phase `faster` and none `slower`. G2 still checks every size, bit for bit.

## How it works

- **`bench/grader/slots.py`:**
  - `build()` reads `min_rows` as it reads `max_rows`: an integer of at least 1, at most `max_rows` when both are given.
  - The function it returns has `hands_off(rows)`, which says whether inputs with that many rows run the compiled reference.
- **`bench/grader/check_candidate.py`:**
  - At each size, a function that hands the rows off is not timed. It takes the compiled reference's times, so for `routing+combine` the part that hands off adds the same time to both sides.
  - A bar's verdict is `handed off` when neither side ran code of its own. Against a baseline that runs its own kernels there, the size is timed as before.
  - `judge()` leaves `handed off` sizes out of a phase. A phase whose sizes are all handed off is `handed off`.
- **`bench/grader/test_hand_off.py`:**
  - checks `build()` with a toy kernel at row counts on both sides of each bound, bit for bit, and that bad bounds are refused;
  - checks `judge()` on five sets of verdicts.
  - Passed on 2026-11-04.
- **A real attempt.** Claude re-graded round 3's routing attempt-6 (`max_rows` 32) with the changed grader ([results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/](../../results/runs/2026-11-04-grader-hand-off/)):
  - G2 passes;
  - decode is `faster` at 1, 8 and 32 rows, on 29, 26 and 27 wins of 30;
  - the three prefill sizes are `handed off`;
  - `beats_compiled` is true.
- **The skill, version 9.**
  - The ready check makes a passing `muse-all` a set.
  - *Ready to test* names a set's attempts together.
  - Builders and boundary agents record `min_rows` and the sizes it hands off.
- **G3 and the ready check are unchanged.** They time whole requests, so a slot's kernels count wherever they run. With 1 request every decode step has 1 row, so an attempt that hands off 1 row runs MLX's own code for the whole 1-request workload. Alone it is then no faster than its compiled bar there, and it can pass G3 only in a set whose other kernels are faster with 1 request. The brief says so.

## Consequences

- **Round 3's pair qualifies for round 4.** Under the set rule, routing attempt-6 with combine attempt-2 would have been `ready` in round 3, because its `muse-all` passed the swarm's ready check. Claude's G3 failed the same pair against the compiled bar at 32 requests of 1,024 tokens, on overlapping ranges, so the pair is still no baseline.
- **A set is judged once.** Its parts are not judged alone, so a set can carry a part that only helps together with the others. G3 still requires the whole set to be faster than both bars, and to be slower nowhere.
- **The interaction of all three slots is untested.** In rounds 1 and 2, replacing all three slots at once lost about 2.8 ms with 8 requests, for an unknown reason ([round 2](../findings/muse-round-2.md), section 4). A set with an experts attempt meets that again.

## Considered options

- **A paired test on medians for the ready check and G3,** so that one outlier repeat can't sink a candidate, as it sank combine attempt-2 in round 3. Not chosen for round 4: it changes ADR 0011's rule for Claude's G3 too, and there was too little time to check it before the deadline.
- **Hand-off by an explicit list of row counts.** More flexible, but no attempt has needed more than one range, and two bounds are simple to check.
